en: I have heard, venerable sir, that it was thus declared by the Blessed One:
"The self is one;
the rod is one."
There is one action; there is one world;
there is one non-world.
There is one thing that is Dhamma; there is one thing that is non-Dhamma; there is one thing that is bondage.
One is liberation;
one is merit;
one is evil.
There is one inflow;
there is one restraint;
there is one feeling.
There is one kind of exhaustion (nirjarā). There is one soul in each individual body. There is one transformation of souls that does not involve the appropriation [of matter].
One [type of] mind,
one [type of] speech,
and one [type of] bodily activity.
One is arising; one is passing away;
one has passed away.
There is one destination; there is one arrival; there is one passing away.
There is one rebirth;
there is one reasoning;
there is one perception.
One is perception; one is cognition;
one is feeling.
For some there is cutting; for some, piercing;
for some, death—of those possessing their final bodies.
Some are pure and become as they truly are;
some are the singular source of suffering for living beings. There is one manifestation of unrighteousness: that by which one’s own self is tormented.

There is one form of the Dharma, namely that which constitutes the soul’s various manifestations. There is one mind among gods, asuras, and humans at any given time; there is one speech among gods, asuras, and humans at any given time; there is one bodily exertion among gods, asuras, and humans at any given time;
and there is one effort, action, strength, vigor, manly endeavor, and perseverance among gods, asuras, and humans at any given time.
There is one knowledge, one vision, and one conduct.
There is one moment,
one space-point, and one atom.
There is one perfection, one who has attained perfection; there is one final liberation, one who has attained final liberation.

One [perceives] sound; one [perceives] form; one [perceives] odor; one [perceives] taste; one [perceives] touch; one [perceives] a pleasant sound; one [perceives] an unpleasant sound; one [perceives] a beautiful form; one [perceives] an ugly form; one [perceives] long; one [perceives] short; one [perceives] round; one [perceives] triangular; one [perceives] quadrangular; one [perceives] broad; one [perceives] circular; one [perceives] black; one [perceives] blue; one [perceives] red; one [perceives] yellow; one [perceives] white; one [perceives] a pleasant odor; one [perceives] an unpleasant odor; one [perceives] bitter; one [perceives] pungent; one [perceives] astringent; one [perceives] sour; one [perceives] sweet; one [perceives] hard, up to one [perceives] rough.

There is one [type of] injury to living beings, [one of] false speech, one of taking what is not given, one of sexual misconduct, and one of possession; one of anger, [one of pride, one of deceit, and one of] greed; one of attachment, one of aversion, one of quarreling, one of slander, one of calumny, one of backbiting, one of delight and resentment, one of deceitful falsehood, and one of the thorn of wrong view.

There is one [vow of] abstention from taking life; [one of] abstention from false speech; one of abstention from taking what is not given; one of abstention from sexual intercourse; and one of abstention from possessiveness. There is one [practice of] detachment from anger; [detachment from pride; detachment from deceit; detachment from greed; detachment from attachment; detachment from aversion; detachment from quarreling; detachment from slander; detachment from backbiting; detachment from discontent and delight; detachment from deceitful falsehood; and detachment from the thorn of wrong view].

One *osappiṇī* (aeon of decrease), one *susama-susamā*, [one *susamā*, one *susama-dūsamā*, one *dūsama-susamā*, one *dūsamā*], one *dūsama-dūsamā*, one *ussappiṇī* (aeon of increase), one *dussama-dussamā*, [one *dussamā*, one *dussama-susamā*, one *susama-dussamā*, one *susamā*, one], *susama-susamā*.

There is one group (vargaṇā) of hell-beings; one group of asura-kumāras; one group of nāga-kumāras; one group of suvarṇa-kumāras; one group of vidyut-kumāras; one group of agni-kumāras; one group of dvīpa-kumāras; one group of udadhi-kumāras; one group of diśā-kumāras; one group of vāyu-kumāras; and one group of stanita-kumāras.

There is one group (vargaṇā) of earth-bodied beings, one group of water-bodied beings, one group of fire-bodied beings, one group of air-bodied beings, one group of plant-bodied beings, one group of two-sensed beings, one group of three-sensed beings, one group of four-sensed beings, one group of five-sensed animals, one group of humans, one group of Vāṇamantara [celestial beings], one group of Jyotiṣka [celestial beings], and one group of Vaimānika [celestial beings]. There is one group of those destined for liberation (bhavasiddhiya), and one group of those not destined for liberation (abhavasiddhiya). There is one group of hell-beings destined for liberation, and one group of hell-beings not destined for liberation; and so on, up to one group of Vaimānika celestial beings destined for liberation, and one group of Vaimānika celestial beings not destined for liberation.

There is one group (*varganā*) of those with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), one group of those with wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and one group of those with mixed view (*samyagmithyādṛṣṭi*). There is one group of hell-beings (*nairayika*) with right view, one group of hell-beings with wrong view, and one group of hell-beings with mixed view; and so on, up to the groups of the *stanitakumāras*. There is one group of earth-bodied beings (*pṛthivīkāyika*) with wrong view, and likewise up to the plant-bodied beings (*vanaspatikāyika*). There is one group of two-sensed beings (*dvīndriya*) with right view, and one group of two-sensed beings with wrong view; and the same applies to three-sensed and four-sensed beings. The rest are as for the hell-beings, up to one group of *vaimānika* gods with mixed view.

There is one group (vargaṇā) of those belonging to the dark side, and one group of those belonging to the bright side; there is one group of hell-beings belonging to the dark side, and one group of hell-beings belonging to the bright side. In this manner, the twenty-four-fold scheme (cauvīsa-daṇḍao) is to be recited.

There is one group (*vargaṇā*) of black-leśyās, one group of blue-leśyās, and so on up to one group of white-leśyās. There is one group of hell-beings with black-leśyās, up to one group of hell-beings with grey-leśyās. Thus, for whichever beings have which leśyās: the Bhavanapatis, Vānamantaras, and the earth-, water-, and plant-bodied beings have four leśyās; fire-, air-, two-sensed, three-sensed, and four-sensed beings have three leśyās; five-sensed animals and humans have six leśyās; the Jyotiṣkas have one, the fiery leśyā; and the Vaimānikas have the three upper leśyās. There is one group of those destined for liberation (*bhavasiddhiya*) with black-leśyās; thus, for all six leśyās, two categories each must be stated. There is one group of hell-beings destined for liberation with black-leśyās, and one group of hell-beings not destined for liberation (*abhavasiddhiya*) with black-leśyās. Thus, for whichever beings have how many leśyās, that many [categories] must be stated, up to the Vaimānikas.

There is one aggregate (*vaggaṇā*) of those with black *leśyā* who possess right view; one aggregate of those with black *leśyā* who possess wrong view; and one aggregate of those with black *leśyā* who possess mixed view. In this same manner, for all six *leśyās*, up to the Vaimānika gods, there are aggregates according to whichever views they hold. There is one aggregate of those with black *leśyā* belonging to the dark faction (*kaṇhapakkhiya*); and one aggregate of those with black *leśyā* belonging to the bright faction (*sukkappakkhiya*), and so on up to the Vaimānikas, according to whichever *leśyās* each possesses. These constitute the eight groups of twenty-four categories (*caüvīsadaṇḍaya*).

There is one group (*varganā*) of those perfected as members of a religious order (*tīrtha-siddha*); one group of those perfected outside of a religious order (*atīrtha-siddha*); [one group of those perfected as Tīrthaṅkaras; one group of those perfected as self-enlightened ones (*svayaṃbuddha-siddha*); one group of those perfected as individually enlightened ones (*pratyekabuddha-siddha*); one group of those perfected through the enlightenment of a Buddha (*buddhabodhita-siddha*); one group of those perfected in the female gender (*strīliṅga-siddha*); one group of those perfected in the male gender (*puruṣaliṅga-siddha*); one group of those perfected in the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga-siddha*); one group of those perfected in another's gender (*anyaliṅga-siddha*); one group of those perfected in the householder's gender (*gṛhiliṅga-siddha*); one group of those perfected alone (*eka-siddha*); one group of those perfected in a company (*aneka-siddha*); one group of those perfected in the first moment (*aprathama-samaya-siddha*), and so on up to one group of those perfected in an infinite number of moments (*ananta-samaya-siddha*).

There is one group (*vaggaṇā*) of single-paramāṇu particles, and so on up to one group of aggregates (*skandha*) consisting of infinite parts (*anantapradeśika*). There is one group of particles occupying one space-point (*pradeśa*), and so on up to one group of particles occupying an innumerable number of space-points. There is one group of particles with a duration of one time-unit (*samaya*), and so on up to one group of particles with an innumerable duration. There is one group of particles with a single-fold black color, and so on up to one group of particles with an innumerable-fold black color, and one group of particles with an infinite-fold black color. In the same way, colors, smells, tastes, and touches are to be described, up to one group of particles with an infinite-fold rough touch. There is one group of aggregates with the minimum number of parts, one group of aggregates with the maximum number of parts, and one group of aggregates with a number of parts that is neither minimum nor maximum. Likewise, there are groups of aggregates with minimum extension, maximum extension, and extension that is neither minimum nor maximum; with minimum duration, maximum duration, and duration that is neither minimum nor maximum; and with minimum black color, maximum black color, and black color that is neither minimum nor maximum. In the same way, groups of aggregates regarding color, smell, taste, and touch are to be described, up to one group of aggregates of particles with a quality of roughness that is neither minimum nor maximum.

Jambudvīpa is one island among all the islands and oceans; it is the innermost of all, the smallest of all, circular, shaped like a cake of sesame oil, circular, shaped like the rim of a chariot wheel, circular, shaped like the seed-vessel of a lotus, and circular, shaped like the full moon. It is one hundred thousand yojanas in length and breadth, and its circumference is three hundred sixteen thousand two hundred twenty-seven yojanas, three krośas, one hundred twenty-eight dhanus, thirteen aṅgulas, and half an aṅgula, with a slight excess.

The one ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, was the last of the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras in this *avasarpinī* era; he has attained perfection (*siddha*), awakened (*buddha*), liberated (*mukta*), reached the end (*antakṛt*), entered final liberation (*parinirvṛta*), and is rid of all suffering.
The gods who have attained the highest rebirth are declared to be one *ratni* in height.
The constellation Ārdrā is declared to have one star; the constellation Citrā is declared to have one star; the constellation Svāti is declared to have one star.

Infinite matter-particles (*pudgala*) are declared to be submerged in a single spatial point; infinite matter-particles are declared to have a duration of a single moment; and infinite matter-particles are declared to possess a single degree of black color, up to infinite matter-particles being declared to possess a single degree of roughness.

Whatever exists in this world, all that is twofold, namely: living beings and non-living things; mobile beings and immobile beings; those born from a womb and those not born from a womb; those with a life-span and those without a life-span; those with sense organs and those without sense organs; those with sensation and those without sensation; those with form and those without form; those consisting of matter and those not consisting of matter; those involved in the cycle of existence and those not involved in the cycle of existence; those that are eternal and those that are non-eternal;
space and non-space; and the medium of motion and the medium of rest.

Regarding bondage and liberation, merit and demerit, influx and restraint, and experience and exhaustion—two types of action (kriyā) are taught, namely: the action of the soul (jīvakriyā) and the action of the non-soul (ajīvakriyā). The action of the soul is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the action of right belief (samyaktvakriyā) and the action of wrong belief (mithyātvakriyā). The action of the non-soul is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that pertaining to movement (iryāpathikā) and that pertaining to the passions (sāmparāyikā).

Two types of action are taught, namely: bodily action and instrumental action. Bodily action is taught to be of two kinds, namely: unrestrained bodily action and improperly directed bodily action. Instrumental action is taught to be of two kinds, namely: instrumental action consisting of accumulation and instrumental action consisting of production.

Two types of action are taught, namely: that which consists of causing injury (*pāōsiyā*) and that which consists of causing torment (*pāriyāvaṇiyā*). Action consisting of causing injury is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which causes injury to living beings (*jīvapāōsiyā*) and that which causes injury to non-living things (*ajīvapāōsiyā*). Action consisting of causing torment is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which causes torment by one's own hand (*sahatthapāriyāvaṇiyā*) and that which causes torment by the hand of another (*parahatthapāriyāvaṇiyā*).

Two types of action are taught, namely: the action of killing living beings and the action of non-renunciation. The action of killing living beings is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the action of killing by one's own hand and the action of killing by the hand of another. The action of non-renunciation is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the action of non-renunciation regarding living beings and the action of non-renunciation regarding non-living things.

Two types of action are taught, namely: that which consists of violence (*ārambhikā*) and that which consists of possession (*pāriggahiyā*). Action consisting of violence is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which involves living beings (*jīvārambhikā*) and that which involves non-living things (*ajīvārambhikā*). Action consisting of possession is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which involves living beings (*jīvapāriggahiyā*) and that which involves non-living things (*ajīvapāriggahiyā*).

Two types of action (kriyā) are taught, namely: that consisting of deceit (māyā) and that consisting of false view (mithyādṛṣṭi). Action consisting of deceit is taught to be of two kinds, namely: crookedness regarding one's own nature (ātmabhāva) and crookedness regarding the nature of others (parabhāva). Action consisting of false view is taught to be of two kinds, namely: false view arising from deficient conduct (ūnācāra-mithyādṛṣṭi) and false view arising from that which is other than such [deficient] conduct (tadviparīta-mithyādṛṣṭi).

Two types of action (kriyā) are taught, namely: that which is through seeing (dṛṣṭijā) and that which is through touching (spṛṣṭijā). Action through seeing is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that of a living being (jīvadṛṣṭijā) and that of a non-living being (ajīvadṛṣṭijā). Action through touching is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that of a living being (jīvaspṛṣṭijā) and that of a non-living being (ajīvaspṛṣṭijā).

Two types of action are taught, namely: that which is dependent on a specific object (*pāḍucciyā*) and that which is incidental (*sāmantovaṇiyāiyā*). Dependent action is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that which is dependent on a living being (*jīva-pāḍucciyā*) and that which is dependent on a non-living thing (*ajīva-pāḍucciyā*); the same applies to incidental action as well.

Two types of action (kiriyā) are taught, namely: that which is performed by one’s own hand (sāhatthiyā) and that which is performed through an instrument (nēsatthiyā). Action performed by one’s own hand is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that performed by the hand of a living being (jīvasāhatthiyā) and that performed by the hand of a non-living thing (ajīvasāhatthiyā); likewise for that performed through an instrument. Two types of action are taught, namely: that which is caused by commanding (āṇavaṇiyā) and that which is caused by requesting (vēyāraṇiyā). Action caused by commanding is taught to be of two kinds, namely: commanding a living being (jīvaāṇavaṇiyā) and commanding a non-living thing (ajīvaāṇavaṇiyā); likewise for that caused by requesting.

Two types of activity (kiriyā) are taught, namely: that consisting of lack of awareness (anābhōgavattiyā) and that consisting of lack of longing (aṇavakaṅkhavattiyā). Activity consisting of lack of awareness is taught to be of two kinds, namely: unintentional taking up [of objects] and unintentional cleaning. Activity consisting of lack of longing is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that consisting of lack of longing regarding one's own body and that consisting of lack of longing regarding the bodies of others.

Two types of action (*kiriyā*) are taught, namely: that consisting of attachment (*pejja*) and that consisting of aversion (*dosa*). Action consisting of attachment is taught to be of two kinds, namely: that consisting of deceit (*māyā*) and that consisting of greed (*lobha*). Action consisting of aversion is taught to be of two kinds, namely: anger (*kōha*) and pride (*māna*). Two types of reproach (*garahā*) are taught, namely: one reproaches at times with the mind, and at times with speech; or alternatively, reproach is taught to be of two kinds, namely: one reproaches half [of the fault] openly, and at times one reproaches half [of the fault] in secret.

Renunciation is twofold, as follows: one renounces at once through the mind, or one renounces at once through speech. Alternatively, renunciation is twofold, as follows: one renounces for a long duration, or one renounces for a short duration.

Endowed with two factors, a mendicant may cross over the wilderness of *saṃsāra*—which is without beginning, without end, long-lasting, and four-cornered—namely: through knowledge and through conduct.

There are two things which, if not fully understood, a person cannot obtain the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin for the sake of hearing: namely, violence (*ārambha*) and possession (*parigraha*). There are two things which, if not fully understood, a person cannot awaken to absolute enlightenment (*kevala-bodhi*): namely, violence and possession. There are two things which, if not fully understood, a person cannot go forth from the home to the homeless state after having shaved his head: namely, violence and possession. Likewise, one cannot dwell in the practice of celibacy; one cannot restrain oneself through self-restraint (*saṃyama*); one cannot restrain oneself through restraint (*saṃvara*); and one cannot produce the knowledge of direct intuition (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*).
Thus there is scriptural knowledge, clairvoyant knowledge, mind-reading knowledge, and omniscience.

Having understood two conditions, a person may obtain the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins for the sake of hearing it; namely, [abstinence from] both violence (*ārambha*) and possession (*parigraha*), up until he may eradicate them—namely, both violence and possession.

There are two conditions by which a person may obtain the hearing of the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins, namely: by having heard it and by having realized it. There are two conditions by which a person may produce absolute, perfect knowledge (kevalajñāna), namely: by having heard it and by having realized it.
Two types of aeons (samā) are taught: the aeon of decrease (avasarpinī) and the aeon of increase (utsarpinī).

Two kinds of madness are taught, namely: that caused by possession by a spirit (*yakṣa*) and that caused by the rising of deluding karma (*mohanīya-karman*). Among these, that which is caused by possession by a spirit is indeed easier to experience and easier to be freed from; whereas that which is caused by the rising of deluding karma is indeed more difficult to experience and more difficult to be freed from.

Two types of violence (daṇḍa) are taught, namely: violence for a purpose and violence without a purpose. Two types of violence are taught for hell-beings, namely: violence for a purpose and violence without a purpose. In this manner, the classification of violence continues through the twenty-four classes of beings up to the Vaimānika gods. Two types of vision (darśana) are taught, namely: right vision and wrong vision.

Right view (samyagdarśana) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: innate right view (nisarga-samyagdarśana) and acquired right view (abhigama-samyagdarśana). Innate right view is declared to be of two kinds, namely: that which is reversible (pratipāti) and that which is irreversible (apratipāti). Acquired right view is declared to be of two kinds, namely: that which is reversible and that which is irreversible. False view (mithyādarśana) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: dogmatic false view (abhigṛhīta-mithyādarśana) and non-dogmatic false view (anabhigṛhīta-mithyādarśana). Dogmatic false view is declared to be of two kinds, namely: that which has an end (saparyavasita) and that which has no end (aparyavasita). The same applies to non-dogmatic false view as well.

Knowledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely: direct (pratyakṣa) and indirect (parokṣa). Direct knowledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely: absolute knowledge (kevalajñāna) and non-absolute knowledge (nokevalajñāna). Absolute knowledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely: absolute knowledge of those still in worldly existence (bhavastha-kevalajñāna) and absolute knowledge of the perfected ones (siddha-kevalajñāna).

Kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence (*bhavastha*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence with activity (*sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence without activity (*ayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*). Kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence with activity is declared to be of two kinds, namely: kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence with activity in the first moment (*prathama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence with activity from the second moment onwards (*aprathama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*); or alternatively, kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence with activity in the final moment (*carama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*) and kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence with activity from the penultimate moment onwards (*acarama-samaya-sayogi-bhavastha-kevalajñāna*). The same applies to kevala-jñāna existing in the state of existence without activity.

Perfect omniscience (*kevalajñāna*) of the perfected ones (*siddha*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the perfect omniscience of those who have just attained perfection (*anantarasiddha*) and the perfect omniscience of those who attained perfection in succession (*paramparasiddha*). The perfect omniscience of those who have just attained perfection is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the perfect omniscience of a single individual who has just attained perfection and the perfect omniscience of multiple individuals who have just attained perfection. The perfect omniscience of those who attained perfection in succession is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the perfect omniscience of a single individual who attained perfection in succession and the perfect omniscience of multiple individuals who attained perfection in succession. Non-omniscient knowledge (*nokevalajñāna*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: clairvoyance (*avadhijñāna*) and mind-reading knowledge (*manahparyayajñāna*).

Avadhi-knowledge (clairvoyance) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: innate (*bhavapratyaya*) and acquired through the subsidence-cum-destruction of karmic veils (*kṣayopaśamika*). Innate avadhi-knowledge is declared to belong to two groups: gods and hell-beings; acquired avadhi-knowledge is declared to belong to two groups: humans and five-sensed animals. Mind-reading knowledge (*manahparyāya-jñāna*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: direct intuition (*ṛjumati*) and expansive intuition (*vipulmati*). Indirect knowledge (*parokṣa-jñāna*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: sensory cognition (*ābhinibodhika-jñāna*) and scriptural knowledge (*śruta-jñāna*). Sensory cognition is declared to be of two kinds, namely: dependent on scripture (*śrutaniśrita*) and independent of scripture (*aśrutaniśrita*). That which is dependent on scripture is declared to be of two kinds, namely: apprehension of meaning (*arthāvagraha*) and apprehension of the phonetic form (*vyañjanāvagraha*); that which is independent of scripture is likewise of these same two kinds.

Scriptural knowledge (śrutajñāna) is of two kinds, namely: that which is included within the scriptures (aṅgapraviṣṭa) and that which is outside the scriptures (aṅgabāhya). That which is outside the scriptures is of two kinds, namely: the essential (āvaśyaka) and that which is beyond the essential (āvaśyakavartiritta). That which is beyond the essential is of two kinds, namely: that which belongs to the proper time (kālika) and that which does not belong to the proper time (utkālika).

Two kinds of Dharma have been taught, namely: the Dharma of scripture (*śrutadharma*) and the Dharma of conduct (*cāritradharma*). The Dharma of scripture is taught as being of two kinds, namely: the Dharma of the conduct of householders (*agāracarittadharma*) and the Dharma of the conduct of the homeless (*anagāracarittadharma*). Two kinds of restraint (*saṃyama*) have been taught, namely: restraint with passion (*sarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion (*vītarāgasaṃyama*). Restraint with passion is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint with passion characterized by subtle delusion (*sūkṣmasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion (*bādarasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*). Restraint with passion characterized by subtle delusion is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint with passion characterized by subtle delusion at the first moment (*prathamasamaya-sūkṣmasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint with passion characterized by subtle delusion at any other moment (*aprathamasamaya-sūkṣmasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*). Alternatively, restraint with passion characterized by subtle delusion is taught as being of two kinds, namely: that which is becoming defiled (*saṃkliśyamāna*) and that which is becoming purified (*viśudhyamāna*). Restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion at the first moment (*prathamasamaya-bādarasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion at any other moment (*aprathamasamaya-bādarasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*). Alternatively, [it is] restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion at the final moment (*caramasamaya-bādarasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion at any other moment (*acaramasamaya-bādarasāmparāya-sarāgasaṃyama*). Alternatively, restraint with passion characterized by gross delusion is taught as being of two kinds, namely: reversible (*pratipātī*) and irreversible (*apratipātī*). Restraint free from passion is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint free from passion through the subsidence of the passions (*upaśāntakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions (*kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*). Restraint free from passion through the subsidence of the passions is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint free from passion through the subsidence of the passions at the first moment (*prathamasamaya-upaśāntakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the subsidence of the passions at any other moment (*aprathamasamaya-upaśāntakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*). Alternatively, [it is] restraint free from passion through the subsidence of the passions at the final moment (*caramasamaya-upaśāntakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the subsidence of the passions at any other moment (*acaramasamaya-upaśāntakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*). Restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for one still in the state of embodied existence (*chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for one possessing omniscience (*kevalin-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*). Restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for one still in the state of embodied existence is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for a self-enlightened one (*svayambuddha-chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for one enlightened by another (*buddhabodhita-chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*). Restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for a self-enlightened one still in the state of embodied existence is taught as being of two kinds, namely: restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for a self-enlightened one at the first moment (*prathamasamaya-svayambuddha-chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for a self-enlightened one at any other moment (*aprathamasamaya-svayambuddha-chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*). Alternatively, [it is] restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for a self-enlightened one at the final moment (*caramasamaya-svayambuddha-chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*) and restraint free from passion through the destruction of the passions for a self-enlightened one at any other moment (*acaramasamaya-svayambuddha-chadmastha-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāgasaṃyama*).

The omniscient with physical body (*chadmastha*) who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment (*kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāga*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the omniscient with physical body who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment at the first moment (*prathama-samaya*), and the omniscient with physical body who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment at a non-first moment (*aprathama-samaya*). Alternatively, there are those at the final moment (*carama-samaya*) and those at a non-final moment (*acarama-samaya*). The omniscient who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment (*kevali-kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāga*) is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the omniscient with activity (*sayogikevali*) who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment, and the omniscient without activity (*ayogikevali*) who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment. The omniscient with activity who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the omniscient with activity at the first moment and the omniscient with activity at a non-first moment. Alternatively, there are those at the final moment and those at a non-final moment. The omniscient without activity who has destroyed the passions and is free from attachment is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the omniscient without activity at the first moment and the omniscient without activity at a non-first moment. Alternatively, there are those at the final moment and those at a non-final moment.

Earth-bodied beings are taught to be of two kinds, namely: subtle and gross; likewise, up to plant-bodied beings, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: subtle and gross. Earth-bodied beings are taught to be of two kinds, namely: developed and undeveloped; likewise, up to plant-bodied beings, they are taught to be of two kinds, namely: developed and undeveloped.

Earth-bodied beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that have undergone transformation (*pariṇata*) and those that have not undergone transformation (*apariṇata*). The same applies up to plant-bodied beings. Substances are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that have undergone transformation and those that have not undergone transformation. Earth-bodied beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that have entered into motion (*gatisamāvaṇṇaga*) and those that have not entered into motion (*agatisamāvaṇṇaga*). The same applies up to plant-bodied beings. Substances are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that have entered into motion and those that have not entered into motion.

Earth-bodied beings are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those immersed immediately and those immersed successively; and so on, up to: substances are taught to be of two kinds, namely: those immersed immediately and those immersed successively.

Time is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the period of decrease (utsarpiṇī) and the period of increase (avasarpiṇī). Space is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the space of the world (loka-ākāśa) and the space beyond the world (aloka-ākāśa).

For hell-beings, two types of bodies are taught, namely: the internal and the external; the internal is composed of karma (*karmaja*), and the external is composed of transformation (*vaikriya*). This should be stated likewise for the gods. For earth-bodied beings, two types of bodies are taught, namely: the internal and the external; the internal is composed of karma, and the external is organic (*audārika*). This continues up to the plant-bodied beings. For two-sensed beings, two types of bodies are taught, namely: the internal and the external; the internal is composed of karma, and the external is organic, consisting of bone, flesh, and blood. Likewise up to four-sensed beings. For five-sensed animals, two types of bodies are taught, namely: the internal and the external; the internal is composed of karma and consists of bone, flesh, blood, nails, teeth, and sinews, while the external is organic. For human beings, it is exactly the same.

For hell-beings who have entered into the state of embodied existence, two types of bodies are taught: namely, the fiery body (*taijasa*) and the karmic body (*kārmaṇa*). This applies continuously up to the beings of the *vaimānika* realm.

The production of bodies for hell-beings occurs through two causes: namely, passion (rāga) and hatred (dosa); and so on, up to the beings of the Vaimānika realm. For hell-beings, the formation of the body is declared to be produced by two factors: namely, produced by passion and produced by hatred; and so on, up to the beings of the Vaimānika realm. Two types of bodies are declared: namely, the mobile body (trasakāya) and the immobile body (sthāvarakāya). The mobile body is declared to be of two kinds: namely, those destined for liberation (bhavasiddhiya) and those not destined for liberation (abhavasiddhiya); the same applies to the immobile body as well.

It is permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to go forth from these two directions—namely, the east and the north. Likewise, it is permissible to shave them, instruct them, initiate them, share food with them, live together with them, assign them a lesson of scripture, direct them in the recitation of scripture, authorize their recitation of scripture, cause them to confess, cause them to repent, cause them to feel remorse, cause them to censure themselves, cause them to reform, cause them to purify themselves, cause them to resolve not to commit [the offense] again, and cause them to undertake appropriate penance and ascetic practice—[all] toward the east and the north.

Having turned toward these two directions, it is permissible for the Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs who have practiced the refinement of the final mortification at the end of life, who have renounced food and drink, who have entered the state of fasting, and who dwell without longing for life—to dwell [in] these two directions, namely: the east and the north.

Those gods who have been reborn in the upper realms, reborn in the celestial abodes (*kalpa*), reborn in the celestial palaces (*vimāna*), reborn in the wandering states (*cāra*), established in their course, fixed in their destiny, and entered upon their path—when sinful karma is performed by those gods constantly and continuously, some experience the sensation there [in that state], while others experience the sensation elsewhere. When sinful karma is performed by hell-beings constantly and continuously, some experience the sensation there, while others experience the sensation elsewhere. This continues up to the five-sensed animals and human beings: when sinful karma is performed by them constantly and continuously, some experience the sensation there, while others experience the sensation elsewhere. With the exception of humans, the rest follow the same pattern.

Hell-beings (nairayika) have two destinies and two origins; that is to say: a hell-being being reborn among hell-beings may be reborn from among humans or from among five-sensed animals. That same hell-being, when relinquishing the state of being a hell-being, goes to the state of being a human or to the state of being a five-sensed animal. The same applies to the Asurakumāras; however, that same Asurakumāra, when relinquishing the state of being an Asurakumāra, goes to the state of being a human or to the state of being an animal. Thus it is for all gods. Earth-bodied beings (pṛthvikāyika) have two destinies and two origins; that is to say: an earth-bodied being being reborn among earth-bodied beings may be reborn from among earth-bodied beings or not from among earth-bodied beings. That same earth-bodied being, when relinquishing the state of being an earth-bodied being, goes to the state of being an earth-bodied being or [to another]; thus it is for all [beings] up to humans.

Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those destined for liberation (bhavasiddhiya) and those not destined for liberation (abhavasiddhiya); and so on up to the Vaimānika gods. Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those who have been reborn immediately (aṇantarōvavaṇṇaga) and those who have been reborn through a succession of births (paramparōvavaṇṇaga); and so on up to the Vaimānika gods. Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those who have attained their destination (gatisamāvaṇṇaga) and those who have not yet attained their destination (agatisamāvaṇṇaga); and so on up to the Vaimānika gods.

Two kinds of hell-beings are taught, namely: those who have just been reborn at the first moment and those who have been reborn for more than the first moment; and so on up to the Vaimānikas. Two kinds of hell-beings are taught, namely: those who breathe and those who do not breathe; and so on up to the Vaimānikas. Two kinds of hell-beings are taught, namely: those with sense-faculties and those without sense-faculties; and so on up to the Vaimānikas.

Nārakas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those who are fully developed (paryāpta) and those who are not fully developed (aparyāpta); this applies up to the Vaimānikas. Nārakas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those with consciousness (saṃjñin) and those without consciousness (asaṃjñin); thus it is for all five-sensed beings, excluding those with fewer than five senses, up to the Vānamantaras. Nārakas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those capable of speech (bhāṣaka) and those incapable of speech (abhāṣaka); thus it is for all except those with one sense-organ. Nārakas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those with right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) and those with wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi); thus it is for all except those with one sense-organ.

Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those with a limited cycle of existence (*parittasaṃsāritā*) and those with an infinite cycle of existence (*anantasaṃsāritā*). This continues up to the Vaimānika gods. Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those with a duration of a numerable number of time-units (*saṅkhejjakālasamayaṭṭhitiyā*) and those with a duration of an innumerable number of time-units (*asaṅkhejjakālasamayaṭṭhitiyā*). In this same way, [the classification applies] to five-sensed beings, one-sensed beings, and all except for those with incomplete sense-faculties, up to the Vānamantara gods.

Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those for whom enlightenment is easily attained and those for whom enlightenment is difficult to attain; this continues up to the Vaimānika gods. Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those belonging to the dark side and those belonging to the bright side; this continues up to the Vaimānika gods. Hell-beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those who are final (having reached the last birth) and those who are not final; this continues up to the Vaimānika gods.

By two conditions, a person knows and sees the lower world: namely, by means of a self that is obstructed (*samohata*), a person knows and sees the lower world; and by means of a self that is unobstructed (*asamohata*), a person knows and sees the lower world. Thus, by means of a self that is both obstructed and unobstructed, a person knows and sees the lower world. In the same way, one knows and sees the horizontal world (*tiriyaloga*), the upper world (*uḍḍhaloga*), and the entire world-system (*kevalakappa loga*).

By two conditions, the self knows and sees the nether world (*adholoka*): namely, by means of the self that has been transformed (*vikurvita*) and by means of the self that has not been transformed. By both—whether transformed or untransformed—the self knows and sees the nether world. In the same way, it knows and sees the horizontal world (*tiryagloka*), the upper world (*ūrdhvaloka*), and the entire world-system (*kevalakalpaloka*).

The self hears sounds in two ways: namely, the self hears sounds through a part [of itself], and the self hears sounds through its whole [self]. In the same way, it sees forms, smells odors, tastes flavors, and experiences tangibles. The self manifests in two ways: namely, the self manifests through a part [of itself], and the self manifests through its whole [self]. In the same way, it speaks, transforms, enjoys, utters speech, assimilates food, undergoes transformation, experiences [karmic results], and effects the wearing away [of karma].
Devas hear sounds in two ways: namely, devas hear sounds with one part of their body, and devas hear sounds with their entire body, up until [the point where they] undergo exhaustion (*nirjarā*).

The Maruts are declared to be of two kinds: namely, those with a single body and those with multiple bodies. Likewise, the Kinnaras, Kimpuruṣas, Gandharvas, Nāgakumāras, Suvarṇakumāras, Agnikumāras, and Vāyukumāra devas are declared to be of two kinds: namely, those with a single body and those with multiple bodies.

Sound is declared to be of two kinds, namely: vocal sound (*bhāsāsadda*) and non-vocal sound (*nōbhāsāsadda*). Vocal sound is declared to be of two kinds, namely: that which is connected with syllables (*akkharasambaddha*) and that which is not connected with syllables (*nōakkharasambaddha*). Non-vocal sound is declared to be of two kinds, namely: elemental sound (*āujjasadda*) and non-elemental sound (*nōāujjasadda*). Elemental sound is declared to be of two kinds, namely: struck (*tata*) and stretched (*vitata*).

That [extended sound] is declared to be of two kinds, namely: solid (*ghana*) and hollow (*susira*). Likewise, non-auditory sound (*nōāujja-sadda*) that is extended is also declared to be of two kinds, namely: the sound of ornaments (*bhūsaṇa-sadda*) and the sound of non-ornaments (*nōbhūsaṇa-sadda*). The sound of non-ornaments is declared to be of two kinds, namely: the sound of clapping hands (*tāla-sadda*) and the sound of the *lattiyā* (a type of percussion instrument). Sound may arise from two conditions: sound may arise from the striking together of material particles (*poggala*), and sound may arise from the breaking apart of material particles.

Matter is joined together in two ways: namely, matter is joined together by itself, or matter is joined together by another. Matter is split in two ways: namely, matter is split by itself, or matter is split by another. Matter falls away in two ways: namely, matter falls away by itself, or matter falls away by another. Likewise, it decays and it disintegrates.

Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that are broken and those that are not broken. Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those characterized by divisibility and those not characterized by divisibility. Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: atoms and those that are not atoms. Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: subtle and gross.

Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that are bound by contact and those that are not bound by contact. Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that are consumed and those that are not consumed. Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those that are self and those that are non-self. Pudgalas are declared to be of two kinds, namely: desirable and undesirable; lovely and unlovely; dear and not dear; pleasant and unpleasant; agreeable and disagreeable.

Sounds are declared to be of two kinds, namely: self-referential and non-self-referential; agreeable and disagreeable; and so on, up to pleasant and unpleasant. Forms are declared to be of two kinds, namely: self-referential and non-self-referential; and so on, up to pleasant and unpleasant. The same applies to odors, tastes, and tangibles; thus, six statements should be recited for each of these.

Conduct is declared to be of two kinds, namely: conduct of knowledge (*jñānācāra*) and non-conduct of knowledge (*no-jñānācāra*). Non-conduct of knowledge is declared to be of two kinds, namely: conduct of perception (*darśanācāra*) and non-conduct of perception (*no-darśanācāra*). Non-conduct of perception is declared to be of two kinds, namely: conduct of character (*cāritrācāra*) and non-conduct of character (*no-cāritrācāra*). Non-conduct of character is declared to be of two kinds, namely: conduct of austerity (*tapācāra*) and conduct of energy (*vīryācāra*).

Two postures (paḍimā) are taught, namely: the posture of meditative absorption (samāhipaḍimā) and the posture of ascetic practice (uvahāṇapaḍimā). Two postures are taught, namely: the posture of seclusion (vivegapaḍimā) and the posture of self-exertion (viusaggapaḍimā). Two postures are taught, namely: the Auspicious One (Bhaddā) and the Very Auspicious One (Subhaddā). Two postures are taught, namely: the Great Auspicious One (Mahābhaddā) and the All-Auspicious One (Savvatobhaddā). Two postures are taught, namely: the Lesser Posture of Emptiness (Khuḍḍiyā Mōyapaḍimā) and the Greater Posture of Emptiness (Mahalliyā Mōyapaḍimā). Two postures are taught, namely: the Moon Posture with a Narrow Middle (Javamajjhā Candapaḍimā) and the Moon Posture with a Wide Middle (Vaïramajjhā Candapaḍimā).

There are two kinds of *sāmāyika* (equanimity/vows), namely: the *sāmāyika* of the householder and the *sāmāyika* of the homeless ascetic. Rebirth is declared for two [classes of beings], namely: gods and hell-beings. Egress from existence is declared for two [classes of beings], namely: hell-beings and the inhabitants of the subterranean palaces (*bhavanavāsī*). Death is declared for two [classes of beings], namely: the celestial luminaries (*jyotiṣka*) and the denizens of the celestial mansions (*vaimānika*). Conception in the womb is declared for two [classes of beings], namely: humans and five-sensed animals.
Food is prescribed for two types of womb-dwellers (*gabbhattha*): namely, humans and five-sensed animals (*pañcendriya-tiryagyoni*).

Growth is prescribed for two types of womb-dwellers: namely, humans and five-sensed animals; likewise for diminution, transformation (*vikurvaṇā*), the transition of states of existence (*gatiparyāya*), the total destruction of karmic matter (*samudghāta*), the conjunction with time, rebirth (*āyāti*), and death.

Two types of skin-covering are taught, namely: that of humans and that of five-sensed animals. Two types of origin from semen and blood are taught, namely: that of humans and that of five-sensed animals. Two types of duration are taught, namely: bodily duration (*kāyaṭṭhitī*) and existential duration (*bhavaṭṭhitī*). Bodily duration is taught for two types of beings, namely: for humans and for five-sensed animals. Existential duration is taught for two types of beings, namely: for gods and for hell-beings.

Life-span (*āyu*) is declared to be of two kinds: namely, life-span by duration (*addhā-āyu*) and life-span by existence (*bhava-āyu*). Life-span by duration is declared for two [categories]: namely, for humans and for five-sensed beings of the animal realm. Life-span by existence is declared for two [categories]: namely, for gods and for hell-beings. Karma is declared to be of two kinds: namely, karma by spatial location (*pada-karma*) and karma by intensity of fruition (*anubhāva-karma*). Two [categories] maintain their life-span as it was: namely, gods and hell-beings. The contraction of life-span (*āyu-saṃvaṭṭa*) is declared for two [categories]: namely, for humans and for five-sensed beings of the animal realm.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two regions (vāsas) are described: they are very similar, without distinction or difference, and do not exceed one another in length, breadth, shape, and circumference; namely, Bharata and Airāvata. In this same manner: Haimavata and Hairaṇyavata; Harivarṣa and Ramyakavarṣa. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east and west of Mount Mandara, two fields (kṣetras) are described: they are very similar, without distinction, and so on, namely Pūrvavideha and Avaravideha. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two continents (kurus) are described: they are very similar, and so on, namely Devakuru and Uttarakuru. Therein, two great and most magnificent Gaja-trees are described: they are very similar, without distinction or difference, and do not exceed one another in length, breadth, height, girth, shape, and circumference; namely, Kūṭaśālmalī and the Jambū tree named Sundarśanā.
Therein dwell two gods of great power, up to great happiness, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely: Garuḍa Vēṇudēva and Anādhṛṣṭa, the sovereign of Jambūdvīpa.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two mountain ranges are described that are almost entirely equal, without distinction or difference, and do not exceed one another in length, breadth, height, depth, shape, or circumference. They are as follows: Cullahimavanta and Siharī; likewise Mahāhimavanta and Ruppī; likewise Nisadha and Nīlavaṃta. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, in the regions of Haimavata and Hairaṇyavata, two circular Vaitāḍhya mountains are described that are almost entirely equal, without distinction or difference, up to [the description of their dimensions]. Therein dwell two gods of great power, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely Sāti and Pabhāsa.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, in the regions of Harivarṣa and Ramyaka, two circular Vaitāḍhya mountains are described—extremely equal [in size] and so forth—as follows: Gandhāvātī and Mālavantapariyāta. There, two gods of great power and so forth, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, reside; namely, Aruṇa and Padma.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, on the eastern and western sides of the region of Devakuru, there are two range-mountains (vakṣāraparvata) described here which resemble the shoulders of a horse and are shaped like half-moons; they are almost exactly equal [in size], namely: Somanasa and Vijjuppabha.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, in the region of Uttarakuru, on the eastern and western sides, there are two mountain ranges described as being like the shoulders of a horse, shaped like half-moons, and mutually equal in all respects—namely, Gandhamādana and Mālyavanta.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two long Vaitāḍhya mountain ranges are described—extremely equal in all respects, as follows: the Long Vaitāḍhya of Bhārata and the Long Vaitāḍhya of Airāvata. In the Long Vaitāḍhya of Bhārata, two caves are described—extremely equal, without distinction or difference, not exceeding one another in length, width, height, shape, and circumference, as follows: the Timisra Cave and the Khaṇḍakapravāda Cave. Therein dwell two gods of great power, [possessing the splendor of a lord of gods, etc.,] with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, as follows: Kayamālaka and Naṭṭamālaka. In the Long Vaitāḍhya of Airāvata, two caves are described, [extremely equal, etc.,] as follows: Kayamālaka and Naṭṭamālaka.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, on the Cullahimavanta range of boundary mountains, two peaks are described—both of which are almost exactly equal in terms of their width, height, shape, and circumference. They are as follows: the Cullahimavanta peak itself and the Vaiśramaṇa peak.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, on the Mahāhimavanta range of boundary mountains, two peaks are described—both being very similar, and so forth—as follows: the Mahāhimavanta peak and the Vairūpyaka peak. Likewise, on the Nisadha range of boundary mountains, two peaks are described—both being very similar, and so forth—as follows: the Nisadha peak and the Rucakaprabha peak.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, on the Nīlavanta range of boundary mountains, two peaks are described—very similar to one another, and so forth—as follows: the Nīlavanta peak and the Uvadaṃsana peak. Likewise, on the Ruppī range of boundary mountains, two peaks are described—very similar to one another, and so forth—as follows: the Ruppī peak and the Maṇikañcana peak. Similarly, on the Siharī range of boundary mountains, two peaks are described—very similar to one another, and so forth—as follows: the Siharī peak and the Tigiñcha peak.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, on the Cullahimavanta and Śikhari mountain ranges which are boundary mountains (*vāsahara-pavvaya*), two great lakes are described—extremely equal, identical, and without distinction, not differing from one another in length, breadth, depth, shape, and circumference. They are as follows: Lake Paumā (Padma) and Lake Poṇḍarīya (Puṇḍarīka). Therein dwell two deities of great power, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely Śrī and Lakṣmī. Likewise, on the Mahāhimavanta and Ruppī boundary mountains, two great lakes are described—extremely equal... [as above] ...namely Lake Mahāpauma (Mahāpadma) and Lake Mahāpoṇḍarīya (Mahāpuṇḍarīka); there dwell two deities, Hiri and Buddhi. Likewise, on the Nisaḍha and Nīlavanta mountains, there are Lake Tigiñcha and Lake Kesarī; there dwell two deities, Dhiti and Kittī.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, two great rivers flow from the Mahāpadma lake and the Mahāhrada lake in the Mahāhimavanta range, namely: the Rohitā and the Harikantā. Likewise, from the Niṣadha range, two great rivers flow from the Tigiñcha lake and the Hrada, namely: the Haritā and the Sītōdā. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, two great rivers flow from the Kesarī lake and the Hrada in the Nīlavanta range, namely: the Sītā and the Nārikantā. Likewise, from the Rukmi range, two great rivers flow from the Mahāpuṇḍarīka lake and the Hrada, namely: the Narakantā and the Rūpyakūlā. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, in the land of Bharata, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar to one another, namely: the Gaṅgā-pravāha lake and the Sindhu-pravāha lake. Likewise, in the land of Haimavata, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar, namely: the Rohitā-pravāha lake and the Rohitaṃsā-pravāha lake. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, in the land of Harivarṣa, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar, namely: the Hari-pravāha lake and the Harikantā-pravāha lake. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, in the land of Mahāvideha, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar, namely: the Sītā-pravāha lake and the Sītōdā-pravāha lake. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, in the land of Ramyaka, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar, namely: the Narakantā-pravāha lake and the Nārikantā-pravāha lake. Likewise, in the land of Hairaṇyavata, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar, namely: the Suvarṇakūla-pravāha lake and the Rūpyakūla-pravāha lake. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, in the land of Airāvata, two outflow lakes are described as being very similar, namely: the Raktā-pravāha lake and the Raktāvatī-pravāha lake. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, in the land of Bharata, two great rivers are described as being very similar, namely: the Gaṅgā and the Sindhu. Just as it was with the outflow lakes, so should the rivers be described; up to the land of Airāvata, two great rivers are described as being very similar, namely: the Raktā and the Raktāvatī.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the past *utsarpiṇī* cycle, in the era of the *susama-duḥṣamā*, the time was two *koṭis* of *sāgaropamas*. Thus it has been declared for this current *avasarpiṇī* cycle; likewise it will be for the future *utsarpiṇī* cycle.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the Susamā period of the past Utsarpiṇī, humans were two *gavyūtis* in height and maintained a maximum lifespan of two *palyopamas*. Likewise, during this current Avasarpiṇī, they have maintained it up to that point; and likewise, in the future Utsarpiṇī, they will maintain it up to that point.

In the continent of Jambudvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, at one time, in one age, two lineages of Arhats have arisen, are arising, or will arise; likewise, two lineages of Cakravartins, and likewise, two lineages of Daśārhas have arisen, are arising, or will arise.

In Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, two Arhats arise, do arise, or will arise at one and the same time and in one and the same age; likewise two Cakravartins, likewise two Baladevas, and likewise two Vāsudevas [of the Daśārha lineage], up to: they have arisen, do arise, or will arise.
In Jambūdvīpa, in the two Kuru regions, humans always dwell experiencing the supreme prosperity of the "most excellent-everywhere" (susamasusama) era, namely in Devakuru and in Uttarakuru.
On the island of Jambudvīpa, in two regions, human beings always dwell enjoying the highest prosperity of the "Perfectly Auspicious" (Susama) age; namely, in Harivāsa and Ramyaka-vāsa.
On the island of Jambudvīpa, in two regions, human beings always dwell enjoying the highest prosperity of the "Auspicious-Afflicted" (Susama-duṣama) age; namely, in Haimavata and Hairaṇyavata.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in two regions, humans always dwell experiencing the supreme prosperity of the Dūṣamasuṣama period; namely, in Pūrvavideha and in Aparavideha. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in two continents, humans dwell experiencing all six types of time; namely, in Bharata and in Airāvata.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, two moons have shone, do shine, or will shine; two suns have blazed, do blaze, or will blaze; two Kattiyās, two Rohiṇīs, two Maggasiras, two Addās—and thus it should be understood according to the sequence of the verses—up to two Bharaṇīs.
Kattiyā, Rohiṇī, Maggasira, Addā, Puṇavvasū, Pūsa, Tatta, Assalēsa, Mahā, and the two Phagguṇīs. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 91)
Hasta, Citrā, Svāti, Viśākhā, and likewise Anurādhā;
Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and likewise Uttarāṣāḍhā. Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, and the two Śatabhiṣaj are the Bhādrapadas. (Ṭhāṇa 92)

Revatī, Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī are to be understood in their proper sequence. (Ṭhāṇa 93) There are two Agnis, two Pajāpatis, two Somas, two Rudras, two Aditis, two Bṛhaspatis, two Sappas, two Pitṛs, two Bhagas, two Aryamans, two Savitas, two Taṭṭhas, two Vāyus, two Indaggis, two Mittas, two Indas, two Niratis, two Āūs, two Vissas, two Brahmas, two Viṇhus, two Vasūs, two Varuṇas, two Ayās, two Vividdhis, two Puṣṣas, two Assas, and two Yamas.

Two are like glowing embers, two are like firebrands, two have red eyes, two are slow-moving, two are occasional, two are frequent, two are grains, two are golden grains, two are golden sparks, two are golden threads, two are golden continuations, two are moons, two are companions, two are consolers, two are those who arrive at work, two are those from market-towns, two are iron-workers, two are drum-makers, two are conchs, two are conch-colored, two are conch-colored in luster, two are bronze, two are bronze-colored, two are bronze-colored in luster, two are silver, two are silver-lustrous, two are blue, two are blue-lustrous, two are radiant, two are masses of radiance, two are sesame seeds, two are sesame-flower-colored, two are water, two are five-colored like water, two are crows, and two are crow-necked.

Two Indaggis, two Dhūmaketus, two Haris, two Piṅgalas, two Buddhas, two Sukkas, two Bahassatis, two Rāhus, two Agatthis, two Māṇavagas, two Kāsas, two Phāsas, two Dhuras, two Pamuhas, two Vigaḍas, two Visandhis, two Ṇiyallas, two Païllas, two Jaḍiyāilagās, two Aruṇas, two Aggillas, two Kālas, two Mahākālagas, two Sotthiyas, two Sovatthiyas, two Vaddhamāṇagas, two Pūsasamāṇagas, two Aṅkusas, two Palambas, two Ṇiccālōgas, two Ṇiccujjētas, two Sayampabhas, two Ōbhāsas, two Sēyaṅkaras, two Khēmaṅkaras, two Ābhaṅkaras, two Pabhaṅkaras, two Aparājitās, two Arayas, two Asōgas, two Vigatasōgas, two Vimalas, two Vitatas, two Vitatthas, two Visālas, two Sālas, two Suvvatās, two Aṇiyaṭṭīs, two Egajaḍīs, two Dujaḍīs, two Karakarigas, two Rāyaggalas, two Pupphukētus, and two Bhāvakētus.
The rampart of Jambūdvīpa is two *gavyūtis* in height.
The salt ocean (*Lavaṇa-samudra*) is two hundred thousand *yojanas* in circumference.
The rampart of the salt ocean is two *gavyūtis* in height.

On the eastern half of the island of Ghātakhaṇḍa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two regions (vāsas) are described, which are almost equal [in size], and so forth; namely, Bharata and Airāvata. Just as it was stated for Jambūdvīpa, so it should be recited here as well, up until: "In these two regions, human beings dwell experiencing the sixfold time, namely—Bharata and Airāvata. However, [the specific trees and deities differ]: the Kūṭaśālmalī tree and the Ghātakī tree; the deities Garuḍa and Veṇudeva, and Sudarśana. On the western half of the island of Ghātakhaṇḍa, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two regions are described, which are almost equal [in size], and so forth; namely, Bharata and Airāvata. Just as it was stated for Jambūdvīpa, so it should be recited here as well, up until: "In these two regions, human beings dwell experiencing the sixfold time, namely—Bharata and Airāvata. However, [the specific trees and deities differ]: the Kūṭaśālmali tree and the Mahāghātakī tree; the deities Garuḍa and Veṇudeva, and Priyadarśana.

In the Ghātyasaṇḍa continent, there are two Bharatas, two Airavatas, two Haimavatas, two Hairanyavatas, two Harivāsas, two Ramyakavāsas, two Pūrvavidehas, and two Aparavidehas; two Devakurus, two great trees of Devakuru, and two gods dwelling in the great trees of Devakuru; two Uttarakurus, two great trees of Uttarakuru, and two gods dwelling in the great trees of Uttarakuru; two Cullahimavantas, two Mahāhimavantas, two Nisadhas, two Nīlavantas, two Ruppis, two Siharīs, two Saddāvātīs, and two Sātī gods dwelling in Saddāvātī; two Viyaḍāvātīs, and two Pabhāsa gods dwelling in Viyaḍāvātī; two Gandhāvātīs, and two Aruṇa gods dwelling in Gandhāvātī; two Mālavantapariyāgas, and two Paüma gods dwelling in Mālavantapariyāga; two Mālavantas, two Cittakūḍas, two Pamhakūḍas, two Naliṇakūḍas, two Egasēlas, two Tikūḍas, two Vēsamaṇakūḍas, two Añjanas, two Mātañjanas, two Sōmaṇasas, two Vijjuppabhas, two Aṅkāvatis, two Pamhāvatis, two Āsīvisas, two Suhāvahas, two Candapavvatas, two Sūrapavvatas, two Nāgapavvatas, two Dēvapavvatas, two Gandhamāyaṇas, two Usugārapavvayas, two Cullahimavantakūḍas, two Vēsamaṇakūḍas, two Mahāhimavantakūḍas, two Vēruliyakūḍas, two Nisaḍhakūḍas, two Ruyagakūḍas, two Nīlavantakūḍas, two Uvadaṁsaṇakūḍas, two Ruppikūḍas, two Maṇikañcaṇakūḍas, two Siharikūḍas, and two Tigiñchikūḍas.

There are two Paumādraha lakes and two goddesses Śrīs residing in those two Paumādraha lakes; two Mahāpaumādraha lakes and two goddesses Hrīs residing in those two Mahāpaumādraha lakes; and so on, up to two Puṇḍarīyadraha lakes and two goddesses Lakṣmīs residing in those two Puṇḍarīyadraha lakes; two Gaṅgāpravāhādraha lakes, up to two Raktāvatīpravāhādraha lakes; two Rohitās, up to two Rūpyakūlās; two Gāhavatīs, two Dahavatīs, two Paṅkavatīs, two Tattajalās, two Mattajalās, two Umattajalās, two Kṣīrodās, two Siṃhasrotas, two Antovāhinīs, two Urmimālinīs, two Phēṇamālinīs, two Gambhīramālinīs; two Kacchas, two Sukacchas, two Mahākacchas, two Kacchāvatīs, two Āvartas, two Maṅgalāvartas, two Pukhalas, two Pukhalāvatīs, two Vacchas, two Suvacchas, two Mahāvacchas, two Vacchagāvatīs, two Rammas, two Rammagas, two Ramaṇijjās, two Maṅgalāvatīs, two Pamhas, two Supamhas, two Mahapamhas, two Pamhagāvatīs, two Saṅkhas, two Naliṇās, two Kumuyās, two Salilāvatīs, two Vappas, two Suvappas, two Mahāvappas, two Vappagāvatīs, two Vaggūs, two Suvaggūs, two Gandhilās, and two Gandhilāvatīs.

There are two Khemās, two Khemapurīs, two Riṣṭās, two Riṣṭapurīs, two Khaggīs, two Mañjūsās, two Oṣadhīs, two Puṇḍarikiṇīs, two Susīmās, two Kuṇḍalās, two Aparājitās, two Pabhaṅkarās, two Aṅkāvatīs, two Pamhāvatīs, two Subhās, two Ratnasañcayās, two Āsapurās, two Siṃhapurās, two Mahāpurās, two Vijayapurās, two Aparājitās, two Aparās, two Aśokās, two Vigataśokās, two Vijayās, two Vējayantīs, two Jayantīs, two Aparājitās, two Cakrapurās, two Khaggapurās, two Avajjhāvas, two Ayōjjhās, two Bhaddasālavaṇas, two Nandanavaṇas, two Sōmaṇasavaṇas, and two Paṇḍagavaṇas; there are two Paṇḍukambala slabs, two Atipaṇḍukambala slabs, two Rattakambala slabs, two Atirattakambala slabs, two Mandaras, and two Mandaracūlikās. Furthermore, the vedikā (railing) of the island of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa is declared to be two gavyūtis in height.

The rampart of the Kālōda ocean is declared to be two *gavyūtas* in height. In the eastern half of the Pukkhara-vara island, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two regions (*vāsas*) are declared—equal in all respects, and so forth—namely: Bharata and Airāvata; likewise, up to two *kurus* are declared: Devakuru and Uttarakuru. Therein, two very great and magnificent trees are declared, namely: the Kūṭaśālmali and the Paümarukkha. The gods Garuḷa Vēṇudēva and Paüma [reside there], enjoying the sixfold pleasures of the senses as they dwell.

In the western half of the Pukkharavara island, to the north and south of Mount Mandara, two regions (varṣas) are described; the distinction is as follows: there is the Kūṭaśālmalī tree and the Mahāpaümarukha tree, and the gods Garuḍa and Vēṇudēva, and Puṇḍarīka. In the Pukkharavara island, there are two Bharatas and two Airāvatas, up to two Mandaras and two Mandara-cūlikās. The rampart (vēdikā) of the Pukkharavara island is described as being two *gavyūtis* in height. The ramparts of all the islands and oceans are described as being two *gavyūtis* in height.

Two lords of the Asura-kumāras are taught, namely: Camara and Bali. Two lords of the Nāga-kumāras are taught, namely: Dharaṇa and Bhūyānanda. Two lords of the Suvarṇa-kumāras are taught, namely: Veṇudeva and Veṇudālī. Two lords of the Vidyut-kumāras are taught, namely: Hari and Harissaha. Two lords of the Agni-kumāras are taught, namely: Agnisīha and Agnimāṇava. Two lords of the Dvīpa-kumāras are taught, namely: Puṇṇa and Visiṭṭha. Two lords of the Udadhi-kumāras are taught, namely: Jalakanta and Jalappabha. Two lords of the Diśā-kumāras are taught, namely: Amitagati and Amitavāhana. Two lords of the Vāyu-kumāras are taught, namely: Velaṃba and Pabhaṃjana. Two lords of the Stanita-kumāras are taught, namely: Ghosa and Mahāghosa. Two lords of the Piśācas are taught, namely: Kāla and Mahākāla. Two lords of the Bhūtas are taught, namely: Surūpa and Paḍirūpa. Two lords of the Yakṣas are taught, namely: Puṇṇabhadda and Māṇibhadda. Two lords of the Rākṣasas are taught, namely: Bhīma and Mahābhīma. Two lords of the Kiṃnaras are taught, namely: Kiṃnara and Kiṃpuruṣa. Two lords of the Kiṃpuruṣas are taught, namely: Sappurisa and Mahāpurisa. Two lords of the Mahoragas are taught, namely: Atikāya and Mahākāya. Two lords of the Gandharvas are taught, namely: Gītarati and Gīyajaśa. Two lords of the Aṇapannas are taught, namely: Saṇṇihiya and Sāmaṇṇa. Two lords of the Paṇapannas are taught, namely: Dhāya and Vihāya. Two lords of the Ṛṣivādas are taught, namely: Ṛṣi and Ṛṣivālaka. Two lords of the Bhūtavādas are taught, namely: Issara and Mahissara. Two Kandīs are taught, namely: Suvaccha and Visāla. Two Mahākandīs are taught, namely: Hassa and Hassarati. Two Kumbhāṇḍas are taught, namely: Sēya and Mahāsēya. Two Patayas are taught, namely: Pattaya and Patayavaī. Of the Jyotiṣka gods, two lords are taught, namely: Candra and Sūra.

In the celestial realms of Saudharma and Īśāna, two Indras are proclaimed, namely: Śakra and Īśāna. In the celestial realms of Sanatkumāra and Māhendra, two Indras are proclaimed, namely: Sanatkumāra and Māhendra. In the celestial realms of Brahma-loka and Lāntaka, two Indras are proclaimed, namely: Brahma and Lāntaka. In the celestial realms of Mahāśukra and Sahasrāra, two Indras are proclaimed, namely: Mahāśukra and Sahasrāra. In the celestial realms of Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta, two Indras are proclaimed, namely: Prāṇata and Acyuta. In the celestial realms of Mahāśukra and Sahasrāra, the palaces (vimānas) are proclaimed to be of two colors, namely: yellow and white. The gods of the Graiveyaka heavens are proclaimed to be two *ratnis* in height.

Whether it is called a *samaya*, or a *āvaliyā*, it is designated as either a living being (*jīva*) or a non-living thing (*ajīva*). Whether it is called a breath (*āṇāpāṇu*), or a *thōva*, it is designated as either a living being or a non-living thing. Whether it is called a *khaṇa*, or a *lava*, it is designated as either a living being or a non-living thing. Likewise, whether it is called a *muhutta*, or a day and night (*ahoratta*), or a fortnight (*pakkha*), or a month (*māsa*), or a season (*uḍu*), or a half-year (*ayaṇa*), or a year (*saṃvacchara*), or a *yuga*, or a hundred years, or a thousand years, or a hundred thousand years, or ten million years (*vāsakoṭī*); or a *puvvaṅga*, or a *puvva*; or a *tuḍiyaṅga*, or a *tuḍiya*; or an *aḍaḍaṅga*, or an *aḍaḍa*; or an *avavaṅga*, or an *avava*; or a *hūhūaṅga*, or a *hūhūya*; or an *uppalaṅga*, or an *uppala*; or a *paümaṅga*, or a *paüma*; or a *naliṇaṅga*, or a *naliṇa*; or an *atthaṇikuraṅga*, or an *atthaṇikura*; or an *aüaṅga*, or an *aüa*, or a *ṇaüaṅga*, or a *ṇaüa*; or a *paütaṅga*, or a *paüta*; or a *cūliyaṅga*, or a *cūliya*; or a *sīsapahēliyaṅga*, or a *sīsapahēliya*; or a *paliōvama*, or a *sāgarōvama*; or an *ōsappiṇī*, or an *ussappiṇī*—it is designated as either a living being or a non-living thing.

Whether it be called a village, a city, a town, a capital, a market-town, a hamlet, a border-village, a port, a capital-city, a mine, a hermitage, a caravan-station, a settlement, a cattle-pen, a grove, a garden, a forest, a thicket, a pond, a lotus-pond, a lake, a series of lakes, a well, a reservoir, a pool, a river, the earth, the ocean, a mass of air, the intermediate quarters, a circle, a formation, an island, a sea, a rampart, a wall, a gate, an archway, hell-beings, the abodes of hell-beings, up to the Vaimānika gods or the abodes of the Vaimānika gods, the celestial realms, the abodes of the celestial palaces, the dwellings, the mountain ranges that support the dwellings, peaks, peak-houses, the regions of victory, royal capitals, or whether they be souls (*jīva*) or non-souls (*ajīva*), these are what are spoken of.

Whether it be called shade, or heat, or moonlight, or darkness, or low ground, or high ground, or a house by a river, or a house in a garden, or a hanging branch, or a place with gentle breezes—it is called either "living" or "non-living.
Two heaps are proclaimed: namely, the heap of living beings and the heap of non-living things.
Two kinds of bondage are proclaimed: namely, the bondage of attachment and the bondage of aversion.

Living beings bind evil karma through two conditions, namely: passion and hatred. Living beings activate evil karma through two conditions, namely: through affliction that occurs spontaneously and through affliction that is induced. Likewise, they experience it and likewise exhaust it—namely, through affliction that occurs spontaneously and through affliction that is induced.

By two conditions the soul departs after having touched the body: namely, either by touching the body partially or by touching the body entirely. Likewise after having shaken it, likewise after having pervaded it, likewise after having contracted it, and likewise after having expanded it. By two conditions the soul may obtain the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins for the purpose of hearing: namely, through destruction alone and through subsidence alone; likewise up to the point where one may produce mind-reading knowledge (*manahparyāya-jñāna*), namely, through destruction alone and through subsidence alone.

Two kinds of *addhōvama* (measures of time) are taught, namely: the *paliōvama* and the *sāgarōvama*. What is the *paliōvama*? It is a pit one *yojana* in width, filled without any gaps up to the brim with the tips of the hair of newborn infants born on successive days. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 104)

The time it takes for each garment to be removed one by one over the course of a hundred years— that time should be understood as the duration of one *palya*. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 105) Ten times the product of ten million of these *palyas* constitutes [the duration of a *sāgaropama*].

That indeed shall be the measure of a single *sāgara*. (Ṭhāṇa 106) Anger is declared to be of two kinds, namely: that directed toward oneself and that directed toward others. Thus it is for hell-beings up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm; and so on, up to the thorn of false view (*micchādamsaṇasalla*).

Living beings who have entered the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) are declared to be of two kinds, namely: mobile (*trasa*) and immobile (*sthāvara*). All living beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: perfected ones (*siddha*) and non-perfected ones (*asiddha*). All living beings are declared to be of two kinds, namely: those with sense organs (*sendriya*) and those without sense organs (*anindriya*). [Those with bodies (*sakāya*) and those without bodies (*akāya*); those with yoga (*sayogin*) and those without yoga (*ayogin*); those with sensation (*saveda*) and those without sensation (*aveda*); those with passions (*sakasāya*) and those without passions (*akasāya*); those with senses (*sendriya*) and those without senses (*anindriya*); likewise, this verse should be applied [to all categories] up to: those with bodies (*sasarīrin*) and those without bodies (*asarīrin*). [The summary verse: Perfected ones, senses, bodies, yoga, sensation, passions, and leśyās.
One who possesses knowledge does not consume subtle food; one who speaks is in his final body and possesses a physical form. (Ṭhāṇa 109)

There are two types of death that were not constantly praised, nor constantly commended, nor constantly spoken of, nor constantly extolled, nor constantly approved by the ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, for the sake of the Nirgrantha ascetics; namely: death in bondage (*valayamaraṇa*) and death under the sway of passion (*vasaṭṭamaraṇa*). Likewise: death due to a vow (*niyāṇamaraṇa*) and death in that very same existence (*tabbhavamaraṇa*); falling from a mountain and falling from a tree; entering water and entering fire; consuming poison and being impaled by a weapon. These two types of death, up to and including being impaled by a weapon, were not constantly approved [by him]. However, for a specific reason, they are not forbidden: namely, death by hanging (*vēhāṇasa*) and death by the vultures’ feast (*giddhapaṭṭha*).

Two modes of death were constantly praised by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, for the Nirgrantha ascetics, and have been approved as such; namely: *pāōvagamaṇa* (fasting unto death) and *bhattapaccakkhāṇa* (renunciation of food). *Pāōvagamaṇa* is declared to be of two kinds: *nīhārima* (with removal of the body) and *anīhārima* (without removal of the body), both necessarily without medical treatment (*apaḍikamma*). *Bhattapaccakkhāṇa* is declared to be of two kinds: *nīhārima* and *anīhārima*, both necessarily with medical treatment (*sapaḍikamma*).

What is this world? It is both the living (jīva) and the non-living (ajīva). What are the infinite worlds? They are both the living and the non-living. What are the eternal worlds? They are both the living and the non-living. Two kinds of awakening (bodhi) are taught: namely, awakening through knowledge (nāṇabodhi) and awakening through vision (daṃsaṇabodhi). Two kinds of awakened ones (buddha) are taught: namely, those awakened through knowledge and those awakened through vision. Two kinds of delusion (mōha) are taught: namely, delusion regarding knowledge and delusion regarding vision. Two kinds of deluded ones (mūḍha) are taught: namely, those deluded regarding knowledge and those deluded regarding vision.

The karma that obscures knowledge (*jñānāvaraṇīya*) is twofold, namely: that which obscures partial knowledge and that which obscures complete knowledge. The karma that obscures vision (*darśanāvaraṇīya*) is likewise twofold.
