The karma that produces feeling (*vedanīya*) is twofold, namely: that which produces pleasant feeling and that which produces unpleasant feeling. The karma that causes delusion (*mohanīya*) is twofold, namely: that which deludes vision and that which deludes conduct. The karma that determines lifespan (*āyuṣka*) is twofold, namely: the lifespan of time (*addhāyuṣka*) and the lifespan of existence (*bhavāyuṣka*). The karma of name (*nāma*) is twofold, namely: auspicious name and inauspicious name. The karma of lineage (*gotra*) is twofold, namely: high lineage and low lineage. The obstructive karma (*antarāyika*) is twofold, namely: that which destroys what is present and that which blocks the path to the future.

Two kinds of delusion (mucchā) are taught, namely: that consisting of attachment (pejja) and that consisting of aversion (dosa). Delusion consisting of attachment is taught to be of two kinds, namely: deceit (māyā) and greed (lōbhā). Delusion consisting of aversion is taught to be of two kinds, namely: anger (kōha) and pride (māna).

Two kinds of attainment are taught, namely: the attainment of the Dharma and the attainment of the Kevalin. The attainment of the Dharma is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the attainment of the Dharma of Scripture and the attainment of the Dharma of Conduct. The attainment of the Kevalin is taught to be of two kinds, namely: the performance of the final act (antakriyā) and rebirth in a celestial mansion (kappavimāṇovavattiya).

Two Tīrthaṅkaras are described as being the color of blue lotuses: namely, Munisuvrata and Ariṣṭanemi. Two Tīrthaṅkaras are described as being the color of yellow *piyaṅgu* (cassia fistula): namely, Malli and Pārśva. Two Tīrthaṅkaras are described as being the color of a red lotus: namely, Padmaprabha and Vāsupūjya. Two Tīrthaṅkaras are described as being the color of the moon: namely, Candraprabha and Puṣpadanta. In the *Saccapravāda-pūrva*, two sections (*vastu*) are described.

The constellation Pūrvābhādrapadā is declared to have two stars; the constellation Uttarābhādrapadā is declared to have two stars; the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī is declared to have two stars; the constellation Uttaraphalgunī is declared to have two stars.
Within the human realm, there are two oceans, namely: the Lavaṇa and the Kāloda.

Two universal monarchs (cakravartins), who did not renounce sensual pleasures, having passed away at the time of death, were reborn as hell-beings in the seventh earth, the Apratiṣṭhāna hell, namely: Subhūma and Brahmadatta.

The maximum lifespan of the gods dwelling in the palaces of the Asurinda-Vajjīyas is taught to be slightly less than two *palyopamas*. In the *Saudharma* kalpa, the maximum lifespan of the gods is taught to be two *sāgaropamas*. In the *Īśāna* kalpa, the maximum lifespan of the gods is taught to be more than two *sāgaropamas*. In the *Sanatkumāra* kalpa, the minimum lifespan of the gods is taught to be two *sāgaropamas*. In the *Māhendra* kalpa, the minimum lifespan of the gods is taught to be slightly more than two *sāgaropamas*.
In two kalpas, the Kappiṭṭhiya gods are found; namely, in Sōhamma and Īsāṇa.
In two kalpas, the gods with fiery radiance (tēulēssa) are found; namely, in Sōhamma and Īsāṇa.

In two kalpas, the gods are declared to be enjoyers of physical contact (*kāyapariyāraga*); namely, in Sōhamma and Īsāṇa. In two kalpas, the gods are declared to be enjoyers of tactile sensation (*phāsapariyāraga*); namely, in Saṇaṅkumāra and Māhinda. In two kalpas, the gods are declared to be enjoyers of visual form (*rūvapariyāraga*); namely, in Bambhalōga and Lantaga. In two kalpas, the gods are declared to be enjoyers of sound (*saddapariyāraga*); namely, in Mahāsukka and Sahassāra. Two Indras are declared to be enjoyers of mental objects (*maṇapariyāraga*); namely, Pāṇaya and Accuya.

Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate matter produced from evil states as sinful karma; namely, that which is produced from the mobile body and that which is produced from the immobile body. In the same way, they have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate; they have bound, are binding, or will bind; they have manifested, are manifesting, or will manifest; they have experienced, are experiencing, or will experience; and they have undergone dissociation, are undergoing dissociation, or will undergo dissociation.

Infinite two-space-point aggregates (dupaesiyā khaṃdhā) are taught; infinite matter-particles (poggalā) occupying two space-points (dupadesōgāḍhā) are taught; and likewise, up to infinite matter-particles possessing double the degree of dryness (duguṇalukkhā poggalā) are taught. Three types of lords (indā) are taught, namely: the nominal lord (nāmindē), the conventional lord (ṭhavaṇindē), and the substantial lord (davvindē). Three types of lords are taught, namely: the lord of knowledge (nāṇindē), the lord of vision (daṃsaṇindē), and the lord of conduct (carittindē). Three types of lords are taught, namely: the lord of gods (dēvindē), the lord of asuras (asurindē), and the lord of humans (maṇussindē).

Three kinds of transformation (*vikurvaṇā*) are taught, namely: one transformation by having consumed external matter; one transformation by not having consumed external matter; and one transformation by having both consumed and not consumed external matter. Three kinds of transformation are taught, namely: one transformation by having consumed internal matter; one transformation by not having consumed internal matter; and one transformation by having both consumed and not consumed internal matter. Three kinds of transformation are taught, namely: one transformation by having consumed both external and internal matter; one transformation by not having consumed both external and internal matter; and one transformation by having both consumed and not consumed both external and internal matter.

Hell-beings are declared to be of three kinds, namely: those with accumulated karma, those with non-accumulated karma, and those with indeterminate karma; likewise for all beings from the one-sensed up to the Vaimānika gods, with the exception of the one-sensed.

Three types of sexual enjoyment (*pariyāraṇā*) are taught, as follows: one god, together with other gods, repeatedly enjoys the goddesses of other gods; he repeatedly enjoys his own personal goddesses; and he repeatedly enjoys himself by transforming himself through his own power. Another god, not together with other gods, does not repeatedly enjoy the goddesses of other gods; he repeatedly enjoys his own personal goddesses; and he repeatedly enjoys himself by transforming himself through his own power. Yet another god, not together with other gods, does not repeatedly enjoy the goddesses of other gods, nor does he repeatedly enjoy his own personal goddesses; he repeatedly enjoys himself by transforming himself through his own power.

Sexual intercourse is declared to be threefold, namely: celestial, human, and animal. Three types of beings engage in sexual intercourse, namely: gods, humans, and animals. Three types of beings practice sexual intercourse, namely: females, males, and hermaphrodites.

Threefold yoga is taught, namely: mental yoga (*manoyoga*), vocal yoga (*vāgyoga*), and bodily yoga (*kāyayoga*). Thus it is for hell-beings, excluding those with fewer than five senses (*vigalindiya*), up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm. Threefold application (*prayoga*) is taught, namely: mental application (*manaprayoga*), vocal application (*vāiprayoga*), and bodily application (*kāyaprayoga*). Just as yoga [is taught] for those excluding those with fewer than five senses, up to that extent is application also. Threefold instrument (*karana*) is taught, namely: mental instrument (*manakarana*), vocal instrument (*vāk-karana*), and bodily instrument (*kāyakarana*); thus [it is taught] for all, excluding those with fewer than five senses, up to the *vaimānika* gods. Threefold instrument is taught, namely: the instrument of undertaking (*ārambhakarana*), the instrument of preparation (*saṃrambhakarana*), and the instrument of execution (*samārambhakarana*); this applies continuously up to the *vaimānika* gods.

By three conditions, living beings produce karma leading to a short lifespan; namely: by killing living beings; by speaking falsehoods; and by providing a monk or a brahmin of such a kind with food, drink, snacks, and delicacies that are unwholesome and unfit for consumption. By these three conditions, they produce karma leading to a short lifespan.

By three conditions, living beings produce karma for a long life-span, namely: they do not kill living beings; they do not speak falsehood; and they provide a worthy ascetic or brahmin with wholesome, acceptable food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. By these three conditions, living beings produce karma for a long life-span.

By three conditions, living beings create karma that results in an impure long life-span (*asubha-dīhāuya*): namely, by killing living beings; by speaking falsehoods; and by treating a worthy ascetic or brahmin with contempt, reviling, mocking, censuring, and insulting them, and by providing them with food or other requisites that are unpleasant and cause displeasure. By these three conditions, living beings create karma for an impure long life-span. By three conditions, living beings create karma that results in a pure long life-span (*subha-dīhāuya*): namely, by not killing living beings; by not speaking falsehoods; and by honoring, saluting, respecting, and revering a worthy ascetic or brahmin, serving them as a source of merit, auspiciousness, divinity, and a sacred object, and by providing them with pleasant and pleasing food, drink, snacks, and delicacies. By these three conditions, living beings create karma for a pure long life-span.

Three types of restraint are taught, namely: restraint of mind, restraint of speech, and restraint of body. Three types of restraint are taught for restrained human beings, namely: restraint of mind, restraint of speech, and restraint of body.

Three types of non-restraint are taught, namely: non-restraint of mind, non-restraint of speech, and non-restraint of body; this applies likewise to hell-beings up to the *stanitakumāras*, to five-sensed animals, to unrestrained human beings, and to the *vāṇamantaras*, the *jyotiṣkas*, and the *vaimānikas*.

Three types of rods are taught, namely: the rod of mind, the rod of speech, and the rod of body. For hell-beings, three rods are taught, namely: the rod of mind, the rod of speech, and the rod of body; this applies to all beings up to the Vaimānikas, with the exception of those with fewer than five senses.

Repentance is declared to be threefold; namely: one repents through the mind, one repents through speech, and one repents through the body for the non-commission of evil karmas. Alternatively, repentance is declared to be threefold; namely: some repent for a long duration, some repent for a short duration, and some withdraw their bodies from the non-commission of evil karmas.

Threefold is renunciation prescribed; namely: one renounces evil impulses through the mind, one renounces evil impulses through speech, and one renounces evil impulses through the body by way of the non-performance of sinful actions. Just as there are two discourses regarding censure (*garahā*), so too should two discourses be understood regarding renunciation (*paccakkhāṇa*).

Three kinds of trees are prescribed, namely: those that provide leaves, those that provide flowers, and those that provide fruit. In the same way, three types of persons are prescribed, namely: one who is like a tree providing leaves, one who is like a tree providing flowers, and one who is like a tree providing fruit.

Three types of persons are taught, namely: the nominal person (*nāma-purisa*), the figurative person (*ṭhavaṇa-purisa*), and the substantial person (*davva-purisa*). Three types of persons are taught, namely: the person of knowledge (*nāṇa-purisa*), the person of vision (*daṃsaṇa-purisa*), and the person of conduct (*caritta-purisa*). Three types of persons are taught, namely: the person of the Veda (*vēda-purisa*), the person of the insignia (*cinda-purisa*), and the person of the designation (*abhilāva-purisa*).

Three kinds of persons are taught, namely: superior persons, middling persons, and inferior persons. Superior persons are taught to be of three kinds, namely: persons of Dharma, persons of enjoyment, and persons of action. Persons of Dharma are Arhats; persons of enjoyment are Universal Monarchs (Cakravartins); persons of action are Vāsudevas. Middling persons are taught to be of three kinds, namely: the Uggas, the Bhogas, and the Rājanyas. Inferior persons are taught to be of three kinds, namely: slaves, servants, and laborers.

Fish are declared to be of three kinds, namely: those born from eggs, those born from wombs, and those born by spontaneous generation. Fish born from eggs are declared to be of three kinds, namely: females, males, and neuters. Fish born from wombs are declared to be of three kinds, namely: females, males, and neuters.

Birds are declared to be of three kinds, namely: egg-born, womb-born, and spontaneously born. Egg-born birds are declared to be of three kinds, namely: female, male, and neuter. Womb-born birds are declared to be of three kinds, namely: female, male, and neuter. In this same manner, they should also be described for the belly-crawlers (uraga-parisappa) and likewise for the arm-crawlers (bhujaga-parisappa).

In this very way, women are declared to be of three kinds, namely: female beings of the animal realm, human females, and female deities. Female beings of the animal realm are declared to be of three kinds, namely: those that move in water, those that move on land, and those that move through the air. Human females are declared to be of three kinds, namely: those from the lands of action (*karmabhūmi*), those from the non-lands of action (*akarmabhūmi*), and those from the intermediate islands (*antaradvīpa*).

Three kinds of males are taught, namely: male beings of the animal realm, male humans, and male gods. Male beings of the animal realm are taught to be of three kinds, namely: those that move in water, those that move on land, and those that move through the air. Male humans are taught to be of three kinds, namely: those from the lands of action (*karmabhūmi*), those from the non-lands of action (*akarmabhūmi*), and those from the intermediate islands (*antaradvīpa*). Three kinds of neuters (*napuṃsaka*) are taught, namely: neuter hell-beings, neuter beings of the animal realm, and neuter humans. Neuter beings of the animal realm are taught to be of three kinds, namely: those that move in water, those that move on land, and those that move through the air. Neuter humans are taught to be of three kinds, namely: those from the lands of action, those from the non-lands of action, and those from the intermediate islands.
There are three types of beings in the animal realm, namely: females, males, and neuters.
For hell-beings, three karmic leśyās (passions) are taught, namely: black leśyā, blue leśyā, and grey leśyā.

For the Asurakumāras, three defiled leśyās are taught, namely: black leśyā, blue leśyā, and grey leśyā; and so on up to the Stanitakumāras. Likewise for the earth-bodied, water-bodied, and plant-bodied beings; and for the fire-bodied, air-bodied, two-sensed, three-sensed, and four-sensed beings, there are three leśyās just as for the hell-beings.

For five-sensed animals (*pañcendriya-tiryag-yoni*), three defiled (*saṅkliṣṭa*) leśyās are taught, namely: black leśyā (*kṛṣṇa-leśyā*), blue leśyā (*nīla-leśyā*), and grey leśyā (*kāpota-leśyā*). For five-sensed animals, three non-defiled (*asaṅkliṣṭa*) leśyās are taught, namely: fiery leśyā (*tejo-leśyā*), lotus leśyā (*padma-leśyā*), and white leśyā (*śukla-leśyā*). It is the same for humans: [for humans] three defiled leśyās are taught, namely: black leśyā, blue leśyā, and grey leśyā; [and three non-defiled leśyās are taught, namely: fiery leśyā, lotus leśyā, and white leśyā. For the *vānamantara* gods, it is the same as for the *asura-kumāra* gods.
For the denizens of the celestial realms (*vemāṇiya*), three types of *leśyās* are taught, namely: the fiery *leśyā*, the lotus *leśyā*, and the white *leśyā*.

A star-form may move for three reasons, namely: when it is undergoing transformation (*vikuvvamāṇe*), when it is enjoying its pleasures (*pariyārēmāṇe*), or when it is moving from one place to another; thus a star-form may move. A god may produce a flash of lightning for three reasons, namely: when he is undergoing transformation, when he is enjoying his pleasures, or when he is displaying the power, splendor, fame, strength, heroism, manly effort, and exertion of a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa of such a kind; thus a god may produce a flash of lightning.

For three reasons a god may produce the sound of thunder: namely, when transforming himself; and just as it was stated regarding lightning, so too for the sound of thunder. For three reasons there may be darkness in the world: namely, when Arhats are passing away, when the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats is passing away, and when the Pūrvas are passing away. For three reasons there may be light in the world: namely, when Arhats are being born, when Arhats are going forth into the religious life, and during the great festivals marking the arising of the knowledge of the Arhats.

There may be darkness among the gods for three reasons, namely: when the Arhats are passing away, when the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats is passing away, and when the Pūrvas are passing away. There may be light among the gods for three reasons, namely: when the Arhats are being born, when the Arhats are going forth into the religious life, and during the great festivals marking the arising of the knowledge of the Arhats.

There may be a gathering of gods for three reasons, namely: when Arhats are being born, when Arhats are renouncing the world, and during the great festivals of the arising of the knowledge of the Arhats; likewise, there are divine festivities and divine conversations.

For three reasons the lords of the gods (devindas) come swiftly to the world of men: namely, when Arhats are being born; when Arhats are renouncing the world; and at the festivals for the arising of the knowledge of Arhats. Likewise, the Sāmāṇika gods, the Tāyattīsaga gods, the World-Guardians (lokapālas), the goddesses who are chief queens, the gods descended from the assemblies, the gods who are commanders of hosts, and the guardian gods (āyarakkhas) come swiftly to the world of men.

On three occasions the gods rise up to greet [the Tirthankara], namely: when the Arhats are being born, and so forth, as before. Likewise, their thrones shake, they let out a lion’s roar, and they scatter flowers. On three occasions the *caitya* trees of the gods shake, namely: when the Arhats are being born, when the Arhats are renouncing the world, and during the great festivals for the arising of the Arhats’ knowledge.

For three reasons the gods belonging to the world of men may quickly come to the human world; namely: when Arhats are being born, when Arhats are renouncing the world, and at the great festivals for the arising of the knowledge of Arhats.

"O venerable ascetic, there are three for whom it is difficult to repay their kindness. They are: one's mother and father, a master, and a teacher of the Dharma. Suppose, O venerable ascetic, some man were to anoint his mother and father with oils refined a hundred or a thousand times, rub them with fragrant unguents, bathe them with the three kinds of water, adorn them with all manner of ornaments, feed them delicious food consisting of pure *thālīpāka* mixed with eighteen kinds of side dishes, and carry them on his back for as long as he lives—even by doing all this, it would still be difficult to repay that mother and father. However, if he were to explain, teach, demonstrate, and establish his mother and father in the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins, only by that means would it be easy to repay that mother and father, O venerable ascetic. Or suppose, O venerable ascetic, some person of high station were to elevate a poor man. Once that poor man has been elevated, he might thereafter live endowed with an abundance of great enjoyments. Then, at some later time, that person of high station might fall into poverty and come quickly to the presence of that poor man. Even if that poor man were to give his master everything he possesses, it would still be difficult to repay him. However, if he were to explain, teach, demonstrate, and establish that master in the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins, only by that means would it be easy to repay that master, O venerable ascetic."

"O venerable ascetics, how many [beings] have there been who, having heard and reflected upon even a single noble and righteous word from the presence of a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, and having passed away at the time of their death, were reborn as gods in one of the celestial realms? Suppose that god, out of gratitude, were to lead his spiritual teacher (dhammāyariya) from a land of famine to a land of plenty, or lead him across a wilderness to a place free of danger, or liberate him when he is overcome by a long-lasting illness—yet even for that, it would be difficult to repay the debt owed to that spiritual teacher. However, O venerable ascetics, if that person were to cause his spiritual teacher, who has fallen away from the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin, to once again accept, understand, explain, and be established in the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin, then by that alone it becomes easy to repay the debt owed to that spiritual teacher."

An ascetic endowed with three qualities may cross over the wilderness of saṃsāra—which is without beginning, without end, long-lasting, and four-cornered—namely: through lack of worldly motives, through being endowed with right view, and through practicing yoga.

Three types of *osappiṇī* (descending cycles) are taught: namely, the highest, the middle, and the lowest; likewise, all six ages should be recited, up to the *dūsama-dūsamā* (the most difficult age).
Three types of *ussappiṇī* (ascending cycles) are taught: namely, the highest, the middle, and the lowest; likewise, all six ages should be recited, up to the *susama-susamā* (the most pleasant age).

Matter may move for three reasons; namely: matter may move when it is being ingested; matter may move when it is undergoing transformation; or matter may move when it is being transferred from one place to another.

Possession (upadhi) is declared to be threefold, namely: possession consisting of karma, possession consisting of the body, and possession consisting of external objects and utensils. This should be stated for the Asurakumāras; likewise, excluding the one-sensed beings and hell-beings, it applies up to the Vaimānikas. Alternatively, possession is declared to be threefold, namely: conscious, unconscious, and mixed. This applies continuously for the hell-beings up to the Vaimānikas.

Possession is declared to be threefold, namely: possession of karma, possession of the body, and possession of external objects and belongings. Thus it is for the Asura-kumāras, and likewise for all beings from the one-sensed hell-beings up to the Vaimānikas. Alternatively, possession is declared to be threefold, namely: sentient, insentient, and mixed. Thus it is for the hell-beings continuously up to the Vaimānikas.

Three kinds of application (praṇidhāna) are taught, namely: mental application, verbal application, and bodily application; likewise for all five-sensed beings up to the Vaimānika gods. Three kinds of right application (supraṇidhāna) are taught, namely: right mental application, right verbal application, and right bodily application. For restrained human beings, three kinds of right application are taught, namely: right mental application, right verbal application, and right bodily application. Three kinds of wrong application (duppraṇidhāna) are taught, namely: wrong mental application, wrong verbal application, and wrong bodily application; likewise for all five-sensed beings up to the Vaimānika gods.

Three kinds of birth-places (yoni) are taught, namely: cold, hot, and cold-hot. Thus [are they] for one-sensed beings, for those with fewer than five senses, for spontaneously born five-sensed animals, and for spontaneously born humans. Three kinds of birth-places are taught, namely: conscious, unconscious, and mixed. Thus [are they] for one-sensed beings, for those with fewer than five senses, for spontaneously born five-sensed animals, and for spontaneously born humans.
Three kinds of birth-places are taught, namely: enclosed, open, and both enclosed and open.

Three kinds of wombs are taught, namely: the tortoise-shaped (*kummuṇṇayā*), the conch-spiral (*saṅkhāvattā*), and the bamboo-joint (*vaṁsīvattiyā*). The tortoise-shaped womb belongs to supreme beings (*uttamapurisa*); from this tortoise-shaped womb, three types of supreme beings descend into the womb, namely: Arhats, Cakravartins, and Baladevas and Vāsudevas. The conch-spiral womb belongs to the Woman-Jewel (*itthīrayaṇa*); from this conch-spiral womb, many living beings (*jīva*) and matter-particles (*poggala*) enter, exit, fall away, and are reborn, yet they do not actually come to fruition [as offspring]. The bamboo-joint womb belongs to ordinary people (*pihajjana*); from this bamboo-joint womb, many ordinary people descend into the womb.
The plant-bodied beings are declared to be of three kinds, namely: those with numerable lives, those with innumerable lives, and those with infinite lives.

On the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, three holy places (tīrtha) are proclaimed, namely: Māgadha, Varadāma, and Prabhāsa. Likewise in Airāvata. On the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Mahāvideha, in each individual Cakravartin-vijaya, three holy places are proclaimed, namely: Māgadha, Varadāma, and Prabhāsa. Likewise on the continent of Ghātakīkhaṇḍa, both in the eastern half and the western half; and likewise on the continent of Puṣkaravaradvīpa, both in the eastern half and the western half.

In the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the past Utsarpiṇī cycle, in the Susama period, the duration was three sāgaropama-koṭākoṭīs. It is likewise declared for the Avasarpiṇī cycle, with this distinction. In the future Utsarpiṇī cycle, it will be the same. Thus, the duration should be stated for the eastern and western halves of Ghanodadhi-samudra, and likewise for the eastern and western halves of Pukkhara-vara-dvīpa.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bhārata and Airāvata during the *susama-susamā* (the most excellent) epoch of the past *utsarpiṇī*, humans were three *gavyūtis* in height and lived for a maximum lifespan of three *palyopamas*. Likewise, in this *avasarpiṇī* and in the future *utsarpiṇī*, on the island of Jambūdvīpa, in Devakuru and Uttarakuru, humans are declared to be three *gavyūtis* in height and live for a maximum lifespan of three *palyopamas*; and so it continues as far as the western half of Puṣkaravaradvīpa.

In Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during each aeon of decrease (avasarpiṇī) and increase (utsarpiṇī), three lineages arise, are arising, or will arise; namely: the lineage of Arhats, the lineage of Cakravartins, and the lineage of Daśārhas. This is likewise true up to the western half of Pukkhara-vara-dvīpa.

In the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during each aeon of decrease (avasarpinī) and increase (utsarpinī), three supreme beings have arisen, are arising, or will arise; namely: Arhats, Cakravartins, Baladevas, and Vāsudevas. This continues as far as the western half of the Pukkhara-vara-dvīpa. There, some maintain a long lifespan—namely: Arhats, Cakravartins, Baladevas, and Vāsudevas; others maintain a medium lifespan—namely: Arhats, Cakravartins, Baladevas, and Vāsudevas.
The maximum lifespan of gross fire-bodied beings is declared to be three days and nights. The maximum lifespan of gross air-bodied beings is declared to be three thousand years.

“Venerable sir, regarding these grains—rice, paddy, wheat, barley, and *javajava*—stored in granaries, in heaps, on platforms, or in attics; plastered over, smeared with lime, marked with seals, stamped, and covered shut—for how long does their *yoni* (vital potential) remain intact? At the minimum, for a period of half a muhūrta; at the maximum, for three years. Beyond that, the *yoni* withers; beyond that, the *yoni* disintegrates; beyond that, the *yoni* is destroyed; beyond that, the seed becomes non-seed; and beyond that, the cessation of the *yoni* is declared.”

In the second hell, the Sakkarappabhā, the maximum lifespan of the hell-beings is declared to be three sāgaropamas; in the third hell, the Vāluyappabhā, the minimum lifespan of the hell-beings is declared to be three sāgaropamas.

In the fifth hell, Dhūmaprabhā, three hundred thousand hell-abodes are declared. In three hells, the hell-beings experience hot suffering; namely, in the first, the second, and the third. In these three hells, the hell-beings dwell experiencing hot suffering; namely, in the first, the second, and the third.

Three things in the world are described as being equal in their respective directions and sub-directions, namely: the Apratiṣṭhāna hell, the Jambūdvīpa continent, and the Sarvārthasiddha great celestial mansion. Three things in the world are described as being equal in their respective directions and sub-directions, namely: the Sīmantaka hell, the Samayakṣetra (the central region of time), and the Īṣatprāgbhārā earth. Three oceans are described as having water by nature, namely: the Kāloda, the Puṣkaroda, and the Svayaṃbhūramaṇa. Three oceans are described as being filled with many fish and crocodiles, namely: the Lavaṇa, the Kāloda, and the Svayaṃbhūramaṇa.

In this world, those who are devoid of virtue, lacking in conduct, devoid of qualities, lacking in self-restraint, and devoid of vows of renunciation and fasting, having met their end at the proper time, are reborn as hell-beings in the seventh earth, the *Appatiṭṭhāṇa* hell. They are as follows: kings, regional lords, and householders who engage in great violence. In this world, those who are virtuous, well-conducted, endowed with qualities, possessed of self-restraint, and observant of vows of renunciation and fasting, having met their end at the proper time, become reborn as gods in the *Sarvārthasiddha* celestial palace. They are as follows: kings who have renounced sensual pleasures, generals, and preceptors.

In the celestial realms of Bambhalōga and Lantaē, the palaces (vimāṇas) are described as being of three colors, namely: black, blue, and red. In the celestial realms of Āṇaya, Pāṇaya, Āraṇa, and Accuya, the bodies of the gods that they maintain throughout their existence (bhavadhāraṇijja-sarīraga) are described as being at most three cubits (rayaṇī) in height.
Three treatises (pannattīs) are studied in due course of time, namely: Candapannattī, Sūrapannattī, and Dīvasāgarapannattī.

The world is declared to be threefold, namely: the nominal world, the conventional world, and the substantial world. The world is declared to be threefold, namely: the world of knowledge, the world of vision, and the world of conduct. The world is declared to be threefold, namely: the upper world, the lower world, and the horizontal world.

The Asura King Camara, lord of the Asurakumāras, has three assemblies, namely: Samitā, Caṇḍā, and Jātā. The inner assembly is Samitā, the middle is Caṇḍā, and the outer is Jātā. Regarding the Sāmānika gods of the Asura King Camara, lord of the Asurakumāras, three assemblies are also declared, namely: Samitā, [Caṇḍā, and Jātā], exactly as for Camara. Likewise for the Thirty-three [Tāvattiṃsa] gods, for the World-protectors (Lokapālas)—[namely] Tumbā, Tuḍiyā, and Pavvā—and likewise for the Chief Queens (Aggramahiṣīs), and for Bali it is exactly the same, up to the Chief Queens.

For Dharaṇa, as well as for his Sāmāṇika and Trāyastriṃśa gods, the assemblies became Samitā, Caṇḍā, and Jātā; for the Lokapālas and their chief queens, they were Īsā, Tuḍiyā, and Daḍharahā. Just as it is for Dharaṇa, so it is for the remaining Bhavanavāsin deities. For Kāla, the lord of the Piśācas and king of the Piśācas, three assemblies are proclaimed: namely, Īsā, Tuḍiyā, and Daḍharahā; likewise for his Sāmāṇikas and chief queens, and so on up to Gīyaratigīyajasas. For Candra, the lord of the Jyotiṣkas and king of the Jyotiṣkas, three assemblies are proclaimed: namely, Tumbā, Tuḍiyā, and Pavvā; likewise for his Sāmāṇikas and chief queens, and so it is for Sūrya as well.

Sakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, has three assemblies proclaimed, namely: Samitā, Caṇḍā, and Jātā; thus as it is for Camara, up to the chief queens, so it is for the world-protectors up to Accuta.

Three watches have been declared, namely: the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. During these three watches, one may obtain the hearing of the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins, namely: during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch. Likewise, up until the arising of kevala-knowledge, [it may occur] during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch.

Three ages are taught, namely: the first age, the middle age, and the last age. Through these three ages, one may obtain the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins for the sake of hearing it, namely: the first age, the middle age, and the last age. This same method is to be understood [as applying] up to omniscience (*kevalajñāna*). Three types of awakening (*bodhi*) are taught, namely: awakening through knowledge (*jñānabodhi*), awakening through vision (*darśanabodhi*), and awakening through conduct (*cāritrabodhi*). Three types of awakened ones (*buddha*) are taught, namely: those awakened through knowledge, those awakened through vision, and those awakened through conduct. The same applies to delusion (*moha*); likewise, there are those who are deluded (*mūḍha*).

Renunciation is declared to be threefold: namely, that which is bound to this world, that which is bound to the next world, and that which is bound to both. Renunciation is declared to be threefold: namely, that which is bound in front, that which is bound behind, and that which is bound on both sides. Renunciation is declared to be threefold: namely, that which causes one to tremble, that which causes one to be pushed forward, and that which causes one to be awakened. Renunciation is declared to be threefold: namely, renunciation through instruction, renunciation through proclamation, and renunciation through an invitation.

Three types of *nirgranthas* are described as not possessed by dejection (*no-sanna-upayukta*), namely: the *pulāka*, the *nirgrantha*, and the *snātaka*. Three types of *nirgranthas* are described as possessed by both dejection and non-dejection (*sanna-no-sanna-upayukta*), namely: the *bakuśa*, the *prati-sevanā-kuśīla*, and the *kaṣāya-kuśīla*. Three stages of the trainee (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*) are described, namely: the highest (*utkṛṣṭā*), the middle (*madhyamā*), and the lowest (*jaghanyā*). The highest lasts six months, the middle four months, and the lowest seven nights and days.

Three grounds for being a senior (thera) are proclaimed, namely: the senior by birth, the senior by learning, and the senior by seniority of ordination. A monk-nirgrantha who is sixty years of age is a senior by birth; a monk-nirgrantha who is a master of the *Sthāna* and *Samavāya* is a senior by learning; a monk-nirgrantha with twenty years of seniority in the order is a senior by seniority of ordination.

Three types of persons are taught, namely: one who is happy, one who is unhappy, and one who is neither happy nor unhappy. Three types of persons are taught, namely: some person going along is happy, some person going along is unhappy, and some person going along is neither happy nor unhappy. Three types of persons are taught, namely: some person while sleeping is happy, some person while sleeping is unhappy, and some person while sleeping is neither happy nor unhappy. Three types of persons are taught, namely: some person thinking "I shall go" is happy, some person thinking "I shall go" is unhappy, and some person thinking "I shall go" is neither happy nor unhappy.
Three types of persons are taught, namely: one who does not go away becomes joyful; one who does not go away becomes dejected; and one who does not go away becomes neither joyful nor dejected.

Three types of persons are taught, namely: one who, upon being born, becomes joyful; one who, upon being born, becomes sorrowful; and one who, upon being born, becomes neither joyful nor sorrowful. Three types of persons are taught, namely: one who, thinking "I shall not be born," becomes joyful; one who, thinking "I shall not be born," becomes sorrowful; and one who, thinking "I shall not be born," becomes neither joyful nor sorrowful.

Likewise: one who, thinking "I am coming," becomes joyful—[the other two] likewise; one who, thinking "I am going," becomes joyful—[the other two] likewise; one who, thinking "I will come," becomes joyful—[the other two] likewise. In this manner, by this same formula.
One who goes and one who does not go, as well as one who comes and likewise one who has not come;
one who stands and one who does not stand, one who sits and likewise one who does not sit.
(Ṭhāṇa 169) One who kills and one who does not kill, as well as one who cuts and likewise one who does not cut.
Having been and not having been; having spoken and not having spoken. (Ṭhāṇa 170) Having given and not having given; likewise, having eaten and not having eaten;
having obtained and not having obtained; having drunk and not having drunk. (Ṭhāṇa 171)
Having tasted what is well-tasted and having tasted what is not well-tasted, having fought and likewise not having fought,
having exerted oneself and not having exerted oneself, having conquered and likewise not having conquered.
(Ṭhāṇaṃga 172) Sounds, forms, smells, tastes, and likewise touches and places.

The unvirtuous are censured, whereas the virtuous are praised. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 173) In this manner, three discourses each are to be recited for every sense-object: having heard a sound, some become joyful—3; likewise, "I am hearing"—3; "I shall hear"—3. Likewise, not having heard [a sound], some become joyful—3; "I am not hearing"—3; "I shall not hear"—3. In the same way, this applies to forms, odors, tastes, and tangibles. For each of these, six discourses are to be recited, making a total of 127 discourses.

There are three states that are censured for one who is ill-behaved, lacking in vows, devoid of virtues, lacking self-restraint, and who does not observe renunciation and fasting; namely: he is censured in this world, his rebirth is censured, and his future state is censured. Conversely, there are three states that are praised for one who is well-behaved, possessed of vows, endowed with virtues, possessing self-restraint, and who observes renunciation and fasting; namely: he is praised in this world, his rebirth is praised, and his future state is praised.

Living beings involved in the cycle of existence are declared to be of three kinds, namely: females, males, and neuters. All living beings are declared to be of three kinds, namely: those with right view, those with wrong view, and those with mixed view. Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be of three kinds, namely: developed (paryāpta), undeveloped (aparyāpta), and neither-developed-nor-undeveloped. Likewise: those with right view, the developed, the limited, the subtle, the conscious, and the perfected (bhavya).

The structure of the world is declared to be threefold, namely: the wind is established in space; the ocean is established in the wind; and the earth is established in the ocean. Three directions are declared, namely: upward, downward, and horizontal. Through these three directions—the upward, the downward, and the horizontal—the movement (*gati*) of living beings proceeds. Through these three directions—the upward, the downward, and the horizontal—the following are declared for living beings: arrival (*āgati*), turning back (*vakkanti*), feeding (*āhāra*), growth (*vuḍḍhi*), decay (*nivuḍḍhi*), the transition of states of existence (*gatipariyāya*), the total mobilization of energy (*samugghāta*), conjunction with time (*kālasañjoga*), the acquisition of right vision (*daṃsaṇābhigama*), and the acquisition of the state of a living being (*jīvābhigama*). That is to say: through the upward, the downward, and the horizontal directions. Likewise, the acquisition of non-living matter (*ajīvābhigama*) by living beings is declared through the upward, the downward, and the horizontal directions. Thus it is for five-sensed animals of the animal realm, and thus also for human beings.

Three types of mobile beings (*trasa*) are taught, namely: fire-bodied beings (*teukāiya*), air-bodied beings (*vāukāiya*), and gross mobile living beings (*urālā-tasa-pāṇā*). Three types of immobile beings (*thāvara*) are taught, namely: earth-bodied beings (*puḍhavikāiya*), water-bodied beings (*āukāiya*), and plant-bodied beings (*vaṇassaïkāiya*). Three things are taught as indivisible (*acchejja*), namely: time (*samae*), space-points (*padese*), and atoms (*paramāṇu*). Likewise, they are taught as inseparable (*abhejja*), uncuttable (*aḍajjha*), ungivable (*agijjha*), non-possessable (*aṇaḍḍha*), having no middle (*amajjha*), and partless (*apaesa*). Three things are taught as impartible (*avibhāima*), namely: time, space-points, and atoms.

The venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, addressing the ascetics and Nirgranthas such as Gautama, spoke thus: "What is the fear of living beings? "Venerable sir," replied the ascetics and Nirgranthas such as Gautama, approaching the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, saluting him, and paying him homage, they said: "Indeed, O Lord, we neither know nor see this matter. If it does not trouble the Lord to explain this matter, we wish to learn this matter from the presence of the Lord. Then the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, addressing the ascetics and Nirgranthas such as Gautama, spoke thus: "Living beings have suffering as their fear, O venerable ones! "Venerable sir, by whom was that suffering created? "It was created by the soul, through negligence. "Venerable sir, how is that suffering destroyed? "Through vigilance."

“Venerable sir, the followers of other sects (annautthiyā) declare, speak, explain, and demonstrate thus: ‘How is action performed for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas? In that regard, they do not ask about that which is done and is being performed; they do not ask about that which is done and is not being performed; they do not ask about that which is not done and is not being performed; and they do not ask about that which is not done but is being performed. Would it be right to say this? That suffering is uncaused, that suffering is untouched, that suffering is neither done nor caused, and that living beings, creatures, souls, and entities experience suffering without having done anything and without having caused anything—that those who speak thus are wrong. I, however, declare, speak, explain, and demonstrate thus: Suffering is caused, suffering is touched, suffering is both done and caused; it should be said that living beings, creatures, souls, and entities experience suffering after having done and having caused it.”

For three reasons, a deceitful person, having committed a deception, would not confess it, would not repent, would not blame himself, would not censure it, would not feel remorse, would not purify himself, would not resolve to refrain from it in the future, and would not undertake the appropriate penance and austerity; namely: "I have done it," "I am doing it," or "I shall do it. For three reasons, a deceitful person, having committed a deception, would not confess it, would not repent, and so on, up to would not undertake [the penance]; namely: "There might be ill-repute for me," "There might be dispraise for me," or "There might be a lack of discipline for me."

There are three reasons why a deceitful person, having committed an act of deceit, would neither confess it nor—up to—renounce it: namely, "My reputation will diminish," "My fame will diminish," or "My honor and respect will diminish. There are three reasons why a deceitful person, having committed an act of deceit, would confess it, repent for it, and—up to—renounce it: namely, "In this world, the deceitful person is censured; his rebirth is censured; and his future destiny is censured."

There are three reasons why a deceitful person, having committed a deception, should confess it and so forth until he undertakes the vow: namely, that for one free from deceit, this world is praised, rebirth is praised, and the future state is praised.

There are three reasons why a deceitful person, having committed a deception, should confess it and so forth until he undertakes the vow: namely, for the sake of knowledge, for the sake of vision, and for the sake of conduct.
Three types of persons are taught: namely, the bearer of the scriptures, the bearer of the meaning, and the bearer of both.

It is permissible for both Niggaṇṭhas and Niggaṇṭhīs to wear or use three kinds of garments, namely: those made of *jaṅgī* (wool), *bhaṅgī* (flax), or *khomiya* (linen). It is permissible for both Niggaṇṭhas and Niggaṇṭhīs to wear or use three kinds of foot-rests, namely: a foot-rest of wicker, a foot-rest of wood, or a foot-rest of clay.
One may wear a garment for three reasons, namely: out of modesty, out of disgust [for impurity], or because of the hardships [of the weather].

Three ways of protecting oneself are taught, namely: by means of the Dharma, by means of a reminder, and having given a reminder, one should either remain silent or, having risen, go to a secluded place by oneself. For a Nirgrantha who is ill, it is permissible to accept three kinds of water for drinking: namely, the best, the middling, and the lowest.

In three circumstances, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha, while making a fellow-monk share in his food or not share in it, does not transgress: namely, having seen it himself; or on the basis of a trustworthy person’s report; or when he turns toward what is true and false, but does not turn toward a fourth [unverified] matter.

Three kinds of authorization (*anuññā*) are taught: namely, for the office of an Ācārya, for the office of an Upādhyāya, and for the office of a Gaṇin. Three kinds of agreement (*samaññā*) are taught: namely, for the office of an Ācārya, for the office of an Upādhyāya, and for the office of a Gaṇin. Likewise for formal admission (*upasampadā*), and likewise for renunciation (*vijahaṇā*).

Speech is declared to be threefold, namely: speech directed toward that [object], speech directed toward something else, and non-speech. Non-speech is declared to be threefold, namely: non-speech directed toward that [object], non-speech directed toward something else, and absolute non-speech. Mind is declared to be threefold, namely: mind directed toward that [object], mind directed toward something else, and non-mind. Non-mind is declared to be threefold, namely: non-mind directed toward that [object], non-mind directed toward something else, and absolute non-mind.

There are three reasons why there might be little rain: namely, in that region or district, many water-born living beings and matter do not emerge from, depart from, decay, or be reborn as water; the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and bhūtas have not properly propitiated [the deities]; and the water-matter that has arisen and transformed there, desiring to rain, is diverted to another region, or the wind disperses the water-matter that has arisen and transformed as a cloudless mist—by these three reasons there might be little rain.

There are three conditions by which there may be heavy rain, namely: (1) in that region or district, many water-born beings and matter emerge as water, depart, decay, and are reborn; (2) gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and bhūtas become properly propitiated and draw in from elsewhere water-matter that has arisen, is transformed, and is about to rain, toward that region; and (3) when such water-matter has arisen, is transformed, and is about to rain, it is not dispersed by the wind. By these three conditions, there may be heavy rain.

By three conditions, a god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods might wish to come quickly to the world of men, yet he is not able to come quickly. They are as follows: the god, having recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods, is infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and immersed in divine sensual pleasures; he does not take up human sensual pleasures, does not recognize them, does not form an attachment to them, does not create a causal basis for them, and does not form a fixed resolve for them. Because that god, having recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods, is infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and immersed in divine sensual pleasures, his affection for the human realm is severed and transferred to the divine realm.

A god who has recently been reborn in the divine worlds, being infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and deeply immersed in celestial sensual pleasures, thinks to himself: "Now I shall go; in a moment I shall go. Yet at that time, human beings have become short-lived and have met their end through the law of time. For these three reasons, a god who has recently been reborn in the divine worlds may wish to come quickly to the world of humans, but he is simply not able to come quickly.

By three conditions, a god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods might desire to come quickly to the world of men, and he is indeed able to come quickly: The god, having recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods, being uninfatuated with, not greedy for, not attached to, and not obsessed by divine sensual pleasures, thinks to himself: "In my human existence, there were teachers, or preceptors, or leaders, or elders, or heads of a group, or holders of a group, or directors of a group, through whose power I obtained, attained, and acquired this kind of divine splendor of a god, divine radiance, and divine majesty. Therefore, I shall go to those Blessed Ones; I shall salute them, revere them, honor them, respect them, and attend upon them as auspicious, blessed, divine, and venerable objects."

A god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds, being uninfatuated with, unattached to, unaddicted to, and not obsessed by divine sensual pleasures, thinks to himself: "In that human existence, there was one who was a man of knowledge or an ascetic, a performer of exceedingly difficult penances; I shall go to those Blessed Ones to pay homage, to bow down, and to attend upon them. Furthermore, a god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds, being uninfatuated with, unattached to, unaddicted to, and not obsessed by divine sensual pleasures, thinks to himself: "In my human existence, there were my mother, or [other relatives] up to my daughter-in-law; I shall go and appear before them so that they may see me and this kind of divine splendor, divine radiance, and divine majesty—attained, reached, and fully acquired by me. For these three reasons, a god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds might wish to come quickly to the human world, and he is indeed able to come quickly.
There are three things that a god would long for, namely: human existence, birth in a noble land, and rebirth in a good family.

A deity may lament on three grounds, as follows: "Alas! While I possessed strength, while I possessed vigor, while I possessed personal power and exertion, during times of peace and plenty, while teachers and preceptors were available, and while my body was healthy, I did not acquire much sacred learning. Alas! Being bound to this world, turning away from the next world, and craving sensual objects, I did not maintain the long course of the ascetic life. Alas! Valuing prestige, sensory flavors, and pleasure, and being greedy for the enjoyment of sense-objects, I did not touch upon the pure conduct. On these three grounds, a deity may lament.

By three conditions a god knows, "I shall depart [from this state]," namely: having seen his celestial palaces and ornaments become lusterless; having seen the wish-fulfilling tree withering; and having perceived his own splendor diminishing. By these three conditions, a god knows, "I shall depart."

By three circumstances a god may experience agitation (*udvega*). They are as follows: "Alas! I must eventually abandon these divine celestial powers, divine celestial splendors, and divine celestial majesties that I have obtained, attained, and fully acquired"; "Alas! I must first of all take as food the mother’s blood and the father’s semen, joined together"; "Alas! I must dwell in the terrifying abode of the womb, which is filthy, like mud and mire, and loathsome. By these three circumstances a god may experience agitation.

The celestial palaces (*vimāṇa*) are described as being of three shapes, namely: circular, triangular, and square. Among them, those celestial palaces which are circular are shaped like the pericarp of a lotus; they are surrounded on all sides by walls, have a single gate, and are so described. Those celestial palaces which are triangular are shaped like a forked road (*siṅghāḍaga*); they are surrounded by walls on two sides and surrounded by a railing (*vēiyā*) on one side, and they are described as having three gates. Those celestial palaces which are square are shaped like a courtyard (*akkhāḍaga*); they are surrounded on all sides by railings and are described as having four gates.

Celestial abodes (*vimāṇa*) are declared to be established in three ways: namely, established upon the dense ocean, established upon the dense wind, and established upon space. Celestial abodes are declared to be of three kinds: namely, permanent, created by supernatural power (*veuvvita*), and those acquired through merit (*pārijāṇiya*). Hell-beings (*nēraïya*) are declared to be of three kinds: namely, those with right view, those with wrong view, and those with right-and-wrong view. The same applies to all beings up to the gods of the celestial realms (*vēmāṇiya*), with the exception of those with incomplete sensory faculties (*vigalindiya*).

Three types of miserable destinies (duggati) are taught, namely: the miserable destiny of hell-beings (nēraïya), the miserable destiny of animal-birth (tirikkhajōṇiya), and the miserable destiny of humans (maṇuya). Three types of happy destinies (sugati) are taught, namely: the happy destiny of the perfected ones (siddha), the happy destiny of gods (dēva), and the happy destiny of humans (maṇussa).

Three types of those in a miserable state (duggata) are taught, namely: those in a miserable state as hell-beings, those in a miserable state as animals, and those in a miserable state as humans. Three types of those in a happy state (sugata) are taught, namely: those in a happy state as perfected ones, those in a happy state as gods, and those in a happy state as humans.

For a monk who observes the fourth-meal fast (caütthabhattiya), it is permissible to accept three kinds of drinks, namely: water from boiled rice, water from soaked rice, and rice-wash water. For a monk who observes the sixth-meal fast (chaṭṭhabhattiya), it is permissible to accept three kinds of drinks, namely: sesame-water, husk-water, and barley-water. For a monk who observes the eighth-meal fast (aṭṭhamabhattiya), it is permissible to accept three kinds of drinks, namely: fermented gruel, sour gruel, and pure water.

There are three kinds of *uvahaḍa* (food brought for a monk) taught: namely, *phali-uvahaḍa* (food brought from a vessel), *suddha-uvahaḍa* (pure food brought), and *saṃsaṭṭha-uvahaḍa* (food brought by one who has handled it). There are three kinds of *oggahita* (appropriated property) taught: namely, that which one appropriates, that which one causes to be brought, and that which one places into one's own mouth. Three kinds of *omoyariyā* (reduction) are taught: namely, reduction of requisites (*uvagaraṇa*), reduction of food and drink (*bhattapāṇa*), and reduction of mental states (*bhāva*). Reduction of requisites is taught as being threefold: namely, using only one garment, using only one bowl, and using only those few personal belongings that are permitted. There are three conditions which lead to the non-benefit, the impurity, the lack of endurance, the lack of excellence, and the lack of future progress for both monks and nuns: namely, scratching, itching, and harmful reflection (*avajjhāṇa*). There are three conditions which lead to the benefit, the happiness, the endurance, the excellence, and the future progress for both monks and nuns: namely, not scratching, not itching, and not having harmful reflections.

Three thorns are taught, namely: the thorn of deceit (*māyā-salla*), the thorn of worldly attachment (*niyāṇa-salla*), and the thorn of false view (*micchā-daṃsaṇa-salla*). By three conditions a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha becomes one whose fiery energy (*teullesa*) is contracted and vast; namely: through the practice of self-heating (*āyāvaṇatā*), through patience and forbearance (*khantikhamā*), and through the austerity-act of fasting (*apāṇaga tava-kamma*). For a monk who has undertaken the Three-Monthly (*timāsiya*) mendicant’s vow (*bhikkhu-paḍima*), it is permissible to accept three portions of food and three portions of drink. For a monk who does not properly maintain the One-Night (*ēgarātiya*) mendicant’s vow, these three conditions lead to his disadvantage, impurity, lack of forbearance, lack of benefit, and lack of future progress; namely: he may suffer madness, he may incur a long-term illness and affliction, or he may fall away from the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalins. For a monk who properly maintains the One-Night mendicant’s vow, three conditions lead to his advantage, purity, forbearance, benefit, and future progress; namely: either clairvoyant knowledge (*ōhināṇa*) arises in him, or mind-reading knowledge (*maṇapajjavanāṇa*) arises in him, or omniscient knowledge (*kēvalanāṇa*) arises in him.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, three karma-bhūmis (lands of action) are taught, namely: Bharata, Airāvata, and Mahāvideha. Likewise on the island of Ghātakasaṇḍa in its eastern half, and so on, up to the western half of the island of Puṣkaravaradvīpa. Three kinds of vision (darśana) are taught, namely: right vision (samyag-darśana), wrong vision (mithyā-darśana), and mixed vision (samyag-mithyā-darśana). Three kinds of inclination (ruci) are taught, namely: right inclination (samyak-ruci), wrong inclination (mithyā-ruci), and mixed inclination (samyag-mithyā-ruci). Three kinds of activity (prayoga) are taught, namely: right activity (samyak-prayoga), wrong activity (mithyā-prayoga), and mixed activity (samyag-mithyā-prayoga).

Three kinds of undertakings (*vavasāya*) are taught, namely: righteous undertaking (*dhammiya*), unrighteous undertaking (*adhammiya*), and both righteous and unrighteous undertaking (*dhammiyādhammiya*). Alternatively, three kinds of undertakings are taught, namely: immediate (*paccakkha*), subsequent (*paccaïya*), and following (*āṇugāmiya*). Alternatively, three kinds of undertakings are taught, namely: pertaining to this world (*ihalōiya*), pertaining to the other world (*paralōiya*), and pertaining to both this world and the other world (*ihalōiyaparalōiya*). Undertaking pertaining to this world is taught as being threefold, namely: worldly (*lōiya*), scriptural (*vēiya*), and conventional (*sāmaïya*). Worldly undertaking is taught as being threefold, namely: wealth (*attha*), righteousness (*dhamma*), and pleasure (*kāma*). Scriptural undertaking is taught as being threefold, namely: the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda. Conventional undertaking is taught as being threefold, namely: knowledge (*nāṇa*), vision (*daṃsaṇa*), and conduct (*caritta*). Three sources of wealth (*atthajōṇī*) are taught, namely: conciliation (*sāma*), force (*daṇḍa*), and sowing dissension (*bhēda*).

Pudgalas (matter) are taught to be of three kinds, namely: those transformed by modification (*prayoga-pariṇata*), those transformed by mixture (*miśra-pariṇata*), and those transformed by their own nature (*visrasā-pariṇata*). Hells are taught to have three foundations, namely: founded on earth, founded on space, and founded on the self (*ātman*). According to the *Nega*, *Saṅgraha*, and *Vyavahāra* [standpoints], they are founded on earth; according to the *Rjusūtra*, they are founded on space; and according to the three verbal standpoints (*śabda-naya*), they are founded on the self.

Threefold is wrongness (micchatta) taught; namely: non-action (akiriya), lack of discipline (aviṇaya), and ignorance (annāṇa). Non-action is taught as threefold; namely: activity of impulse (paoga-kiriya), activity of accumulation (samudāṇa-kiriya), and activity of ignorance (annāṇa-kiriya). Activity of impulse is taught as threefold; namely: activity of mental impulse (maṇa-paoga-kiriya), activity of vocal impulse (vai-paoga-kiriya), and activity of bodily impulse (kāya-paoga-kiriya). Activity of accumulation is taught as threefold; namely: immediate activity of accumulation (aṇantara-samudāṇa-kiriya), successive activity of accumulation (parampara-samudāṇa-kiriya), and activity of accumulation of both (tadubhaya-samudāṇa-kiriya). Activity of ignorance is taught as threefold; namely: activity of sensory ignorance (mati-annāṇa-kiriya), activity of scriptural ignorance (suta-annāṇa-kiriya), and activity of deluded insight-ignorance (vibhaṅga-annāṇa-kiriya). Lack of discipline is taught as threefold; namely: partial transgression (dēsaccāī), lack of support (nirālambaṇatā), and various forms of attachment and aversion (nānā-peja-dōsa). Ignorance is taught as threefold; namely: partial ignorance (dēsa-annāṇa), total ignorance (savva-annāṇa), and ignorance regarding the nature of existence (bhāva-annāṇa).

The Dharma is declared to be threefold, namely: the Dharma of scripture (*śrutadharma*), the Dharma of conduct (*cāritradharma*), and the Dharma of the substance-constituents (*astikāyadharma*). Threefold service (*upakrama*) is declared, namely: righteous service, unrighteous service, and both righteous and unrighteous service. Alternatively, threefold service is declared, namely: service for oneself, service for others, and service for both. In the same way, there are three discourses each regarding assistance (*vaiyāvṛttya*), favor (*anugraha*), instruction (*anuśāsti*), and reproach (*upālambha*), just as in the case of service.

Three kinds of discourse are taught, namely: discourse on wealth (*atthakahā*), discourse on Dharma (*dhammakahā*), and discourse on pleasure (*kāmakahā*). Three kinds of adjudication are taught, namely: adjudication regarding wealth (*atthaviṇicchaya*), adjudication regarding Dharma (*dhammaviṇicchaya*), and adjudication regarding pleasure (*kāmaviṇicchaya*). "Venerable sir, for one who pays homage to such a monk or brahmin, what is the fruit of that homage? "The fruit is hearing [the teaching]. "Venerable sir, what is the fruit of that hearing? "The fruit is knowledge (*nāṇa*). "Venerable sir, what is the fruit of that knowledge? "The fruit is discernment (*vinnāṇa*). In this same manner, by this formula, the following verse is to be understood: [Verse: "Hearing has knowledge as its fruit; knowledge has discernment as its fruit; Discernment has the abandonment of defilements as its fruit; from the abandonment of defilements comes liberation."

"In hearing, knowledge, discernment, renunciation, self-restraint, freedom from craving, austerity, purification, non-action, and nirvana. (Thāṇaṃ 204) "Venerable sir, what is the fruit of that non-action? "Its fruit is nirvana. "Venerable sir, what is the fruit of that nirvana? "O venerable ascetic, it is taught that its fruit is the ultimate goal of reaching the state of perfection (siddhi)."

For an ascetic who has undertaken the vow (paḍimā), it is permissible to inspect three types of lodgings (*uvassaya*), namely: a house for arriving travelers, a house for those seeking shelter, or a house at the foot of a tree; in this manner he should seek permission, and in this manner he should enter. For an ascetic who has undertaken the vow, it is permissible to inspect three types of bedding (*santhāraga*), namely: a stone slab on the ground, a wooden slab, or simply as it is spread out; in this manner he should seek permission, and in this manner he should enter.

Threefold time is taught, namely: past, present, and future. Threefold temporal division is taught, namely: past, present, and future. Likewise, the *āvalikā*, breath (*ānāpāṇu*), *thōva*, *lava*, *muhūrta*, day and night, up to a hundred thousand years, a *pūrvāṅga*, a *pūrva*, up to an *avasarpiṇī*—threefold is the cycle of matter (*pudgalaparivarta*) taught, namely: past, present, and future.

Speech is declared to be threefold, namely: singular speech, dual speech, and plural speech; or alternatively, speech is declared to be threefold, namely: feminine speech, masculine speech, and neuter speech; or alternatively, speech is declared to be threefold, namely: past speech, present speech, and future speech.

Threefold exposition is taught, namely: exposition of knowledge, exposition of vision, and exposition of conduct. Threefold rightness is taught, namely: rightness of knowledge, rightness of vision, and rightness of conduct. Threefold obstruction is taught, namely: obstruction regarding procurement, obstruction regarding acquisition, and obstruction regarding search. Threefold purification is taught, namely: purification regarding procurement, purification regarding acquisition, and purification regarding search.

Threefold is the attainment declared; namely: attainment of knowledge, attainment of vision, and attainment of conduct. Attainment of knowledge is declared to be threefold; namely: superior, middling, and inferior. Likewise for the attainment of vision and likewise for the attainment of conduct. Threefold is defilement declared; namely: defilement of knowledge, defilement of vision, and defilement of conduct. Likewise for non-defilement, likewise for transgression (*atikamma*), likewise for violation (*vaikkama*), likewise for error (*aiyāra*), and likewise for improper conduct (*aṇāyāra*).

One should confess, repent, reproach oneself, and censure oneself—up to the point of undertaking the remedy—for the transgression of three things, namely: the transgression of knowledge, the transgression of vision, and the transgression of conduct; likewise for the violations (vaikkama), the excesses (aticāra), and the improprieties (anāyāra).

Three kinds of atonement (pāyacchitta) are prescribed, namely: that which requires confession (āloyaṇāriha), that which requires repentance (paḍikkamaṇāriha), and that which requires both (tadubhayāriha).

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, three non-karmabhūmis are declared, namely: Haimavata, Harivarṣa, and Devakuru. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, three non-karmabhūmis are declared, namely: Uttarakuru, Ramyaka-varṣa, and Hiraṇyavata.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, three regions are declared; namely: Bharata, Haimavata, and Harivarṣa. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, three regions are declared; namely: Ramyaka-varṣa, Hairaṇyavata, and Airāvata.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, three mountain ranges that serve as boundaries between regions (*vāsaharapavvaya*) are declared; namely: Cullahimavanta, Mahāhimavanta, and Nisadha. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, three mountain ranges that serve as boundaries between regions are declared; namely: Nīlavanta, Ruppī, and Siharī. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, three great lakes are declared; namely: Paümadaha (Lotus Lake), Mahāpaümadaha (Great Lotus Lake), and Tigiñchadaha (Tigiñcha Lake). Therein dwell three deities of great power, possessing a lifespan of one *palyopama*; namely: Śrī, Hrī, and Dhṛti. Likewise, to the north [there are three lakes]: Kesari-daha, Mahāpoṇḍarīya-daha, and Poṇḍarīya-daha; and there dwell the deities Kīrti, Buddhi, and Lakṣmī.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, from the Culla-Himavanta range of boundary mountains, three great rivers flow forth from the Padma lakes, namely: the Gaṅgā, the Sindhu, and the Rohitaṃsā. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, from the Śikhari range of boundary mountains, three great rivers flow forth from the Puṇḍarīka lakes, namely: the Suvarṇakūlā, the Rattā, and the Rattavatī.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, three intermediate rivers are described, namely: Gāhāvatī, Dahavatī, and Paṅkavatī. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītā, three intermediate rivers are described, namely: Tattajalā, Mattajalā, and Umattajalā. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītōdā, three intermediate rivers are described, namely: Khīrōdā, Sīhasōtā, and Antōvāhiṇī. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītōdā, three intermediate rivers are described, namely: Ummimāliṇī, Phēṇamāliṇī, and Gambhīramāliṇī.

In this same manner, on the eastern half of the continent of Ghātyaṣaṇḍa, one should describe everything in full, beginning from the non-karmabhūmis up to the intermediate rivers; likewise, it should be described in full for the western half of the Pukkhara-vara-dvīpa island.

By three causes the earth may shake in a particular region (*deśa*); namely: (1) if great matter-particles (*pudgala*) descend into this *Ratnaprabhā* earth, then those descending great matter-particles cause a part of the earth to shake; (2) or if a great serpent (*mahoraga*), possessing great power, up to great majesty, performs the act of emerging and submerging beneath this *Ratnaprabhā* earth, he causes a part of the earth to shake; (3) or when a battle between *Nāgas* and *Suvargas* is taking place, a part of the earth in that region shakes. By these three causes, the earth may shake in a particular region.

The entire earth may shake for three reasons, namely: (1) when the dense wind beneath this Jewel-Lustre Earth (Rayaṇappabhā) is agitated; then that dense wind, being agitated, would stir the dense water; then that dense water, being stirred, would cause the entire earth to shake. (2) Or, a god of great power, up to one of great influence, displaying his supernatural power, splendor, fame, strength, heroism, manly effort, and exertion, might cause the entire earth to shake. (3) Or, while a battle between gods and asuras is taking place, the entire earth may shake. For these three reasons, the entire earth may shake.

Three types of *devakibbisiya* (divine penitents) are taught, namely: those with a lifespan of three *palyopamas*, those with a lifespan of three *sāgaropamas*, and those with a lifespan of thirteen *sāgaropamas*.

"Venerable Sir, where do the *devakibbisiya*s with a lifespan of three *palyopamas* reside? "Above the Jyotiṣkas and below the *Saudharma* and *Īśāna* heavens; it is here that the *devakibbisiya*s with a lifespan of three *palyopamas* reside."

"Venerable sir, where do the celestial *kibbisikas* with a lifespan of three *sāgaropamas* reside? Above the *kalpas* of Sōhamma and Īsāṇa, and below the *kalpas* of Saṇaṅkumāra and Māhinda—there the celestial *kibbisikas* with a lifespan of three *sāgaropamas* reside.

Venerable sir, where do the celestial *kibbisikas* with a lifespan of thirteen *sāgaropamas* reside? Above the *kalpa* of Bambhalōga and below the *kalpa* of Lantaga—there the celestial *kibbisikas* with a lifespan of thirteen *sāgaropamas* reside."

The lifespan of the gods in the outer assembly of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of gods, is declared to be three *palyopamas*. The lifespan of the goddesses in the inner assembly of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of gods, is declared to be three *palyopamas*. The lifespan of the goddesses in the outer assembly of Īsāna, the lord of gods and king of gods, is declared to be three *palyopamas*.

Three kinds of penance (*pāyacchitta*) are prescribed, namely: penance for knowledge (*nāṇapāyacchitta*), penance for vision (*daṃsaṇapāyacchitta*), and penance for conduct (*carittapāyacchitta*). Three [offenses] involving non-expiation (*aṇugghātima*) are prescribed, namely: performing manual labor (*hatthakamma*), engaging in sexual intercourse (*mēhuṇa*), and eating at night (*rāībhōyaṇa*). Three [offenses] involving *pārañcita* (requiring exclusion) are prescribed, namely: *pārañcita* for one who is wicked (*duṭṭha*), *pārañcita* for one who is negligent (*pamatta*), and *pārañcita* for those acting against one another. Three [offenses] involving suspension (*aṇavaṭṭhapta*) are prescribed, namely: committing theft against one's own co-religionists (*sāhammiya*), committing theft against those of other religions (*aṇṇadhammiya*), and clapping one's hands in derision.

It is not appropriate for three types of persons to be ordained, namely: the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), the one who has lost his virility (*vātīka*), and the impotent (*kīva*). It is not appropriate for these three to have their heads shaved, to be instructed, to be initiated, to share in the community, or to live in association with the order; namely: the eunuch, the one who has lost his virility, and the impotent. Three types of persons are declared to be unfit for instruction: the undisciplined, the one obsessed with worldly attachments, and the one who has not mastered the fundamentals. Three types of persons are appropriate for instruction: the disciplined, the one free from obsession with attachments, and the one who has mastered the fundamentals.

Three types of ill-disposed beings are taught, namely: the wicked, the deluded, and the agitated. Three types of well-disposed beings are taught, namely: the non-wicked, the non-deluded, and the non-agitated.
Three circular mountains are taught, namely: Mānuṣottara, Kuṇḍalavara, and Rucakavara.

Three things of immense magnitude are taught, namely: Jambudvīpa among islands, Mount Mandara among mountains, and the Saṃbhūramaṇa ocean among oceans; likewise, the Brahma-loka heaven among the heavens.

The duration of the disciplinary code (kappaṭhitī) is declared to be threefold, namely: the duration of the code for general conduct (sāmāiyakappa), the duration of the code for re-establishment after a breach (chedovaṭṭhāvaṇiyakappa), and the duration of the code for those undergoing penance (ṇivvisamāṇakappa). Alternatively, the duration of the disciplinary code is declared to be threefold, namely: the duration of the code for those who have completed their penance (nivviṭṭhakappa), the duration of the code for the Jina-type ascetics (jiṇakappa), and the duration of the code for the elder-type ascetics (thērakappa).

For hell-beings, three types of bodies are taught: the transformation body (*vaikriyika*), the fiery body (*taijasa*), and the karmic body (*kārmaṇa*). For the asura-kumāras, three types of bodies are taught: the transformation body, the fiery body, and the karmic body. Thus it is for all gods. For earth-bodied beings, three types of bodies are taught: the physical body (*audārika*), the fiery body, and the karmic body. Thus it is for all up to the four-sensed beings, with the exception of the air-bodied beings.

With respect to the teacher (*guru*), three types of adversaries are taught, namely: the adversary of the preceptor (*ācārya*), the adversary of the instructor (*upādhyāya*), and the adversary of the elder (*sthavira*). With respect to the realm (*gati*), three types of adversaries are taught, namely: the adversary of this world, the adversary of the other world, and the adversary of both worlds. With respect to the community (*samūha*), three types of adversaries are taught, namely: the adversary of the family (*kula*), the adversary of the group (*gaṇa*), and the adversary of the Saṅgha. With respect to compassion (*anukampā*), three types of adversaries are taught, namely: the adversary of the ascetic (*tapasvin*), the adversary of the sick (*glāna*), and the adversary of the novice (*śaikṣa*). With respect to state (*bhāva*), three types of adversaries are taught, namely: the adversary of knowledge (*jñāna*), the adversary of vision (*darśana*), and the adversary of conduct (*cāritra*). With respect to the teaching (*śruta*), three types of adversaries are taught, namely: the adversary of the scripture (*sūtra*), the adversary of the meaning (*artha*), and the adversary of both.
Three paternal parts are taught, namely: bone, marrow, and hair of the head, beard, and body hair. Three maternal parts are taught, namely: flesh, blood, and brain.

By three conditions, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha becomes one of great shedding [of karma] and of great final liberation; that is to say: "When shall I study the sacred word, whether little or much? When shall I dwell having undertaken the vow of solitary wandering? When shall I, having practiced the refinement of the body through the final mortification at the time of death, having renounced food and drink, and having entered the state of total fasting, dwell without longing for life? Thus, by making it manifest through mind, speech, and body, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha becomes one of great shedding and of great final liberation.

By three conditions, a lay follower (*śramaṇopāsaka*) becomes one of great exhaustion of karma and reaches a great final goal. They are as follows: "When shall I renounce my possessions, whether small or great? When shall I, having become shaven-headed, go forth from the home to the homeless state? When shall I, having practiced the refinement of the final fast unto death, having renounced food and drink, having entered the state of fasting, dwell without longing for life? Thus, making it manifest through his mind, his speech, and his body, the lay follower becomes one of great exhaustion of karma and reaches a great final goal.

Three kinds of obstruction of matter (*poggalapaḍighāta*) are taught, namely: a single atom (*paramāṇupoggala*) may be obstructed upon encountering another atom; it may be obstructed due to dryness (*lukkhattāē*); or it may be obstructed at the end of the world (*lōganta*). Three kinds of eyes (*cakkhu*) are taught, namely: the single eye, the two eyes, and the three eyes. A human being with physical vision (*chaümattha*) has one eye; a deity has two eyes; and a monk (*samaṇa*) or brahmin (*māhaṇa*) who possesses the attained knowledge and vision (*uppaṇṇanāṇadaṃsaṇadhara*) should be called "one who has three eyes."

Threefold is the range of perception declared; namely: upward, downward, and across. When such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa possesses extraordinary knowledge and vision arising, it first perceives upward, then across, and after that, downward.
