O venerable śramaṇa, the lower world is declared to be difficult to perceive.

Threefold prosperity is taught; namely: the prosperity of gods (*deviḍḍhi*), the prosperity of kings (*rāiḍḍhi*), and the prosperity of the community (*gaṇiḍḍhi*). The prosperity of gods is taught as threefold: the prosperity of celestial mansions (*vimāṇiḍḍhi*), the prosperity of transformation (*viguvvaṇiḍḍhi*), and the prosperity of attendants (*pariyāraṇiḍḍhi*); or alternatively, the prosperity of gods is taught as threefold: animate (*sacittā*), inanimate (*acittā*), and mixed (*mīsitā*). The prosperity of kings is taught as threefold: the prosperity of a king’s entry (*atiyāṇiḍḍhi*), the prosperity of a king’s departure (*nijjāṇiḍḍhi*), and the prosperity of a king’s army, vehicles, treasury, and granaries (*bala-vāhaṇa-kōsa-koṭṭhāgāriḍḍhi*); or alternatively, the prosperity of kings is taught as threefold: animate, inanimate, and mixed.

The power of the Gaṇin (the leader of a group) is declared to be threefold; namely: the power of knowledge, the power of vision, and the power of conduct. Alternatively, the power of the Gaṇin is declared to be threefold; namely: conscious, unconscious, and mixed.
Three kinds of pride are declared; namely: pride in power, pride in taste, and pride in pleasure.
Three kinds of activity are declared; namely: righteous activity, unrighteous activity, and both righteous and unrighteous activity.

The Blessed One has proclaimed the Dhamma in three ways: namely, well-studied (*su-adhijjhata*), well-reflectively-meditated upon (*su-jjhāita*), and well-practiced (*su-tavassita*). When it is well-studied, then it is well-reflectively-meditated upon; when it is well-reflectively-meditated upon, then it is well-practiced. Thus, this Dhamma—well-studied, well-reflectively-meditated upon, and well-practiced—has been well-expounded by the Blessed One.
Three kinds of wavering (*vāvatti*) have been proclaimed: namely, ignorance (*ajāṇu*), lack of knowledge (*vitigicchā*), and likewise, attachment (*ajjhōvavajjaṇā*) and obsession (*pariyāvajjaṇā*).

Three kinds of limits are taught, namely: the limit of the world (*loka-anta*), the limit of the Vedas (*veda-anta*), and the limit of the systems (*samaya-anta*). Three types of Jinas are taught, namely: the Jina of clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhi-jñāna*), the Jina of mind-reading knowledge (*manaḥparyāya-jñāna*), and the Jina of omniscient knowledge (*kevala-jñāna*). Three types of Kevalins are taught, namely: the Kevalin of clairvoyant knowledge, the Kevalin of mind-reading knowledge, and the Kevalin of omniscient knowledge. Three types of Arhats are taught, namely: the Arhat of clairvoyant knowledge, the Arhat of mind-reading knowledge, and the Arhat of omniscient knowledge.

Three leśyās are declared to be foul-smelling, namely: black leśyā, blue leśyā, and grey leśyā. Three leśyās are declared to be sweet-smelling, namely: fiery leśyā, lotus leśyā, and white leśyā. Likewise, they are those leading to an evil destiny and those leading to a happy destiny; those that are defiled and those that are undefiled; those that are unpleasant and those that are pleasant; those that are impure and those that are pure; those that are censured and those that are praised; and those that are cold-dry and those that are hot-dry.

Three kinds of death are taught, namely: the death of the ignorant (*bālamaraṇa*), the death of the wise (*paṇḍiyamaraṇa*), and the death of the both-ignorant-and-wise (*bālapaṇḍiyamaraṇa*). The death of the ignorant is taught to be of three kinds, namely: one with steady passion (*ṭhitalessa*), one with defiled passion (*saṅkiliṭṭhalessa*), and one with passion arising from modifications (*pajjavajātalessa*). The death of the wise is taught to be of three kinds, namely: one with steady passion, one with undefiled passion (*asaṅkiliṭṭhalessa*), and one with passion arising from modifications. The death of the both-ignorant-and-wise is taught to be of three kinds, namely: one with steady passion, one with undefiled passion, and one with passion not arising from modifications (*apajjavajātalessa*).

There are three states that lead to the disadvantage, the impurity, the lack of forbearance, the lack of excellence, and the lack of future benefit for one who is undetermined. They are as follows: having become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home to the homeless life, he is suspicious, wavering, and filled with doubt regarding the Nigrantha doctrine; he has fallen into division and fallen into turbidity. He does not have faith in, does not trust in, and does not delight in the Nigrantha doctrine. Thus, various hardships (parīsaha) repeatedly assail him and overcome him; he does not overcome those hardships as they repeatedly assail him. Furthermore, having become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home to the homeless life, he is suspicious regarding the five great vows (mahāvratas), up to being filled with turbidity; he does not have faith in the five great vows, up to [the point where] various hardships repeatedly assail him and overcome him. Furthermore, having become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home to the homeless life, he is suspicious regarding the six classes of living beings (jīvanikāyas), up to [the point where] [hardships] overcome him.

There are three states that, when undertaken, lead to one's welfare and even to a favorable rebirth. They are as follows: having become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home life into homelessness, he becomes free from doubt and free from hesitation regarding the Nigaṇṭha doctrine; being thus free from turbidity, he believes in, trusts in, and finds delight in the Nigaṇṭha doctrine. Having repeatedly confronted the hardships, he overcomes them; the hardships do not overcome him, however many times he is confronted by them.

Having become shaven-headed and having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, if he—free from doubt and free from hesitation regarding the five great vows—repeatedly encounters and overcomes the hardships, then those hardships do not repeatedly encounter and overcome him. Having become shaven-headed and having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, if he—free from doubt regarding the six classes of living beings—repeatedly encounters and overcomes the hardships, then those hardships do not repeatedly encounter and overcome him.

Each individual earth [hell] is completely surrounded on all sides by three layers, namely: the layer of dense water (ghanodadhi-valaya), the layer of dense wind (ghanavāta-valaya), and the layer of subtle wind (tanuvāta-valaya).

Beings in the hells are born with a maximum body-formation (vigraha) lasting for three time-units (samaya); this applies to all beings up to the Vaimānikas, with the exception of the one-sensed beings.

For the Arhat whose delusion is exhausted, three types of karma are simultaneously destroyed: knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇīya), and obstructive (antarāya) karma.
The Abhijit constellation is declared to have three stars; likewise for Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, and Jyeṣṭhā.
From the Arhat Dharma, the Arhat Śānti appeared after three *sāgaropamas* less three-fourths of a *palyopama* had elapsed.

For the ascetic, the Blessed Mahāvīra, the stage of the end of the lineage lasted until the third generation of men. The Arhat Malli, together with three hundred men, shaved his head and went forth from the home to the homeless state; the same applies to Pārśva.

The ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, had three hundred *caturdaśapūrvins*—those who possessed the fourteen *pūrvas*, who were not yet Jinas but resembled Jinas, who had mastered the entire range of syllables and phonemes, and who spoke as truly as a Jina would. This was the highest possible attainment among those possessing the fourteen *pūrvas*. Furthermore, there were three Tīrthaṅkaras who were also Cakravartins, namely: Śānti, Kuṃthu, and Ara.

There are three tiers of Graiveyaka palaces described, namely: the lower tier of Graiveyaka palaces, the middle tier of Graiveyaka palaces, and the upper tier of Graiveyaka palaces. The lower tier of Graiveyaka palaces is described as being of three kinds, namely: the lowest-of-the-lower tier of Graiveyaka palaces, the middle-of-the-lower tier of Graiveyaka palaces, and the highest-of-the-lower tier of Graiveyaka palaces. The middle tier of Graiveyaka palaces is described as being of three kinds, namely: the lowest-of-the-middle tier of Graiveyaka palaces, the middle-of-the-middle tier of Graiveyaka palaces, and the highest-of-the-middle tier of Graiveyaka palaces. The upper tier of Graiveyaka palaces is described as being of three kinds, namely: the lowest-of-the-upper tier of Graiveyaka palaces, the middle-of-the-upper tier of Graiveyaka palaces, and the highest-of-the-upper tier of Graiveyaka palaces.

Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate matter (pudgala) produced from the three states as sinful karma; namely: produced from females, produced from males, and produced from neuters. Likewise for accumulation (ciṇa), gathering (uvaciṇa), bondage (bandha), activation (udīra), experience (vēda), and shedding (nijjarā).
Infinite aggregates (skandhas) consisting of three categories are taught; likewise, up to infinite particles of matter possessing the three qualities of roughness are taught.

Four ways of making an end [to suffering] are taught, as follows: First, there is the first way of making an end, which involves little karma remaining. He becomes shaven-headed and goes forth from the home life into homelessness; he is abundant in self-restraint, abundant in restraint, abundant in concentration, austere, striving for the further shore, possessed of ascetic practices, and a destroyer of suffering through penance. Yet, his penance is not of such a kind, nor is his painful sensation of such a kind, that such a person attains perfection, awakens, is liberated, and reaches final nirvana, making an end to all suffering, after a long course of practice—just like King Bharata, the universal monarch of the four continents. This is the first way of making an end.

Furthermore, there is a second way of making an end [to suffering], which occurs through the maturation of great karma. He, having become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home life into homelessness, is abundant in self-restraint and abundant in restraint; he is possessed of ascetic practices, a destroyer of suffering, and an ascetic. For him, such is his austerity and such is his experience of sensation; when his course of life has been brought to an end, that kind of person attains perfection and makes an end [of suffering], just as did the ascetic Gayasūmāla. This is the second way of making an end.

Furthermore, there is another way of making an end [to suffering], which occurs through the retribution of great karma. He, having become shaven-headed and gone forth from the home life into homelessness, proceeds as in the second case; however, he attains perfection through a long period of practice, up until he makes an end of all suffering—just like King Saṇaṅkumāra, the universal monarch of the four quarters. This is the third way of making an end.

Furthermore, there is another fourth way of making an end [to suffering]: it is characterized by few karmic consequences. Having become shaven-headed and gone forth as a monk, he is abundant in self-restraint; yet for him there is no such kind of asceticism, nor does there arise such kind of painful sensation. Such a person, through the completion of his religious career, attains perfection and makes an end of all suffering—just like the venerable lady Marudevā. This is the fourth way of making an end.

Four kinds of trees are taught, namely: one that is tall and remains tall; one that is tall but becomes low; one that is low but becomes tall; and one that is low and remains low. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is tall and remains tall, and so on, until: one who is low and remains low.

Four kinds of trees are taught, namely: one that is tall and has a tall growth-pattern; one that is tall and has a short growth-pattern; one that is short and has a tall growth-pattern; and one that is short and has a short growth-pattern. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is tall and has a tall disposition, and so forth, in four permutations.

Four types of trees are taught, namely: one that is tall and has a tall form; likewise, there is the fourfold permutation. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is tall and has a tall form; [and so on with] the fourfold permutation. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is tall and has a lofty mind; [and so on with] the fourfold permutation. Likewise regarding intention (*saṅkappa*), wisdom (*panna*), view (*diṭṭhi*), conduct (*sīlāyāra*), conduct in practice (*vavahāra*), and exertion (*parakkama*); for one type of person, there is no counterpart.

There are four kinds of trees, namely: one called straight that is straight; one called straight that is crooked; [and so on for] the four permutations (catubhaṅgo). In the same way, there are four types of persons, namely: one called straight that is straight; [and so on for] the four permutations. Just as the section concerning the upright and the bent was explained, so too should it be recited regarding the straight and the crooked, up to "exertion" (parakkama). For a monk who has undertaken the vows, it is appropriate to speak four kinds of speech, namely: speech for requesting, speech for questioning, speech for obtaining permission, and speech for answering when asked.
Four types of speech are taught, namely: the first type of speech is truth; the second is falsehood; the third is both truth and falsehood; and the fourth is neither truth nor falsehood.

Four types of cloth are taught, namely: one called pure that is pure, one called pure that is impure, one called impure that is pure, and one called impure that is impure. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one called pure who is pure—this constitutes a fourfold permutation (caubhaṅgo). Likewise, regarding cloth in terms of its transformed state (*pariṇata-rūve*), there are four types of persons with their opposites: one called pure whose mind (*maṇa*) is pure—this constitutes a fourfold permutation. Thus it continues for intention (*saṅkappa*) up to exertion (*parakkama*).

Four types of threads are taught, namely: the over-born, the under-born, the ill-born, and the firebrand. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is truthful in name and is actually truthful; one who is truthful in name but is untruthful; one who is untruthful in name but is truthful; and one who is untruthful in name and is untruthful. The same applies to transformation, up to exertion.

Four types of cloth are taught, namely: one is clean and clean, one is clean and unclean; thus there are four permutations (*caübbhaṅgō*). In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one is clean and clean, [and so on]—thus there are four permutations. Just as it was stated regarding clean cloth, so it is also for the learned (*suti*), up to the point of exertion (*parakkama*).

Four types of *kōrava* fruits are taught, namely: the *ambapalambaka-kōrava*, the *tālapalambaka-kōrava*, the *vallipalambaka-kōrava*, and the *meṇḍhavisāṇa-kōrava*. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is like the *ambapalambaka-kōrava*, one who is like the *tālapalambaka-kōrava*, one who is like the *vallipalambaka-kōrava*, and one who is like the *meṇḍhavisāṇa-kōrava*.

Four types of wood for scraping are taught, namely: the outer bark, the inner bark, the wood itself, and the heartwood. In the same way, four types of alms-seekers are taught, namely: one who is like the outer bark, up to one who is like the heartwood. For the alms-seeker who is like the outer bark, austerity like that of the heartwood is taught; for the alms-seeker who is like the heartwood, austerity like that of the outer bark is taught; for the alms-seeker who is like the inner bark, austerity like that of the wood itself is taught; and for the alms-seeker who is like the wood itself, austerity like that of the inner bark is taught.

The vegetable-bodied beings are taught to be of four kinds, namely: those whose seeds are at the tip, those whose seeds are at the root, those whose seeds are at the joints, and those whose seeds are at the trunk.

There are four reasons why a newly reborn hell-being in the hell-world might wish to come quickly to the human world, yet is unable to come quickly: first, a newly reborn hell-being in the hell-world, while experiencing the intense agony that has arisen there, might wish to come quickly to the human world, yet is unable to come quickly.
A newly reborn hell-being in the hell-world, being repeatedly tormented by the hell-wardens, might wish to come quickly to the human world, yet he is simply not able to come quickly.

A newly reborn hell-being, while the karma to be experienced as hellish suffering has not yet been exhausted, not yet been undergone, and not yet been worn away, might wish to come quickly to the world of men, yet he is simply unable to come quickly. A newly reborn hell-being, while the karma in hell has not yet been exhausted, not yet been undergone, and not yet been worn away, might wish to come quickly to the world of men, yet he is simply unable to come quickly.
By these four conditions, a newly reborn hell-being in the hell-world might desire to come quickly to the world of humans, yet he is simply not able to come quickly.
Four sets of robes are permitted for the nuns to wear or carry: namely, one two-cubit wide, two three-cubit wide, and one four-cubit wide.
Four meditations are taught: namely, the meditation of suffering, the meditation of cruelty, the meditation of dharma, and the meditation of purity.

The sorrowful meditation (*ārta-dhyāna*) is declared to be fourfold, as follows: being possessed of association with the unpleasant, one is likewise endowed with mindfulness of separation from it; being possessed of association with the pleasant, one is likewise endowed with mindfulness of non-separation from it; being possessed of association with affliction, one is likewise endowed with mindfulness of separation from it; being possessed of association with the enjoyment of cherished sensual pleasures, one is likewise endowed with mindfulness of non-separation from them. Four characteristics of this sorrowful meditation are declared, as follows: weeping, lamenting, moaning, and wailing.

Fierce meditation (*rōddhajhāṇa*) is declared to be fourfold, namely: that which is connected with violence (*hiṁsāṇubandhi*), that which is connected with falsehood (*mōsāṇubandhi*), that which is connected with theft (*tēṇāṇubandhi*), and that which is connected with guarding [possessions] (*sārakkhaṇāṇubandhi*). Four characteristics of fierce meditation are declared, namely: the fault of excessive indulgence (*ōsaṇṇadōsa*), the fault of abundance [of evil] (*bahudōsa*), the fault of ignorance (*annāṇadōsa*), and the fault of persisting until death (*āmaraṇantadōsa*).

The meditation on the Dharma (*dhamma-jhāṇa*) is taught to be fourfold and characterized by four modes of entry, namely: investigation into the command (*āṇā-vijaya*), investigation into danger (*avāya-vijaya*), investigation into karmic fruition (*vivāga-vijaya*), and investigation into structure (*saṇṭhāṇa-vijaya*). Regarding this meditation on the Dharma, four characteristics are taught, namely: delight in the command (*āṇā-rui*), natural delight (*nisagga-rui*), delight in scripture (*sutta-rui*), and profound delight (*ogāḍha-rui*). Regarding this meditation on the Dharma, four supports are taught, namely: recitation (*vāyaṇā*), questioning (*paḍipucchaṇā*), reviewing (*pariyaṭṭaṇā*), and reflection (*aṇuppehā*). Regarding this meditation on the Dharma, four reflections are taught, namely: reflection on solitude (*egāṇuppehā*), reflection on impermanence (*aṇiccāṇuppehā*), reflection on the lack of refuge (*asaraṇāṇuppehā*), and reflection on the cycle of existence (*saṃsārāṇuppehā*).

The white meditation (*śukla-dhyāna*) is declared to be fourfold and to have four entrances, namely: with discursive thought of multiplicity and with mental activity (*pṛthaktva-vitarka-savicāra*); with discursive thought of unity and without mental activity (*ekatva-vitarko-avicāra*); subtle activity and without purpose (*sūkṣma-kriyā-anivarti*); and completely ceased activity and non-returning (*samucchinnakriyā-apratipāti*). Four characteristics of the white meditation are declared, namely: absence of distress (*avyatha*), absence of delusion (*asammoha*), detachment (*viveka*), and renunciation (*vyutsarga*). Four supports (*ālambana*) of the white meditation are declared, namely: forbearance (*kṣānti*), liberation (*mukti*), uprightness (*ārjava*), and gentleness (*mārdava*). Four reflections (*anuprekṣā*) of the white meditation are declared, namely: reflection on infinity (*anantatva-anuprekṣā*), reflection on transformation (*vipariṇāma-anuprekṣā*), reflection on impurity (*aśubha-anuprekṣā*), and reflection on danger (*apāya-anuprekṣā*).
The duration of life for gods is declared to be fourfold; namely: some are gods by name, some are kinsmen of gods, some are priests of gods, and some are flames of gods.

Four types of cohabitation are declared; namely: one god may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; one god may enter into cohabitation with a female spirit (chavī); one female spirit may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; and one female spirit may enter into cohabitation with another female spirit.

Four passions (*kaṣāya*) are taught, namely: the passion of anger (*krodha*), the passion of pride (*māna*), the passion of deceit (*māyā*), and the passion of greed (*lobha*). This is the case for hell-beings up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm. Anger is taught to be established in four ways, namely: established in oneself (*ātmapratiṣṭhita*), established in another (*parapratiṣṭhita*), established in both (*tadubhayapratiṣṭhita*), and unestablished (*apratiṣṭhita*). This is the case for hell-beings up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm; and so it is for each [passion] up to greed, up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm.

The arising of anger is declared to occur through four causes, namely: with reference to land, with reference to a building, with reference to the body, and with reference to possessions. This applies to hell-beings up to the gods of the Vaimānika realm; likewise for pride up to greed, up to the gods of the Vaimānika realm. Anger is declared to be of four kinds, namely: anger of infinite bondage (*anantānubandhī-krodha*), anger of non-renunciation (*apaccakkhāṇa-krodha*), anger of the veil of renunciation (*paccakkhāṇāvaraṇa-krodha*), and burning anger (*sañjalaṇa-krodha*). This applies to hell-beings up to the gods of the Vaimānika realm; likewise for pride up to greed, up to the gods of the Vaimānika realm.

Anger is declared to be fourfold, namely: produced through conscious intent (*ābhoga-nirvartita*), produced without conscious intent (*anābhoga-nirvartita*), subsided (*upaśānta*), and unsubsided (*anuśānta*). In this same way, for hell-beings up to the gods of the *Vaimānika* realm, pride is declared to be fourfold, namely: produced through conscious intent, produced without conscious intent, subsided, and unsubsided. In this same way, [this applies] up to greed, up to the *Vaimānika* gods.

Living beings, indeed, have accumulated the eight types of karma through four causes, namely: through anger, pride, deceit, and greed; and so on, up to the Vaimānika gods. Thus they have accumulated, thus they are accumulating, and thus they will accumulate—this is the *daṇḍa* (karmic burden). Thus they bound [the karma]—threefold; thus they experienced [it]—threefold; thus they felt [it]—threefold; thus they underwent [it]—threefold; thus they shed [it]—threefold; and so on, up to the Vaimānika gods.

Four postures (paḍimā) are taught, namely: the posture of meditative absorption (samāhipaḍimā), the posture of ascetic practice (uvahāṇapaḍimā), the posture of seclusion (vivegapaḍimā), and the posture of renunciation (viussaggapaḍimā). Four postures are taught, namely: Bhaddā, Subhaddā, Mahābhaddā, and Savvatobhaddā. Four postures are taught, namely: the minor Mōyapaḍimā, the major Mōyapaḍimā, the Javamajjhā, and the Vaïramajjhā.

Four astikāyas, which are non-living bodies (ajīvakāya), are taught; namely: the dharma-astikāya, the adharma-astikāya, the space-astikāya (ākāśa-astikāya), and the matter-astikāya (pudgala-astikāya). Four astikāyas, which are formless bodies (arūpi-kāya), are taught; namely: the dharma-astikāya, the adharma-astikāya, the space-astikāya, and the soul-astikāya (jīva-astikāya).

Four fruits are declared, as follows: some that are raw and sweet when raw; some that are raw and sweet when ripe; some that are ripe and sweet when raw; and some that are ripe and sweet when ripe. In the very same way, four types of persons are declared, as follows: one who is like a fruit that is raw and sweet when raw—[and so on for the other three]. Truth is declared to be fourfold: uprightness of body, uprightness of speech, uprightness of mind, and the practice of non-deception. Falsehood is declared to be fourfold: crookedness of body, crookedness of speech, crookedness of mind, and the practice of deception.

Fourfold concentration is taught, namely: mental concentration, vocal concentration, bodily concentration, and concentration regarding requisites; thus it is for hell-beings, five-sensed beings, and so on, up to the Vaimānika gods.

Fourfold is well-directedness (suppaṇihāṇa) as it is taught, namely: well-directedness of mind, well-directedness of speech, well-directedness of body, and well-directedness of requisites; likewise for restrained human beings. Fourfold is ill-directedness (duppaṇihāṇa) as it is taught, namely: ill-directedness of mind, ill-directedness of speech, ill-directedness of body, and ill-directedness of requisites; likewise for five-sensed beings up to the Vaimānika gods.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is pleasant in conversation but not pleasant in association; one who is pleasant in association but not pleasant in conversation; one who is both pleasant in conversation and pleasant in association; and one who is neither pleasant in conversation nor pleasant in association. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who perceives his own fault but not another’s; one who perceives another’s fault but not his own; [the remaining two are] likewise. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who confesses his own fault but not another’s; [the remaining three are] likewise. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who pacifies his own fault but not another’s; [the remaining three are] likewise. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who rises to greet others but does not cause others to rise; [the remaining three are] likewise. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who pays homage but does not cause others to pay homage; [the remaining three are] likewise. In the same way: one who honors, one who respects, one who worships, one who praises, one who asks questions back, one who asks questions, one who explains; and four types of persons are taught, namely: one who holds the scriptures but not their meaning; one who holds the meaning but not the scriptures; [the remaining two are] likewise.

The Asura lord Camara, king of the Asura-kumāras, has four world-protectors (lokapālas) prescribed, namely: Soma, Yama, Varuṇa, and Vaiśramaṇa. Likewise for Bali: Soma, Yama, Vaiśramaṇa, and Varuṇa. For Dharaṇa: Kālapāla, Kolapāla, Śailapāla, and Śaṅkhapāla. For Bhūtānanda: Kālapāla, Kolapāla, Śaṅkhapāla, and Śailapāla. For Veṇudeva: Citra, Vicitra, Citrapakṣa, and Vicitrapakṣa. For Veṇudāli: Citra, Vicitra, Vicitrapakṣa, and Citrapakṣa. For Harikānta: Prabha, Suprabha, Prabhakānta, and Suprabhakānta. For Harissaha: Prabha, Suprabha, Suprabhakānta, and Prabhakānta. For Agniśikha: Tejas, Tejaḥśikha, Tejaḥkānta, and Tejaḥprabha. For Agnimāṇava: Tejas, Tejaḥśikha, Tejaḥprabha, and Tejaḥkānta. For Pūrṇa: Rūpa, Rūpāṃśa, Rūpakānta, and Rūpaprabha. For Viśiṣṭa: Rūpa, Rūpāṃśa, Rūpaprabha, and Rūpakānta. For Jalakānta: Jala, Jalarata, Jalakānta, and Jalaprabha. For Jalaprabha: Jala, Jalarata, Jalaprabha, and Jalakānta. For Amitagati: Tvaritagati, Kṣipragati, Siṃhagati, and Siṃhavikramagati. For Amitavāhana: Tvaritagati, Kṣipragati, Siṃhavikramagati, and Siṃhagati. For Velaṃba: Kāla, Mahākāla, Añjana, and Riṣṭa. For Pabhañjana: Kāla, Mahākāla, Riṣṭa, and Añjana. For Dhoṣa: Āvarta, Vyāvarta, Nandiyāvarta, and Mahānandiyāvarta. For Mahādhoṣa: Āvarta, Vyāvarta, Mahānandiyāvarta, and Nandiyāvarta. For Śakra: Soma, Yama, Varuṇa, and Vaiśramaṇa. For Īśāna: Soma, Yama, Vaiśramaṇa, and Varuṇa. In this manner, they alternate one by one up to Acyuta. There are four types of Vāyu-kumāras prescribed, namely: Kāla, Mahākāla, Velaṃba, and Pabhañjana.
Four kinds of gods are taught, namely: the Bhavanavāsins, the Vāṇamantaras, the Jyotiṣkas, and the Vimānavāsins.
Four kinds of measurement are taught, namely: measurement of substance, measurement of space, measurement of time, and measurement of state.
Four great matrons among the Disākumāris are taught, namely: Rūpā, Rūpāṃśā, Surūpā, and Rūpāvatī.
Four great queens of the Vidyutkumāras are taught, namely: Citrā, Cittakaṇagā, Satērā, and Sōtāmaṇī.

The lifespan of the gods in the middle assembly of Sakra, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is taught to be four palyopamas. The lifespan of the goddesses in the middle assembly of Īśāna, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is taught to be four palyopamas.

The cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is taught to be fourfold, namely: the cycle of existence of substance (dravya), the cycle of existence of space (kṣetra), the cycle of existence of time (kāla), and the cycle of existence of state (bhāva).
The *Dṛṣṭivāda* is taught to be fourfold, namely: *parikarma*, *sūtra*, *pūrvagata*, and *anuyoga*.

Fourfold penance (*prāyaścitta*) is taught, namely: penance for [defects in] knowledge, penance for [defects in] vision, penance for [defects in] conduct, and penance for [neglect of] essential duties. Fourfold penance is taught, namely: penance for transgression, penance for association, penance for imposition, and penance for concealment.
Time is declared to be fourfold, namely: time as measurement (pamāṇakāla), time as the completion of the life-span (ahāuyanivvattikāla), time as death (maraṇakāla), and time as duration (addhākāla).

Transformation of matter is declared to be fourfold, namely: transformation of color (vaṇṇapariṇāma), transformation of odor (gandhapariṇāma), transformation of taste (rasapariṇāma), and transformation of touch (phāsapariṇāma).

In the Bharaha and Eravața regions, the twenty-two Arhat Blessed Ones, excluding those of the first and last [ages], proclaim the fourfold Dharma as follows: abstention from all taking of life, abstention from all false speech, abstention from all taking of what is not given, and abstention from all external possessions. In all the Mahāvideha regions, the Arhat Blessed Ones proclaim the fourfold Dharma as follows: abstention from all taking of life, up to and including abstention from all external possessions.

Four miserable destinies are proclaimed, namely: the miserable destiny of hell-beings, the miserable destiny of animal-births, the miserable destiny of humans, and the miserable destiny of gods. Four happy destinies are proclaimed, namely: the happy destiny of the perfected ones (*siddha*), the happy destiny of gods, the happy destiny of humans, and rebirth in a good family. Four miserable states are proclaimed, namely: the miserable state of hell-beings, the miserable state of animal-births, the miserable state of humans, and the miserable state of gods. Four happy states are proclaimed, namely: the happy state of the perfected ones, the happy state of gods, the happy state of humans, and rebirth in a good family.

In the first moment of being a Jina, four types of karma are destroyed, namely: knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇīya), perception-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇīya), deluding (mohanīya), and obstructive (antarāyika). The Arhat, Jina, and Kevalin, possessing arisen knowledge and perception, experiences four types of karma, namely: feeling-producing (vedanīya), life-determining (āyuṣka), name (nāman), and status (gotra).
In the first moment of attaining perfection (siddha), four types of karma are simultaneously exhausted, namely: feeling-producing, life-determining, name, and status.
There are four causes for the arising of laughter; they are as follows: having seen, having heard, having smelled, and having remembered.

Four kinds of intervals are taught; they are as follows: the interval of wood, the interval of lotus-fibers, the interval of iron, and the interval of stone. In the same way, four kinds of intervals are taught for a woman or a man; they are as follows: equal to the interval of wood, equal to the interval of lotus-fibers, equal to the interval of iron, and equal to the interval of stone. Four types of fear are taught; they are as follows: fear of the day, fear of a journey, fear of heat, and fear of a wrestling match.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is an open transgressor but not a secret transgressor; one who is a secret transgressor but not an open transgressor; one who is both an open transgressor and a secret transgressor; and one who is neither an open transgressor nor a secret transgressor.

The great king Soma, the chief queen of the asura lord Camara, the king of the asura-kumāras, has four chief queens, namely: Kaṇagā, Kaṇagalatā, Cittaguttā, and Vasundharā. It is the same for Yama, Varuṇa, and Vaiśramaṇa. The great king Soma, the chief queen of the Vairocana lord Bali, the king of the Vairocanas, has four chief queens, namely: Mitagā, Subhaddā, Vijjutā, and Aśanī. It is the same for Yama, Vaiśramaṇa, and Varuṇa. The great king Kālavāla, the chief queen of Dharaṇa, the lord of the nāga-kumāras, the king of the nāga-kumāras, has four chief queens, namely: Aśokā, Vimalā, Suprabhā, and Sundarasanā. It is the same up to Śaṅkhavāla. The great king Kālavāla, the chief queen of Bhūtānanda, the lord of the nāga-kumāras, the king of the nāga-kumāras, has four chief queens, namely: Sunandā, Subhaddā, Sujātā, and Sumanā. It is the same up to Śailavāla, as in the case of Dharaṇa.

In this same manner, it applies to all the world-guardians of the southern quarter, up to Ghosa, just as it was for Bhūtānanda; and likewise for the world-guardians up to Mahāghosa. Of Kāla, the lord of the Piśācas and king of the Piśācas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Kamalā, Kamalappabhā, Utpalā, and Sudarśanā. It is the same for Mahākāla. Of Surūpa, the lord of the Bhūtas and king of the Bhūtas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Rūpavatī, Bahurūpā, Surūpā, and Subhagā. It is the same for Pratirūpa. Of Puṇyabhadra, the lord of the Yakṣas and king of the Yakṣas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Puṇṇā, Bahupuṇṇittā, Uttamā, and Tārakā. It is the same for Māṇibhadra. Of Bhīma, the lord of the Rākṣasas and king of the Rākṣasas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Padmā, Vasumatī, Kanakā, and Ratnaprabhā. It is the same for Mahābhīma. Of Kiṃnara, the lord of the Kiṃnaras, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Vaḍeṃsā, Ketumatī, Ratisenā, and Ratiprabhā. It is the same for Kumpuruṣa. Of Sappuruṣa, the lord of the Kiṃpuruṣas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Rohiṇī, Navamitā, Hrī, and Puṣpavatī. It is the same for Mahāpuruṣa. Of Atikāya, the lord of the Mahoragas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Bhujagā, Bhujagāvatī, Mahākacchā, and Phuḍā. It is the same for Mahākāya. Of Gītarati, the lord of the Gandharvas and king of the Gandharvas, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Sughoṣā, Vimalā, Susvarā, and Sarasvatī. It is the same for Gītyayaśas. Of Candra, the lord of the luminaries and king of the luminaries, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Candraprabhā, Dosiṇābhā, Arcimālī, and Pabhaṅkarā. It is the same for Sūra, with the exception that [the names are] Sūraprabhā, Dosiṇābhā, Arcimālī, and Pabhaṅkarā. Of Aṅgāra, the great planet, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Vijayā, Vaijayantī, Jayantī, and Aparājitā. It is the same for all the great planets, up to Bhāvaketu.

Of Soma, the great king of the gods, the lord of the gods, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Rohiṇī, Mayaṇā, Cittā, and Sāmā; and so on up to Vessamaṇa. Of Īśāna, the lord of the gods, the lord of the gods, Soma, the great king, four chief queens are proclaimed, namely: Puḍhavī, Rātī, Rayanī, and Vijjū; and so on up to Varuṇa.

Four types of milk-products are taught, namely: milk, curd, clarified butter, and fresh butter; four types of oily substances are taught, namely: oil, ghee, fat, and fresh butter; four great delicacies are taught, namely: honey, meat, liquor, and fresh butter.

Four types of gabled houses are taught, namely: one called "guarded" which is guarded; one called "guarded" which is unguarded; one called "unguarded" which is guarded; and one called "unguarded" which is unguarded. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one called "guarded" who is guarded—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four types of gabled halls are taught, namely: one that is guarded and has guarded doors; one that is guarded but has unguarded doors; one that is unguarded but has guarded doors; and one that is unguarded and has unguarded doors. In the very same way, four types of women are taught, namely: one who is guarded and has guarded senses; one who is guarded but has unguarded senses; [and so on for the remaining two]. There are four kinds of occupation (ogāhaṇā), namely: occupation by substance (davvōgāhaṇā), occupation by space (khettōgāhaṇā), occupation by time (kālōgāhaṇā), and occupation by state (bhāvōgāhaṇā).
Four *prajñaptis* (cosmological treatises) external to the *aṅgas* are taught, namely: the *Candraprajñapti*, the *Sūryaprajñapti*, the *Jambūdvīpaprajñapti*, and the *Dvīpasāgaraprajñapti*.

Four types of retraction (*paḍisaṃlīṇa*) are taught, namely: retraction from anger, retraction from pride, retraction from deceit, and retraction from greed. Four types of non-retraction are taught, namely: non-retraction from anger, up to non-retraction from greed. Four types of retraction are taught, namely: retraction of the mind, retraction of speech, retraction of the body, and retraction of the senses. Four types of non-retraction are taught, namely: non-retraction of the mind, up to non-retraction of the senses.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wretched and wretched [in disposition], one who is wretched but not wretched [in disposition], one who is not wretched but wretched [in disposition], and one who is not wretched and not wretched [in disposition]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wretched and wretched in his transformation, one who is wretched but not wretched in his transformation, one who is not wretched but wretched in his transformation, and one who is not wretched and not wretched in his transformation.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is miserable and has a miserable appearance; one who is miserable but has a non-miserable appearance; one who is non-miserable but has a miserable appearance; and one who is non-miserable and has a non-miserable appearance.

In the same way, there are four types each for those with a miserable mind (dīnamaṇe), a miserable intention (dīnasaṅkappe), a miserable wisdom (dīnapanne), a miserable view (dīnaditthī), a miserable conduct and observance (dīnasīlācāre), and a miserable mode of livelihood (dīnavavahāre). Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is miserable and has miserable exertion (dīnaparakkame); one who is miserable but has non-miserable exertion; and so on for all [the preceding categories], with the fourfold permutation (caübbhaṅgo) to be recited for each.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wretched and of wretched exertion; one who is wretched but of noble exertion; one who is noble but of wretched exertion; and one who is noble and of noble exertion. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wretched and of wretched livelihood—likewise [wretched] in birth, wretched in speech, and wretched in appearance. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wretched and serves the wretched—likewise [serves the wretched] in conduct, [serves the wretched] in religious status, and [serves the wretched] in retinue. One who is wretched and has a wretched retinue—likewise [has a wretched retinue] in conduct, [has a wretched retinue] in religious status, and [has a wretched retinue] in birth. In all cases, there is a fourfold permutation (catubhaṅga).

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is noble (*ajja*) by name but is actually ignoble; one who is noble by name but is actually ignoble; one who is ignoble by name but is actually noble; and one who is ignoble by name and is actually ignoble. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is noble by name and noble in conduct (*pariṇae*); likewise, one who is noble in appearance (*rūve*), noble in mind (*maṇe*), noble in intention (*saṅkappe*), noble in wisdom (*panne*), noble in view (*diṭṭhī*), noble in conduct and observance (*sīlācāre*), noble in behavior (*vavahāre*), noble in effort (*parakkame*), noble in livelihood (*vittī*), noble in birth (*jātī*), noble in speech (*bhāsī*), noble in both [speech and action] (*ōbhāsī*), noble in service (*sevī*), and likewise noble in the religious life (*pariyāē*), noble in companionship (*pariyālē*). Thus there are seventeen statements. Just as they were spoken with respect to the "miserable" (*dīṇē*), so too should they be spoken with respect to the "noble" (*ajjē*).

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is noble by name but of ignoble disposition; one who is noble by name but of ignoble disposition; one who is ignoble by name but of noble disposition; and one who is ignoble by name and of ignoble disposition.

Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one endowed with birth, one endowed with lineage, one endowed with strength, and one endowed with beauty. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one endowed with birth, up to one endowed with beauty.

Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth but not with a good lineage; one who is endowed with a good lineage but not with noble birth; one who is endowed with both noble birth and a good lineage; and one who is endowed with neither noble birth nor a good lineage. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth... [and so on, up to] ...one who is endowed with neither noble birth nor a good lineage. Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth but not with strength... [and so on, up to] ...one who is endowed with neither noble birth nor strength. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth... [and so on].

Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth but not endowed with beauty; [and so on for the other three combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons born in society are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth but not endowed with beauty; one who is endowed with beauty but not endowed with noble birth; [and so on for the other two combinations].

Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one who is endowed with lineage but not endowed with strength; [and so on for the other three combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with lineage but not endowed with strength; [and so on for the other three combinations]. Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one who is endowed with lineage but not endowed with beauty; [and so on for the other three combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with lineage but not endowed with beauty; [and so on for the other three combinations]. Four types of bulls are taught, namely: one who is endowed with strength but not endowed with beauty; [and so on for the other three combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with strength but not endowed with beauty; [and so on for the other three combinations].

Four types of elephants are taught, namely: the *bhadra*, the *manda*, the *mṛga*, and the *saṅkīrṇa*. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: the *bhadra*, the *manda*, the *mṛga*, and the *saṅkīrṇa*. Four types of elephants are taught, namely: one who is *bhadra* but has a *manda* mind; one who is *bhadra* but has a *mṛga* mind; one who is *bhadra* but has a *saṅkīrṇa* mind. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is *bhadra* and has a *bhadra* mind; one who is *bhadra* and has a *manda* mind; one who is *bhadra* and has a *mṛga* mind; one who is *bhadra* and has a *saṅkīrṇa* mind. Four types of elephants are taught, namely: one who is *manda* but has a *bhadra* mind; one who is *manda* and has a *manda* mind; one who is *manda* but has a *mṛga* mind; one who is *manda* but has a *saṅkīrṇa* mind. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is *manda* but has a *bhadra* mind, and so forth, exactly as before.

Four types of elephants are taught, namely: one who is mild but of auspicious mind; one who is mild but of dull mind; one who is mild but of wavering mind; and one who is mild but of agitated mind. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is mild but of auspicious mind, and so forth, as before.

Four types of elephants are taught, as follows: one that is well-bred (*saṅkiṇṇa*) but of a gentle mind (*bhaddamaṇa*); one that is well-bred but of a dull mind (*mandamaṇa*); one that is well-bred but of a timid mind (*miyamaṇa*); and one that is well-bred and of a well-bred mind (*saṅkiṇṇamaṇa*). In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, as follows: one who is well-bred but of a gentle mind, and so on, up to one who is well-bred and of a well-bred mind.

The "gentle" (*bhadra*) elephant has honey-colored, reddish-brown eyes; his long tail-tuft is well-formed and grows in regular succession; he is exalted and steadfast in front, and is perfectly composed in all his limbs. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 296)
One with moving, thick, and uneven skin, a large head,
a broad chest, thick nails, teeth, and hair, and yellowish-red eyes is dull-witted.
(Ṭhāṇa 297) One who is thin, has a weak digestive fire, a slender body, and thin teeth, nails, and hair [is likewise dull].
One who is timid, agitated, and fearful therein is called a "meager" elephant. Among these elephants,
that one which resembles others only slightly, whether in form or in character, is to be known as "mixed."
The excellent person drinks in the autumn; the dull-witted person drinks in the spring; the mild person drinks in the winter; and the one who is well-restrained drinks at all times. (Sthāna 300)

Four types of talk are taught, namely: talk about women, talk about food, talk about the country, and talk about kings. Talk about women is taught to be fourfold, namely: talk about the birth of women, talk about the family of women, talk about the beauty of women, and talk about the dress of women. Talk about food is taught to be fourfold, namely: talk about the acquisition of food, talk about the consumption of food, talk about the preparation of food, and talk about the distribution of food. Talk about the country is taught to be fourfold, namely: talk about the customs of the country, talk about the products of the country, talk about the preferences of the country, and talk about the dress of the country. Talk about kings is taught to be fourfold, namely: talk about the arrival of the king, talk about the departure of the king, talk about the army and vehicles of the king, and talk about the treasury and storehouses of the king. Four types of discourse are taught, namely: the introductory (akkhevaṇī), the expansive (vikkhevaṇī), the stirring (saṃveyaṇī), and the liberating (nivveyaṇī). Introductory discourse is taught to be fourfold, namely: introductory discourse on conduct (āyāra), introductory discourse on legal procedure (vavahāra), introductory discourse on cosmology (paṇṇatti), and introductory discourse on philosophical tenets (diṭṭhivāta). Expansive discourse is taught to be fourfold, namely: he explains his own doctrine, and having explained his own doctrine, he explains the doctrine of others; having explained the doctrine of others, he establishes his own doctrine. He explains right view, and having explained right view, he explains wrong view; having explained wrong view, he establishes right view. Stirring discourse is taught to be fourfold, namely: stirring discourse regarding this world, stirring discourse regarding the next world, stirring discourse regarding one's own body, and stirring discourse regarding the bodies of others. Liberating discourse is taught to be fourfold, namely: [the teaching that] evil deeds performed in this world result in the ripening of painful fruits in this world; evil deeds performed in this world result in the ripening of painful fruits in the next world; evil deeds performed in the next world result in the ripening of painful fruits in this world; evil deeds performed in the next world result in the ripening of painful fruits in the next world. Good deeds performed in this world result in the ripening of pleasant fruits in this world; good deeds performed in this world result in the ripening of pleasant fruits in the next world—thus there are four permutations.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is thin and thin; one who is thin and strong; one who is strong and thin; and one who is strong and strong. Four types of persons are taught: one who is thin with a thin body; one who is thin with a strong body; one who is strong with a thin body; and one who is strong with a strong body. Four types of persons are taught: for one who is thin with a thin body, knowledge and vision arise; not for one who is thin with a strong body. For one who is strong with a strong body, knowledge and vision arise; not for one who is strong with a thin body. For some, knowledge and vision arise both for one with a thin body and for one with a strong body. For others, knowledge and vision do not arise for one with a thin body nor for one with a strong body.

There are four conditions by which, for monks or nuns, although there may be a desire for extraordinary knowledge and vision (*atisesa-ñāṇadassana*) to arise in this present time, it does not arise. Namely: they frequently engage in talk about women, talk about food, talk about the countryside, and talk about kings; they do not properly cultivate themselves through seclusion and renunciation; they do not remain awake in the practice of spiritual vigilance (*dhamma-jāgarikā*) during the first and last watches of the night; and they do not properly seek out pure, acceptable, and gathered alms-food. By these four conditions, for monks or nuns, [extraordinary knowledge and vision] will not arise.

By four conditions, for either monks or nuns, extraordinary knowledge and vision may arise in this present time when they are desirous of its arising. They are as follows: they do not engage in talk about women, talk about food, talk about the country, or talk about kings; they have properly cultivated themselves through detachment and renunciation; they remain awake in the practice of spiritual vigilance during the first and last parts of the night; and they have properly sought out pure, acceptable, and collected alms-food. By these four conditions, for either monks or nuns, extraordinary knowledge and vision may arise in this present time when they are desirous of its arising.

It is not permitted for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to perform the recitation (*svādhyāya*) on four great festival days (*mahāpāḍivayā*), namely: the first day of Āṣāḍha, the festival of Indra, the first day of Kārttika, and the first day of Sugimha (the beginning of summer).

It is not permitted for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to perform the recitation during four twilights (*saṃdhyā*), namely: the first [twilight], the last [twilight], at midday, and at midnight. It is permitted for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to perform the recitation at four times of the day, namely: the forenoon, the afternoon, the evening, and the dawn.

The stability of the world is declared to be fourfold, namely: the wind is established in space; the ocean is established in the wind; the earth is established in the ocean; and mobile and immobile living beings are established upon the earth.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a "Taha" (a person of integrity), but not one who is a "No-taha" (a person lacking integrity); one who is a "Sovatthi" (one who prospers), but not one who is a "Padhāṇa" (an exertor); four types of persons are taught, namely: one who benefits himself but does not benefit others; one who benefits others but does not benefit himself; one who benefits both himself and others; and one who benefits neither himself nor others.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: some who are masters of themselves but not masters of others; some who are masters of others but not masters of themselves; some who are masters of both themselves and others; and some who are masters of neither themselves nor others. Four types of persons are taught, namely: some who are masters of themselves but not masters of others—[the same fourfold set as above].

Four kinds of censuring are taught, namely: censuring by way of undertaking [a practice]; censuring by way of doubt; censuring by way of whatever is mistaken; and censuring by way of what is thus declared.

Four types of persons have been declared, namely: one who is sufficient for himself but not for another; one who is sufficient for another but not for himself; one who is sufficient both for himself and for another; and one who is sufficient neither for himself nor for another.

Four kinds of roads are taught, namely: one road that is straight and is called "straight," one road that is straight but is called "crooked," one road that is crooked but is called "straight," and one road that is crooked and is called "crooked. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one person who is straight and is called "straight"—[and so on for the other three]. Four kinds of roads are taught, namely: one road that is secure and is called "secure," one road that is secure but is called "insecure," one road that is insecure but is called "secure," and one road that is insecure and is called "insecure. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one person who is secure and is called "secure"—[and so on for the other three].

Four paths are taught, namely: one called secure that is secure in nature; one called secure that is insecure in nature; one called insecure that is secure in nature; and one called insecure that is insecure in nature. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one called secure who is secure in nature—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four kinds of whirlpools are taught, namely: one that is crooked and turns to the left; one that is crooked and turns to the right; one that is straight and turns to the left; and one that is straight and turns to the right. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is crooked and turns to the left—[and so on for the other three].

Four kinds of smoke-tips are taught, namely: one that is crooked and turns to the left—[and so on for the other three]. In the same way, four types of women are taught, namely: one who is crooked and turns to the left—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of fire-flames are taught, namely: one is called *vāmā* (leftward) and turns to the right (*dāhiṇāvattā*), [and so on up to four]. In the same way, four types of women are taught, namely: one is called *vāmā* and turns to the right, [and so on up to four]. Four types of wind-circles are taught, namely: one is called *vāmā* and turns to the left (*vāmāvattā*), [and so on up to four]. In the same way, four types of women are taught, namely: one is called *vāmā* and turns to the left, [and so on up to four].

There are four types of forest groves that are secluded, namely: one that is crooked and turns to the left, and so on [up to four]. In the same way, four types of persons are declared, namely: one who is crooked and turns to the left, and so on [up to four]. For four reasons, a *nirgrantha* (monk) does not overstep [the bounds of propriety] when speaking to or conversing with a *nirgranthī* (nun), namely: when asking the way, when showing the way, when giving food, drink, soft food, or solid food, or when having food, drink, soft food, or solid food given.

Regarding the body of darkness (*tamukkāya*), four names have been declared, namely: "darkness" (*tama*), or "the body of darkness" (*tamukkāya*), or "gloom" (*andhakāra*), or "great gloom" (*mahandhakāra*). Regarding the body of darkness, four names have been declared, namely: "the world's storehouse of darkness" (*logandhagāra*), or "the world's darkness" (*logatamasa*), or "the gods' storehouse of darkness" (*devandhagāra*), or "the gods' darkness" (*devatamasa*). Regarding the body of darkness, four names have been declared, namely: "the wind-wall" (*vātaphaliha*), or "the agitation of the wind-wall" (*vātaphalihakhobha*), or "the army of the gods" (*dēvaranna*), or "the host of the gods" (*dēvavūha*).
Having descended from there, he remains having covered four kalpas, namely: those of the Sōdhamma, Īsāṇa, Saṇaṅkumāra, and Māhinda heavens.

Four types of persons are proclaimed, namely: one who is called an open practitioner, one who is called a secret practitioner, one who is called a delighter in the present, and one who is called a delighter in the escape.

Four types of armies are taught, namely: one that conquers but does not vanquish; one that vanquishes but does not conquer; one that both conquers and vanquishes; and one that neither conquers nor vanquishes. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who conquers but does not vanquish—[and so on for the remaining three]. Four types of armies are taught, namely: one that conquers and is victorious; one that conquers and is defeated; one that vanquishes and is victorious; and one that vanquishes and is defeated. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who conquers and is victorious—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four types of traps are taught, namely: the bamboo-root trap, the ram-horn trap, the cow’s urine trap, and the licking trap. In the same way, four kinds of deceit are taught, namely: that which is like the bamboo-root trap, up to that which is like the licking trap. A living being who dies having entered into deceit like the bamboo-root trap is reborn among the denizens of hell. A living being who dies having entered into deceit like the ram-horn trap is reborn among the animals. [A living being who dies having entered into deceit] like the cow’s urine trap is reborn among humans. [A living being who dies having entered into deceit] like the licking trap is reborn among the gods.

Four types of pillars are taught, namely: stone pillars, bone pillars, wooden pillars, and *tiṇisalatā* (creeper) pillars. In the same way, four kinds of pride (*māna*) are taught, namely: pride equal to a stone pillar, up to pride equal to a *tiṇisalatā* pillar. A living being who dies having entered into pride equal to a stone pillar is reborn among the denizens of hell; likewise, up to a living being who dies having entered into pride equal to a *tiṇisalatā* pillar is reborn among the gods.

Four types of cloth are prescribed, namely: cloth dyed with *kimirāga* (red dye from insects), cloth dyed with *kaddamarāga* (muddy red dye), cloth dyed with *khañjaṇarāga* (soot-red dye), and cloth dyed with *haliddarāga* (turmeric dye). In the same way, fourfold greed (*lobha*) is prescribed, namely: greed similar to cloth dyed with *kimirāga*, greed similar to cloth dyed with *kaddamarāga*, greed similar to cloth dyed with *khañjaṇarāga*, and greed similar to cloth dyed with *haliddarāga*. A living being who dies having entered into greed similar to cloth dyed with *kimirāga* is reborn among the denizens of hell (*nairayika*). [The same applies] up to: a living being who dies having entered into greed similar to cloth dyed with *haliddarāga* is reborn among the gods (*deva*).
The cycle of existence is declared to be fourfold; namely: the cycle of existence of hell-beings, up to the cycle of existence of gods.
Life-span is declared to be fourfold; namely: the life-span of hell-beings, up to the life-span of gods.
Existence is declared to be fourfold; namely: the existence of hell-beings, up to the existence of gods.

Fourfold food is taught, namely: solid food (*aśana*), drink (*pāna*), soft food (*khādima*), and delicacy (*svādima*). Fourfold food is taught, namely: that which is endowed with preparation (*upakṣara-sampanna*), that which is endowed with cooking (*upakvaḍa-sampanna*), that which is endowed with its natural state (*svabhāva-sampanna*), and that which is endowed with being thoroughly purified (*parijuṣita-sampanna*).

Fourfold bondage is taught, namely: bondage of type (*prakṛti-bandha*), bondage of duration (*sthiti-bandha*), bondage of intensity (*anubhāva-bandha*), and bondage of space-points (*pradeśa-bandha*).

Fourfold effort (*upakrama*) is taught, namely: the effort of binding (*bandhana-upakrama*), the effort of activation (*udīraṇa-upakrama*), the effort of pacification (*upaśamana-upakrama*), and the effort of transformation (*vipariṇāmana-upakrama*).

The instrumental cause of bondage (*bandhanopkrama*) is taught to be fourfold, namely: the instrumental cause of the bondage of nature (*prakṛti-bandhana*), the instrumental cause of the bondage of duration (*sthiti-bandhana*), the instrumental cause of the bondage of intensity (*anubhāva-bandhana*), and the instrumental cause of the bondage of space-points (*pradeśa-bandhana*). The instrumental cause of activation (*udīraṇopakrama*) is taught to be fourfold, namely: the instrumental cause of the activation of nature, the instrumental cause of the activation of duration, the instrumental cause of the activation of intensity, and the instrumental cause of the activation of space-points. The instrumental cause of subsidence (*upaśamanopakrama*) is taught to be fourfold, namely: the instrumental cause of the subsidence of nature, the instrumental cause of the subsidence of duration, the instrumental cause of the subsidence of intensity, and the instrumental cause of the subsidence of space-points. The instrumental cause of transformation (*vipariṇāmanopakrama*) is taught to be fourfold, namely: the instrumental cause of the transformation of nature, the instrumental cause of the transformation of duration, the instrumental cause of the transformation of intensity, and the instrumental cause of the transformation of space-points.

Fourfold is the comparison of relative smallness and greatness (*appābahua*) as it is taught, namely: comparison of relative smallness and greatness of nature (*pagati*), comparison of relative smallness and greatness of duration (*ṭhiti*), comparison of relative smallness and greatness of intensity (*aṇubhāva*), and comparison of relative smallness and greatness of space-points (*paesa*).

Fourfold is transference (*saṅkama*) as it is taught, namely: transference of nature, transference of duration, transference of intensity, and transference of space-points. Fourfold is stasis (*nidhatta*) as it is taught, namely: stasis of nature, stasis of duration, stasis of intensity, and stasis of space-points.

The fourfold *nigāyita* (classification) is taught as follows: *pagati-nigāyita* (classification by nature), *ṭhiti-nigāyita* (classification by duration), *aṇubhāva-nigāyita* (classification by intensity), and *paesa-nigāyita* (classification by spatial extension).

Four types of unity (*ekka*) are taught as follows: unity of substance (*daviekkaya*), unity of mother [cause] (*māuekkaya*), unity of modification (*pajjavekkaya*), and unity of collection (*saṅgahekkaya*). Four types of plurality (*katī*) are taught as follows: plurality of substance (*davikatī*), plurality of mother [cause] (*māuyakatī*), plurality of modification (*pajjavakatī*), and plurality of collection (*saṅgahakatī*).
There are four kinds of totality (sarva), namely: nominal totality (nāma-sarva), notional totality (sthāpanā-sarva), possessive totality (ādeśa-sarva), and exhaustive totality (niravaśeṣa-sarva).
On the four sides of the mountain Mānuṣottara, four peaks are proclaimed, namely: Ratna, Ratnoccaya, Sarvaratna, and Ratnasañcaya.

In the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the era of the Susama-susamā (the most excellent) period of the past Utsarpiṇī, the duration was four koṭākoṭis of sāgaropamas; in the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the era of the Susama-susamā period of this present Avasarpiṇī, the duration is taught to be four koṭākoṭis of sāgaropamas; and in the continent of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the era of the Susama-susamā period of the future Utsarpiṇī, the duration will be four koṭākoṭis of sāgaropamas.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, four non-action lands (*akarmabhūmi*) are taught, excluding Devakuru and Uttarakuru; namely: Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, and Ramyakavarṣa. Four circular Vaitāḍhya mountains are taught; namely: Saddāvātī, Viyaḍāvātī, Gandhāvātī, and Mālavantaparitātē. Therein dwell four gods of great power, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely: Sātī, Pabhāse, Aruṇe, and Paüme. On the island of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Mahāvideha, four types are taught; namely: Pūrvavideha, Aparavideha, Devakurā, and Uttarakurā. All the boundary mountains (*vāsahara-pavvata*), such as Nisadha and Nīlavanta, are taught to be four hundred *yojanas* in height and four hundred *gavyūtis* in width. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara, on the northern bank of the great river Sītā, four range-mountains (*vakkhāra-pavvaya*) are taught; namely: Cittakūḍa, Pamhakūḍa, Naliṇakūḍa, and Ega-sēla. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara, on the southern bank of the great river Sītā, four range-mountains are taught; namely: Tikūḍa, Vēsamaṇakūḍa, Añjana, and Mātañjana.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, on the southern bank of the great river Sītodā to the west of Mount Mandara, four range-mountains (vakkhārapavvaya) are declared; namely: Aṅkāvatī, Pamhāvatī, Āsīvisa, and Suhāvaha.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, on the northern bank of the great river Sītodā to the west of Mount Mandara, four range-mountains are declared; namely: Candapavvata, Sūrapavvata, Dēvapavvata, and Nāgapavvata.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the four intermediate directions from Mount Mandara, four Vakkhāra mountains are proclaimed, namely: Somaṇasa, Vijjuppabha, Gandhamāyana, and Mālavanta.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Mahāvideha, at the minimum [period], four Arhats, four Cakravartins, four Baladevas, and four Vāsudevas have arisen, are arising, or will arise.

On Mount Mandara on the island of Jambudvīpa, four forests are proclaimed, namely: Bhaddasālavaṇa, Nandanavana, Somanasavana, and Paṇḍagavana. On Mount Mandara on the island of Jambudvīpa, in the Paṇḍagavana, four consecration-slates (abhiṣeka-śilā) are proclaimed, namely: Paṇḍukambalaśilā, Aïpaṇḍukambalaśilā, Rattakambalaśilā, and Atirattakambalaśilā. Above the summit of Mandara, it is proclaimed to be four yojanas in width. In the same manner, in the eastern half of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa island, starting from Kāla and so forth, up to the summit of Mandara; likewise, up to the western half of Puṣkaravaradvīpa, up to the summit of Mandara.

The *Āvaśyaka* pertaining to Jambūdvīpa extends from the *Cūlikā* up to Ghātakasaṇḍa and Puṣkaravara on the eastern and western sides. (Sthānāṅga 322) Regarding the island of Jambūdvīpa, four gates are proclaimed, namely: Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, and Aparājita. These gates are each four *yojanas* in width and an equal distance in depth. Therein dwell four gods of great power and influence, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely: Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, and Aparājita.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara and in the four intermediate directions of the Cullahimavanta range—the mountain that acts as a boundary for the region—having entered the Lavaṇa Ocean by three hundred yojanas each, there are four intermediate islands (antaradvīpas) described, namely: Egurūyadvīpa, Ābhāsiyadvīpa, Vēsāṇiyadvīpa, and Naṅgōliyadvīpa. On those islands dwell four types of humans, namely: the Egurūyas, the Ābhāsiyas, the Vēsāṇiyas, and the Naṅgōliyas. In the four intermediate directions of those islands, having entered the Lavaṇa Ocean by four hundred yojanas each, there are four intermediate islands described, namely: Hayakaṇṇadvīpa, Gayakaṇṇadvīpa, Gōkaṇṇadvīpa, and Sakkulikannadvīpa. On those islands dwell four types of humans, namely: the Hayakaṇṇas, the Gayakaṇṇas, the Gōkaṇṇas, and the Sakkulikannas.

In the four intermediate directions of those islands, after entering the Salt Ocean for five hundred yojanas each, there are four intermediate islands situated there, namely: Āyaṃsamuhadīva, Meṇḍhamuhadīva, Aōmuhadīva, and Gōmuhadīva. On those islands, the four types of humans are to be described. In the four intermediate directions of those islands, after entering the Salt Ocean for six hundred yojanas each, there are four intermediate islands situated there, namely: Āsamuhadīva, Hatthimuhadīva, Sīhamuhadīva, and Vagghamuhadīva. On those islands, the four types of humans are to be described.

In the four intermediate directions of those islands, having entered the Salt Ocean for seven hundred yojanas, there are four inner islands (antaradīva) situated; namely: Āsakarṇadvīpa, Hastikarṇadvīpa, Akarṇadvīpa, and Karṇaprāvaraṇadvīpa. Regarding these islands, the inhabitants—human beings—are to be described [in the same manner as those on the main islands].

In the four intermediate directions of those islands, having entered the Salt Ocean by eight hundred yojanas each, there are four intermediate islands (antaradvīpa) situated, namely: Ukkāmuhadvīpa, Mēhamuhadvīpa, Vijjumuhadvīpa, and Vijjudantadvīpa. Regarding these islands, the inhabitants—human beings—should be described [in the same manner as the inhabitants of the main islands].

In the four intermediate directions of those islands, having entered nine hundred yojanas into the salt ocean, there are four intermediate islands (antaradvīpa) situated there, namely: Dhaṇadantadīva, Laṭṭhadantadīva, Gūḍhadantadīva, and Suddhadantadīva. On those islands dwell four kinds of humans, namely: the Dhaṇadantas, the Laṭṭhadantas, the Gūḍhadantas, and the Suddhadantas.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara and at the four intermediate corners of the Vāsahara mountain range Śikhari, having entered the Lavaṇa ocean by three hundred yojanas each, there are four intermediate islands (antaradvīpas) described; namely: Eguruyadvīpa. The rest is to be recited exactly as before without omission, up to Suddhadanta.

To the north, south, east, and west, extending ninety-five thousand yojanas from the outer edge of the Jambudvīpa continent into the Lavaṇasamudra ocean, there are four great hells (mahāpāyālas) described as being of immense size, situated like large jars with wide openings. They are as follows: Valayāmukha, Keua, Jūvaka, and Īsara. Therein dwell four gods of great power and majesty, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely: Kāla, Mahākāla, Velaṃba, and Pabhañjana.

To the four directions, extending forty-two thousand yojanas from the outer edge of the Jambudvīpa continent into the Lavaṇasamudra ocean, there are four mountain-dwellings of the four Velandhara nāga kings, namely: Gōthūbha, Udakōbhāsa, Saṅkha, and Dagasīma. Therein dwell four gods of great power, [possessing the splendor of a universal monarch] with a lifespan of one palyopama, namely: Gōthūbha, Siva, Saṅkha, and Maṇōsilā.

To the north-east, south-east, north-west, and south-west of the outer boundary wall of Jambūdvīpa, having entered forty-two thousand yojanas into the Lavaṇa Ocean, there are four mountain-dwellings of the four Anuvelandhara Naga kings, namely: Kakkoḍaya, Vijjuppabha, Kailāsa, and Aruṇappabha. Therein dwell four gods of great power, [possessing all the divine attributes] up to a lifespan of one palyopama, namely: Kakkoḍaya, Kaddama, Kailāsa, and Aruṇappabha.

In the salt ocean, four moons have shone, do shine, or will shine; four suns have blazed, do blaze, or will blaze; [the lunar mansions] from Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, four fires, up to four Yamas, four Aṅgāras, up to four Bhāvaketus. Four gates of the salt ocean are declared, namely: Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, and Aparājita. These gates are declared to be four yojanas in width and the same in depth. Therein dwell four gods of great power, up to a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely: Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, and Aparājita.

The island of Ghātakhaṇḍa is declared to be four hundred thousand yojanas in circumference; outside of the island of Jambūdvīpa, there are four Bharatas and four Airāvatas. Just as it was described in detail in the Saddaśeṣaka, so too should it be stated here in its entirety, up to the four Mandaras and the four Mandara-cūlikās.

In the exact center of the circular perimeter of the island of Nandīśvaravaradvīpa, in the four cardinal directions, there are four Añjana mountains described, namely: the eastern Añjana mountain, the southern Añjana mountain, the western Añjana mountain, and the northern Añjana mountain. These Añjana mountains are eighty-four thousand *yojanas* in height and one thousand *yojanas* in depth. At their base, they are ten thousand *yojanas* in width; thereafter, gradually decreasing, they are at the top one thousand *yojanas* in width. At the base, they are thirty-one thousand six hundred and twenty-three *yojanas* in circumference; at the top, they are three thousand six hundred and sixty-six *yojanas* in circumference. They are broad at the base, narrow in the middle, and slender at the top, shaped like a cow’s tail (*gopuccha*). They consist entirely of Añjana stone, are clear, smooth, glossy, polished, refined, stainless, pure, free from impurities, with unblemished luster, radiant, brilliant, luminous, beautiful, lovely to behold, handsome, and perfect in form. On the tops of these Añjana mountains, very level and delightful ground-sites are described. In the exact center of those very level and delightful ground-sites, four Siddhāyatana (shrines of the perfected ones) are described. These Siddhāyatanas are one hundred *yojanas* in length, fifty *yojanas* in width, and seventy-two *yojanas* in height. In the four cardinal directions of these Siddhāyatanas, four gates are described, namely: the Deva gate, the Asura gate, the Nāga gate, and the Suvarṇa gate. In these gates dwell four kinds of deities, namely: Devas, Asuras, Nāgas, and Suvarṇas. In front of these gates, four entrance-halls (*mukhamaṇḍapa*) are described. In front of these entrance-halls, four viewing-hall pavilions (*prekṣāgṛhamaṇḍapa*) are described. In the exact center of these viewing-hall pavilions, four diamond-studded wrestling-grounds (*vajramayā akkhāḍā*) are described. In the exact center of these diamond-studded wrestling-grounds, four jeweled pedestals (*maṇipīṭhikā*) are described. Above these jeweled pedestals, four lion-thrones are described. Above these lion-thrones, four victory-banners (*vijayadūṣya*) are described. In the exact center of these victory-banners, four diamond-studded hooks (*vajramayā aṅkuśā*) are described. On these diamond-studded hooks, four *kumbhika* pearl-garlands are described. Each of these *kumbhika* pearl-garlands is surrounded on all sides by four half-*kumbhika* pearl-garlands, each of which is half the height of the former. In front of these viewing-hall pavilions, four jeweled pedestals are described. Above these jeweled pedestals, four shrine-stūpas (*caityastūpa*) are described. Around each of these shrine-stūpas, in the four cardinal directions, four jeweled pedestals are described. Above these jeweled pedestals, four Jina images made of all kinds of jewels are situated in the lotus posture (*sampaliyaṅkanisanna*), facing the stūpas, namely: Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, Candrānana, and Vāriṣeṇa. In front of these shrine-stūpas, four jeweled pedestals are described. Above these jeweled pedestals, four shrine-trees (*caityavṛkṣa*) are described. In front of these shrine-trees, four jeweled pedestals are described. Above these jeweled pedestals, four Mahendra banners are described. In front of these Mahendra banners, four Nandā lotus-pools are described. Around each of these lotus-pools, in the four cardinal directions, four forest groves are described, namely: in the east, south, west, and north.
To the east is the Aśoka grove, to the south is the Saptaparṇa grove, to the west is the Campaka grove, and on the northern side is the Mango grove. (Ṭhāṇa 328)

Therein, on that eastern Añjana mountain, four Nanda lotus-ponds are described in the four directions, namely: Nandottarā, Nandā, Ānandā, and Nandivardhanā. These Nanda lotus-ponds are one hundred thousand *yojanas* in length, fifty thousand *yojanas* in width, and ten hundred *yojanas* in depth. On each side of these lotus-ponds, in the four directions, four triple-staircase structures are described. In front of those triple-staircase structures, four archways (*toraṇas*) are described, namely: in the east, south, west, and north. On each side of these lotus-ponds, in the four directions, four groves (*vanaṣaṇḍas*) are described, namely: in the east, south, west, and north. In the exact center of these lotus-ponds, four Curd-Face (*dadhimukha*) mountains are described. Those Curd-Face mountains are sixty-four thousand *yojanas* in height, one thousand *yojanas* in depth, level everywhere, shaped like a plowshare, ten thousand *yojanas* in width, and thirty-one thousand six hundred twenty-four *yojanas* in circumference. They are composed entirely of jewels, transparent, and so forth, up to "exquisite. On top of those Curd-Face mountains, very level and delightful ground-areas are described; the rest is to be recited exactly as for the Añjana mountains, without omission, up to the Mango Grove on the northern side. Therein, on that southern Añjana mountain, four Nanda lotus-ponds are described in the four directions, namely: Bhadrā, Viśālā, Kumudā, and Puṇḍarīkiṇī.
