These Nanda lotus-ponds are one hundred thousand *yojanas* [in length], and the rest is the same as before, up to the Curd-Face mountains and the groves. Therein, on that western Añjana mountain, four Nanda lotus-ponds are described in the four directions, namely: Nandiṣeṇā, Amoghā, Gostūmā, and Sudarśanā. The rest is the same as before; likewise the Curd-Face mountains, likewise the Siddhāyatana shrines, up to the groves. Therein, on that northern Añjana mountain, four Nanda lotus-ponds are described in the four directions, namely: Vijayā, Vaijayantī, Jayantī, and Aparājitā. These Nanda lotus-ponds are one hundred thousand *yojanas* [in length], and the rest is the same as before regarding their dimensions; likewise the Curd-Face mountains, likewise the Siddhāyatana shrines, up to the groves.

In the middle portion of the circumference of the island of Nandīśvaravaradvīpa, in the four intermediate directions, there are four pleasure-mountains (*ratikara-ga-parvata*) described, namely: the pleasure-mountain in the northeast, the pleasure-mountain in the southeast, the pleasure-mountain in the southwest, and the pleasure-mountain in the northwest. These pleasure-mountains are ten hundred *yojanas* (1,000 *yojanas*) in height, ten *gavyūta*-hundreds (100 *gavyūtas*) in depth, equal everywhere, and shaped like a drum (*jhallari*). They are ten thousand *yojanas* in width and thirty-six hundred and twenty-four *yojanas* (36,240 *yojanas*) in circumference. They are made entirely of jewels, clear, and so forth, up to "exquisite. Therein, as for that pleasure-mountain in the northeast, in its four directions, there are four royal capitals (*rājadhānī*) equal in size to Jambūdvīpa belonging to the four chief queens of Īśāna, the lord of gods and king of gods, namely: Nandottarā, Nandā, Uttarakurā, and Devakurā; [belonging to] Kṛṣṇā, Kṛṣṇarājī, Rāmā, and Rāmarakṣitā. Therein, as for that pleasure-mountain in the southeast, in its four directions, there are four royal capitals equal in size to Jambūdvīpa belonging to the four chief queens of Śakra, the lord of gods and king of gods, namely: Śramaṇā, Saumanasā, Arcirmālī, and Manoramā; [belonging to] Padmā, Śivā, Satī, and Añjū. Therein, as for that pleasure-mountain in the southwest, in its four directions, there are four royal capitals equal in size to Jambūdvīpa belonging to the four chief queens of Śakra, the lord of gods and king of gods, namely: Bhūtā, Bhūtāvataṃsā, Gothūbhā, and Sundarasanā; [belonging to] Amalā, Accharā, Navamikā, and Rohiṇī.

Therein, on that Ratikara mountain situated to the north-west, there are four royal capitals, equal in size to Jambudvīpa, belonging to the four chief queens of Īśāna, the lord of gods and king of the gods; they are as follows: Rayanā, Ratanuccayā, Savvarayaṇā, and Ratanasañcayā; and Vasuē, Vasuguttāē, Vasumittāē, and Vasundharāē.
Fourfold is truth (sacca); it is thus: name-truth (nāmasacca), representation-truth (ṭhavaṇasacca), substance-truth (davvasacca), and state-truth (bhāvasacca).
The austerity of the Ājīvikas is declared to be fourfold, namely: fierce austerity, terrible austerity, the extraction of the tongue, and the withdrawal of the faculty of taste.

Restraint is declared to be fourfold, namely: restraint of mind, restraint of speech, restraint of body, and restraint of requisites. Accumulation is declared to be fourfold, namely: accumulation of mind, accumulation of speech, accumulation of body, and accumulation of requisites.
Fourfold non-possession is taught, namely: non-possession of mind, non-possession of speech, non-possession of body, and non-possession of requisites.

Four types of rivers are taught, namely: the mountain river, the earth river, the sand river, and the water river. In the same way, fourfold anger is taught, namely: that which is like a mountain river, that which is like an earth river, that which is like a sand river, and that which is like a water river. A living being who dies while possessed by anger like a mountain river is reborn among the denizens of hell. A living being who dies while possessed by anger like an earth river is reborn in the animal realm. A living being who dies while possessed by anger like a sand river is reborn among human beings. A living being who dies while possessed by anger like a water river is reborn among the gods.

Four types of water are taught, namely: muddy water, turbid water, sandy water, and rocky water. In the same way, four kinds of dispositions (*bhāva*) are taught, namely: that which is similar to muddy water, that which is similar to turbid water, that which is similar to sandy water, and that which is similar to rocky water. A soul that dies having entered into a disposition similar to muddy water is reborn among the denizens of hell (*nairayika*). Likewise, up to: a soul that dies having entered into a disposition similar to rocky water is reborn among the gods (*deva*).

Four types of birds are taught, as follows: one that is endowed with song but not endowed with beauty; one that is endowed with beauty but not endowed with song; one that is both endowed with song and endowed with beauty; and one that is neither endowed with song nor endowed with beauty. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, as follows: one who is endowed with song but not endowed with beauty—[and so on for the other three]. Four types of persons are taught, as follows: one who, when asked to give testimony, gives testimony; one who, when asked to give testimony, does not give testimony; one who, when asked not to give testimony, gives testimony; and one who, when asked not to give testimony, does not give testimony. Four types of persons are taught, as follows: one who gives testimony concerning himself but not concerning another; one who gives testimony concerning another but not concerning himself; one who gives testimony concerning both himself and another; and one who gives testimony concerning neither himself nor another.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who, saying "I shall enter with trust," enters with trust; one who, saying "I shall enter with trust," enters without trust—[these four]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who enters with trust regarding his own name, but not that of another—[these four].

There are four kinds of trees, namely: those that provide leaves, those that provide flowers, those that provide fruit, and those that provide shade. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, as follows: one who is like a tree providing leaves, one who is like a tree providing flowers, one who is like a tree providing fruit, and one who is like a tree providing shade.

For one carrying a burden, four refreshments are prescribed, as follows: when he shifts the burden from one shoulder to the other, that is prescribed as one refreshment for him; when he voids excrement or urine, that too is prescribed as one refreshment for him; when he goes to dwell in a residence of the Nāgakumāras or a residence of the Suvarṇakumāras, that too is prescribed as one refreshment for him; and when he stands until the end of his task, that too is prescribed as one refreshment for him.

In the same way, four consolations are declared for a lay follower (*śrāvaka*). They are as follows: First, wherever he undertakes the vows of morality (*śīla*), the vows of virtue (*guṇavrata*), the prohibitions (*viramaṇa*), renunciations (*pratyākhyāna*), and the fasting observances (*poṣadhopavāsa*), there too one consolation is declared for him. Second, wherever he correctly observes the *sāmāyika* (equanimity) and the *deśāvakāśika* (restricted activity), there too one consolation is declared for him. Third, wherever he correctly observes the complete *poṣadha* on the fourteenth, eighth, and full moon days, there too one consolation is declared for him. Fourth, wherever he correctly observes the complete *poṣadha* on the fourteenth, eighth, and the specific full moon days, there too one consolation is declared for him. Fifth, wherever he dwells having practiced the refinement of the body through the final mortification at the end of life, having renounced food and drink, having entered the state of total withdrawal (*pāovagama*), and not longing for further time, there too one consolation is declared for him.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is risen and has risen; one who is risen and has set; one who has set and has risen; and one who has set and has set. King Bharata, the universal monarch of the four continents, is "risen and risen"; King Bambhadatta, the universal monarch of the four continents, is "risen and set"; the ascetic Hariesabala is "set and risen"; and Kāla the Śoṇāyanin is "set and set."

Four groups (jummā) are taught, namely: the black group (kaḍajumma), the white group (tēōya), the mixed group (dāvarajumma), and the grey group (kaliōya). Four groups are taught for the hell-beings (nēraïyā), namely: the black group, the white group, the mixed group, and the grey group. Thus it is for the asura-kumāras up to the stanita-kumāras; likewise for the earth-bodied beings, water-bodied, fire-bodied, air-bodied, and plant-bodied beings; for two-sensed, three-sensed, and four-sensed beings; for five-sensed animals, humans, the Vāṇamantara gods, the Jyotiṣka gods, and the Vaimānika gods—for all of them, just as for the hell-beings.

Four types of heroes are taught, namely: the hero of forbearance, the hero of austerity, the hero of generosity, and the hero of battle. The Arhats are heroes of forbearance; the houseless ascetics (anagāras) are heroes of austerity; Vaiśramaṇa is a hero of generosity; and Vāsudeva is a hero of battle. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is high by birth but low in inclination; one who is high by birth but low in inclination; one who is low by birth but high in inclination; and one who is low by birth and low in inclination.

The Asurakumāras are declared to have four leśyās, namely: black leśyā (kaṇha), blue leśyā (nīla), grey leśyā (kāu), and fiery leśyā (teu). Thus it is for all [beings] up to the Stanitakumāras; likewise for the earth-bodied beings, water-bodied beings, plant-bodied beings, and the Vānamantaras—all of them are as with the Asurakumāras.

Four types of vehicles are taught, namely: one vehicle that is yoked is indeed yoked; one vehicle that is yoked is not yoked; one vehicle that is not yoked is yoked; and one vehicle that is not yoked is not yoked. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one person who is yoked is indeed yoked; one person who is yoked is not yoked; one person who is not yoked is yoked; and one person who is not yoked is not yoked.

Four types of vehicles are taught, namely: one that is yoked and has been yoked for travel; one that is yoked but has not been yoked for travel; [and the other two]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is yoked and has been yoked for practice; [and so on].

Four types of vehicles are taught, namely: one that is yoked and has a yoked appearance; one that is yoked but has an unyoked appearance; one that is unyoked but has a yoked appearance; and one that is unyoked and has an unyoked appearance. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is yoked and has a yoked appearance; [and so on].

Four types of carriages are taught, namely: one that is yoked and beautiful, one that is yoked but not beautiful—thus four. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is yoked and beautiful—thus four.

Four types of draft animals are taught, namely: one that is yoked and yoked, one that is yoked but not yoked—thus four. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is yoked and yoked—thus four.

Just as there are four statements regarding the *jñāna* (knowledge), so too are there four regarding the *yuga* (yoke). The opposites are exactly the same, from the types of men (*purisajāta*) up to "splendor" (*sōbha*). Four types of charioteers (*sārathi*) are taught, namely: one who yokes but does not cause to unyoke; one who causes to unyoke but does not yoke; one who both yokes and causes to unyoke; and one who neither yokes nor causes to unyoke. In the very same way, four types of persons (*purisajāta*) are taught, namely: one who yokes but does not cause to unyoke—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four types of horses are taught, namely: one that is yoked and is indeed yoked; one that is yoked but is not yoked; [and so on for the remaining two]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is yoked and is indeed yoked; [and so on for the remaining three]. Likewise, there are those who are yoked-perfected, yoked-formed, and yoked-beautiful; for all of these, there are corresponding types of persons as their opposites.

Four types of elephants are taught, namely: one that is yoked is indeed yoked, one that is yoked is not yoked, and so on, up to four [combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is yoked is indeed yoked, and so on, up to four. Just as it was stated regarding horses, so too should it be recited for elephants; the opposites are likewise the types of persons.

Four types of travelers are taught, namely: one who is a traveler on the path but not on a bypath; one who is a traveler on a bypath but not on the path; one who is both a traveler on the path and on a bypath; and one who is neither a traveler on the path nor on a bypath. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a traveler on the path but not on a bypath—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four kinds of flowers are taught, namely: one that is endowed with beauty but not endowed with fragrance; one that is endowed with fragrance but not endowed with beauty; one that is endowed with both beauty and fragrance; and one that is neither endowed with beauty nor endowed with fragrance. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with beauty but not endowed with virtue—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth but not with noble lineage; one who is endowed with noble lineage but not with noble birth—[these four]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with noble birth but not with strength; one who is endowed with strength but not with noble birth—[these four].

In this manner, there are four discourses on birth with respect to form (4); likewise, four on birth with respect to learning (4); likewise, four on birth with respect to conduct (4); likewise, four on birth with respect to character (4). Likewise, there are four on family with respect to strength (4); likewise, four on family with respect to form (4); four on family with respect to learning (4); four on family with respect to conduct (4); and four on family with respect to character (4). Four types of persons are taught, namely: one endowed with strength but not endowed with form; [and so on for the other three combinations]—making four. Likewise, there are four on strength with respect to learning (4); likewise, four on strength with respect to conduct (4); and likewise, four on strength with respect to character (4).

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with beauty but not with learning; [and so on for four combinations]. Likewise, [four] with respect to beauty and conduct; [and so on for four combinations]. [Four] with respect to beauty and character; [and so on for four combinations]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with learning but not with conduct; [and so on for four combinations]. Likewise, [four] with respect to scripture and conduct; [and so on for four combinations]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is endowed with conduct but not with character; [and so on for four combinations]. These twenty-one permutations (bhaṅgas) are to be recited.

Four kinds of fruits are taught, namely: the sweet amala fruit, the sweet grape, the sweet milk, and the sweet sugar-candy. In the same way, four kinds of teachers are taught, namely: those equal to the sweet amala fruit, up to those equal to the sweet sugar-candy fruit.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who performs services for himself but not for others; one who performs services for others but not for himself; one who performs services both for himself and for others; and one who performs services neither for himself nor for others. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who performs service but does not receive it; one who receives service but does not perform it; [and so on for the remaining two]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who causes distress but does not cause pride; one who causes pride but does not cause distress; one who causes both distress and pride; and one who causes neither distress nor pride. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who causes distress to the group but does not cause pride [and so on for the remaining three]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who maintains the group but does not cause pride [and so on for the remaining three]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who beautifies the group but does not cause pride [and so on for the remaining three]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who purifies the group but does not cause pride [and so on for the remaining three].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who abandons outward form but not the Dharma; one who abandons the Dharma but not outward form; one who abandons both outward form and the Dharma; and one who abandons neither outward form nor the Dharma. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who abandons the Dharma but not membership in a community; one who abandons membership in a community but not the Dharma; [and so on for the remaining two].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who loves the Dharma but is not firm in the Dharma; one who is firm in the Dharma but does not love the Dharma; one who both loves the Dharma and is firm in the Dharma; and one who neither loves the Dharma nor is firm in the Dharma. Four types of preceptors are taught, namely: one who is a preceptor for ordination but not a preceptor for initiation; one who is a preceptor for initiation but not a preceptor for ordination; one who is both a preceptor for ordination and a preceptor for initiation; and one who is neither a preceptor for ordination nor a preceptor for initiation, but is a preceptor of the Dharma (*dhammāyariya*). Four types of preceptors are taught, namely: one who is a preceptor for recitation (*uddesa*) but not a preceptor for instruction (*vāyaṇa*); one who is a preceptor for instruction but not a preceptor for recitation; [and so on, up to: four [types of preceptors are taught, namely: one who is a preceptor for both recitation and instruction; and one who is neither a preceptor for recitation nor a preceptor for instruction]. (4)

Four types of disciples are taught, namely: some are disciples by initiation but not disciples by attendance—[the fourfold set]—disciples by the Dharma; four types of disciples are taught, namely: some are disciples by recitation but not disciples by instruction—[the fourfold set]—disciples by the Dharma.

Four types of *nirgrantha* ascetics have been described, namely: a senior (*rātinīya*) *śramaṇa* *nirgrantha* who possesses great karma and great activity, who is not self-disciplined and lacks restraint, and who does not become an achiever of the Dharma; a senior *śramaṇa* *nirgrantha* who possesses little karma and little activity, who is self-disciplined and restrained, and who becomes an achiever of the Dharma; a junior (*ōmarātinīya*) *śramaṇa* *nirgrantha* who possesses great karma and great activity, who is not self-disciplined and lacks restraint, and who does not become an achiever of the Dharma; and a junior *śramaṇa* *nirgrantha* who possesses little karma and little activity, who is self-disciplined and restrained, and who becomes an achiever of the Dharma.

Four types of female ascetics (nirgranthīs) are taught, namely: the female ascetic who is a householder’s wife (rātinī), who possesses great karma, great activity, is not free from deceit, is not restrained, and does not fulfill the Dharma; likewise—4.

Four types of male lay disciples (śramaṇopāsakas) are taught, namely: the male lay disciple who is a householder’s wife, who possesses great karma, great activity, is not free from deceit, is not restrained, and does not fulfill the Dharma; likewise—4.

Four types of female lay disciples (śramaṇopāsikās) are taught, namely: the female lay disciple who is a householder’s wife, who possesses great karma, great activity, is not free from deceit, and is not restrained; likewise, there are four [other] groups.

Four types of lay followers (*śramaṇopāsaka*) are taught, namely: those who are like parents, those who are like brothers, those who are like friends, and those who are like co-wives. Four types of lay followers are taught, namely: those who are like a mirror, those who are like a banner, those who are like a stump, and those who are like a thorny bush.
For the lay followers of the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, their lifespan is taught to be four *palyopamas* in the Aruṇābha celestial palace in the Saudharma realm.

There are four reasons why a god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods might wish to come quickly to the world of men, yet is unable to come quickly. They are as follows: (1) A god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods is infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and absorbed in divine sensual pleasures; he does not take interest in, does not recognize, does not form an attachment to, does not create a causal basis for, nor does he establish a fixed intention toward human sensual pleasures. (2) A god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods is infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and absorbed in divine sensual pleasures; his love for humans has ceased and has shifted toward the divine. (3) A god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods is infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and absorbed in divine sensual pleasures; it occurs to him: "I shall go now; I shall go in a moment. But by that time, humans have become short-lived and have met their end through the law of time. (4) A god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods is infatuated with, greedy for, attached to, and absorbed in divine sensual pleasures; human odors become repulsive and contrary to him, and even from above, human odors do not reach him quickly, extending only as far as four or five hundred *yojanas*. By these four reasons, a god who has recently been reborn in the worlds of the gods might wish to come quickly to the world of men, yet is unable to come quickly.

There are four circumstances by which a god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds might desire to come quickly to the world of men, and is indeed able to come quickly. They are as follows: (1) A god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds, being uninfatuated, ungreedy, unattached, and not obsessed by divine sensual pleasures, thinks to himself: "In my human existence, there were indeed teachers, preceptors, leaders, elders, heads of groups, holders of the scriptures, or directors of groups, through whose power I obtained, attained, and acquired this kind of divine splendor, divine radiance, and divine majesty. Therefore, I shall go to those Blessed Ones to pay homage, to bow down, to honor, to respect, and to attend upon them as auspicious, auspicious, divine, and venerable objects. (2) A god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds... [as above] ...up to... not obsessed, thinks to himself: "In that human existence, there was one who was a man of knowledge or an ascetic, a performer of exceedingly difficult penances. Therefore, I shall go to those Blessed Ones to pay homage... up to... attend upon them. (3) A god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds... [as above] ...up to... not obsessed, thinks to himself: "In my human existence, there were indeed mothers... up to... daughters-in-law. Therefore, I shall go and appear before them so that they may see me with this kind of divine splendor, divine radiance, and divine majesty obtained, attained, and acquired. (4) A god who has recently been reborn in the celestial worlds... [as above] ...up to... not obsessed, thinks to himself: "In my human existence, there were indeed friends, companions, associates, or intimates, and we had made a mutual agreement: 'Whoever among us passes away first must inform the other. Because of these [reasons], he is able to come quickly."

There are four occasions on which the world becomes darkened: namely, when the Arhats are passing away; when the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats is passing away; when the Pūrvas are passing away; and when the Jātatejas are passing away.

There are four occasions on which the world becomes illuminated: namely, when the Arhats are being born; when the Arhats are going forth into the religious life; during the festivals for the arising of the knowledge of the Arhats; and during the festivals for the final liberation (parinirvāṇa) of the Arhats.

They come quickly to the human world; even as it is stated in the *Tiṭhāṇa*, up until: "The gods who have reached the end of the world may come quickly to the human world, namely, when Arhats are striving [for liberation], and so forth, up to the great festivals for the final nirvāṇa of the Arhats."

Four types of difficult beds (*duḥśayyā*) are taught, namely: First, regarding the first difficult bed: Here, one who has gone forth from the home to the homeless state after being shaven, having become a *nirgrantha* in the *pravacana*, yet is suspicious, wavering, possessed by doubt, overcome by fear, and possessed by turbidity; he does not have faith in the *nirgrantha* *pravacana*, does not trust it, and does not find pleasure in it. Not having faith, not trusting, and not finding pleasure in the *nirgrantha* *pravacana*, he directs his mind toward high and low things and falls into ruin. This is the first difficult bed. Furthermore, the second difficult bed: One who has gone forth from the home to the homeless state after being shaven, is not satisfied with his own gains, but covets, longs for, desires, and yearns for the gains of others. Coveting, longing for, desiring, and yearning for the gains of others, he directs his mind toward high and low things and falls into ruin. This is the second difficult bed. Furthermore, the third difficult bed: One who has gone forth from the home to the homeless state after being shaven, up to that point, covets, longs for, desires, and yearns for divine and human sensual pleasures (*kāma-bhoga*). Coveting, longing for, desiring, and yearning for divine and human sensual pleasures, he directs his mind toward high and low things and falls into ruin. This is the third difficult bed. Furthermore, the fourth difficult bed: One who has gone forth from the home to the homeless state after being shaven, thinks to himself: "When I lived in the household life, I received massages, rubdowns, body-anointings, and body-washes. But ever since I became a shaven ascetic and went forth, I no longer receive such massages and body-washes. He then covets, longs for, desires, and yearns for those massages and body-washes. Coveting, longing for, desiring, and yearning for those massages and body-washes, he directs his mind toward high and low things and falls into ruin. This is the fourth difficult bed.

Four types of comfortable beds (*suhasejjā*) have been declared, as follows: First, regarding the first comfortable bed: Here, one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness as a monk, having become shaven-headed, is free from doubt, free from hesitation, and free from indecision regarding the Nirgrantha doctrine; he is neither fallen into schism nor fallen into impurity. He believes in, trusts in, and finds pleasure in the Nirgrantha doctrine. While believing, trusting, and finding pleasure in the Nirgrantha doctrine, he does not direct his mind toward high or low [states], nor does he undergo destruction. This is the first comfortable bed. Now, the second comfortable bed: Here, one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness as a monk, having become shaven-headed, is satisfied with his own gains. He does not hope for, desire, long for, or crave the gains of others. Not hoping for, nor craving the gains of others, he does not direct his mind toward high or low states, nor does he undergo destruction. This is the second comfortable bed. Now, the third comfortable bed: Here, one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness as a monk, having become shaven-headed, does not hope for, nor crave divine or human sensual pleasures. Not hoping for, nor craving divine or human sensual pleasures, he does not direct his mind toward high or low states, nor does he undergo destruction. This is the third comfortable bed. Now, the fourth comfortable bed: Here, one who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness as a monk, having become shaven-headed, thinks thus: "If the Arhats, the Blessed Ones—who are healthy, disease-free, strong, and possessed of sound bodies—undertake various sublime, auspicious, extensive, strenuous, exalted, and highly powerful ascetic practices for the sake of destroying karma, how much more so should I endure, tolerate, bear, and withstand the internal and external pains that come upon me? Since I do not properly endure, tolerate, bear, or withstand these internal and external pains, what indeed will happen to me? [It will be] absolute ruin. (This concludes the section on the four comfortable beds.)

Four types of persons are declared who are unfit to teach: one who is undisciplined, one who is addicted to sensory luxuries, one who has not mastered the scriptures, and one who is deceitful. Four types of persons are declared who are fit to teach: one who is disciplined, one who is not addicted to sensory luxuries, one who has mastered the scriptures, and one who is free from deceit.

Four types of persons are declared: some are those who support only themselves and not others; some are those who support others and not themselves; some are those who support both themselves and others; and some are those who support neither themselves nor others.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is miserable and remains miserable; one who is miserable but becomes happy; one who is happy but remains miserable; and one who is happy and remains happy.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is miserable and has bad conduct; one who is miserable but has good conduct; one who is happy but has bad conduct; and one who is happy and has good conduct. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is miserable and finds it difficult to find rest; one who is miserable but finds it easy to find rest; [and so on for the remaining three]. (4)
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is unfortunate and destined for an unhappy state; one who is unfortunate but destined for a happy state; [and so on for the remaining two].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who was unfortunate and has gone to an unhappy state; one who was unfortunate but has gone to a happy state; [and so on for the remaining two]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is dark and remains dark; one who is dark but becomes luminous; one who is luminous but remains dark; and one who is luminous and remains luminous.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is dark and possesses the power of darkness; one who is dark but possesses the power of light; one who is light but possesses the power of darkness; and one who is light and possesses the power of light. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is dark and takes pride in the power of darkness; one who is dark but takes pride in the power of light—[the remaining two being] four.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who has comprehended karma but not the perception [of its nature]; one who has comprehended the perception but not the karma; and one who has comprehended both—[the remaining two being] four.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who has understood his karmic actions but not the household life; one who has understood the household life but not his karmic actions; one who has understood both; and one who has understood neither.
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who has understood his perceptions but not the household life; one who has understood the household life but not his perceptions; and so on, up to four.
Furthermore, four types of persons are taught, namely: one whose aim is this world but not the next; one whose aim is the next world but not this one; and so on, up to four.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one by name increases by one and decreases by one; one by name increases by two and decreases by two; one by name increases by one and decreases by two; and one by name increases by two and decreases by one.

Four types of thoroughbred horses are taught, namely: one that is a thoroughbred and is well-trained; one that is a thoroughbred but is a wild colt; one that is a wild colt but is well-trained; and one that is a wild colt and is a wild colt. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a thoroughbred and is well-trained; [and so on]—there are four permutations.

Four types of thoroughbred horses are taught, as follows: one that is a thoroughbred and carries in the manner of a thoroughbred; one that is a thoroughbred but carries in the manner of a wild horse. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, as follows: one who is a thoroughbred and carries in the manner of a thoroughbred; [and so on,] there are four permutations.

Four types of crossroads are taught, namely: one who is well-born but not of noble family; one who is of noble family but not well-born; [the other two completing the fourfold set]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is well-born but not of noble family; [and so on for the four permutations]. Four types of crossroads are taught, namely: one who is well-born but not strong; [and so on for the four permutations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is well-born but not strong; [and so on for the four permutations].

Four types of crossroads are taught, namely: one that is well-endowed with its birthplace but not well-endowed with beauty—[and so on for the other three combinations]—making four. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is well-endowed with his lineage but not well-endowed with beauty—[and so on for the other three combinations]—making four.

Four types of crossroads are taught, namely: one that is well-endowed with its birthplace but not well-endowed with victory—[and so on for the other three combinations]—making four. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is well-endowed with his lineage but not well-endowed with victory—[and so on for the other three combinations]—making four.

Thus, there are four types of persons endowed with noble birth but not with strength; four types endowed with noble birth but not with beauty; four types endowed with noble birth but not with victory; and likewise, four types endowed with strength but not with beauty; and four types endowed with strength but not with victory. (4) In all these cases, the categories of persons are opposites. There are four types of persons regarding the throat [or the neck], namely: one who is endowed with beauty but not with victory, and so on, up to four; even so, there are four types of persons, namely: one who is endowed with beauty but not with victory, and so on, up to four.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who, having gone forth as a lion, dwells as a lion; one who, having gone forth as a lion, dwells as a jackal; one who, having gone forth as a jackal, dwells as a lion; and one who, having gone forth as a jackal, dwells as a jackal.

Four things in the world are declared to be equal, namely: the Apratiṣṭhāna hell, Jambūdvīpa island, the Pālaka celestial vehicle, and the Sarvārthasiddha great celestial palace. Four things in the world are declared to be equal in their respective directions and intermediate directions, namely: the Sīmantaka hell, the Samaya-kṣetra (the field of time), the Uḍu celestial vehicle, and the Isīpabbhārā earth.

In the upper world, four types of bodies are taught, namely: earth-bodied beings, water-bodied beings, plant-bodied beings, and gross mobile living beings. In the lower world, four types of bodies are taught, namely: earth-bodied beings, and so forth, exactly as before. Likewise in the intermediate world—[four each].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one whose strength is modesty (*hirisatta*), one whose strength is the mind of modesty (*hirimaṇasatta*), one whose strength is wavering (*calasatta*), and one whose strength is firm (*thirasatta*).
Four postures for the bed are taught; four postures for clothing are taught; four postures for the alms-bowl are taught; four postures for standing are taught.

Four bodies are taught as being in contact with the soul (*jīva*); namely: the transformation body (*vaikriyika*), the assimilative body (*āhāraka*), the fiery body (*taijasa*), and the karmic body (*kārmaṇa*). Four bodies are taught as being mixed with karma; namely: the gross body (*audārika*), the transformation body, the assimilative body, and the fiery body. The world is taught as being pervaded by four substantial entities (*astikāya*); namely: the substance of motion (*dharmāstikāya*), the substance of rest (*adharmāstikāya*), the substance of souls, and the substance of matter (*pudgalāstikāya*). The world is taught as being pervaded by beings taking birth in four coarse categories of organisms; namely: earth-bodied beings, water-bodied beings, air-bodied beings, and plant-bodied beings.

Four things are declared to be equal in terms of spatial extension: the substance of motion (dharma-astikāya), the substance of rest (adharma-astikāya), the space of the world (loka-ākāśa), and a single soul (eka-jīva). The body of four types of beings is not easily perceived: that of the earth-bodied (pṛthvī-kāyika), the water-bodied (ap-kāyika), the fire-bodied (tejas-kāyika), and the plant-bodied (vanaspati-kāyika).

Four types of sensory objects, when contacted, are experienced: the object of the sense of hearing, the object of the sense of smell, the object of the sense of taste, and the object of the sense of touch.

By four causes, living beings and matter are unable to go beyond the limits of the world; namely: due to the absence of motion, due to the lack of support, due to dryness, and due to the inherent nature of the world.

There are four kinds of *nāta* (exemplification) taught, namely: *āharaṇa* (the example itself), *āharaṇataddesa* (the partial example), *āharaṇataddosa* (the defective example), and *uvaṇṇāsōvaṇaya* (the illustrative application). *Āharaṇa* is taught as being fourfold, namely: *avāya* (the refutation), *uvāya* (the proof), *ṭhavaṇākamma* (the establishment of the thesis), and *paḍuppaṇṇavināsī* (that which perishes as soon as it arises). *Āharaṇataddesa* is taught as being fourfold, namely: *aṇusiṭṭhī* (instruction), *uvālambha* (reproach), *pucchā* (inquiry), and *nissāvayana* (causing to flow out/extraction). *Āharaṇataddosa* is taught as being fourfold, namely: *adhammajutta* (unrighteous), *paḍilōbha* (deceptive), *attōvaṇīta* (self-applied), and *duruvaṇīta* (ill-applied). *Uvaṇṇāsōvaṇaya* is taught as being fourfold, namely: *tavvatthuta* (praise of that very thing), *tavaṇṇatthuta* (praise of its qualities), *paḍiṇibha* (analogy), and *hetu* (reason). *Hetu* is taught as being fourfold, namely: *jāvae* (that which causes birth), *thāvae* (that which causes stability), *vaṁsaē* (that which causes lineage), and *lūsaē* (that which causes destruction). Alternatively, *hetu* is taught as being fourfold, namely: *paccakkha* (direct perception), *anumāna* (inference), *ōvamma* (analogy), and *āgama* (scriptural authority). Alternatively, *hetu* is taught as being fourfold, namely: existence exists, that is a *hetu*; existence does not exist, that is a *hetu*; non-existence exists, that is a *hetu*; non-existence does not exist, that is a *hetu*.
Fourfold is calculation taught; namely: computation (*parikamma*), practical application (*vavahāra*), the cord (*rajju*), and the heap (*rāsī*).

In the lower world, four things produce darkness: namely—hells, hell-beings, evil karmas, and impure matter-particles. In the middle world, four things produce light: namely—the moon, the sun, jewels, and fire. In the upper world, four things produce light: namely—gods, goddesses, celestial palaces (*vimāna*), and ornaments.

Four types of pursuit are taught, namely: one pursues by producing enjoyments not yet arisen; one pursues by not being separated from enjoyments already arisen; one pursues by producing happinesses not yet arisen; and one pursues by not being separated from happinesses already arisen.
Fourfold food is taught for hell-beings, namely: like glowing coals, like embers, cold, and as cold as ice.

Four kinds of food are prescribed for animals of the animal realm (*tirikkhajōṇiya*): namely, the consumption of dung (*kaṅkōvama*), the consumption of soil (*bilōvama*), the consumption of the flesh of relatives by name (*nāmamaṁsōvama*), and the consumption of the flesh of one's own offspring (*puttamaṁsōvama*).

Four kinds of food are prescribed for humans: namely, solid food (*asaṇa*), drinks (*pāṇa*), chewed food (*khāima*), and tasted food (*sāima*). Four kinds of food are prescribed for gods: namely, possessing color (*vaṇṇamanta*), possessing fragrance (*gandhamanta*), possessing taste (*rasamanta*), and possessing touch (*phāsamanta*).

Four types of venomous beings by birth (*jātiāsīvisa*) are prescribed: namely, the scorpion species of venomous beings, the frog species of venomous beings, the serpent species of venomous beings, and the human species of venomous beings.

“Venerable sir, what is the extent of the range of a scorpion-type venomous snake? A scorpion-type venomous snake is capable of making its body as large as half of Bhārata, transforming it with venom so that it expands; yet this is merely its range for expansion—it has not, does not, nor will it ever actually do so. Venerable sir, what is the extent of the range of a frog-type venomous snake? A frog-type venomous snake is capable of making its body as large as the whole of Bhārata, transforming it with venom so that it expands... [the rest] is exactly the same, up to ‘nor will it ever do so. Question regarding the serpent-type: A serpent-type venomous snake is capable of making its body as large as Jambudvīpa, transforming it with venom... [the rest] is exactly the same, up to ‘nor will it ever do so. Question regarding the human-type: A human-type venomous snake is capable of making its body as large as the entire *samaya*-kṣetra (the inhabited world), transforming it with venom so that it expands; yet this is merely its range for expansion—it has not, does not, nor will it ever actually do so.”
Disease is declared to be fourfold; namely: wind-born, bile-born, phlegm-born, and combined (sannivātie).
Medical treatment is declared to be fourfold; namely: the physician, medicines, the patient, and the attendant.
Four types of physicians are declared; namely: one who treats himself but not others; one who treats others but not himself; [and so on for the remaining two].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a wound-maker but not a reviler of wounds; one who is a reviler of wounds but not a wound-maker; one who is both a wound-maker and a reviler of wounds; and one who is neither a wound-maker nor a reviler of wounds. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a wound-maker but not a protector of wounds—[the same fourfold formula applies].
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a wound-maker but not a healer of wounds—[the same fourfold formula applies].

Four types of wounds are taught, namely: one that has a thorn within but no thorn without; [and so on for the other three combinations]. Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who has a thorn within but no thorn without; [and so on for the other three combinations].

Four types of wounds are taught, namely: one that is corrupt within but not corrupt without; one that is corrupt without but not corrupt within; [and so on for the other two combinations]. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is corrupt within but not corrupt without; [and so on for the other three combinations].

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is fortunate but is known as fortunate; one who is fortunate but is known as unfortunate; one who is unfortunate but is known as fortunate; and one who is unfortunate and is known as unfortunate.
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is fortunate and is similar to one who is fortunate; one who is fortunate and is similar to one who is unfortunate—[and so on for the remaining two].
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is fortunate and considers himself fortunate; one who is fortunate and considers himself unfortunate—[and so on for the remaining two].
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is virtuous and considers himself virtuous; one who is virtuous but considers himself sinful—these four.
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who proclaims [the truth] but does not practice it; one who practices it but does not proclaim it—these four.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who proclaims [the truth] but is not endowed with the livelihood of gleaning; one who is endowed with the livelihood of gleaning but does not proclaim [the truth]—these four.
The fourfold multiplication of trees is taught as follows: in the form of shoots, leaves, flowers, and fruits.

Four assemblies of disputants are taught, namely: the proponents of action (kriyāvādins), the proponents of non-action (akriyāvādins), the proponents of ignorance (ajñānavādins), and the proponents of chance (vainayikavādins).

For hell-beings, four assemblies of disputants are taught, namely: the proponents of action up to the proponents of chance; likewise for the asura-kumāras, and so on up to the stanitakumāras; and thus for all [beings] except those with fewer than five senses, up to the vaimānikas.

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: some that thunder but do not rain; some that rain but do not thunder; some that both thunder and rain; and some that neither thunder nor rain. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: some who thunder but do not rain—[and so on, up to] four.

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: some that thunder but do not flash, some that flash but do not thunder, [and so on for the other two combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: some who thunder but do not flash, [and so on for the other three combinations].

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: some that rain but do not flash, some that flash but do not rain, [and so on for the other two combinations]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: some who rain but do not flash, [and so on for the other three combinations].

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: one that rains at the proper time but not at the improper time; one that rains at the improper time but not at the proper time; [the remaining two combinations]; and one that rains neither at the proper time nor at the improper time. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who rains at the proper time but not at the improper time; [the remaining two combinations]; and one who rains neither at the proper time nor at the improper time.

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: one that rains in a field but not in a non-field; one that rains in a non-field but not in a field; [the remaining two combinations]; and one that rains neither in a field nor in a non-field. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who rains in a field but not in a non-field; [the remaining two combinations]; and one who rains neither in a field nor in a non-field.

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: one that produces [rain] but does not create [it], one that creates but does not produce, and so on—making four. In the same way, four types of parents are taught, namely: one who gives birth but does not fashion [the child], one who fashions but does not give birth, and so on—making four.

Four types of clouds are taught, namely: one that rains locally but not everywhere, one that rains everywhere but not locally, and so on—making four. In the same way, four types of kings are taught, namely: one who rules over a region but not over everything, one who rules over everything but not a region, and so on—making four.

Four types of clouds are proclaimed, namely: Pukkhalasaṃvaṭṭa, Pajjuṇṇa, Jīmūta, and Jimha. The great cloud Pukkhalasaṃvaṭṭa nourishes [the earth] for ten thousand years with a single rainfall; the great cloud Pajjuṇṇa nourishes it for one thousand years with a single rainfall; the great cloud Jīmūta nourishes it for ten years with a single rainfall; and the great cloud Jimha nourishes it for a single year through many rainfalls, or perhaps does not nourish it at all.

Four types of baskets are taught, namely: the basket of a *śvapāka* (outcaste), the basket of a *vaiśika* (courtesan), the basket of a householder, and the basket of a king. In the same way, four types of teachers are taught, namely: one who is like the basket of a *śvapāka*, one who is like the basket of a *vaiśika*, one who is like the basket of a householder, and one who is like the basket of a king.

Four kinds of trees are taught, namely: one called a *sāla* tree which has a *sāla* as its surrounding, one called a *sāla* tree which has an *eraṇḍa* as its surrounding, one called an *eraṇḍa* tree which has a *sāla* as its surrounding, and one called an *eraṇḍa* tree which has an *eraṇḍa* as its surrounding. In the same way, four kinds of teachers are taught, namely: one called a *sāla* teacher who has a *sāla*-like following, one called a *sāla* teacher who has an *eraṇḍa*-like following, [and so on for the remaining two].

Four types of trees are taught, namely: some called *sāla* have a *sāla* retinue; some called *sāla* have an *eraṇḍa* retinue; [and so on for the remaining two]. In the same way, four types of teachers are taught, namely: some called *sāla* have a *sāla* retinue; some called *sāla* have an *eraṇḍa* retinue; [and so on for the remaining two].
Just as a king of trees named *sāla* may stand in the midst of a *sāla* grove, even so should a beautiful teacher with beautiful disciples be understood. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 372)
Just as a king of trees called the *sāla* might be found in the midst of castor-oil plants (*eraṇḍa*),
so too should the teacher Sundara be understood as a "king of disciples" among those of ill conduct.
(Ṭhāṇa 373) Conversely, a king of trees called the castor-oil plant might be found in the midst of *sāla* trees.
Thus, one should understand the "inauspicious teacher" (maṅgula-ācārya) as the head of the Sundarī [sect]. Ṭhāṇa 374.
Just as in the midst of castor-oil plants there is a king of trees named the castor-oil plant, so too should one understand the "inauspicious teacher" as the head of the Maṅgula [sect]. Ṭhāṇa 375.

Four types of fish are taught, namely: one that moves with the current, one that moves against the current, one that moves along the edge, and one that moves in the middle. In the same way, four types of alms-seekers are taught, namely: one who moves with the current, one who moves against the current, one who moves along the edge, and one who moves in the middle.

Four kinds of balls are taught, namely: a ball of honey and flour, a ball of molasses, a ball of wood, and a ball of clay. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: those similar to a ball of honey and flour—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of balls are taught, namely: an iron ball, a copper ball, a brass ball, and a silver ball. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is like an iron ball, up to one who is like a silver ball. Four types of balls are taught, namely: a gold ball, a silver ball, a jewel ball, and a diamond ball. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is like a gold ball, up to one who is like a diamond ball.

Four kinds of leaf-baskets are taught, namely: the sword-leaf basket, the hand-leaf basket, the razor-leaf basket, and the *kalambacīriyā* leaf basket. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is like the sword-leaf basket, up to one who is like the *kalambacīriyā* leaf basket. Four kinds of baskets are taught, namely: the wicker-basket, the split-bamboo basket, the leather basket, and the woolen blanket basket. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is like the wicker-basket, up to one who is like the woolen blanket basket.
Fourfold are the four-footed beings taught; namely: those with solid hooves, those with cloven hooves, those with webbed feet, and those with claws.
Fourfold are the winged beings taught; namely: those with leather wings, those with feathered wings, those with folded wings, and those with outspread wings.
Fourfold are the small creatures taught; namely: two-sensed, three-sensed, four-sensed, and spontaneously born five-sensed animals.

Four types of birds are taught, namely: some that have descended but not circled; some that have circled but not descended; some that have both descended and circled; and some that have neither descended nor circled. In the very same way, four types of mendicants are taught, namely: some who have descended but not circled; some who have circled but not descended; [and so on]—four.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is both expelled and [of] an expelled nature; one who is expelled but [of] an unexpelled nature; one who is unexpelled but [of] an expelled nature; and one who is both unexpelled and [of] an unexpelled nature.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is expelled and has an expelled self; one who is expelled but has an unexpelled self; one who is unexpelled but has an expelled self; and one who is unexpelled and has an unexpelled self.

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wise and lives wisely; one who is wise but does not live wisely; one who is unwise but lives wisely; and one who is unwise and does not live wisely.

(4) Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is wise and has a wise heart; one who is wise but has an unwise heart; one who is unwise but has a wise heart; and one who is unwise and has an unwise heart.

(4) Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is compassionate toward oneself but not toward others; one who is compassionate toward others but not toward oneself; [one who is compassionate toward both]; and one who is compassionate toward neither. (4)

Fourfold cohabitation is taught, namely: celestial, demonic, rakshasa, and human. Fourfold cohabitation is taught, namely: one who is a god may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; one who is a god may enter into cohabitation with an asura-woman; one who is an asura may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; and one who is an asura may enter into cohabitation with an asura-woman.

Fourfold cohabitation is declared; namely: one who is a god may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; one who is a god may enter into cohabitation with a rākṣasī; one who is a rākṣasa may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; and one who is a rākṣasa may enter into cohabitation with a rākṣasī.

Four kinds of cohabitation are taught, namely: one who is a god may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; one who is a god may enter into cohabitation with a human woman; one who is a human may enter into cohabitation with a goddess; and one who is a human may enter into cohabitation with a human woman.

Four kinds of cohabitation are taught, namely: one who is an asura may enter into cohabitation with an asuri; one who is an asura may enter into cohabitation with a rakkhasi; one who is a rakkhasa may enter into cohabitation with an asuri; and one who is a rakkhasa may enter into cohabitation with a rakkhasi.

Four kinds of cohabitation are declared, namely: some asura cohabits with an asuri; some asura cohabits with a human female; some human cohabits with an asuri; and some human cohabits with a human female.

Four kinds of cohabitation are taught, namely: one who is a *rākṣasa* enters into cohabitation with a *rākṣasī*; one who is a *rākṣasa* enters into cohabitation with a human woman; one who is a human enters into cohabitation with a *rākṣasī*; and one who is a human enters into cohabitation with a human woman.

The non-falling-away [karmic states] are declared to be fourfold, namely: the demonic (*āsura*), the coercive (*ābhiyogika*), the delusive (*saṃmoha*), and the divine *kiṃbhisa*. By four conditions, living beings produce karma leading to a demonic state, namely: by a nature prone to anger, by a nature prone to greed, by ascetic practices associated with worldly attachment, and by living off omens.

By four conditions, living beings produce karma leading to a coercive state, namely: by self-exaltation, by disparaging others, by performing rites for prosperity (*bhūtikamma*), and by practicing sorcery (*kōuya*).

By four causes, living beings project karma that results in delusion; namely: by teaching a false path, by hostility toward the true path, by the improper enjoyment of sensual pleasures, and by making a false resolution regarding one's future existence.

By four causes, living beings project karma that results in the status of a divine outcaste (*devakibbisiya*); namely: by speaking dispraise of the Arhats, by speaking dispraise of the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats, by speaking dispraise of the teachers and preceptors, and by speaking dispraise of the fourfold community (*cātuvarṇa saṃgha*).

Renunciation is taught to be fourfold, namely: bound to this world, bound to the other world, bound to both worlds, and unbound. Renunciation is taught to be fourfold, namely: bound in front, bound behind, bound on both sides, and unbound.
Renunciation is taught to be fourfold, namely: renunciation by inclination, renunciation by proclamation, renunciation by association, and renunciation like the flight of a bird.

Fourfold renunciation is taught, namely: renouncing oneself, renouncing one's wife, renouncing one's children, and renouncing one's grandchildren. Fourfold renunciation is taught, namely: that which is like a reaper of actors, that which is like a reaper of soldiers, that which is like a reaper of hunters, and that which is like a reaper of jackals.

Fourfold agriculture is taught, namely: plowing, weeding, gleaning, and gathering the gleanings. In the same way, fourfold renunciation is taught, namely: plowed, weeded, gleaned, and gathered the gleanings.
Renunciation is declared to be fourfold, namely: like a heap of grain, like scattered grain, like strewed grain, and like gathered grain.
Four cravings are declared, namely: craving for food, craving for fear, craving for sexual intercourse, and craving for possession.

Craving for food arises from four causes, namely: from the state of having an empty stomach, from the rising of karma that produces the sensation of hunger, from mental inclination, and from application toward that purpose.

The perception of fear arises through four conditions, namely: due to a state of weakness, due to the rising of karma to be experienced as fear, due to the intellect, and due to application to that object.

The perception of sexual desire arises through four conditions, namely: due to the presence of mind, flesh, and blood, due to the rising of deluding karma (*mohanīya-karma*), due to the intellect, and due to application to that object.

The perception of possessiveness arises through four conditions, namely: due to a lack of liberation, due to the rising of karma to be experienced as greed (*lobha-vedanīya-karma*), due to the intellect, and due to application to that object.

There are four kinds of sensual pleasures, namely: the graceful, the pathetic, the loathsome, and the cruel. Graceful sensual pleasures belong to the gods; pathetic sensual pleasures belong to humans; loathsome sensual pleasures belong to those of the animal realm; and cruel sensual pleasures belong to the denizens of hell.

There are four kinds of ponds, namely: one that is shallow and has shallow water; one that is shallow and has deep water; one that is deep and has shallow water; and one that is deep and has deep water. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is shallow and has shallow intent; one who is shallow and has deep intent; one who is deep and has shallow intent; and one who is deep and has deep intent.

Four kinds of water are taught, namely: one that is shallow and appears shallow; one that is shallow and appears deep; one that is deep and appears shallow; and one that is deep and appears deep. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is shallow and appears shallow; one who is shallow and appears deep; [and so on for the remaining two].

Four oceans are proclaimed, namely: one that is shallow and has shallow waters; one that is shallow and has deep waters—[and so on for the remaining two]. In the same way, four types of persons are proclaimed, namely: one who is shallow and has a shallow heart—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four oceans are proclaimed, namely: one that is shallow and appears shallow; one that is shallow and appears deep—[and so on for the remaining two]. In the same way, four types of persons are proclaimed, namely: one who is shallow and appears shallow—[and so on for the remaining three].

Four types of swimmers are taught, as follows: some who say "I will cross the ocean" actually crosses the ocean; some who say "I will cross the ocean" actually crosses a puddle; some who say "I will cross a puddle" [actually crosses the ocean]—[the fourth case is implied].

Four types of swimmers are taught, as follows: having crossed the ocean, some sink in the ocean; having crossed the ocean, some sink in a puddle; having crossed a puddle, some sink in the ocean—[the fourth case is implied].

Four types of jars are taught, namely: one that is full and called "full," one that is full and called "empty," one that is empty and called "full," and one that is empty and called "empty. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught: one who is full and called "full"—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of jars are taught, namely: one that is full and appears full; one that is full but appears empty; one that is empty but appears full; and one that is empty and appears empty. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is full and appears full—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of jars are taught, namely: one that is full and has the appearance of being full; one that is full but has the appearance of being empty—[and so on for the other three]. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is full and has the appearance of being full—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of jars are taught, namely: one that is full and pleasing, one that is full but unpleasant, one that is empty but pleasing, and one that is empty and unpleasant. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is full and pleasing.

Four types of jars are taught, namely: one that is full and leaking, one that is full and not leaking, one that is empty and leaking, and one that is empty and not leaking. In the same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is full and leaking—[and so on for the other three].

Four types of jars are taught, namely: one that is broken, one that is cracked, one that is porous, and one that is non-porous. In the same way, fourfold conduct is taught, namely: broken [conduct], up to non-porous [conduct].

Four kinds of jars are taught, namely: one jar of honey with a honey stopper; one jar of honey with a poison stopper; one jar of poison with a honey stopper; and one jar of poison with a poison stopper. In the very same way, four types of persons are taught, namely: [one who is] like a jar of honey with a honey stopper—4. He in whom there is a heart free from evil and impurity, and whose tongue also always speaks sweetly—that person is like a jar of honey with a honey stopper. (Sthānāṅga 388)
That man in whom there is a heart that is impure and turbid, yet a tongue that always speaks sweet words—he is like a jar of honey with poison hidden beneath the lid.
(Sūtrakṛtāṅga 3.89) But that man in whom the heart is pure and the tongue always speaks sweet words—[he is like a jar of poison with a lid of honey]. (Sūtrakṛtāṅga 3.89)
In that man in whom there exists a jar of poison with honey for its lid— Ṭhāṇa 390—
in whom the heart is turbid and the tongue speaks bitter words, in that man always resides a jar of poison with poison for its lid. Ṭhāṇa 391.

Four kinds of obstacles (*upasarga*) are taught, namely: divine, human, animal, and those resulting from one's own actions (*āyasacceyaṇijja*). Divine obstacles are taught to be fourfold, namely: through laughter, through anger, through suspicion, and through individual hostility. Human obstacles are taught to be fourfold, namely: through laughter, through anger, through suspicion, and through the practice of misconduct (*kusīlapaḍisēvaṇayā*). Animal obstacles are taught to be fourfold, namely: through fear, through anger, for the sake of food, and for the protection of offspring. Obstacles resulting from one's own actions are taught to be fourfold, namely: by being struck, by falling, by becoming paralyzed (*thambhaṇatā*), and by being smeared (*lesaṇatā*).

Karma is declared to be fourfold; namely: some karma that is auspicious is auspicious; some karma that is auspicious is inauspicious; some karma that is inauspicious is auspicious; and some karma that is inauspicious is inauspicious.

Karma is declared to be fourfold; namely: some karma that is auspicious has an auspicious fruition; some karma that is auspicious has an inauspicious fruition; some karma that is inauspicious has an auspicious fruition; and some karma that is inauspicious has an inauspicious fruition.
Karma is declared to be fourfold; namely: karma of type (*prakṛti-karman*), karma of duration (*sthiti-karman*), karma of intensity (*anubhāva-karman*), and karma of location (*pradeśa-karman*).
The Saṅgha is declared to be fourfold, namely: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen.
Intelligence is declared to be fourfold, namely: innate, acquired, karmic, and developmental.

Wisdom is declared to be fourfold, namely: wisdom of perception, wisdom of investigation, wisdom of judgment, and wisdom of retention; or alternatively, wisdom is declared to be fourfold, namely: like the water of a rain-puddle, like the water of a stream, like the water of a lake, and like the water of the ocean.

Living beings involved in the cycle of existence are declared to be fourfold, namely: hell-beings, animals, humans, and gods. All living beings are declared to be fourfold, namely: those with mental activity (*manoyogin*), those with vocal activity (*vāgyogin*), those with bodily activity (*kāyayogin*), and those without activity (*ayogin*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be fourfold, namely: those with female gender (*strīvedaka*), those with male gender (*puruṣavedaka*), those with neuter gender (*napuṃsakavedaka*), and those without gender (*avedaka*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be fourfold, namely: those with visual perception (*cakṣurdarśin*), those with non-visual perception (*acakṣurdarśin*), those with clairvoyant perception (*avadhidarśin*), and those with omniscient perception (*kevaladarśin*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be fourfold, namely: the self-restrained (*saṃyata*), the unrestrained (*asaṃyata*), the partially restrained (*saṃyatāsaṃyata*), and those who are neither restrained nor unrestrained (*no-saṃyata-no-asaṃyata*).

Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is a friend and is indeed a friend; one who is a friend but is not a friend; one who is not a friend but is a friend; and one who is not a friend and is not a friend. Four types of persons are taught: one who is a friend and has the appearance of a friend; [and so on for] the four permutations.
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is liberated and is indeed liberated; one who is liberated but is not liberated—[four permutations].
Four types of persons are taught, namely: one who is liberated and has the appearance of being liberated; one who is liberated but does not have the appearance of being liberated—[four permutations].

The five-sensed beings of the animal realm are described as having four destinations and four origins; namely: a five-sensed being of the animal realm, when being reborn among five-sensed beings of the animal realm, may be reborn from among hell-beings, or from among animals, or from among humans, or from among gods. And that same five-sensed being of the animal realm, when relinquishing its status as a five-sensed being of the animal realm, may go toward the state of a hell-being, or [the other states] up to the state of a god. Humans have four destinations and four origins; it is exactly the same for humans as well.

For one who does not initiate violence against living beings with the five sense-faculties, fourfold self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is accomplished; namely: he becomes one who has desisted from the pleasure consisting of the tongue; he becomes one who is unattached to the suffering consisting of the tongue; he becomes one who has desisted from the pleasure consisting of touch; and likewise for the other [senses]—four [in each].

For one who instigates violence against two-sensed beings, fourfold non-restraint is produced, namely: by depriving them of the pleasure consisting of the tongue, he becomes joined with the pain consisting of the tongue; and by depriving them of the pleasure consisting of touch, [he becomes joined with the pain consisting of touch]. For the hell-beings of right view, four types of karma-activity (kriyā) are taught, namely: activity pertaining to violence (ārambhikī), activity pertaining to possessiveness (pārigrahikī), activity pertaining to deceit (māyāpratyayikī), and activity of non-renunciation (apratyākhyānakriyā).

For the Asurakumāras of right view, four types of karma-activity (kiriyā) are taught; namely, the same as before. In this same way, [this applies] for all beings down to the Vaimānikas, with the exception of those with incomplete sense-faculties (vigaliṃdiya). By four causes one may destroy existing virtues: namely, by anger, by malice, by lack of compassion, and by adherence to false views.
By four causes one may display non-existent virtues: namely, through flattery, through compliance with another's will, for the sake of some purpose, or as a form of ingratitude.

The production of the bodies of hell-beings occurs through four causes, namely: anger, pride, deceit, and greed; and so on up to the Vaimānika gods. The bodies of hell-beings are declared to be produced by four factors, namely: produced by anger, produced by pride, produced by deceit, and produced by greed; and so on up to the Vaimānika gods. Four gateways of Dharma have been taught, namely: forbearance, equanimity, uprightness, and gentleness.

By four causes, living beings project karma for the duration of a hellish existence, namely: through great violence, through great possessiveness, through the killing of five-sensed beings, and through the consumption of raw flesh.

By four causes, living beings project karma for the duration of an animal existence, namely: through deceitfulness, through guile, through false speech, and through the use of false weights and measures.

By four conditions, living beings project karma for a human lifespan, namely: by being naturally kind, naturally disciplined, compassionate, and free from envy. By four conditions, living beings project karma for a divine lifespan, namely: through self-restraint with passion, through partial restraint (of the layperson), through the penance of the ignorant, and through involuntary shedding of karma.

Four kinds of musical instruments are taught, namely: stringed (*tata*), percussion (*vitata*), solid (*ghana*), and wind (*jhusira*). Four kinds of dance are taught, namely: *añcita*, *ribhita*, *ārabhaṭa*, and *bhasola*. Four kinds of song are taught, namely: *ukkhitaka*, *pattaka*, *mandaka*, and *rovindaka*. Four kinds of garlands are taught, namely: woven (*ganthima*), braided (*vēḍhima*), filled (*pūrima*), and assembled (*saṅghātima*). Four kinds of ornaments are taught, namely: ornaments for the hair, ornaments for the clothing, ornaments for the garlands, and ornaments for the body.
The fourfold *abhinaya* (dramatic performance) is taught as follows: *diṭṭhantia*, *pāḍisuta*, *sāmaṇṇaviṇivāiya*, and *logamajjhāvasita*.

In the celestial realms of Sanatkumāra and Māhendra, the palaces (*vimāṇa*) are taught to be of four colors, namely: blue, red, yellow, and white. In the celestial realms of Mahāśukra and Sahasrāra, the bodies maintained by the gods (*bhavadhāraṇijja*) are taught to be at most four *ratni*s in height.

Four types of water-wombs are taught, namely: hot, cold, cool, and warm. Four types of water-wombs are taught, namely: those born in winter, those enveloped by clouds, those that are both cold and warm, and those possessing five forms. In the month of Māgha, the womb-born are those of winter; in Phagguṇa, they are those enveloped by clouds; in Caitra and Vaiśākha, they are those that are both cold and warm, and those possessing five forms. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 408)
Four types of human wombs are taught, namely: for the state of a female, for the state of a male, for the state of a neuter, and for the state of a *bimba*.
When the semen is small and the *ojas* (vital essence) is abundant, a female is born there; when the *ojas* is small and the semen is abundant, a male is born there. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 410)
When both the dark and white [seminal fluids] are in equal proportion, a neuter being is produced;
when there is a conjunction with female vitality (*ojas*), a female form is produced therein. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 411) Four powerful bases are taught in the *Utpādapūrva*.
Poetry is declared to be fourfold, namely: prose (gajja), verse (pajja), mixed prose and verse (kattha), and song (geya).

For hell-beings, four types of total mobilization (samugghāta) are declared, namely: the mobilization of pain (veyaṇā-samugghāta), the mobilization of passions (kasāya-samugghāta), the mobilization at the time of death (māraṇantiya-samugghāta), and the mobilization for the transformation body (veuvviya-samugghāta); it is the same for the wind-bodied beings as well.

During the time of the Arhat Ariṭṭhanemi, there were four hundred masters of the fourteen-fold scriptures (cauddasa-puvvi) who were not yet Jinas but resembled Jinas, possessing the complete mastery of all syllables; like Jinas themselves, they spoke without error, and their supreme attainment of the fourteen-fold scriptures was unsurpassed.
The Blessed One, the ascetic Mahāvīra, had four hundred disputants who were invincible in assemblies consisting of gods, humans, and asuras; they possessed the highest excellence in debate.

The four lower celestial realms (kalpas) are described as being shaped like a half-moon; namely: Sōhamma, Īsāṇa, Saṇaṅkumāra, and Māhinda. The four middle celestial realms are described as being shaped like a full moon; namely: Bambhalōga, Lantaē, Mahāsukka, and Sahassāra. The four upper celestial realms are described as being shaped like a half-moon; namely: Āṇata, Pāṇata, Āraṇa, and Accuta. There are four oceans with distinct tastes described; namely: Lavaṇōda, Varuṇōda, Khīrōda, and Ghatōda.

Four whirlpools are taught, namely: the rough whirlpool, the high whirlpool, the hidden whirlpool, and the baited whirlpool. In the same way, four passions are taught, namely: anger is like the rough whirlpool, pride is like the high whirlpool, deceit is like the hidden whirlpool, and greed is like the baited whirlpool. A living being who has entered into anger like the rough whirlpool, when he dies, is reborn among the denizens of hell. One who has entered into pride like the high whirlpool... [is reborn] among the denizens of hell. One who has entered into deceit like the hidden whirlpool... [is reborn] among the denizens of hell. A living being who has entered into greed like the baited whirlpool, when he dies, is reborn among the denizens of hell.

The constellation Anurādhā is declared to have four stars; Pūrvāṣāḍhā is likewise, and Uttarāṣāḍhā is likewise. Souls have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate matter formed into the state of evil karma (pāpakarma); [matter] formed as hell-beings, formed as animals, formed as humans, and formed as gods—they have thus accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate it. In this same manner apply the categories of accumulation (ciṇa), further accumulation (uvaciṇa), bondage (bandha), activation (udīra), experience (vēya), and likewise destruction (nijjarā).

Infinite four-partite aggregates are taught; infinite matter-particles (pudgala) occupying four spatial points are taught; infinite matter-particles with a duration of four time-units (samaya) are taught; infinite matter-particles with four qualities of blackness are taught, up to infinite matter-particles with four qualities of roughness are taught.

The five great vows are proclaimed as follows: abstention from all killing of living beings; [abstention from all false speech; abstention from all taking of what is not given; abstention from all unchastity]; abstention from all possessions. The five minor vows are proclaimed as follows: abstention from gross killing of living beings; abstention from gross false speech; abstention from gross taking of what is not given; contentment with one’s own wife; limitation of desires.

Five colors are declared, namely: black, blue, red, yellow, and white; five tastes are declared, namely: bitter, pungent, astringent, sour, and sweet; five strands of sensual pleasure are declared, namely: sounds, forms, smells, tastes, and tactile objects. By these five factors, living beings become attached—namely, by sounds up to tactile objects—and likewise they become impassioned, infatuated, greedy, and obsessed.

Living beings encounter destruction through five conditions, namely: sounds, up to tactile sensations. Five conditions, when not fully understood, lead to the detriment, the impurity, the lack of forbearance, the lack of security, and the lack of favorable consequence for living beings, namely: sounds, up to tactile sensations.
