Five conditions, when well understood, lead to the welfare, the purity, up to the favorable consequence for living beings, namely: sounds, up to tactile sensations. Five conditions, when not fully understood, lead to the going to an evil destination for living beings, namely: sounds, up to tactile sensations. Five conditions, when well understood, lead to the going to a happy destination for living beings, namely: sounds, up to tactile sensations.

By five causes, living beings go to an evil destination (*durgati*); namely: by killing living beings, up to by possession (*parigraha*). By five causes, living beings go to a happy destination (*sugati*); namely: by abstaining from killing living beings, up to by abstaining from possession. Five vows (*pratimā*) are taught; namely: the Auspicious (*Bhaddā*), the Very Auspicious (*Subhaddā*), the Greatly Auspicious (*Mahābhaddā*), the All-Auspicious (*Savvatobhaddā*), and the Most Excellent Auspicious Vow (*Bhadduttarapaḍimā*).

Five stationary bodies (*thāvarakāya*) are taught; namely: the Indra stationary body, the Brahma stationary body, the Artisan stationary body, the Saṃmati stationary body, and the Pātāvacca stationary body.

Regarding the stationary beings, five lords of the stationary bodies are proclaimed, namely: Indra, the lord of the stationary bodies; Brahmā, the lord of the stationary bodies; Śilpī, the lord of the stationary bodies; Sammati, the lord of the stationary bodies; and Pātāvacca, the lord of the stationary bodies.

There are five circumstances in which one who desires to produce limited vision (*avadhidarśana*) should, at the very outset, fix his gaze. They are as follows: First, having seen the earth as it was when it first came into being, he should fix his gaze at the very outset. Second, having seen the earth as it has become a mass of small insects (*kunthu*), he should fix his gaze at the very outset. Third, having seen the body of a very large serpent (*mahoraga*), he should fix his gaze at the very outset. Fourth, having seen a god of great power, up to one of great happiness, he should fix his gaze at the very outset. Fifth, having seen ancient, magnificent, and very large great treasures in cities—treasures whose owners have perished, whose lineages have perished, whose guards and keepers have perished; which have been abandoned by their masters, abandoned by their lineages, and abandoned by their guards and keepers; and which remain deposited in villages, towns, cities, hamlets, market towns, ports, caravan settlements, royal camps, and encampments; or in crossroads, trijunctions, quadrangles, junctions, four-way intersections, main roads, and paths; or in the drainage channels of cities; or in cemeteries, empty houses, mountain caves, sanctuaries, rock shelters, palaces, and dwellings—he should fix his gaze at the very outset. In these five circumstances, one who desires to produce limited vision should, at the very outset, fix his gaze.

There are five situations in which one desiring the arising of supreme, excellent knowledge and vision (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*) should not, at the very outset, lean against [a support]. They are as follows: having seen the earth to be sparse, one should not, at the very outset, lean against it; the rest is the same as before, up to: having seen objects placed within houses or dwellings, one should not, at the very outset, lean against them. By these five situations, one desiring the arising of supreme knowledge and vision should not, at the very outset, lean against [a support].

The bodies of hell-beings are described as having five colors and five tastes, namely: black up to white, and bitter up to sweet. In this same manner, without interruption, up to the Vaimānika gods, five types of bodies are described, namely: the physical (audārika), the transformational (vaikriya), the assimilative (āhāraka), the fiery (taijasa), and the karmic (kārmaṇa). The physical body is described as having five colors and five tastes, namely: black up to white, and bitter up to sweet; and so on, up to the karmic body. Furthermore, all gross, skeletal corpses have five colors, five tastes, two odors, and eight tactile qualities.

There are five conditions by which the path of the first and last Jinas is difficult to traverse: namely, it is difficult to explain, difficult to analyze, difficult to perceive, difficult to endure, and difficult to practice. There are five conditions by which the path of the middle Jinas is easy to traverse: namely, it is easy to explain, easy to analyze, easy to perceive, easy to endure, and easy to practice.

There are five points which have been constantly praised, constantly extolled, constantly spoken of, constantly commended, and constantly approved by the ascetic Lord Mahāvīra for the sake of the ascetic Nigranthas; namely: forbearance, equanimity, uprightness, gentleness, and lightness. There are five points... [as above]... namely: truthfulness, self-restraint, austerity, renunciation, and living in celibacy. There are five points... [as above]... namely: wandering for alms at the beginning of the meal-time, wandering for alms at the end of the meal-time, wandering for alms in between, wandering for alms in secluded places, and wandering for alms on coarse food. There are five points... [as above]... namely: wandering for alms without prior announcement, wandering for alms with restricted acceptance, practicing silence while wandering for alms, accepting what is prepared by a householder who has already made his preparations, and accepting what is prepared by a householder who makes his preparations specifically for the mendicant. There are five points... [as above]... namely: receiving food that is brought near, receiving pure food, receiving a measured amount, receiving only what is seen, and receiving only what is offered after being asked.

There are five practices authorized by the ascetic Blessed One, namely: eating only once a day, abstaining from food at night, eating only the first half of the meal, eating a limited amount of alms-food, and eating broken-off morsels of alms-food. There are five practices authorized by the ascetic Blessed One, namely: consuming tasteless food, consuming distasteful food, consuming the last of the alms-food, consuming coarse food, and consuming rough food. There are five practices authorized by the ascetic Blessed One, namely: subsisting on tasteless food, subsisting on distasteful food, subsisting on the last of the alms-food, subsisting on coarse food, and subsisting on rough food. There are five practices authorized by the ascetic Blessed One, namely: standing in one place, sitting in the *utkuṭuka* posture, remaining in the meditative posture (*pratimā*), sitting in the *vīrāsana* posture, and sitting cross-legged. There are five practices authorized by the ascetic Blessed One, namely: standing like a staff, lying on the bare ground, exposing oneself to the heat, not wearing a cloak, and not using a mat.

By five conditions, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha becomes one of great shedding of karma and great final liberation: namely, by performing service for the teacher without weariness; by performing service for the preceptor without weariness; by performing service for the elder without weariness; by performing service for the ascetic without weariness; by performing service for the sick without weariness. By five conditions, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha becomes one of great shedding of karma and great final liberation: namely, by performing service for the novice without weariness; by performing service for the family without weariness; by performing service for the group without weariness; by performing service for the Saṅgha without weariness; by performing service for his fellow-monks without weariness.

A Śramaṇa Nirgrantha does not transgress when he renders a fellow member of the community (sādharmika) who has committed an offense subject to reconciliation (saṃbhōiya) into one requiring non-reconciliation (visaṃbhōiya) for five reasons, namely: he has practiced an act involving formal action (sakiriyaṭṭhāṇa); having practiced it, he does not confess it; having confessed it, he does not undertake the penance (paṭṭhaveti); having undertaken it, he does not perform the purification (nivvisati); and he repeatedly practices those established rules of conduct (ṭhitipakappa) of the Elders (theras), thinking, "I am practicing this; what can the Elders do to me? A Śramaṇa Nirgrantha does not transgress when he renders a fellow member of the community subject to banishment (pārañcitta) for five reasons, namely: he dwells in a family and strives for the division of that family; he dwells in a group (gaṇa) and strives for the division of that group; he seeks out faults (hiṃsappēhī); he seeks out vulnerabilities (chiddappēhī); and he repeatedly raises questions and challenges (pasiṇāyataṇāiṃ).

There are five grounds for dispute regarding a teacher or preceptor within a community (*gaṇa*). They are as follows: (1) The teacher or preceptor does not properly carry out the commands or instructions within the community; (2) The teacher or preceptor does not properly perform the ritual of prostration (*kitikamma*) as part of the daily observances (*ādhārātiṇiya*) within the community; (3) The teacher or preceptor retains the various categories of scriptures (*sutta-pajjava-jāta*) but does not properly recite them from time to time within the community; (4) The teacher or preceptor does not properly attend to the service of the sick and novices within the community; (5) The teacher or preceptor moves about within the community without having asked permission, rather than moving about after having asked permission.

Regarding the teacher and preceptor (*ācāryopādhyāya*), five points of non-grasping (*an-avagraha-sthāna*) are prescribed within the community (*gaṇa*). They are as follows: The teacher and preceptor, within the community, correctly carries out commands and instructions; likewise, they correctly perform the ritual homage (*kṛtikarma*) with full devotion. The teacher and preceptor, within the community, maintains the various categories of the scriptures (*sūtra-paryāya-jāta*) and correctly transmits them from time to time. The teacher and preceptor, within the community, properly attends to the service of the sick and novices (*śaikṣa-vaiyāvṛtya*). Furthermore, the teacher and preceptor, within the community, conducts themselves by seeking permission before acting, and not by acting without seeking permission.
Five postures are taught: the squatting posture, the cow’s-hoof posture, the even-footed posture, the lotus posture, and the half-lotus posture.
Five bases for uprightness are taught, namely: uprightness in speech, uprightness in gentleness, uprightness in humility, uprightness in patience, and uprightness in self-restraint.
Five types of celestial beings are taught, namely: the moons, the suns, the planets, the constellations, and the stars.

There are five kinds of gods, namely: gods by potentiality (*bhaviyadavvadēva*), gods among men (*naradēva*), gods by righteousness (*dhammadēva*), gods beyond gods (*dēvātidēva*), and gods by state (*bhāvadēva*).
Five kinds of enjoyment (*pariyāraṇā*) are taught, namely: bodily enjoyment, tactile enjoyment, visual enjoyment, auditory enjoyment, and mental enjoyment.
Of Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asura-kumāras, five chief queens are taught, namely: Kālī, Rātī, Rayanī, Vijjū, and Mehā.
Vairocana Indra, the king of Vairocana, has five chief queens, namely: Sumbhā, Nisumbhā, Rambhā, Nirambhā, and Madanā.

For Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asura-kumāras, five types of battle-armies and five commanders of those battle-armies are proclaimed, namely: the infantry commander, the chariot commander, the elephant commander, the buffalo commander, and the chariot-warrior commander. Duma is the commander of the infantry; Sōdāma, the king of horses, is the commander of the chariots; Kūnthu, the king of elephants, is the commander of the elephants; Lōhitakkha is the commander of the buffaloes; and Kiṇṇara is the commander of the chariot-warriors.

To Bali, the lord of Vairoṇa, the king of Vairoṇa, five military divisions and five commanders of the military divisions are proclaimed; namely: the commander of the infantry up to the commander of the chariots. Mahādruma was the commander of the infantry; Mahāsodāma, the king of horses, was the commander of the cavalry; Mālaṅkāra, the king of elephants, was the commander of the elephant corps; Mahālohitākṣa was the commander of the buffalo corps; and Kupuruṣa was the commander of the chariot corps.

For Dharaṇa, the lord of the Nāgakumāras and king of the Nāgakumāras, five types of military divisions and five commanders of those military divisions are proclaimed, namely: the infantry division up to the chariot division.

Bhaddasena is the commander of the infantry division; Yasodhara is the king of horses and commander of the cavalry division; Sudarśana is the king of elephants and commander of the elephant division; Nīlakaṇṭha is the commander of the buffalo division; and Ānanda is the commander of the chariot division.

For Bhūyānanda, the lord of the Nāgakumāras and king of the Nāgakumāras, five types of military forces and five commanders of those forces are proclaimed; namely: the infantry force up to the chariot force. The skilled commander of the infantry is Suggīva, the king of horses; the commander of the elephant force is Pīḍhāṇiya, the king of elephants; the commander of the buffalo force is Seyakaṇṭha; and the commander of the chariot force is Nanduttara.

For Veṇudeva, the lord of the Suvarṇas and king of the Suvarṇakumāras, five types of battle arrays and five commanders of battle arrays are prescribed, namely: the infantry array, and so forth, just as for Dharaṇa; likewise for Veṇudālī; and just as for Bhūtānanda. Just as it was for Dharaṇa, so it is for all those on the right side up to Ghosa; and just as it was for Bhūtānanda, so it is for all those on the left side up to Mahāghosa.

Of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, five military divisions and five commanders of those military divisions are proclaimed, as follows: the infantry division, the ox-division, the deer-leader as commander of the infantry division, Vāyu the horse-king as commander of the chariot division, Airāvaṇa the elephant-king as commander of the elephant division, Dāmaḍḍhi the ox-king as commander of the ox division, and Māḍhara the camel-king as commander of the camel division.

The divine lord Īśāna, king of the gods, has five military divisions: the infantry division (*pāyattāṇiya*), the chariot division (*pīḍhāṇiya*), the elephant division (*kuñjarāṇiya*), the bull division (*usabhāṇiya*), and the chariot-army division (*radhāṇiya*). Lahuparakkama, the commander of the infantry division, is the great wind; Āsarāya, the commander of the chariot division, is the flower-toothed one; Mahādāmaḍḍhi, the commander of the elephant division, is the great wreath-bearer; and Mahāmāḍhara, the commander of the bull division, is the great wreath-wielder. As it is for Śakra, so it is for all [the lords] of the southern quarter up to Āraṇa; as it is for Īśāna, so it is for all [the lords] of the northern quarter up to Accuta.

The lifespan of the gods in the inner assembly of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is declared to be five *palyopamas*. The lifespan of the goddesses in the inner assembly of Īsāna, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is declared to be five *palyopamas*.

Five kinds of obstructions are declared, namely: obstruction of movement, obstruction of duration, obstruction of bondage, obstruction of enjoyment, and obstruction of strength, heroism, manly effort, and prowess.
Five kinds of non-living beings (*ajīva*) are declared, namely: those who live by birth, those who live by clan, those who live by karma, those who live by craft, and those who live by outward marks.
There are five insignia of royalty, namely: the sword, the parasol, the head-ornament, the sandals, and the fly-whisk.

There are five grounds by which an ordinary person (*chaumattha*) should properly endure, forgive, tolerate, and bear up against arisen hardships and calamities (*parīsaha-uvassagga*). They are as follows: (1) This man is indeed possessed by karma that has arisen and is like one who is insane; therefore, this man reviles me, or mocks me, or scolds me, or insults me, or binds me, or obstructs me, or cuts my skin, or leads me to death, or harms me, or snatches away, tears apart, breaks, or steals my robe, bowl, blanket, or broom. (2) This man is indeed possessed by a spirit (*jakkha*); therefore, this man reviles me, and so on, up to stealing from me. (3) Karma to be experienced in this very life (*tabbhava-veyaṇijja*) has arisen for me; therefore, this man reviles me, and so on, up to stealing from me. (4) If I were not to properly endure, forgive, tolerate, or bear up against [these things], what do you think would happen? Only evil karma would be produced for me. (5) But if I properly endure, and so on, up to bearing them up, what do you think would happen? Only the shedding of karma (*nijjarā*) would be produced for me. By these five grounds, an ordinary person should properly endure, and so on, up to bearing up against arisen hardships and calamities.

There are five reasons why a Kevalin should properly endure, and so forth, up to tolerate, arisen hardships and afflictions when someone robs him; namely: (1) "This man has a distracted mind; that is why this man reviles me," or [robs me], up to "robs me. (2) "This man has a deranged mind; that is why this man [reviles me], up to robs me. (3) "This man is possessed by a spirit; that is why this man [reviles me], up to robs me. (4) "Karma to be experienced in this very life has arisen for me; that is why this man [reviles me], up to robs me. (5) "Seeing me properly enduring, forbearing, patient, and tolerating, many other Śramaṇas and Nirgranthas with limited vision will likewise properly endure, and so forth, up to tolerate, whenever such arisen hardships and afflictions occur. For these five reasons, a Kevalin should properly endure, and so forth, up to tolerate, arisen hardships and afflictions.

Five causes are taught, namely: he does not know the cause, he does not see the cause, he does not understand the cause, he does not attain the cause, and he dies an ignorant death because of the cause.
Five causes are taught, namely: through the cause he does not know, and so on, up to: through the cause he dies an ignorant death.
Five causes are taught, namely: he knows the cause, and so on, up to: he dies a death of one still possessed of veils (chaumattha-maraṇa) because of the cause.
Five causes are taught, namely: by means of a cause one knows, [and so on] up to: by means of a cause one dies a death of a *chaumattha* (one with veiled vision).
Five non-causes are taught, namely: without a cause one does not know, [and so on] up to: without a cause one dies a death of a *chaumattha*.
Five non-causes are taught, namely: without a cause one does not know, [and so on] up to: without a cause one dies a death of a *chaumattha*.

Five reasons are taught, namely: he knows without a reason, and so on, up to he dies the death of a kevalin without a reason. Five reasons are taught, namely: he knows by means of no-cause, and so on, up to he dies the death of a kevalin by means of no-cause. For the kevalin, five unsurpassed qualities are taught, namely: unsurpassed knowledge, unsurpassed vision, unsurpassed conduct, and unsurpassed vigor.

The Arhat Paumappaha had five [lunar] asterisms associated with him, as follows: under the asterism Citrā he descended from his previous existence and entered the womb; under Citrā he was born; under Citrā, having become shaven-headed, he went forth from the household life into homelessness; under Citrā, infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, absolute, and perfect supreme knowledge and vision arose; and under Citrā he attained final liberation. The Arhat Pupphadanta had five [lunar] roots associated with him, as follows: under the root [asterism] he descended from his previous existence and entered the womb.
The constellation Citrā is for Paumappabha; furthermore, Puṣpadanta’s is Mūla.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā belongs to Sīyala, and Uttarāṣāḍhā to Vimala.
Bhaddavayā (Śravaṇā) is for Anantajina, Revatī for Dharma, and Bharaṇī for Śānti.
For Kunthu, the birth was under Kṛttikā; likewise for Ara, it was under Revatī.
For Munisuvrata, it was Śravaṇa; for Nami, Āśvinī; for Nemi, Citrā;
for Pārśva, Viśākhā; and for Vīra, the five [nakṣatras] beginning with Uttarā-phalgunī. (Ṭhāṇa 447–448)

The Blessed One, the Great Hero, was associated with the constellation Uttaraphalguni (Hastottara) on five occasions: namely, having passed away from his previous existence and descended into the womb under Uttaraphalguni; having been transferred from one womb to another under Uttaraphalguni; having been born under Uttaraphalguni; having gone forth from the household life into homelessness as a shramana by shaving his head under Uttaraphalguni; and when infinite, supreme, unobstructed, unimpeded, complete, and perfect supreme knowledge and vision arose under Uttaraphalguni.

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to cross, whether once, twice, or thrice within a month, any of these five great oceanic rivers that have been enumerated: namely, the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarayū, Airāvatī, and Mahī.

However, it is permissible under five circumstances: in the event of fear, in the event of famine, if someone should carry them across, if a flood is approaching, or if there are many non-Aryans [on the opposite bank].

It is not permissible for Nirgranthas or Nirgranthīs to travel from village to village during the first rains; however, it is permissible under five circumstances, namely: in the event of danger, in the event of famine, or even when there is a great threat from non-Aryans.

For those who have entered the rainy-season retreat, it is not permissible for monks or nuns to travel from village to village during that time. However, it is permissible under five circumstances, namely: for the sake of knowledge; for the sake of vision; for the sake of conduct; if their preceptor or teacher should become separated from them; or for the sake of performing services for a preceptor or teacher who is away.

Five things that cause a downfall are prescribed, namely: performing manual labor, engaging in sexual intercourse, eating at night, eating food belonging to a householder, and eating food belonging to a king.

Under five circumstances, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha entering a royal harem does not transgress [the rule]. They are as follows: (1) If the city were guarded on all sides and its gates secured, and many Śramaṇas and Brāhmaṇas were unable to go out or come in for the sake of food or drink, he may enter the royal harem for the purpose of informing them; (2) he may enter the royal harem while returning borrowed items such as stools, planks, beds, or bedding; (3) he may enter the royal harem out of fear of an approaching wild horse or elephant; (4) another person might suddenly or by force seize him by the arm and bring him into the royal harem; (5) or the people of the royal harem, having surrounded him on all sides outside while he is in a grove or a garden, might detain him there. Under these five circumstances, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha entering a royal harem does not transgress.

There are five circumstances under which a woman, even while not living with a man, may conceive a fetus: namely, if the woman is unchaste and sits in a compromising position and becomes possessed by semen-particles; or if semen-particles mixed with her own [secretions] enter into her womb; or if she herself introduces semen-particles [into her womb]; or if another person introduces semen-particles [into her womb]; or if semen-particles enter her as she is bathing with cold water. By these five circumstances, she may conceive.

There are five circumstances under which a woman, even while living with a man, will not conceive: namely, being too young, being past her youth, being naturally barren, being afflicted by disease, or being dejected. In these five circumstances, she will not conceive.

There are five conditions by which a woman, even while living with a man, would not conceive a fetus: namely, she is constantly menstruating, she does not menstruate at all, her menstrual flow is discolored, her menstrual flow is obstructed, or she lacks sexual intercourse. By these five conditions, even while living with a man, she would not conceive a fetus.

There are five circumstances under which a woman, even while living together with a man, would not conceive a child: namely, she does not engage in intercourse during the fertile season; or the semen that has been emitted is discharged [before union]; or her bile and blood are disturbed; or there is the influence of past karmic deeds; or the fruit of a son has not yet been destined for her. For these five reasons, up to and including the last, she would not conceive.

Nirgranthas and Nirgranthīs do not overstep [the rule] when they occupy a place, a bed, or a sitting area together for five reasons, as follows: First, some Nirgranthas and Nirgranthīs have entered upon a long journey through a large, trackless wilderness where no path exists; there, occupying a place or a bed together, they do not overstep [the rule]. Second, some Nirgranthas and Nirgranthīs have arrived to stay in a village, a town, or even a capital city; where some obtain lodging and others do not, there, occupying a place or [other accommodations] together, they do not overstep [the rule]. Third, some Nirgranthas and Nirgranthīs have arrived to stay in a region inhabited by Nāgakumāras; there, [occupying a place] together, they do not overstep [the rule], because seductive spirits (*āmōsaga*) are seen who wish to take possession of the Nirgranthīs for the sake of their robes. Fourth, young men are seen who wish to take possession of the Nirgranthīs for the sake of sexual intercourse; there, [occupying a place] together, they do not overstep [the rule]. Thus, for these five reasons, they do not overstep [the rule].

Under five circumstances, a naked (*acelaka*) Śramaṇa Nirgrantha living together with clothed (*sacelika*) Nirgranthīs does not transgress [the rule]. They are as follows: a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha whose mind is deranged, living together with clothed Nirgranthīs in the absence of other Nirgranthas, does not transgress; likewise, by this same method, one who is possessed by a spirit (*yakṣāviṣṭa*), one who is insane (*unmādaprāpta*), or a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha who has been ordained by a Nirgranthī—living together with clothed Nirgranthīs in the absence of other Nirgranthas—does not transgress.

Five doors of influx (*āsava-dvāra*) are taught, namely: wrong belief (*micchatta*), non-restraint (*avirati*), negligence (*pamāda*), passions (*kasāya*), and activities (*joga*). Five doors of restraint (*saṃvara-dvāra*) are taught, namely: right belief (*sammatta*), restraint (*virati*), vigilance (*apamāda*), absence of passions (*akasāitta*), and absence of activities (*ajogitta*).

Five types of violence (*daṇḍa*) are taught, namely: violence for a purpose (*aṭṭhā-daṇḍa*), violence without a purpose (*aṇaṭṭhā-daṇḍa*), violence through injury (*hiṃsā-daṇḍa*), accidental violence (*akasmā-daṇḍa*), and violence due to perversion of view (*diṭṭhī-vippariyāsiyā-daṇḍa*).

For those with wrong view, five types of activity (*kriyā*) are taught, namely: activity pertaining to violence (*ārambhikī*), activity pertaining to possession (*pārigrahikī*), activity pertaining to deceit (*māyāpratyayā*), activity of non-renunciation (*apratyākhyānakriyā*), and activity pertaining to wrong belief (*mithyādarśanapratyayā*). For hell-beings with wrong view, five types of activity are taught, namely: from activity pertaining to violence up to activity pertaining to wrong belief. Thus it continues without interruption for all [beings] up to the Vaimānika gods who hold wrong views; however, those with deficient sense-faculties (*vikaḷendriya*) who hold wrong views are not mentioned, while the rest is exactly the same.

Five types of action (kriyā) are taught, namely: bodily action (kāyikī), possessive action (ādhikaraṇikī), injurious action (pāuṃsīyā), afflictive action (pāritāvaṇikī), and the action of taking life (prāṇātipāta-kriyā). For hell-beings there are exactly these five; thus continuously up to the gods of the Vaimānika realm. Five types of action are taught, namely: those beginning with the action of violence (ārambhikī) up to the action arising from false view (mithyādṛṣṭi-pratyayā). For hell-beings there are these five actions; [this continues] continuously up to the gods of the Vaimānika realm.

Five types of action (*kriyā*) are taught, namely: that which arises from seeing (*dṛṣṭijā*), that which arises from touching (*spṛṣṭijā*), that which arises from dependence on another (*prātītyajā*), that which arises from proximity (*sāmantopanipātikā*), and that which is performed by one's own hand (*sāhastikā*). This applies to hell-beings (*nairayika*) up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm. Five types of action are taught, namely: that which arises from seeking (*naiṣpeṣikī*), that which arises from commanding (*ājñāpanīyā*), that which arises from requesting (*vaitaraṇīyā*), that which arises from lack of awareness (*anābhogapratyayā*), and that which arises from lack of desire (*anavakāṅkṣā-pratyayā*). This applies likewise up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm. Five types of action are taught, namely: that which arises from attachment (*premapratyayā*), that which arises from aversion (*doṣapratyayā*), the action of formation (*prāyogikī-kriyā*), the action of accumulation (*samudāna-kriyā*), and the action of movement (*airyāpathikī-kriyā*). These apply to humans as well; for the others, they do not exist.
Five kinds of renunciation are taught, namely: renunciation of possessions, renunciation of lodgings, renunciation of passions, renunciation of activities, and renunciation of food and drink.

Five kinds of legal procedures (*vavahāra*) are taught, namely: scripture (*āgama*), tradition (*sutta*), command (*āṇā*), retention (*dhāraṇā*), and custom (*jīta*). If, in a given case, there should be scripture, one should initiate the legal procedure by means of scripture; if there should be no scripture in that case, and if there should be tradition, one should initiate the legal procedure by means of tradition; if there should be no tradition in that case, and so on, up until: if there should be custom in that case, one should initiate the legal procedure by means of custom. One should initiate the legal procedure by means of these five—from scripture down to custom—in whatever manner scripture, or down to custom, may exist in that case. In each respective instance, one should initiate the legal procedure accordingly.

"What do you say to this, venerable sir? Are the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas authoritative on the basis of scripture? Thus, when a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha practices this fivefold procedure—whether at whatever time, wherever, or in whatever manner—remaining independent and well-established, he becomes one who fulfills the command. For restrained persons, five things are declared to be sleep; namely: sounds, and so forth, up to tactile sensations. For those restrained persons who are awake, five things are declared to be sleep; namely: sounds, and so forth, up to tactile sensations.
For humans, whether asleep or awake, there are five types of objects of awakening proclaimed: namely, sounds up to tactile sensations.
By five causes, living beings take on karmic dust (rajas): namely, by killing living beings up to by possession.
By five causes, living beings cast off karmic dust: namely, by abstaining from killing living beings up to by abstaining from possession.
For a homeless ascetic who has undertaken the five-month mendicant’s vow (bhikkhu-paḍimā), it is permissible to accept five morsels of solid food and five sips of drink.

Five types of defilement are taught, namely: defilement regarding origin (uggama-uvadhāta), defilement regarding procurement (uppāyana-uvadhāta), defilement regarding search (esaṇa-uvadhāta), defilement regarding preparation (parikamma-uvadhāta), and defilement regarding consumption (pariharaṇa-uvadhāta).

Five kinds of purification are taught, namely: purification regarding origin (uggama-visōhī), purification regarding procurement (uppāyana-visōhī), purification regarding search (esaṇa-visōhī), purification regarding preparation (parikamma-visōhī), and purification regarding consumption (pariharaṇa-visōhī).

By five causes, living beings create karma that makes enlightenment difficult to attain, namely: by speaking dispraise of the Arhats; by speaking dispraise of the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats; by speaking dispraise of the teachers and preceptors; by speaking dispraise of the fourfold Saṅgha; and by speaking dispraise of the gods who have practiced austerities and celibacy.

By five conditions, living beings perform karma that leads to the state of having easily attainable enlightenment (*sulabhabodhitā*). They are as follows: praising the Arhats; [praising the *siddhas*, praising the *ācāryas*, praising the *upādhyāyas*, and] praising the gods who possess right view and who practice austerity and celibacy.

Five types of withdrawal (*paḍisaṃlīṇa*) are taught: withdrawal of the sense of hearing, up to withdrawal of the sense of touch. Five types of non-withdrawal (*apaḍisaṃlīṇa*) are taught: non-withdrawal of the sense of hearing, up to non-withdrawal of the sense of touch.

Fivefold restraint is taught, namely: restraint of the sense of hearing, up to restraint of the sense of touch. Fivefold non-restraint is taught, namely: non-restraint of the sense of hearing, up to non-restraint of the sense of touch.

Fivefold self-discipline is taught, namely: the discipline of equanimity (*sāmāyika-saṃyama*), the discipline of re-establishment (*chedopasthāpanīya-saṃyama*), the discipline of purification through penance (*parihāraviśuddhi-saṃyama*), the discipline of subtle passion (*sūkṣmasāmparāya-saṃyama*), and the discipline of conduct as it has been proclaimed (*yathākhyāta-cāritra-saṃyama*).
For one who does not harm one-sensed beings, fivefold restraint is practiced, namely: restraint toward the earth-body, up to restraint toward the plant-body.
For one who harms one-sensed beings, fivefold non-restraint is practiced, namely: non-restraint toward the earth-body, up to non-restraint toward the plant-body.

For one who does not harm the five sense-faculties of living beings, fivefold restraint is produced; namely: restraint of the ear-faculty, up to restraint of the body-faculty. For one who harms the five sense-faculties of living beings, fivefold non-restraint is produced; namely: non-restraint of the ear-faculty, up to non-restraint of the body-faculty. For one who does not harm any breathers, beings, souls, or creatures, fivefold restraint is produced; namely: restraint of the one-sensed beings, up to restraint of the five-sensed beings.

For one who instigates violence against all breathers, beings, souls, and living creatures, fivefold non-restraint (*asaṃyama*) is produced, namely: non-restraint regarding one-sensed beings, up to non-restraint regarding five-sensed beings.

Five types of the body of subtle plants (*tanu-vanaspati-kāya*) are taught, namely: those propagated from the tip, those propagated from the root, those propagated from the joint, those propagated from the trunk, and those propagated from seeds.
Fivefold conduct (*ācāra*) is taught, namely: conduct of knowledge, conduct of vision, conduct of character, conduct of austerity, and conduct of energy.

The fivefold rules of conduct (*āyārapakappa*) are taught as follows: the monthly with suspension (*māsiya-ugghāiya*), the monthly without suspension (*māsiya-aṇugghāiya*), the four-monthly with suspension (*caumāsiya-ugghāiya*), the four-monthly without suspension (*caumāsiya-aṇugghāiya*), and the formal imposition (*ārōvaṇā*). The formal imposition is taught as fivefold: that which is sent forth (*paṭṭhaviyā*), that which is established (*ṭhaviyā*), the complete (*kasiṇā*), the incomplete (*akasiṇā*), and the immediate (*hāḍahaḍā*).

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, five Vakkhāra mountains are declared; namely: Mālavanta, Cittakūḍa, Pamhakūḍa, Nalinakūḍa, and Egasēla. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītā, five Vakkhāra mountains are declared; namely: Tikūḍa, Vēsamaṇakūḍa, Añjana, Māyañjana, and Sōmaṇasa. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītoyā, five Vakkhāra mountains are declared; namely: Vijjuppabha, Aṅkāvatī, Pamhāvatī, Āsīvisa, and Suhāvaha. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītoyā, five Vakkhāra mountains are declared; namely: Pacandapavvata, Sūrapavvata, Nāgapavvata, Dēvapavvata, and Gandhamādana.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, in the region of Devakurū, five great lakes are proclaimed, namely: Nisaha-daha, Duvakuru-daha, Sūra-daha, Sulasa-daha, and Vijjuppabha-daha. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, in the region of Uttarakurū, five great lakes are proclaimed, namely: Nīlavanta-daha, Uttaraku-rū-daha, Pañca-daha, Erāvaṇa-daha, and Mālavanta-daha.
All the Vakkhāra mountains and the great rivers Sītā and Sītōdā rise five hundred *yojanas* in height and extend five hundred *gavyūtas* in width.

On the eastern half of the island of Ghātakīṣaṇḍa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, five Vakkhāra mountains are described; namely: Mālavaṃta, and so forth, just as on Jambudvīpa, up to the western half of the island of Puṣkaravaradvīpa, where the Vakkhāra mountains and the lakes are to be described with the same heights.

In the Samayakṣetra, there are five Bharatas and five Airāvatas; thus, as it was stated in the second chapter of the *Caüṭṭhāṇa*, so it should be recited here as well, up to "five Mandaras and five Mandara-cūlikās," with the exception that the *usuyāra* (sunbeams) do not exist.
The Arhat Ṛṣabha, the descendant of Kośala, was five hundred *dhanus* in height. King Bharata, the universal monarch (*cāurantacakkavaṭṭī*), was five hundred *dhanus* in height.

The ascetic Bāhubalī and likewise the nun Bambhī, and similarly Sundarī as well—by five conditions one may wake from sleep: namely, by sound, by touch, by the digestion of food, by the exhaustion of sleep, and by the seeing of a dream.

There are five circumstances in which a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha, while taking hold of or supporting a Nirgranthī, does not transgress [the rule]. They are as follows: (1) If a Nirgranthī should be carried off by some kind of beast or bird, then the Nirgrantha, while taking hold of or supporting the Nirgranthī, does not transgress.

A *nirgrantha* does not transgress [the rule] when taking hold of or supporting a *nirgranthī* who is stumbling or falling on a difficult path or uneven ground; he does not transgress when taking hold of or supporting a *nirgranthī* who is sinking or being submerged in water, mud, moss, or a pool; he does not transgress when helping a *nirgranthī* to board or disembark from a boat; nor does he transgress when taking hold of or supporting a *nirgranthī* who is deranged in mind, possessed by a spirit, obsessed by a *yakṣa*, afflicted by madness, beset by calamity, involved in a legal dispute, subject to penance, one who has renounced food and drink, or one who is suffering from illness.

In the community of the teacher-preceptor (ācārya-upādhyāya), five privileges are prescribed, namely: 1. When the teacher-preceptor repeatedly shakes or sweeps his feet inside the residence (upāśraya), he does not commit an offense. 2. When the teacher-preceptor disposes of or cleans away excrement or urine inside the residence, he does not commit an offense. 3. The teacher-preceptor may, at his own will, perform services for others, or he may choose not to do so. 4. When the teacher-preceptor stays alone for one night or two nights within the residence, he does not commit an offense. 5. When the teacher-preceptor stays alone for one night or two nights outside the residence, he does not commit an offense.

There are five grounds for which the departure from the community (gaṇa) of an Ācārya or Upādhyāya is prescribed, namely: 1. An Ācārya or Upādhyāya does not properly exercise authority or maintain discipline within the community; 2. An Ācārya or Upādhyāya does not properly perform the ritual salutation (kṛtikarma) and respectful service (veṇaiya) toward those senior to him in the community; 3. An Ācārya or Upādhyāya does not properly recite, from time to time, those scriptural portions that he has memorized and mastered within the community; 4. An Ācārya or Upādhyāya maintains external contact with a nun belonging to his own community or another community; 5. Or, if his circle of friends or kinsmen should depart from the community, his departure from the community is prescribed for the sake of supporting and assisting them.
Five kinds of people possessing supernatural power (ṛddhi) are taught, namely: Arhats, universal monarchs (cakravartins), Baladevas, Vāsudevas, and monks who have cultivated their souls.

Five astikāyas (ontological categories) are taught, namely: the astikāya of dharma, the astikāya of adharma, the astikāya of space, the astikāya of soul, and the astikāya of matter. The astikāya of dharma is without color, without smell, without taste, without touch, formless, insentient, eternal, stable, and a substance of the world (*loka-dravya*). In brief, it is taught to be fivefold: by way of substance (*dravyataḥ*), by way of space (*kṣetrataḥ*), by way of time (*kālataḥ*), by way of state (*bhāvataḥ*), and by way of quality (*guṇataḥ*). By way of substance, the astikāya of dharma is a single substance. By way of space, it is co-extensive with the dimensions of the world. By way of time, there never was a time when it did not exist, there never is a time when it does not exist, and there never will be a time when it will not exist; it has existed, it exists, and it will exist—it is constant, permanent, eternal, indestructible, unchanging, stable, and everlasting. By way of state, it is without color, without smell, without taste, and without touch. By way of quality, its characteristic is the quality of facilitating motion.

The description of the non-substance of matter (adhamma-astikāya) is exactly like this; however, in terms of its qualities, it has the quality of providing space for movement (sthāna-guṇa). The description of the non-substance of space (ākāśa-astikāya) is exactly like this; however, in terms of its extent, it is equal in measure to the universe and the non-universe (loka-aloka), and in terms of its qualities, it has the quality of providing accommodation (avagāhana-guṇa); the rest is exactly the same. The description of the non-substance of souls (jīva-astikāya) is exactly like this; however, in terms of substance, there are infinite substances in the non-substance of souls; they are formless (arūpi), eternal (sāśvata), and in terms of their qualities, they have the quality of consciousness (upayoga-guṇa).

The substance of matter (*poggalatthikā*) possesses five colors, five tastes, two odors, and eight tangibles; it is material, non-sentient, eternal, and stable. As for its substantial nature (*davvaō*), the substance of matter consists of infinite substances. As for its spatial nature (*khettaō*), it occupies the extent of the universe. As for its temporal nature (*kālaō*), it has never been non-existent and is eternal. As for its modal nature (*bhāvaō*), it possesses color and so forth up to tangibility. As for its quality (*guṇaō*), its characteristic quality is the property of being grasped. Five destinies (*gatī*) are taught, namely: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of humans, the destiny of gods, and the destiny of the perfected ones (*siddhigatī*). Five objects of the senses (*indiyattha*) are taught, namely: the object of the sense of hearing, and so forth, up to the object of the sense of touch.

Five types of "shaven" (muṇḍa) are taught: the ear-faculty-shaven, up to the touch-faculty-shaven; or alternatively, five types of "shaven" are taught: the anger-shaven, the pride-shaven, the deceit-shaven, the greed-shaven, and the head-shaven.

In the lower world, five types of gross beings are taught, namely: earth-bodied, water-bodied, air-bodied, plant-bodied, and coarse mobile living beings. In the upper world, five types of gross beings are taught, namely: exactly the same.
In the middle world, five types of gross beings are taught, namely: one-sensed beings up to five-sensed beings.

Five types of gross fire-bodied beings are taught, namely: embers, flames, glowing coals, sparks, and meteors. Five types of gross air-bodied beings are taught, namely: east wind, west wind, south wind, north wind, and wind from the intermediate directions.

Five types of non-conscious air-bodied beings are taught, namely: that which is drawn out [from a wound], that which is blown [by a bellows], that which is compressed, that which is inherent in bodies, and that which is spontaneously generated.

Five types of *nigganthas* (ascetics) are taught, namely: the *pulāga*, the *baüsa*, the *kusīla*, the *niggantha*, and the *siṇāta*. The *pulāga* is taught to be of five kinds, namely: the *pulāga* of knowledge, the *pulāga* of vision, the *pulāga* of conduct, the *pulāga* of outward marks, and the fifth is called the *pulāga* according to subtlety (*ahāsuhuma*). The *baüsa* is taught to be of five kinds, namely: the *baüsa* through deliberation (*ābhoga*), the *baüsa* without deliberation (*aṇābhoga*), the *baüsa* who is restrained (*saṃvuḍa*), the *baüsa* who is unrestrained (*asaṃvuḍa*), and the fifth is called the *baüsa* according to subtlety. The *kusīla* is taught to be of five kinds, namely: the *kusīla* of knowledge, the *kusīla* of vision, the *kusīla* of conduct, the *kusīla* of outward marks, and the fifth is called the *kusīla* according to subtlety. The *niyaṇṭha* is taught to be of five kinds, namely: the *niyaṇṭha* of the first moment, the *niyaṇṭha* of the non-first moment, the *niyaṇṭha* of the last moment, the *niyaṇṭha* of the non-last moment, and the fifth is called the *niyaṇṭha* according to subtlety. The *siṇāta* (the one who has bathed) is taught to be of five kinds, namely: one who is skinless (*acchavī*), one who is unblemished (*asabala*), one who is free from karma-matter (*akammaṃsa*), one who possesses perfectly pure knowledge and vision, an Arhat, a Jina, a Kevalin, and one who is stainless (*aparissāī*).

It is permissible for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to wear or use five types of garments, namely: those made of *jaṅgī*, those made of *bhaṅgī*, those made of wool (*sāṇa*), the *pottī*, and fifthly, that which is called the *tiriḍapaṭṭa*.

It is permissible for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to wear or use five types of brooms (*rayaharaṇī*), namely: those made of wool, those made of camel-hair, those made of wool, those made of *paccāpicca* grass, and fifthly, those made of *muñjāpicca* grass.
For one practicing the Dharma, five bases of support (*nissāṭṭhāṇa*) have been taught, namely: the six classes of living beings, the community (*gaṇa*), the king, the householder, and one’s own body.
Five treasures are proclaimed, namely: the treasure of sons, the treasure of friends, the treasure of crafts, the treasure of wealth, and the treasure of grain.
Five kinds of poison are proclaimed, namely: earth-poison, water-poison, fire-poison, mantra-poison, and the poison of Brahman (sacred knowledge).

There are five things that one who is still a *chaumattha* (one with veils) does not know and does not see in their entirety: namely, the substance of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), the substance of rest (*adhammatthikāya*), the substance of space (*āgāsatthikāya*), the soul unbound by a body (*jīva asarīrapaḍibaddha*), and the infinitesimal atom (*paramāṇupoggala*). However, the Arhat, Jina, Kevalin, who possesses arisen knowledge and vision, knows and sees these very same things in their entirety: namely, from the substance of motion up to the infinitesimal atom.

In the lower world, five unsurpassed, vast, and great hells are taught, namely: Kāla, Mahākāla, Raurava, Mahāraurava, and Apratiṣṭhāna. In the upper world, five unsurpassed, vast, and great celestial palaces are taught, namely: Vijaya, Vaijayanta, Jayanta, Aparājita, and Sarvārthasiddha.

Five types of persons are taught, namely: one whose essence is modesty (hirisatta), one whose mind is modesty (hirimaṇasatta), one of wavering essence (calasatta), one of firm essence (thirasatta), and one of rising essence (udayaṇasatta).

Five kinds of fish are taught, namely: one that swims with the current, one that swims against the current, one that moves along the edge, one that moves in the middle, and one that moves everywhere. In the same way, five types of alms-seekers are taught, namely: one who follows the current, and so on, up to one who moves everywhere. Five kinds of mendicants are taught, namely: the mendicant who is a guest, the mendicant who is a poor man, the mendicant who is a Brahmin, the mendicant who is a householder, and the mendicant who is an ascetic.

A naked ascetic (*acelaka*) is praised for five reasons, namely: his fewness of possessions (*appa-ḍilehā*), his praise-worthy lightness (*lāghaviya*), his lack of concern for his appearance (*rūve vesāsie*), his acceptance of austerity (*tave aṇuṇṇāte*), and his extensive restraint of the senses (*viule indiya-niggahē*).

Five types of transgressors (*ukkala*) are taught, namely: the transgressor with a staff (*daṇḍukkale*), the transgressor with a rope (*rajjukkale*), the transgressor who is a thief (*tēṇukkale*), the transgressor regarding a region (*dēsukkale*), and the transgressor regarding everything (*savvukkale*).

Five kinds of carefulness (*samiti*) are taught, namely: carefulness in walking (*iriyā-samiti*), carefulness in speech (*bhāsā-samiti*), carefulness in seeking alms (*esaṇā-samiti*), carefulness in taking up and putting down utensils and belongings (*āyāṇa-bhaṇḍa-matta-nikkhevaṇā-samiti*), and carefulness in the disposal of excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and sweat (*uccāra-pāsavaṇa-khēla-siṃdhāṇa-jalla-pāriṭṭhāvaṇiyā-samiti*).
Living beings who have entered into the cycle of existence are declared to be of five kinds, namely: those with one sense organ, up to those with five sense organs.

One-sensed beings are described as having five destinies and five origins; namely: when a one-sensed being is being reborn among one-sensed beings, it may be reborn from among one-sensed beings up to five-sensed beings. Furthermore, when that same one-sensed being relinquishes its state of being one-sensed, it may go to the state of one-sensed beings up to the state of five-sensed beings. Two-sensed beings likewise have five destinies and five origins; and so on, up to five-sensed beings who are described as having five destinies and five origins; namely: a five-sensed being [may be reborn] up to [the point where it] may go [to any of the five states].

All living beings are declared to be of five kinds, namely: those with anger-passion (kōhakasāī), those with pride-passion (māṇakasāī), those with deceit-passion (māyākasāī), those with greed-passion (lōbhakasāī), and those without passions (akasāī). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be of five kinds, namely: hell-beings (nēraïyā), animals (tirikkha-jōṇiyā), humans (maṇussā), gods (dēvā), and perfected beings (siddhā).

"Venerable Sir, regarding these grains—black lentils, masūra, sesame, mung beans, black gram, niṣpāva, horse gram, ālisandaga, and satīṇa—when they are stored in granaries, baskets, on couches, on shelves, in layers, plastered over, sealed, marked, and covered, for how long does their *yoni* (germinal capacity) persist? "Gautama, at the minimum for a moment (*antarmuhūrta*), and at the maximum for five years. Beyond that, the *yoni* withers; beyond that, the *yoni* is destroyed; beyond that, the *yoni* is utterly ruined; beyond that, the seed becomes non-seed; beyond that, the cessation of the *yoni* is declared."

Five kinds of years are prescribed, namely: the lunar year (*nakkhatta-saṃvacchara*), the yoke-year (*juga-saṃvacchara*), the measure-year (*pamāṇa-saṃvacchara*), the characteristic-year (*lakkhaṇa-saṃvacchara*), and the Saturn-year (*saṇiñcara-saṃvacchara*). The yoke-year is prescribed as fivefold, namely: the moon-year, the moon-year, the intercalary moon-year, the intercalary moon-year, and indeed [the fifth]. The measure-year is prescribed as fivefold, namely: the lunar, the moon, the season, the sun, and the intercalary. The characteristic-year is prescribed as fivefold, namely: [as follows]...
The conjunction of the constellations occurs evenly; the seasons change evenly;
it is neither too hot nor too cold, and there is abundant rain—such is the constellation.
(Ṭhāṇa 499) It joins with the full moon night together with the moon while the constellations are moving unevenly.
When there is much bitterness and many [unseasonable] rains, they call that the *cāndra* year.

When the clouds ripen out of season, giving flowers and fruits even to those trees that do not yet bear them, and when the rain does not fall properly, they call that the *kārmika* year. (Ṭhāṇa 500–501)
The sun gives its essence to the earth and water, as well as to the flowers and fruits;
even with little rain, the harvest ripens properly.
(Ṭhāṇaṅga 502) Through the heat of the sun’s rays, the moments, instants, days, and seasons pass away.
Know, O Renu, that this is called "the dust has settled," which signifies that it has increased. (Sutta Nipata 503)

Fivefold is the path of departure for a living being as it has been taught, namely: by means of the feet, by means of the thighs, by means of the chest, by means of the head, and by means of all the limbs. One departing by means of the feet becomes a goer to hell; one departing by means of the thighs becomes a goer to the animal realm; one departing by means of the chest becomes a goer among humans; one departing by means of the head becomes a goer among humans [or] becomes a goer to the world of gods; one departing by means of all the limbs is taught to have the attainment of perfection (siddhigati) as its ultimate end.

Five kinds of disintegration (*chēyaṇa*) are taught, namely: disintegration of arising (*uppā-chēyaṇa*), disintegration of disappearance (*viya-chēyaṇa*), disintegration of bondage (*bandha-chēyaṇa*), disintegration of space-points (*paēsa-chēyaṇa*), and disintegration of the two-edged [soul] (*dōdhāra-chēyaṇa*). Five kinds of immediate succession (*āṇantariya*) are taught, namely: immediate succession of arising (*uppā-āṇantariya*), immediate succession of disappearance (*viya-āṇantariya*), immediate succession of space-points (*paēsa-āṇantariya*), immediate succession of time-units (*samaya-āṇantariya*), and immediate succession of generality (*sāmaṇṇa-āṇantariya*). Five kinds of infinity (*aṇanta*) are taught, namely: nominal infinity (*nāmāṇanta*), conventional infinity (*ṭhavaṇāṇanta*), substantial infinity (*davvāṇanta*), numerical infinity (*gaṇaṇāṇanta*), and spatial infinity (*paēsa-aṇanta*). Alternatively, five kinds of infinity are taught, namely: absolute infinity (*ēganta-aṇanta*), dual-ended infinity (*duhaō-aṇanta*), partial extension infinity (*dēsavitthārāṇanta*), total extension infinity (*savvavitthārāṇanta*), and eternal infinity (*sāsayāṇanta*).

Knowledge is taught to be fivefold, namely: sensory knowledge (*ābhinibōhiya-nāṇa*), scriptural knowledge (*suya-nāṇa*), clairvoyance (*ōhi-nāṇa*), mind-reading knowledge (*maṇapajjava-nāṇa*), and omniscience (*kevala-nāṇa*).

The karma that obscures knowledge is taught to be fivefold, namely: the karma that obscures sensory knowledge, the karma that obscures scriptural knowledge, the karma that obscures clairvoyance, the karma that obscures mind-reading knowledge, and the karma that obscures omniscience.
Recitation (*sajjhāya*) is taught to be fivefold, namely: teaching (*vāyaṇā*), questioning (*pucchaṇā*), reviewing (*pariyaṭṭaṇā*), reflecting (*aṇuppēhā*), and religious discourse (*dhammakahā*).

Five kinds of renunciation (paccakkhāṇa) are taught, namely: purity through faith, purity through discipline, purity through recitation, purity through preservation, and purity through inner disposition (bhāva).

Five kinds of confession (paḍikkamaṇa) are taught, namely: confession regarding the doors of influx (āsava), confession regarding false belief (micchatta), confession regarding the passions (kasāya), confession regarding activity (joga), and confession regarding inner disposition (bhāva).

One should recite the scripture for five reasons: for the sake of gathering [disciples], for the sake of assisting [others], for the sake of self-purification (*nijjarā*), so that the scripture may be mastered by me, or for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of the scriptural tradition. One should study the scripture for five reasons: for the sake of knowledge, for the sake of right vision, for the sake of conduct, for the sake of releasing [others] from conflict, or thinking, "I shall know the reality within my own hands.
In the celestial realms of *Saudharma* and *Īśāna*, the palaces (*vimānas*) are described as being of five colors, namely: black, up to white.
In the Saṃhama and Īśāna heavens, the celestial palaces (vimānas) are declared to be five hundred yojanas in height.
In the Brahma and Lāntaka heavens, the bodies maintained by the gods (bhavadhāraṇija-sarīraga) are declared to be at most five cubits (rayanī) in height.

Hell-beings (nēraïya) have bound, do bind, or will bind matter (poggala) of five colors and five tastes; namely, from black to white, and from bitter to sweet. This applies likewise up to the Vaimānika gods.
On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, five great rivers join the great river Gaṅgā; namely: the Jaūṇā, Saraū, Āvī, Kōsī, and Mahī.
On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, five great rivers join the great river Sindhu; namely: the Sataddū, Vitatthā, Vibhāsā, Erāvatī, and Candabhāgā.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, five great rivers flow into the Raktā Mahānadī; namely: Kiṇhā, Mahākiṇhā, Nīlā, Mahānīlā, and Mahātīrā.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, five great rivers flow into the Raktāvati Mahānadī; namely: Indā, Indasenā, Susenā, Vārisenā, and Mahābhogā.

Five Tīrthaṅkaras, having lived in the state of householders during their youth, became shaven-headed and went forth from the home to the homeless life; namely: Vāsupūjya, Malli, Ariṣṭanemi, Pārśva, and Vīra. In the royal capital Camaracañcā, five assembly halls are proclaimed; namely: the Sudharmā assembly hall, the Upapāta assembly hall, the Abhiṣeka assembly hall, the Alaṅkārika assembly hall, and the Vyavasāya assembly hall. In each individual position of Indra, five assembly halls are proclaimed; namely: the Sudharmā assembly hall, the Upapāta assembly hall, the Abhiṣeka assembly hall, the Alaṅkārika assembly hall, and the Vyavasāya assembly hall.
Five constellations with five stars each are proclaimed, namely: Dhanisthā, Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Hastā, and Viśākhā.

Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate matter formed in five ways as sinful karma; namely: that which is formed by one-sensed organisms, up to that which is formed by five-sensed organisms. Likewise, the aggregates (skandhas) consisting of five space-points (*pradeśa*), which are subject to accumulation (*ciṇa*), further accumulation (*uvaciṇa*), bondage (*bandha*), activation (*udīra*), experience (*vēda*), and likewise destruction (*nijjarā*), are taught to be infinite. Infinite particles of matter (*poggala*) occupying five space-points are taught to be infinite, up to infinite particles of matter possessing the quality of dryness (*lukkha*) to the fifth degree.

An ascetic endowed with six qualities is worthy of maintaining a community (*gaṇa*); namely: one who is full of faith, one who is truthful, one who is wise, one who is learned, one who possesses strength, and one who is free from legal disputes.

A *nirgrantha*, when accepting or supporting a female *nirgrantha*, does not transgress [the rule] in six cases; namely: one whose mind is deranged, one whose mind is obsessed by passion, one possessed by a spirit, one who has become insane, one who is undergoing affliction, and one who is involved in a legal dispute.

In six circumstances, the *nirgranthas* and *nirgranthīs*, while attending to a fellow member of the community who has passed away, do not transgress: namely, when they are carrying [the body] from the interior to the exterior, or from the exterior out beyond [the boundary]; or when they are observing it; or when they are sitting near it; or when they are taking leave [of the deceased]; or when they proceed in silence.

There are six things that one who is still in the state of a *chaumattha* (one with veils) does not know and does not see in their entirety: namely, the substance of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), the substance of rest (*adhammatthikāya*), space (*āyāsa*), the soul unbound by a body (*jīvamasarīrapaḍibaddha*), the atom (*paramāṇupoggala*), and sound (*sadda*). However, the Arhat, Jina, Kevalin, who possesses arisen knowledge and vision, knows and sees these very same things in their entirety: namely, the substance of motion, and so on, up to sound.

There are six conditions in which all living beings possess no supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), nor splendor (*dyuti*), nor fame (*yaśas*), nor strength (*bala*), nor vigor (*vīrya*), nor personal exertion (*puruṣakāra-parākrama*). They are as follows: making a living being into a non-living thing; making a non-living thing into a living being; speaking two languages simultaneously; experiencing or not experiencing the fruit of karma created by oneself; cutting or breaking a single atom (*paramāṇu-pudgala*); or passing beyond the limits of the world with one's own body.

Six classes of living beings are taught, namely: the earth-bodied, up to the mobile-bodied. Six planets are taught, namely: Venus, Jupiter, Mars, Rāhu, Saturn, and Ketu. Six types of living beings involved in the cycle of existence are taught, namely: the earth-bodied, up to the mobile-bodied.

Earth-bodied beings have six destinations and six origins; that is to say: when an earth-bodied being is being reborn among earth-bodied beings, it may be reborn from among earth-bodied beings or even from among mobile-bodied beings. Furthermore, when that same earth-bodied being relinquishes its state as an earth-bodied being, it may go to the state of an earth-bodied being or even to the state of a mobile-bodied being. Water-bodied beings also have six destinations and six origins; likewise for all others up to mobile-bodied beings.

All living beings are declared to be of six kinds, namely: those with sensory-cognition knowledge (*ābhinibodhika-jñānī*), up to those with omniscience (*kevala-jñānī*), and those with non-knowledge (*ajñānī*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be of six kinds, namely: one-sensed beings (*ekendriya*), up to five-sensed beings (*pañcendriya*), and those without senses (*anindriya*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be of six kinds, namely: those possessing a physical body (*audārika-śarīrin*), those possessing a transformation body (*vaikriyika-śarīrin*), those possessing an assimilative body (*āhāraka-śarīrin*), those possessing a fiery body (*taijasa-śarīrin*), those possessing a karmic body (*kārmaṇa-śarīrin*), and those without a body (*aśarīrin*).

The minute vegetable-bodied beings are declared to be of six kinds, namely: those propagated from the tip (*agrabīja*), those propagated from the root (*mūlabīja*), those propagated from the joint (*porabīja*), those propagated from the trunk (*skandhabīja*), those propagated from seeds (*bījaruha*), and those produced by spontaneous generation (*saṃmūrchima*).

There are six conditions that are not easily obtained by all living beings, namely: birth in a human existence; birth in a noble land; rebirth in a good family; hearing the Dharma proclaimed by the Kevalin; faith in what has been heard; and the proper practice with the body of that which has been heard, believed, or approved.
There are six objects of the senses, namely: the object of the sense of hearing, up to the object of the sense of touch, and the object of the mind-sense (no-indriya).

Sixfold restraint is taught; namely: restraint of the ear-faculty, up to restraint of the body-faculty, and restraint of the mind-faculty (*no-indriya*). Sixfold non-restraint is taught; namely: non-restraint of the ear-faculty, up to non-restraint of the body-faculty, and non-restraint of the mind-faculty.
Sixfold pleasure is taught; namely: pleasure of the ear-faculty, up to pleasure of the mind-faculty.
Sixfold pain is taught; namely: pain of the ear-faculty, up to pain of the mind-faculty.

Sixfold is the expiation prescribed, namely: that which is worthy of confession, that which is worthy of repentance, that which is worthy of both, that which is worthy of separation, that which is worthy of relinquishment, and that which is worthy of austerity.

Six kinds of humans are taught, namely: those of Jambūdvīpa; those of the eastern half of Ghātakīkhaṇḍa-dvīpa; those of the western half of Ghātakīkhaṇḍa-dvīpa; those of the eastern half of Puṣkaravaradvīpa; those of the western half of Puṣkaravaradvīpa; and those of the intermediate islands (antaradvīpa). Alternatively, six kinds of humans are taught: spontaneously born humans (saṃmūrchima-manuṣya) of the karma-bhūmis, of the non-karma-bhūmis, and of the intermediate islands; and womb-born humans (garbhavyutkrāntika-manuṣya) of the karma-bhūmis, of the non-karma-bhūmis, and of the intermediate islands.

Six kinds of humans possessing supernatural powers (*ṛddhimanta*) are taught, namely: Arhats, universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), Baladevas, Vāsudevas, Cāraṇas, and Vidyādharas. Six kinds of humans lacking supernatural powers are taught, namely: those from the Haimavata region, those from the Hairaṇyavata region, those from Harivarṣa, those from Ramyakavarṣa, the inhabitants of Kuru, and those from the intermediate islands (*antaradvīpa*).

The *osappiṇī* (descending cycle) is taught to be sixfold, namely: *susama-susamā*, *susamā*, *susama-duṣamā*, *duṣama-susamā*, *duṣamā*, and *duṣama-duṣamā*. The *ussappiṇī* (ascending cycle) is taught to be sixfold, namely: from *duṣama-duṣamā* up to *susama-susamā*.

In the regions of Bhārata and Airāvata on the island of Jambūdvīpa, during the *susama-susamā* period of the past *ussappiṇī*, humans were six thousand *dhanus* in height and lived for a maximum lifespan of six and a half *palyopamas*.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during this *susama-susamā* (the most excellent) period of the current *avasarpinī*, it was exactly thus. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Bharata and Airāvata, during the *susama-susamā* period of the future *utsarpinī*, it will be exactly thus, up until they shall maintain a maximum lifespan of six and a half *palyopamas*.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the regions of Devakuru and Uttarakuru, humans are declared to be six thousand *dhanus* in height and to live for a maximum of six and a half *palyopamas*. Likewise, there are four such discourses for the eastern half of Dhātakīkhaṇḍadvīpa, up to four discourses for the western half of Puṣkaravaradvīpa.

There are six types of bone-joints (saṅghayaṇa), namely: the adamantine-ox-bolt joint (vairōsabhanārāyasaṅghayaṇa), the ox-bolt joint (usabhanārāyasaṅghayaṇa), the bolt joint (nārāyasaṅghayaṇa), the half-bolt joint (addhanārāyasaṅghayaṇa), the pin joint (khīliyāsaṅghayaṇa), and the unclosed joint (chēvaṭṭasaṅghayaṇa).

There are six types of bodily figures (saṇṭhāṇa), namely: symmetrical and square (samacaüraṁsa), globular (naggōhaparimaṇḍala), triangular (sāī), hunchbacked (khujjē), dwarf-like (vāmaṇē), and misshapen (huṇḍē).

There are six conditions that, when not practiced by oneself, lead to harm, impurity, lack of forbearance, lack of excellence, and a lack of future benefit; namely: seniority (*pariyāya*), retinue (*pariyāla*), learning (*suta*), austerity (*tava*), gain (*lābha*), and honor and respect (*pūyāsakkāra*). There are six conditions that, when practiced by oneself, lead to welfare, purity, forbearance, excellence, and future benefit; namely: seniority, retinue, learning, austerity, gain, and honor and respect. Six types of noble-born humans (*jāti-āriya*) are declared;
namely: the Ambaṭṭhas, the Kalandas, the Vedehas, and the Vedigādikas.
The Haritas, the Cuñcus, and these six are the Ibbha castes.
(Ṭhāṇa 541) Six kinds of noble families of humans are taught, namely: Uggas, Bhogas, Rāiṇṇas, Ikkhāgas, Nātas, and Kauravyas.

Sixfold is the stability of the world taught, as follows: wind is established in space; the ocean is established in wind; the earth is established in the ocean; mobile and immobile beings are established on the earth; non-living things are established in living beings; and living beings are established in karma.

Six directions are taught, namely: east, west, south, north, upward, and downward. In these six directions, the movement (*gati*) of living beings proceeds, namely: eastward up to downward. Likewise [apply this to] coming (*āgati*), turning away (*vakkantī*), nutrition (*āhāra*), growth (*vuḍḍhī*), decline (*nivuḍḍhī*), transformation (*viguvvaṇā*), the cycle of existence (*gatipariyāya*), the total mobilization of the body (*samugghāta*), conjunction with time (*kālasañjoga*), the attainment of right vision (*daṃsaṇābhigama*), the attainment of knowledge (*nāṇābhigama*), the comprehension of living beings (*jīvābhigama*), and the comprehension of non-living beings (*ajīvābhigama*). The same applies to five-sensed animals and humans. There are six conditions by which a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha, while taking food, does not transgress [the rule], namely...

For the sake of alleviating pain, for the sake of service, for the sake of proper conduct (*īryāpatha*), for the sake of self-restraint (*saṃyama*), for the sake of protecting living beings, and sixthly, for the sake of reflecting upon the Dharma. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 546) A Śramaṇa Nirgrantha who discontinues food intake does not transgress [the rule] in six circumstances, namely:—

[One may undergo] the cutting off of the body for the sake of enduring illness and calamities, for the sake of guarding celibacy, for the sake of compassion toward living beings, or for the sake of austerity.

(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 548) There are six causes by which a person may fall into madness, namely: speaking ill of the Arhats; speaking ill of the Dharma proclaimed by the Arhats; speaking ill of the teachers and preceptors; speaking ill of the fourfold community; being possessed by a spirit; and through the rising of deluding karma (*mohanīya-karman*).

Six kinds of negligence (*pramāda*) are taught, namely: negligence due to intoxicants, negligence due to sleep, negligence due to the objects of the senses, negligence due to the passions (*kaṣāya*), negligence due to gambling, and negligence regarding inspection (*pratilekhanā*).
Six kinds of negligent inspection are taught, namely:
the hurried (*ārabhaḍā*), the crushing (*saṃmardā*), and the third, the shoving (*mosalī*), which should be avoided.
Shaking off [dust] is the fourth; scattering [it] is the sixth. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 552) Sixfold is the inspection for non-negligence as it is taught, namely:
not shaking excessively, not shaking too much, not continuous, and indeed without the *mosalī* gesture.
The six *purimas* and nine *khōḍas* are for the purification of water-drinking.

(Ṭhāṇa 554) Six *leśyās* are taught, namely: black *leśyā*, blue *leśyā*, grey *leśyā*, yellow *leśyā*, pink *leśyā*, and white *leśyā*. Six *leśyās* are taught for five-sensed animals (*pañcendriya-tirikkhajōṇiya*), namely: black *leśyā* up to white *leśyā*. Likewise for humans and gods.

Of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, the moon-god Mahārāja, six chief queens are taught. Of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, the sun-god Mahārāja, six chief queens are taught.
The lifespan of the gods in the middle assembly of Īśāna, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is declared to be six *palyopamas*.
Six great female elders among the *Diśākumāris* are declared, namely: Rūpā, Rūpaṃsā, Surūpā, Rūpavatī, Rūpakāntā, and Rūpaprabhā.
Six great female elders among the *Vidyutkumāris* are declared, namely: Alā, Śakrā, Satārā, Sotāmaṇī, Indrā, and Dhanavidyutā.
The Nāga-kumāra lord, Dharaṇa, the king of the Nāga-kumāras, has six chief queens (agramahiṣīs), namely: Alā, Śakrā, Satārā, Sautāmanī, Indrā, and Dhanavidyutā.
The Nāga-kumāra lord, Bhūtānanda, the king of the Nāga-kumāras, has six chief queens, namely: Rūpā, Rūpāṃśā, Surūpā, Rūpavatī, Rūpakāntā, and Rūpaprabhā.
As it is for Dharaṇa, so it is for all those on the southern side up to Ghoṣa; as it is for Bhūtānanda, so it is for all those on the northern side up to Mahāghoṣa.
The Nāgakumāra lord and king Gharagaṇa has six thousand *sāmānika* deities; likewise for Bhūtānanda up to Mahāghoṣa.

Sixfold is the cognition of apprehension (*ōgahamati*) taught: namely, it apprehends quickly, it apprehends much, it apprehends manifoldly, it apprehends firmly, it apprehends independently, and it apprehends without doubt. Sixfold is the cognition of inquiry (*īhāmati*) taught: namely, it inquires quickly, it inquires much, [and so on] up to it inquires without doubt.
The intellect of comprehension (*avāya-mati*) is declared to be sixfold; namely: it comprehends quickly, and so on, up to it comprehends without doubt.

The intellect of retention (*dhāraṇā-mati*) is declared to be sixfold; namely: it retains much, it retains manifold, it retains what is ancient, it retains what is difficult to retain, it retains independently, and it retains without doubt.

External austerity (*bāhiraya-tava*) is declared to be sixfold; namely: fasting (*aṇasaṇa*), reduction of the appetite (*ōmōdariyā*), the practice of begging for alms (*bhikkhāyariyā*), renunciation of delicious flavors (*rasapari-cāē*), mortification of the body (*kāyakilēsa*), and seclusion (*paḍisaṁlīṇatā*).
Sixfold internal austerity is taught, namely: expiation, humility, service, study, meditation, and renunciation.
Sixfold dispute is taught, namely: by stepping down, by stepping up, by following the grain, by going against the grain, by breaking, and by splitting.
Sixfold small living beings are taught, namely: two-sensed, three-sensed, four-sensed, five-sensed terrestrial animals born of moisture, fire-bodied beings, and air-bodied beings.

Sixfold is the alms-round prescribed, namely: the cart-like (pēḍā), the half-cart-like (addhapēḍā), the cow’s urination (gōmuttiyā), the locust-path (pataṅgavīhiyā), the conch-spiral (sambukkāvaṭṭā), and the going-and-returning (gantumpaccāgatā).

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, on this Jewel-Luster Earth (Rayaṇappabhā puḍhavī), six great descending hells are prescribed, namely: Lōla, Lōluē, Uddaḍḍha, Nidaḍḍha, Jarā, and Pajjarā.
On the fourth earth, the Mud-Luster Earth (Paṅkappabhā puḍhavī), six great descending hells are prescribed, namely: Āra, Vāra, Māra, Rōra, Rōrūva, and Khāḍakhaḍa.
In the Brahma-world kalpa, six tiers of celestial mansions are proclaimed, namely: Ara, Viraja, Niraja, Nirmala, Vitimira, and Viśuddha.

Of the moon, the lord of luminaries and refuge of luminaries, six constellations are proclaimed as belonging to the eastern half, having equal fields, and consisting of thirty muhūrtas, namely: Pūrvabhādrapadā, Kṛttikā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Mūla, and Pūrvāṣāḍhā.

Of the moon, the lord of luminaries and refuge of luminaries, six constellations are declared to be night-partakers, having half-fields and fifteen muhūrtas each; namely: Śatabhiṣaj, Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Aśleṣā, Svātī, and Jyeṣṭhā.

Of the moon, the lord of luminaries and refuge of luminaries, six constellations are declared to be both-day-and-night-partakers, having one and a half fields and forty-five muhūrtas each; namely: Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Uttaraphalgunī, Viśākhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarābhādrapadā.
The Kulakara Abhicaṇḍa was six hundred *dhanus* in height.
King Bharata, the universal monarch (*cāurantacakkavaṭṭī*), was a great king for six hundred thousand *pūrva*s.
Of the Arhat Pārśva, the foremost among men, there was an assembly of six hundred disputants who were undefeated in the presence of the assembly of gods, humans, and asuras.
The Arhat Vāsupūjya went forth into homelessness as a monk together with six hundred men.
The Arhat Candraprabha remained a *chaumattha* (one still possessing physical obscuration) for six months.

For one who does not harm three-sensed beings, sixfold restraint is accomplished; namely: he becomes one who does not deprive [beings] of olfactory pleasure, nor does he become one who joins them with olfactory pain; likewise for gustatory pleasure, and so too for tactile pleasure.

For one who begins the destruction of three-sensed beings, sixfold non-restraint is produced, namely: by depriving them of olfactory pleasure, he becomes joined with olfactory pain; [and so on] up to: by depriving them of tactile pleasure, he becomes joined with tactile pain.
In the island of Jambudvīpa, six non-karmabhūmis are proclaimed, namely: Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, Ramyakavarṣa, Devakuru, and Uttarakuru.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, six regions (varṣas) are taught, namely: Bharata, Airāvata, Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, and Ramyakavarṣa.
On the island of Jambūdvīpa, six mountain ranges (varṣadhara-parvatās) are taught, namely: Cullahimavanta, Mahāhimavanta, Nisadha, Nīlavanta, Rūpyī, and Śikhari.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, six peaks are declared, namely: Cullahimavanta-peak, Vessamaṇa-peak, Mahāhimavanta-peak, Vairuliya-peak, Nisadha-peak, and Ruyaga-peak. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, six peaks are declared, namely: Nīlavanta-peak, Uvadaṃsaṇa-peak, Ruppika-peak, Maṇikacaṇa-peak, Sihari-peak, and Tigiccha-peak.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, six great lakes are proclaimed, namely: Paumaddaha, Mahāpaumaddaha, Tigiñchiddaha, Kesariddaha, Mahāpoṇḍarīyaddaha, and Puṇḍarīyaddaha. Therein dwell six goddesses of great power, [possessing splendor, fame, and glory], with a lifespan of a *palyopama*, namely: Śrī, Hrī, Dhṛti, Kīrti, Buddhi, and Lakṣmī.

On the continent of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, six great rivers are declared; namely: Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Rohitā, Rohitaṃsā, Harī, and Harikāntā. On the continent of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, six great rivers are declared; namely: Narakāntā, Nārikāntā, Suvarṇakūlā, Rūpyakūlā, Raktā, and Raktavatī.
