On the island of Jambudvīpa, on both banks of the great river Sītā to the east of Mount Mandara, six intermediate rivers are declared; namely: Gāhāvatī, Dahavatī, Paṅkavatī, Tattajalā, Mattajalā, and Ummattajalā. On the island of Jambudvīpa, on both banks of the great river Sītōdā to the west of Mount Mandara, six intermediate rivers are declared; namely: Khīrōdā, Sīhasōtā, Antōvāhiṇī, Ummimāliṇī, Phēṇamāliṇī, and Gambhīramāliṇī.

In the eastern half of the island of Ghātakhaṇḍa, six non-karmabhūmi regions are taught, namely: Haimavata, and so forth; just as it is described for Jambūdvīpa, up to the intermediate rivers, so it should be recited up to the western half of Pukkhavaradvīpa.
Six seasons are taught, namely: the rainy season (pāuṣa), the monsoon (varṣārātra), autumn (śarad), winter (hemanta), spring (vasanta), and summer (grīṣma).

Six deficient nights (ōmaratta) are taught, namely: on the third lunar day, the seventh lunar day, the eleventh lunar day, the fifteenth lunar day, the nineteenth lunar day, and the twenty-third lunar day.
Six nights are prescribed, namely: on the fourth day, the eighth day, the twelfth day, the sixteenth day, the twentieth day, and the twenty-fourth day.

Regarding the knowledge of sensory perception (*ābhinibōhiya-ñāṇa*), there are six kinds of grasping of objects (*atthoggaha*), namely: grasping of objects by the sense of hearing, grasping of objects by the sense of sight, grasping of objects by the sense of smell, grasping of objects by the sense of taste, grasping of objects by the sense of touch, and grasping of objects by the mind-sense (*nōindiya*).

Clairvoyant knowledge (*avadhijñāna*) is declared to be of six kinds, namely: that which follows one (*ānugāmika*), that which does not follow one (*anānugāmika*), that which increases (*vardhamānaka*), that which decreases (*hīyamānaka*), that which is reversible (*pratipāti*), and that which is irreversible (*apratipāti*).

It is not permitted for *nirgranthas* or *nirgranthīs* to utter these six types of speech, namely: false speech (*aliyavayana*), slanderous speech (*hāliyavayana*), contemptuous speech (*khiṃsitavayana*), harsh speech (*pharusavayana*), worldly speech (*gāratthiyavayana*), or to repeat what has already been discussed.

Six extensions of the *kalpa* are proclaimed, namely: speaking the vow of taking life, speaking the vow of false speech, speaking the vow of taking what is not given, speaking the vow of non-abstinence, speaking the vow of being no man, and speaking the vow of being a slave. Having extended these six extensions of the *kalpa*, one who does not fulfill them correctly reaches that state.

Six obstacles to the spiritual life have been declared; namely: being quarrelsome is an obstacle to self-restraint; being deceitful is an obstacle to truthful speech; being fickle-eyed is an obstacle to careful movement (*īryāpatha*); being greedy for food is an obstacle to the sphere of pure alms-seeking; being overcome by desire is an obstacle to the path of liberation; making a vow for future existence is an obstacle to the path of liberation. In all respects, the Blessed One has praised freedom from such vows.

There are six types of disciplinary standing (kappaṭṭhitī), namely: the standing of the Sāmāyika discipline, the standing of the Chedopasthāpanika discipline, the standing of the Nivvisamāṇaka discipline, the standing of the Nivviṭṭha discipline, the standing of the Jina-discipline, and the standing of the Thera-discipline.
The venerable ascetic Mahāvīra went forth as a renunciant, shaven-headed, after six meals without water.
For the venerable ascetic Mahāvīra, after six meals without water, infinite, supreme [knowledge] arose, up to [the attainment of omniscience].
The Blessed One, the Great Hero, the ascetic, attained perfection on the sixth meal without water, having reached the state of a *siddha* and being liberated from all suffering.

In the Saṇaṅkumāra and Māhinda heavens, the celestial palaces (*vimāṇa*) are declared to be six hundred *yojanas* in height. In the Saṇaṅkumāra and Māhinda heavens, the gods are declared to be [six] hundred *yojanas* in height. In the Saṇaṅkumāra and Māhinda heavens, the bodies of the gods maintained by their own existence (*bhavadhāraṇijja*) are declared to be at most six *ratnīs* in height.
Sixfold is the transformation of food as it is taught, namely: pleasant, savory, nourishing, invigorating, intoxicating, and exhilarating.

Sixfold is the transformation of poison as it is taught, namely: that which is bitten, that which is eaten, that which has entered the body, that which follows the flesh, that which follows the blood, and that which follows the marrow.

Sixfold is the inquiry as it is taught, namely: inquiry based on doubt, inquiry based on contention, sequential inquiry, conformable inquiry, knowledge of things as they are, and knowledge of things not as they are.
The royal city of Camaracañcā is, at most, six months devoid of a new arrival by way of rebirth.
Each individual position of an Indra is, at most, six months devoid of a new arrival by way of rebirth.

The seventh nether earth (Aghasaptama) is, at most, six months devoid of a new arrival by way of rebirth. The state of the perfected ones (Siddhagati) is, at most, six months devoid of a new arrival by way of rebirth.

The bondage of life-span (*āyu-bandha*) is declared to be sixfold, namely: life-span bound by the name-karma of birth (*jāti-nāma-nidhattāyu*), life-span bound by the name-karma of destiny (*gati-nāma-nidhattāyu*), life-span bound by the name-karma of duration (*sthiti-nāma-nidhattāyu*), life-span bound by the name-karma of body-extent (*avagāhanā-nāma-nidhattāyu*), life-span bound by the name-karma of location (*pradeśa-nāma-nidhattāyu*), and life-span bound by the name-karma of intensity (*anubhāga-nāma-nidhattāyu*).

The bondage of life-span for hell-beings (*nairayika*) is declared to be sixfold, namely: life-span bound by the name-karma of birth, up to life-span bound by the name-karma of intensity; and so on, up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm.

Hell-beings (*nairayika*) necessarily project the life-span of their next existence when six months of their current life remain; the same applies to the asura-kumāras up to the stanita-kumāras. Five-sensed subhuman beings (*tiryagyoni*) with an incalculable lifespan (*asaṃkhyeyavarṣāyuṣka*) who possess consciousness (*saṃjñin*) necessarily project the life-span of their next existence when six months of their current life remain. Conscious human beings (*manuṣya*) with an incalculable lifespan necessarily project the life-span of their next existence when six months of their current life remain. The *vānamantara*, *jyotiṣka*, and *vaimānika* [gods] are like the hell-beings.

Six kinds of dispositions (*bhāva*) are taught, namely: innate (*audayika*), subsidential (*upaśamika*), destructive (*kṣāyika*), destructive-subsidential (*kṣayopaśamika*), transformational (*pāriṇāmika*), and combined (*sānnipātika*).
Six kinds of confession (*pratikramaṇa*) are taught, namely: confession for excrement, confession for urine, temporary, lifelong, and that which consists of "whatever is wrong" or "pleasing.
The constellation Kṛttikā is taught to have four stars; the constellation Aśleṣā is taught to have four stars.

Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate matter formed into six types of entities as sinful karma (*pāvakamma*). They are as follows: those formed from the earth-body (*puḍhavikāiya*) up to those formed from the mobile-body (*tasakāiya*). Likewise, there are the six processes: accumulation (*ciṇa*), further accumulation (*uvaciṇa*), bondage (*bandha*), activation (*udīra*), experience (*veya*), and likewise, shedding (*nijjarā*).

Infinite aggregates (*khandha*) consisting of six space-points (*pradeśa*) are taught; infinite matter-particles (*poggala*) occupying six space-points are taught; infinite matter-particles with a duration of six time-units (*samaya*) are taught; and infinite matter-particles with sixfold black color, up to infinite matter-particles with sixfold roughness, are taught.

There are seven ways of departing from the community, as follows: (1) I find pleasure in all teachings; (2) I find pleasure in some, but not in others; (3) I have doubt regarding all teachings; (4) I have doubt regarding some, but not regarding others; (5) I reject all teachings; (6) I reject some, but do not reject others; (7) I accept all teachings. "Venerable Sir, I desire to adopt and dwell in the practice of the solitary wandering ascetic."

Sevenfold is the knowledge of analysis (vibhaṅga-ñāṇa) taught; namely: the penetration of the world in one direction, the penetration of the world in five directions, the soul as subject to karmic obstructions, the soul as pure, the soul as impure, the soul as possessing form, and all this as souls.

In this regard, first is the knowledge of discernment (*vibhaṅganāṇa*): when such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa acquires the knowledge of discernment, by means of that arisen knowledge of discernment he perceives in the east, west, south, north, or upwards as far as the *Saudharma* heaven. It occurs to him: "An extraordinary knowledge and vision has arisen in me regarding the comprehension of the world in one direction; yet some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas have said that there is a comprehension of the world in all five directions. Those who have spoken thus have spoken falsely. This is the first knowledge of discernment.

Furthermore, this is the second type of analytical knowledge (*vibhaṅga-jñāna*): when such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa possesses arisen analytical knowledge, by means of that arisen analytical knowledge he perceives in the east, west, south, north, or upwards as far as the *Saudharma* heaven. To him it occurs: "An extraordinary knowledge and vision has arisen in me regarding the penetration of the world in five directions. There are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who say that the penetration of the world is in only one direction; those who speak thus speak falsely. This is the second type of analytical knowledge.

Furthermore, regarding the third type of analytical knowledge (*vibhaṅganāṇa*): when such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa attains analytical knowledge, by means of that attained analytical knowledge he perceives beings killing living creatures, speaking falsehoods, taking what is not given, indulging in sexual misconduct, and accumulating possessions; yet he does not perceive evil karma being committed. Then it occurs to him: "I possess a superior knowledge and vision that has arisen, [according to which] the soul is obscured by action (*kiriyāvaraṇa*). There are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who say, 'The soul is not obscured by action'; those who speak thus speak falsely. This is the third type of analytical knowledge.

Furthermore, regarding the fourth type of analytical knowledge (*vibhaṅga-jñāna*): when such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa possesses arisen analytical knowledge, by means of that arisen analytical knowledge he perceives the gods themselves. Without having grasped external or internal matter, yet having touched, pervaded, and permeated it as a single entity and in its diversity, and having transformed it, he remains [there]. Then this thought occurs to him: "An extraordinary knowledge and vision has arisen in me: 'The soul is powerful. Yet some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas say, 'The soul is not powerful. Those who speak thus speak falsely. This is the fourth type of analytical knowledge.

Furthermore, there is a fifth type of analytical knowledge (*vibhaṅga-jñāna*). When such a kind of ascetic [as previously described] attains it, by means of that arisen analytical knowledge he perceives only the gods. He sees external and internal matter that has not been exhausted; having manifested various forms and bodies, he remains so. Then this thought occurs to him: "There exists... [the self] has arisen as an immortal soul. Those ascetics or brahmins who say 'the soul is mortal'—those who speak thus have spoken falsely. This is the fifth type of analytical knowledge.

Furthermore, regarding the sixth type of analytical knowledge (*vibhaṅganāṇa*): when such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa possesses arisen analytical knowledge, by means of that arisen analytical knowledge he perceives the gods themselves. He perceives material bodies (*poggala*), whether they have been appropriated or not appropriated, having touched, vibrated, burst, and transformed them into various states of unity and diversity. To him it occurs: "An extraordinary knowledge and vision has arisen in me: 'The soul (*jīva*) is possessed of form (*rūvī*). Yet some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas say: "The soul is formless (*arūvī*). Those who speak thus speak falsely. This is the sixth type of analytical knowledge. Furthermore, regarding the seventh type of analytical knowledge: when such a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa possesses arisen analytical knowledge, by means of that arisen analytical knowledge he perceives the body of matter (*poggalakāya*) permeated by the subtle wind-element (*vāyukāya*), moving, shifting, trembling, quivering, vibrating, striking, and rising up, transforming into this or that state. To him it occurs: "An extraordinary knowledge and vision has arisen in me: 'All this consists of souls. Yet some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas say: "'Living beings' and 'non-living things'—those who speak thus speak falsely. For him, these four classes of living beings (*jīvanikāya*) do not come into his right comprehension: namely, the earth-bodied, water-bodied, fire-bodied, and wind-bodied beings. Through these four classes of living beings, he applies wrong punishment (*micchadaṇḍa*). This is the seventh type of analytical knowledge.

Sevenfold is the classification of birth-sources (yoni) as follows: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, soil-born, spontaneously generated, and those born from sprouts. Egg-born beings are declared to have seven destinies and seven origins, as follows: when an egg-born being is reborn among egg-born beings, it may be reborn from among egg-born, womb-born, up to and including sprout-born beings; and likewise, when that same egg-born being relinquishes its state of being egg-born, it may pass into the state of being egg-born, womb-born, up to and including sprout-born.
Pōtaga, regarding the seven destinies of beings, in the same manner the coming and going of all seven [classes of beings] should be recited, up to the *ubbhiya* (the celestial beings).

In the community (*gaṇa*) of an *ācārya-uvajjhāya*, seven points of support (*saṅgahaṭhāṇā*) are proclaimed, namely: the *ācārya-uvajjhāya* in the community correctly exercises command or maintains discipline; thus as in the *pañcaṭṭhāṇa* [scripture], up to: the *ācārya-uvajjhāya* in the community is one who acts with permission and not one who acts without permission.

The teacher and preceptor, within the community, properly procures requisites that have not yet been obtained; and the teacher and preceptor, within the community, properly protects and preserves requisites already obtained, and does not protect or preserve them improperly.

Regarding the teacher-preceptor (*ācāryopādhyāya*), seven grounds for non-inclusion in the community (*gaṇa*) have been declared, as follows: the teacher-preceptor does not properly exercise command or authority within the community; and so on, up to: he does not properly protect and preserve the requisites. Seven rules for seeking alms-food (*piṇḍaiṣaṇā*) have been declared. Seven rules for seeking water (*pānaiṣaṇā*) have been declared. Seven postures for receiving instruction (*avagrahapratimā*) have been declared. Seven sets of seven [disciplinary] points (*saptasaptikā*) have been declared. Seven great chapters (*mahādhyayana*) have been declared.

The seventh vow of the monks (*bhikkhupaḍimā*), consisting of forty-nine days and nights and one hundred and ninety-nine alms-rounds, has been fully accomplished according to the scriptures. Below [the world-system], seven earths (*puḍhavī*) are proclaimed; seven dense oceans (*ghaṇōdahi*) are proclaimed; seven dense winds (*ghaṇavāta*) are proclaimed; seven subtle winds (*taṇuvāta*) are proclaimed; and seven intermediate spaces (*ōvāsantara*) are proclaimed. Within these seven intermediate spaces, the seven subtle winds are established; within these seven dense winds, the seven dense oceans are established.

Within these seven dense oceans, there exist seven earths (pudgalas) situated in a massed, broad, and circular configuration, namely: the first up to the seventh. Regarding these seven earths, seven names are proclaimed, as follows: Dhammā, Vaṃsā, Selā, Añjanā, Riṣṭā, Maghā, and Māghavatī. Regarding these seven earths, seven lineages (gottas) are proclaimed, as follows: Ratnaprabhā, Śarkarāprabhā, Vālukāprabhā, Paṅkaprabhā, Dhūmaprabhā, Tamaḥprabhā, and Tamastamaḥprabhā.
Seven types of gross air-bodied beings are taught, namely: east wind, west wind, south wind, north wind, upward wind, downward wind, and diagonal wind.
Seven shapes are taught, namely: long, short, round, triangular, square, broad, and circular.
Seven bases of fear are taught, namely: fear of this world, fear of the next world, fear of seizure, fear of the unexpected, fear of pain, fear of death, and fear of ill repute.

One should recognize an ordinary person (chadmastha) by seven criteria, namely: he has killed living beings; he has spoken falsehoods; he has taken what was not given; he has indulged in sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells; he has accepted honor and respect; having declared "this is blameworthy," he nevertheless continues to practice it; and he does not act according to what he preaches.
One should recognize an omniscient one (kevalin) by seven criteria, namely: he has not killed living beings, and so on [up to], he acts exactly as he preaches.
Seven root lineages are proclaimed, namely: Kāśyapas, Gautamas, Vatsas, Kaucchas, Kauśikas, Māṇḍavas, and Vāsiṣṭhas.

Those who are Kāśyapas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: the Kāśyapas, the Saṇḍillas, the Golas, the Vālas, the Muñjajiṇas, the Parvapekṣatṛṇas, and the Varṣakṛṣṇas. Those who are Gautamas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: the Gautamas, the Gaggas, the Bhāradvājas, the Aṅgirasas, the Śakkarābhas, the Bhakkharābhas, and the Udattābhas.

Those who are Vatsas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: those Vatsas who are Agneyas, those Maitreyas, those Śālmalinas, those Selayatas, those Asthiṣeṇas, and those Vītakarmas. Those who are Kaucchas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: those Kaucchas who are Maudgalyāyanas, those Piṅgalāyanas, those Kauṇḍinyas, those Maṇḍalinas, those Hāritas, and those Saumayas. Those who are Kausikas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: those Kausikas who are Kātyāyanas, those Śālaṅkāyanas, those Gōlikāyanas, those Pakṣikāyanas, those Āgniccas, and those Lauhiccas.

Those Maṇḍavas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: the Tē Maṇḍavas, the Tē Ariṭṭhas, the Tē Saṃmutas, the Tē Telās, the Tē Elāvaccās, the Tē Kaṇḍillas, and the Tē Khārāyaṇas. Those Vasiṭṭhas are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: the Tē Vāsiṭṭhas, the Tē Ujāyaṇas, the Tē Jārukaṇhas, the Tē Vagghāvaccās, the Tē Koṇḍiṇṇas, the Tē Saṇṇīs, and the Tē Pārāsarās. Seven root standpoints (mūlanayas) are declared, namely: Naigama, Saṅgraha, Vyavahāra, Rjusūtra, Śabda, Samabhirūḍha, and Evambhūta.
Seven musical notes (saras) are taught, namely:
*ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *dhaivata*, and *naiṣāda*. These seven notes are thus declared. (Ṭhāṇa 605)
Regarding these seven notes, there are seven locations for the notes, as follows:
the *ṣaḍja* note is produced from the tip of the tongue; the *ṛṣabha* note from the chest;
the *gāndhāra* note from the throat; and the *madhyama* note from the middle of the tongue. (Ṭhāṇa 607)
One should declare the fifth [note] from the nose, the *dhaivata* from the teeth and lips, and the *naiṣāda* from the head; these are explained as the locations of the notes.
(Ṭhāṇa 608) Seven notes dependent on living beings are taught, namely: [list follows].

The peacock cries out its prepared note; the cock utters the *ṛṣabha* tone; the swan calls with the *gāndhāra*; but the *gavēlayas* [cranes] sound the *madhyama*. At the time of the blossoming of flowers, the cuckoo utters the *pañcama* tone. *Ṭhāṇaṅga Sutta* 610. aha. kusuma-sambhave kāle. koilā pañcamaṃ saraṃ.

The sixth is the crane, the koñca bird; this elephant is the seventh. (Ṭhāṇa 611) Seven tones not dependent on living beings are taught, namely: the muiṅga shell sounds the *sajja* tone, and the gomuhī [horn] the *risabha* tone.
The *saṅkha* sounds the *gandhāra* note, while the *majjhima* is sounded by the *jhallarī*.
The *caücalaṇapatiṭṭhāṇā* and the *gōhiyā* sound the fifth note (*pañcama*).
The *āḍambara*, the *dhēvatiyā*, and the great drum (*mahābhērī*) sound the seventh note. (Ṭhāṇa 613–614)
For these seven notes, seven characteristics of the notes are declared, namely:
Through the *ṣaḍja* note, one obtains a livelihood, and what is done does not perish;
one possesses cattle, friends, and sons, and is indeed beloved by women. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 616)
Riṣabha [bestowed] upon him the priesthood, the command of the army, wealth, clothing,
perfumes, ornaments, women, and couches.
(Ṭhāṇa 617) In Gandhāra, those skilled in song, whose livelihood was music, and who were proficient in the arts—
There are poets whose wisdom extends to other sciences as well;
they possess a moderate tone and lead a happy life.
One who is endowed with a moderate tone eats, drinks, and gives while remaining composed in that moderate tone. (Ṭhāṇa 618–619)
Those endowed with the fifth *sāra* become lords of the earth,
heroes, organizers, and leaders of many groups. (Ṭhāṇa 620) Those endowed with the *Revatī-sāra* become fond of quarrels.
Fowlers, trappers, hunters, and fishermen; outcasts, boxers, and scavengers, as well as others who perform evil deeds;
those who kill iguanas, thieves, and those who live by trapping deer with snares. (Ṭhāṇa 621–622)

Of these seven notes (svara), three groups (grāma) are taught, namely: the *Ṣaḍja* group, the *Madhyama* group, and the *Gāndhāra* group. Of the *Ṣaḍja* group, seven modulations (*mūrcchanā*) are taught, namely:
Maṅgī, Kauravvīyā, Harī, Rayanī, Sārakaṃtā, the sixth named Sārasī, and the seventh, the pure *Ṣaḍja*. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 624)
Seven types of intoxication are declared for Majjhima Village, namely:
Uttaramandā, Rayanī, Uttarā, Uttarāyatā, Assōkantā, Sovīrā, and Abhirū is the seventh. (Ṭhāṇa 626)
Seven modulations (*mucchaṇā*) of the Gandhāra scale are taught, namely:
Nandī, Khuddimā, Pūrimā, and the fourth, Suddhagandhārā; Uttaragandhārā is the fifth modulation. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 628)
The sixth [note], Suṭṭhuttaramāyāmā, should be known as necessarily being *niyamaso* (fixed);
if it is extended upward (*uttarāyatā*) and possesses a *koḍimā* (peak), it is the seventh, *mucchā*. (Ṭhāṇa 629) From where do the seven notes arise? What is the source (*jōṇī*) of song?
How many breaths [are there] in a measure, and how many are the modes of song? Seven notes arise from the navel, and song is known to be accompanied by weeping;
there are measures according to the words, breaths, and three are the modes of singing.
Beginning at the start, carrying it through the middle,
and meditating upon it at the end— these are the three modes of singing.
(Ṭhāṇa 632) There are six faults, eight qualities, three meters, and two styles of recitation.

Just as one who is well-trained will take hold of the net in the middle of the arena, so too [should the monk be disciplined]. (Ṭhāṇa 633) Do not sing with a frightened voice, nor in secret, nor with excessive volume;
moreover, a faltering tone and a nasal quality are two faults of singing. (Ṭhāṇa 634)

Full, resonant, adorned, rhythmic, likewise undistorted, sweet, even, and well-modulated— these are the eight qualities of song. (Ṭhāṇa 635) It is sung with excellence of chest, throat, and head, composed of soft and expanded words.
Thus, song (*gēya*) possesses the seven musical scales (*sattasara*), is rhythmic (*samatāla*), free from suffering,
and is faultless, substantial, endowed with reason, adorned, refined, courteous, measured, and indeed sweet. (Ṭhāṇa 636–637)
That which is even, half-even, and uneven everywhere—these are the three types of meter; a fourth is not found.
(Ṭhāṇa 638) Two styles of speech are declared: the refined (sakkata) and the vernacular (pāgata).
While the *Sāramaṇḍala* is being sung, these are the praises spoken by the seers (*Ṛṣis*):
"Who sings sweetly? Who sings harshly? Who sings roughly? Who sings with four [vocal registers]? Who sings slowly? Who sings quickly? (Ṭhāṇaṃga 640)

Furthermore, what is the *vissara* [melody] like? A female jackal sings sweetly; a black woman sings harshly; a fair-complexioned woman sings with a fourfold [tempo]; a one-eyed person sings slowly; a blind person sings quickly. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 641) Furthermore, the *piṅgalā* [melody] is equal to the strings, equal to the rhythm (*tāla*), equal to the feet, equal to the tempo (*laya*), and equal to the grasp (*graha*).
The seven notes are equal in their inhalation and exhalation, and equal in their movement.
(Ṭhāṇa 642) There are seven notes, three scales (*grāmas*), twenty-one *mūrcchanās*, and forty-nine *tānas*;
thus the circle of notes (*svara-maṇḍala*) is complete. (Ṭhāṇa 643)

Seven types of bodily mortifications are taught, namely: standing on one foot, sitting in the *ukkuḍuka* posture, remaining in the *pratimā* (meditative) posture, the *vīrāsana* posture, the *naiṣadyika* posture, the staff-like posture (*daṇḍāyatika*), and the *lagaṇḍaśāyin* posture.
In the island of Jambūdvīpa, seven regions (*varṣa*) are taught, namely: Bharata, Airāvata, Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, Ramyakavarṣa, and Mahāvideha.
In the island of Jambūdvīpa, seven mountain ranges (*varṣadhara-parvata*) are taught, namely: Cullahimavanta, Mahāhimavanta, Nisadha, Nīlavanta, Rūpyī, Śikhari, and Mandara.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, seven great rivers flow toward the east and enter the salt ocean; namely: the Gaṅgā, Rohitā, Harī, Sītā, Narakantā, Suvaṇṇakūlā, and Rattā. On the island of Jambudvīpa, seven great rivers flow toward the west and enter the salt ocean; namely: the Sindhu, Rohitaṃsā, Harikantā, Sītōdā, Nārikantā, Rūppakūlā, and Rattāvatī. In the eastern half of the island of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, seven regions (vāsas) are declared; namely: Bharaha, [and so on] up to Mahāvideha.
In the eastern half of the island of Ghātakhaṇḍa, seven mountain ranges are proclaimed, namely: Cullahimavanta, and so on, up to Mandara.

In the eastern half of the continent of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, seven great rivers flow toward the east and enter the Kāloda Ocean; namely, from the Gaṅgā up to the Raktā. In the eastern half of the continent of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, seven great rivers flow toward the west and enter the Lavaṇa Ocean; namely, from the Sindhu up to the Raktavatī. In the western half of the continent of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, there are likewise seven regions (*varṣa*); however, [the rivers] flow toward the east and enter the Lavaṇa Ocean, and toward the west they enter the Kāloda Ocean; the rest is exactly as before. In the eastern half of the Pukkhara-vara-dvīpa-continent, there are likewise seven regions; however, [the rivers] flow toward the east and enter the Pukkhara-oda Ocean, and toward the west they enter the Kāloda Ocean; the rest is exactly as before. Likewise in the western half; however, [the rivers] flow toward the east and enter the Kāloda Ocean, and toward the west they enter the Pukkhara-oda Ocean. In all cases, the regions, the mountain ranges that separate the regions, and the rivers are to be described in this manner.
In the island of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, during the past *utsarpiṇī*, there were seven Kulakaras, namely:
Mittadāma, Sudāma, Supāsa, Sayampabha, Vimaladhosa, Sudhosa, and Mahādhosa as the seventh. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 647)
In Jambūdvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, during this *avasarpinī*, there were seven Kulakaras.
Here, first was Vimalavāhana, Cakṣuṣman, Yaśas, fourth was Abhicandra, then Prasenajit, Marudeva, and Nābhi. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 649)
These seven Kulakaras had seven wives, namely:
Candrayasā, Candrakāntā, Surūpā, Pratirūpā, Cakṣuḥkāntā, Śrīkāntā, and Marudevī; these are the names of the women who were the Kulakaras. (Ṭhāṇaṅga Sutta 651)

In the continent of Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhārata, during the future *utsarpiṇī* era, there will be seven Kulakaras: Mittavāhana, Subhoma, Suprabha, Sayampabha, Datta, Sūkṣma, and Subandhu; these will exist in the future. (Ṭhāṇa 653)
When Vimalavāhana was the Kulakara, seven kinds of trees appeared for his enjoyment, namely:
the Mataṅga, the Bhiṅga, the Cittaṅga, the Cittarasa, the Maṇiyaṅga, the Aṇiyaṇa as the seventh, and the Kalpavr̥kṣa. (Āyāraṅga Sutta Ṭhāṇa 655)
The sevenfold administration of punishment is proclaimed, namely: reprimand, reproach, censure, public rebuke, confinement within a circle, banishment, and mutilation.

For each universal monarch (cakravartin) who rules over the four quarters, seven single-sensed jewels are proclaimed, namely: the wheel-jewel, the parasol-jewel, the leather-shield-jewel, the staff-jewel, the sword-jewel, the gem-jewel, and the money-jewel.

For each individual universal monarch (cakravartin) who rules over the four quarters, seven precious jewels of the five senses are proclaimed; namely: the general-jewel, the householder-jewel, the treasurer-jewel, the priest-jewel, the woman-jewel, the horse-jewel, and the elephant-jewel.

One should recognize that a deeply degenerate age has arrived by means of seven signs; namely: it rains out of season, it does not rain at the proper time, the unrighteous are honored while the righteous are not honored, the people have adopted false views, there is mental distress, and there is physical distress.

By seven conditions one should know that a period of great peace has arrived, namely: it does not rain out of season; it rains at the proper time; the unrighteous are not honored; the righteous are honored; people are properly submissive to their elders; there is mental happiness; and there is physical happiness.
Seven types of beings involved in the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) are declared, namely: hell-beings, male animals, female animals, males, females, gods, and goddesses.
Sevenfold is the classification of life-span (*āyu-bheda*) declared, namely: [the life-spans of the aforementioned seven classes of beings].

Life-span (*āyu*) is determined by seven factors: mental resolve (*ajjhavasāṇa*), signs (*nimitta*), food (*āhāra*), sensation (*vēyaṇā*), injury caused by others (*parādhāta*), touch (*phāsa*), and inhalation and exhalation (*āṇāpāṇu*).

(Ṭhāṇaṅga 661) All living beings (*savvajīva*) are declared to be of seven kinds, namely: earth-bodied beings (*puḍhavikāiya*), water-bodied beings (*āukāiya*), fire-bodied beings (*tēukāiya*), air-bodied beings (*vāukāiya*), plant-bodied beings (*vaṇassatikāiya*), mobile-bodied beings (*tasakāiya*), and those without a body (*akāiya*).
Alternatively—seven types of all living beings are taught, namely: black-leśyā, blue-leśyā, grey-leśyā, yellow-leśyā, pink-leśyā, white-leśyā, and leśyā-less.

King Bambhadatta, the universal monarch of the four quarters, seven *dhanus* in height, having lived a maximum lifespan of seven hundred years, at the time of his death passed away and was reborn as a hell-being in the seventh underworld, the *Appatiṭṭhāṇa* hell.

The Arhat Malli, having become a shaven-headed ascetic for the seventh time, went forth from the home life into homelessness; namely: Malli, the noble princess of Videha; Pratibuddhi, the king of the Ikṣvākus; Candracchāya, the king of Aṅga; Rūpin, the lord of Kuṇāla; Śaṅkha, the king of Kāśī; Adīnaśatru, the king of Kuru; and Jitaśatru, the king of Pañcāla.
Sevenfold vision is taught; namely: right vision, wrong vision, right-and-wrong vision, visual vision, non-visual vision, limited vision, and omniscient vision.

An omniscient being who is free from passion (vītarāga) but still possesses the physical body (chaumattha) experiences seven types of karmic matter, excluding deluding karma (mōhaṇijja); namely: knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, life-span-determining, name-determining, status-determining, and obstructive.

A person with limited vision (*chaumattha*) does not know and does not see seven things in their true nature: namely, the substance of motion (*dhammatthikāya*), the substance of rest (*adhammatthikāya*), the substance of space (*āgāsatthikāya*), a soul (*jīva*) unattached to a body, a single atom (*paramāṇupoggala*), and sound (*sadda*). However, one who has attained knowledge knows and sees these very same things—namely, from the substance of motion down to smell (*gandha*). The ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, possessed the *vajra-ṛṣabha-nārāca* bone-joint structure, was shaped with a symmetrical quadrangular form, and was seven *ratnīs* in height.

Seven types of frivolous talk are proclaimed, namely: talk about women, talk about food, talk about the country, talk about kings, talk that is soft and piteous, talk that causes schism in right view, and talk that causes schism in right conduct.

Seven special privileges are prescribed for an *ācārya* or *upādhyāya* within the *gaṇa*, namely: (1) an *ācārya* or *upādhyāya* does not transgress [the rules] when repeatedly shaking or sweeping his feet inside the residence; (2) likewise, as described in the *Pañcasthāna*, up until: (3) staying alone outside the residence for one night or two nights; (4) special privileges regarding requisites; and (5–7) special privileges regarding food and drink.

Sevenfold restraint is proclaimed, namely: restraint regarding the earth-bodied beings, up to restraint regarding the mobile-bodied beings, and restraint regarding non-living beings. Sevenfold non-restraint is proclaimed, namely: non-restraint regarding the earth-bodied beings, up to non-restraint regarding the mobile-bodied beings, and non-restraint regarding non-living beings.

There are seven types of undertaking (*ārambha*), namely: undertaking involving the earth-body, up to undertaking involving non-living bodies (*ajīvakāya*). Likewise for non-undertaking (*anārambha*), likewise for undertaking with violence (*sārambha*), likewise for undertaking without violence (*asārambha*), likewise for thorough undertaking (*samārambha*), and likewise for thorough non-undertaking (*asamārambha*), up to thorough non-undertaking involving non-living bodies.
Now, venerable sir, regarding these grains—adhasi, kusumbha, koddava, kaṅgu, rālaka, varaṭṭa, koddasaga, saṇa, sarisava, and mulaga—which are stored in granaries, in storehouses, and so forth...

Thus regarding non-commencement, thus regarding commencement, thus regarding non-commencement, thus regarding undertaking, thus regarding non-undertaking, up to the non-undertaking of the non-living bodies (*ajīvakāya*).

For those who have closed [the doors of the senses], for how long does the womb (*yoni*) persist? Gautama! At the minimum for one *muhūrta*, at the maximum for seven years; beyond that, the womb withers, until the cessation of the womb is declared. The maximum lifespan of gross water-bodied beings (*bādarāpkāyika*) is declared to be seven thousand years.

And in that Vālukāprabhā earth, the maximum lifespan of the hell-beings is taught to be seven sāgaropamas; in the fourth Paṅkaprabhā earth, the minimum lifespan of the hell-beings is taught to be seven sāgaropamas.

Seven chief queens are proclaimed for Varuṇa, the great king of the gods, [who is under] Sakka, the lord of the gods and king of the gods; seven chief queens are proclaimed for Soma, the great king of the gods, [who is under] Īsāna, the lord of the gods and king of the gods; seventy chief queens are proclaimed for Yama, the great king of the gods, [who is under] Īsāna, the lord of the gods and king of the gods.
For the gods in the inner assembly of Īsāna, the lord of the gods and king of the gods, a lifespan of seven *palyopamas* is proclaimed.
The lifespan of the principal queens of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is declared to be seven *palyopamas*.
In the Sōhamma heaven, the maximum lifespan of the queens who are under his personal care is declared to be seven *palyopamas*.
Among the Sārassaya and Māicca gods, seven classes of gods and seven hundred [individual] gods are declared.
Seven gods and seven thousand gods are described as belonging to the Gaddatōya and Tusita devas.
In the Saṇaṅkumāra realm, the maximum lifespan of the gods is described as seven sāgarōvamas.
In the Māhinda realm, the maximum lifespan of the gods is described as slightly more than seven sāgarōvamas.
In the Brahma-world realm (Brahmaloka-kalpa), the lifespan of the gods is declared to be at least seven sāgaropamas.
In the Brahma-world and Lāntaka realms, the celestial palaces (vimānas) are declared to be seven hundred yojanas in height.

The bodies maintained by the gods dwelling in the celestial abodes (*bhavanavāsin*) are, at most, seven *ratni*s in height; likewise for the *vānamantara* gods, and likewise for the *jyotiṣka* gods. In the *Saudharma* and *Īśāna* heavens, the bodies maintained by the gods are, at most, seven *ratni*s in height.

Within the island of Nandīśvaravara, seven islands are described, namely: Jambūdvīpa, Ghātakīṣaṇḍa, Puṣkaravara, Varuṇavara, Kṣīravara, Ghṛtavara, and Kṣodavara. Within the island of Nandīśvaravara, seven oceans are described, namely: Lavaṇa, Kāloda, Puṣkarauda, Varuṇoda, Kṣīroda, Ghṛtoda, and Kṣodauda.
Seven mountain ranges (śreṇīs) are described, namely: straight and extended, curved on one side, curved on both sides, bent at one end, bent at both ends, circular, and semi-circular.

Of Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asurakumāras, seven armies and seven commanders of armies are proclaimed, namely: the infantry army, the elephant army, the chariot army, the buffalo army, the dance army, and the Gandharva army. Druma is the commander of the infantry army; likewise, as described in the *Pañcaṭṭhāna*, up to Kinnara, who is the commander of the chariot army; Riṣṭa is the commander of the dance army; and Gītarati is the commander of the Gandharva army.

To Bala, the lord of Vairocana and king of Vairocana, seven commanders of the seven divisions are proclaimed, as follows: the commander of the infantry division up to the commander of the Gandharva division; Mahādruma is the commander of the infantry division, up to Kimpurisa as the commander of the elephant division, Mahāriṣṭha as the commander of the dance division, and Gītayaśas as the commander of the Gandharva division.

Of Gharana, the lord of the Nāgakumāras and king of the Nāgakumāras, seven armies and seven army commanders are proclaimed; namely: the infantry, and so on up to the musicians. Bhaddasena is the commander of the infantry, and so on up to Ānanda, who is the commander of the chariot forces; Nandana is the commander of the dancers and actors; and Tetali is the commander of the musicians.

For Bhūtānanda, the lord of the Nāga-kumāras and king of the Nāga-kumāras, seven armies and seven commanders of the armies are proclaimed, as follows: the infantry army, up to the Gandharva army; Dakṣa, the commander of the infantry army, up to Nandottara, the commander of the chariot army; Rati, the commander of the dance army; and Mānasa, the commander of the Gandharva army. In this same manner, it should be understood for Ghoṣa and Mahāghoṣa as well.

For Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, seven armies and seven commanders of armies are proclaimed, as follows: the infantry army, up to the gandharva army; Hariṇegamesī is the commander of the infantry army, up to Māḍhara, who is the commander of the chariot army; Seta is the commander of the dance army; and Tumburu is the commander of the gandharva army. For Īsāna, the lord of gods and king of the gods, seven armies and seven commanders of armies are proclaimed, as follows: the infantry army, up to the gandharva army; Lahuparakkama is the commander of the infantry army, up to Mahāseta, who is the commander of the dance army; and Rata is the commander of the gandharva army. The rest is as in the *Pañcaṭṭhāṇa* [Sūtra]; in this manner, it should be understood up to Accuta as well.

For Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asurakumāras, and for Duma, the commander of the infantry, seven girth-straps are prescribed, namely: the first girth-strap up to the seventh girth-strap.

In the first girth of Duma, the commander of the infantry for Camara, the lord of the Asura-kumāras and king of the Asuras, sixty-four thousand gods are declared to reside; as many as there are in the first girth, twice that number are in the second girth; as many as there are in the second girth, twice that number are in the third girth; and so on, until as many as there are in the sixth girth, twice that number are in the seventh girth.

The same applies to Bali; however, his great tree has sixty thousand days of existence, and the rest is exactly as for Dharaṇa. Likewise for the others, with the exception that there are twenty-eight thousand gods; the rest is the same, just as for Dharaṇa, up to Mahāghosa; however, the commanders of the infantry are different from those previously mentioned.

Of Sakka, the lord of gods, the king of gods, Hariṇegamesi, seven divisions (kacchā) are proclaimed, as follows: the first division. Just as it was for Camara, so it is up to Accuta; the only difference is regarding the commanders of the infantry (pāyattāṇiyādhipatī), who have been previously described. The measure of the gods is this: for Sakka there are eighty-four thousand gods, and so on, up to the sixth division; the seventh division consists of twice that number of gods. This is to be understood from the following verse: up to Accuta Lahuparakkama, there are ten thousand gods, and so on, up to the sixth division; the seventh division consists of twice that number.
Eighty-four thousand, eighty thousand, seventy-two thousand, seventy thousand, sixty thousand, fifty thousand, forty thousand, thirty thousand, twenty thousand, and ten thousand.

(Āvaśyaka Niryukti 684) Seven types of verbal expressions are taught, namely: conversation (*ālāpa*), non-conversation (*anālāpa*), dialogue (*ullāpa*), non-dialogue (*anullāpa*), discourse (*saṃlāpa*), idle chatter (*palāpa*), and confused chatter (*vippalāpa*).

Sevenfold discipline (*vinaya*) is taught, namely: discipline of knowledge (*jñāna-vinaya*), discipline of vision (*darśana-vinaya*), discipline of conduct (*cāritra-vinaya*), discipline of mind (*manas-vinaya*), discipline of speech (*vāc-vinaya*), discipline of body (*kāya-vinaya*), and discipline of courtesy toward the world (*lokopacāra-vinaya*). The sevenfold commendable discipline of mind is taught, namely: that which is sinless (*apāpaka*), blameless (*asāvadya*), non-active (*akriya*), untroubled (*nirupakleśa*), not causing influx (*anāsravakara*), not causing affliction (*acchavikara*), and free from false suspicion (*abhūtābhiśaṅkana*). The sevenfold uncommendable discipline of mind is taught, namely: that which is sinful (*pāpaka*), blameworthy (*sāvadya*), active (*sakriya*), troubled (*sopakleśa*), causing influx (*āsravakara*), causing affliction (*chavikara*), and involving false suspicion (*bhūtābhiśaṅkana*). The sevenfold commendable discipline of speech is taught, namely: that which is sinless, blameless, and so forth, up to being free from false suspicion. The sevenfold uncommendable discipline of speech is taught, namely: that which is sinful, and so forth, up to involving false suspicion.

Seven types of commendable bodily discipline (*kāyavinaya*) are taught, namely: deliberate walking, deliberate standing, deliberate sitting, deliberate lying down, deliberate stretching out, deliberate contracting, and the application of all sense-faculties with deliberation. Seven types of uncommendable bodily discipline are taught, namely: undeliberate walking, and so on, up to undeliberate application of all sense-faculties. Seven types of discipline for social courtesy (*logovayāravinaya*) are taught, namely: acting in the presence [of others], complying with the wishes of others, acting for the sake of a task, repaying what has been done for one, seeking one's own welfare, knowing the proper place and time, and being non-oppositional in all matters.

Seven types of total disintegration (samugdhāta) are taught; namely: the disintegration of pain (vēyaṇā-samugdhāta), the disintegration of passions (kasāya-samugdhāta), the disintegration at the time of death (māraṇantiya-samugghāta), the disintegration of the transformation-body (vēuvviya-samugghāta), the disintegration of fiery energy (tējasa-samugghāta), the disintegration of the assimilative body (āhāraga-samugghāta), and the disintegration of the omniscient (kevali-samugghāta). Seven types of total disintegration are taught for human beings; it is exactly the same.

In the dispensation (*tittha*) of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, seven heretics (*pavayaṇa-niṇhaga*) are proclaimed, namely: the Bahuratās, the Jīvapaeṣiyas, the Avattiyas, the Sāmuccheiyas, the Dōkiriyas, the Tērāsiyas, and the Abaddhiyas. Of these seven heretics of the doctrine, there were seven teachers of the Dharma (*dhammāyariya*), namely: Jamālī, Tīsagutta, Āsāḍha, Āsamitta, Gaṅga, Chaluja, and Goṭṭhāmāhila. For these seven heretics of the doctrine, there were seven cities of origin (*uppatti-nagara*), namely: [the following list follows].

Śrāvastī, Ṛṣabhapura, Sētavyā, Mithilā, Ullakātīra, Purimatālā, Daśapura, and Niṇhaguppatti are the cities [associated with these events]. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 689) Regarding the karma to be experienced as pleasant (*sātāvedanīya*), seven kinds of fruition (*anubhāva*) are taught, namely: pleasant sounds, pleasant forms, pleasant smells, pleasant tastes, pleasant tangibles, mental happiness, and vocal happiness. Regarding the karma to be experienced as unpleasant (*asātāvedanīya*), seven kinds of fruition are taught, namely: unpleasant sounds, and so on, up to vocal misery.

The great constellation is declared to have seven stars. Seven constellations beginning with Abhijit are declared to be those of the eastern gate, namely: Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvabhadrapadā, Uttarabhadrapadā, and Revatī. Seven constellations beginning with Aśvinī are declared to be those of the southern gate, namely: Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, and Punarvasu. Seven constellations beginning with Puṣya are declared to be those of the western gate, namely: Puṣya, Aśleṣā, Maghā, Pūrvaphalgunī, Uttaraphalgunī, Hasta, and Citrā. Seven constellations beginning with Svātī are declared to be those of the northern gate, namely: Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mūla, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Uttarāṣāḍhā.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, on the Somanasa Vakkhāra mountain, seven peaks are proclaimed, namely: Siddha, Somanasa, and Maṅgalāvatīkūḍa should be known; Devakuru, Vimala, Kāñcana, and Visiṭṭhakūḍa should also be known. (Ṭhāṇa 693)

On Mount Gandhamādana, a transverse mountain (vakkhārapavvata) in Jambudvīpa, seven peaks are enumerated, as follows: namely—Siddha, Gandhamādana (should be known), Gandhilāvatī-peak, Uttarakuru, Phalika, Lohitākṣa, and Ānandana. (Ṭhāṇa 695)
Seven hundred thousand times one million species of birth-places for the two-sensed beings are taught.

Living beings have accumulated, do accumulate, or will accumulate matter formed in seven locations as sinful karma; namely: that formed in hellish beings, up to that formed in female deities. In the same way, there is accumulation and shedding. Seven types of infinite aggregates with distinct divisions are taught; seven types of matter with distinct degrees of penetration, up to seven types of matter with infinite degrees of dryness, are taught.

An ascetic endowed with eight qualities is worthy of undertaking and dwelling in the practice of solitary wandering. They are as follows: he is a man of faith, a man of truth, a man of wisdom, a man of great learning, one possessed of strength, one who does not cause self-affliction, one possessed of fortitude, and one endowed with vigor.

There are eight categories of birth (yonisaṅgraha) taught, namely: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, soil-born, spontaneously born, germinating-born, and apparitional-born. Regarding the egg-born, there are eight types of destinies and eight types of origins taught, as follows: when an egg-born being is reborn, it may be reborn from among egg-born beings, or from among womb-born, moisture-born, soil-born, spontaneously born, germinating-born, or apparitional-born beings. Furthermore, that very same egg-born being, when relinquishing its state of being egg-born, may go to the state of being egg-born, or to the state of being womb-born, up to the state of being apparitional-born. The same applies to the womb-born; the same applies to the moisture-born; for the remaining [categories], there is no coming or going.

Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate eight types of karmic matter (*karmaprakṛti*). They are as follows: knowledge-obscuring, perception-obscuring, feeling-producing, deluding, life-determining, name-determining, status-determining, and obstructive. Hell-beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate these same eight types of karmic matter; and so on without interruption up to the gods of the *vaimānika* realm.
Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate [these] eight types of karmic matter in exactly the same way.

In this same manner, these twenty-four groups (daṇḍakas) concerning acquisition (ciṇa), accumulation (uvaciṇa), bondage (bandha), activation (udīra), experience (vēya), and likewise destruction (nijjarā) are to be recited.

In eight circumstances, a deceitful person, having committed an act of deceit, would neither confess it, nor repent for it; [nor would he blame himself, nor censure it, nor turn away from it, nor purify himself, nor resolve not to do it again, nor undertake the appropriate penance and austerity]; namely: "I have done it," "I am doing it," or "I shall do it"; or "there will be ill-repute for me," or "there will be dispraise for me," or "there will be misfortune for me," or "my reputation will diminish," or "my fame will diminish."

In eight circumstances, one who is deceitful, having committed a deception, should confess it and so forth until he undertakes the vow: namely—deceitfulness is censured in this world; rebirth [in an evil state] is censured; future destiny is censured. Even for a single instance, if one who is deceitful, having committed a deception, does not confess it and so forth until he undertakes the vow, there is no spiritual perfection for him. But even for a single instance, if one who is deceitful, having committed a deception, confesses it and undertakes the vow, there is spiritual perfection for him.

Even if a deceitful person, having committed a transgression, should confess it—even up to undertaking a penance—there is still no fulfillment for him; or if extraordinary knowledge and vision should arise in his teacher or preceptor, and that [teacher] should then confess it on his behalf, he is still a deceitful person.

A deceitful person, having practiced deceit, is like this: for example, an iron forge, or a copper forge, or a tin forge, or a lead forge, or a silver forge, or a gold forge; or a fire of sesame husks, or a fire of chaff, or a fire of grain-husks, or a fire of reeds, or a fire of bark; or a furnace for *soṇḍiyā* (a type of vessel), or a furnace for *bhaṇḍiyā*, or a furnace for *gōliyā*; or a potter’s kiln, or a smithy, or a brick-maker’s kiln, or a furnace for making *jantu* (a type of clay product); or the bellows of a blacksmith—all these, when heated until they become uniform in temperature, emitting thousands of sparks like the blossoms of the *kiṁśuka* tree, releasing thousands of flames, scattering thousands of embers, and burning intensely within—just so does the deceitful person, having practiced deceit, burn intensely within. Furthermore, whatever others say, the deceitful person knows: "I am suspected, I am suspected. The deceitful person, having practiced deceit and failing to confess or repent, at the time of death passes away and is reborn among the gods in certain celestial realms. However, he is not among those of great power, nor among those of far-reaching influence, nor among those of long duration. There he becomes a god who is not of great power, nor of far-reaching influence, nor of long duration. Whatever assembly of outsiders or insiders he has there, they do not honor him, nor recognize him, nor invite him to a worthy seat. Even as he speaks, only four or five gods rise up to attend him, thinking, "Let the noble one speak much, let the noble one speak! When his lifespan in that celestial realm is exhausted, and his existence and duration have ended, he falls from there and is reborn in this very human world in such families as these: low-caste families, outcaste families, destitute families, poor families, beggars' families, or miserly families. He is reborn as a male in such families. There he becomes a man who is ugly in form, ill-favored in appearance, foul-smelling, bad-tasting, unpleasant to the touch; undesirable, unlovely, unpleasing, disagreeable, and repulsive; with a weak voice, a feeble voice, an undesirable voice, an unpleasant voice, an unpleasing voice, a disagreeable voice, and an unattractive voice. He is reborn with speech that is untrustworthy. Whatever assembly of outsiders or insiders he has there, they do not honor him, nor recognize him, nor invite him to a worthy seat. Even as he speaks, only four or five people rise up to attend him, saying, "Let the master speak much, let the master speak!"

Indeed, one who possesses deceit, having committed a deceitful act and then reflected upon it and repented, at the time of death, passes away and is reborn among the gods in certain celestial realms as a deity. That is to say: among those of great power, up to those of long duration. There he becomes a god of great power, up to one of long duration; his chest is adorned with necklaces, his arms are encased in bracelets and armlets, he wears earrings that grace the surface of his cheeks, and he possesses various hand-ornaments, various garments and ornaments, and a variegated garland and crown. He is clothed in auspicious, excellent raiment and wears auspicious, excellent perfumes, garlands, and ointments. With a radiant body, wearing a long hanging forest garland, he shines and illuminates the ten directions with divine color, divine fragrance, divine taste, divine touch, divine compactness, divine shape, divine prosperity, divine splendor, divine radiance, divine luster, divine heat, and divine effulgence. Amidst the sound of great drums, dancing, singing, instrumental music, strings, cymbals, clapping, armlets, and the resonance of *dhaṇa*, *muiṅga*, and other instruments, he dwells enjoying divine pleasures. Furthermore, whatever assembly—outer or inner—he has there, they honor him, recognize him, and invite him to a highly worthy seat. And while he is speaking, even four or five deities rise from their seats [to attend] him, saying, "Let the god speak much! Let him speak!"

When his lifespan in that celestial world has expired, having passed away from there, he is reborn here in this human existence in such families as are wealthy, prosperous, and beyond the reproach of many people; he is reborn there as a male. There he becomes handsome, well-formed, fragrant, delicious, pleasant to the touch, desirable, lovely, dear, agreeable, with a voice that is not deficient and is pleasing to the mind, and he is reborn with speech that is persuasive. Furthermore, whatever assembly—whether external or internal—he has there, they all show him respect and say, "O noble sir, speak! Speak much!"

Eightfold restraint is taught, as follows: restraint of the sense of hearing, up to restraint of the sense of touch; restraint of the mind, restraint of speech, and restraint of the body. Eightfold non-restraint is taught, as follows: non-restraint of the sense of hearing, up to non-restraint of the body.
Eight kinds of tangibles are taught, as follows: hard, soft, heavy, light, cold, hot, smooth, and rough.

The eightfold stability of the world is taught as follows: wind is established in space; water is established on wind; the earth is established on water; mobile and immobile living beings are established on the earth; non-living things are established in living beings; living beings are established in karma; non-living things are comprised within living beings; and living beings are comprised within karma.

The eightfold excellence of a teacher (gaṇi) is taught as follows: excellence of conduct, excellence of learning, excellence of body, excellence of speech, excellence of recitation, excellence of intelligence, excellence of application, and the eighth is the comprehension of the means of gathering disciples.
The great treasure Egameṇa is established upon the circumference of the eight-fold world-system (cakravāla) and is declared to be eight yojanas in height.

Eight kinds of carefulness (samiti) are taught, namely: carefulness in walking (iryāsamiti), carefulness in speech (bhāṣāsamiti), carefulness in seeking alms (eṣaṇāsamiti), carefulness in taking up and setting down utensils and belongings (ādānabhāṇḍamātranikṣepaṇāsamiti), carefulness in the disposal of excrement, urine, saliva, mucus, and ear-wax (uccāraprasravaṇakhelasindhāṇāñjallapariṣṭhāpanikāsamiti), carefulness of mind (manaḥsamiti), carefulness of speech (vāksamiti), and carefulness of body (kāyasamiti).

An ascetic endowed with eight qualities is worthy of receiving confession: namely, one who possesses right conduct (*āyāra*), who possesses right doctrine (*āhāra*), who possesses right legal procedure (*vavahāra*), who is not secretive, who acts for the benefit [of others], who is not forgetful, who is capable of leading [others] out [of faults], and who perceives danger.

An ascetic endowed with eight qualities is worthy of confessing his own faults: namely, one who is perfected in birth, perfected in lineage, perfected in discipline, perfected in knowledge, perfected in vision, perfected in conduct, patient, and self-controlled.

Eight types of penance (*prāyaścitta*) are taught, namely: that which is fit for confession (*ālocanā-arha*), that which is fit for repentance (*pratīkramaṇa-arha*), that which is fit for both, that which is fit for separation (*viveka-arha*), that which is fit for exertion (*vyutsarga-arha*), that which is fit for austerity (*tapa-arha*), that which is fit for diminution (*cheda-arha*), and that which is fit for root-reinstatement (*mūla-arha*).

Eight grounds for pride (*mada-sthāna*) are taught, namely: pride of birth, pride of family, pride of strength, pride of beauty, pride of austerity, pride of learning, pride of gain, and pride of power.

Eight proponents of non-action (*akriyāvādin*) are taught, namely: the proponent of unity (*ekavādin*), the proponent of plurality (*anekavādin*), the proponent of limited existence (*mitavādin*), the proponent of creation (*nirmitavādin*), the proponent of experience (*sātavādin*), the proponent of annihilation (*samucchedavādin*), the proponent of eternity (*nitavādin*), and the proponent of the non-existence of the next world (*nāsti-paralokavādin*).
The eightfold great signs are proclaimed, namely: terrestrial, atmospheric, dream, celestial, bodily, vocal, characteristic, and symbolic.
The eightfold division of speech is proclaimed, namely: the first [case] occurs in designation, while the second is for instruction.
The third [case] is used in the sense of an instrument; the fourth is for the purpose of bestowing;
the fifth is for taking away; the sixth is for salutation along with one's lineage;
the seventh is for the purpose of proximity; and the eighth is the vocative case. (Ṭhāṇa 715–716)

Therein, the first case (nominative) is used in description—as in "this is he" or "I am this"; the second (accusative), however, is used in instruction—as in "say this," "do that," or "this or that"; the third (instrumental) is used in the sense of an agent—as in "done by him" or "done by me. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 717)

"Handi namo sāhāe" constitutes the fourth word-group. In "avaṇe giṇhasu," "tattō" or "ittō" is the fifth [word-group]. In "avādāṇe," "chaṭṭhī" [the sixth case] is used for that, for this, or for one who has gone, in relation to a master (sāmi). (Ṭhāṇa 718–719)

Furthermore, the seventh [case] occurs in the sense of "in that" (*tasmim*), and the eighth becomes the vocative in the sense of "time for food," as in: "O youth! (Ṭhāṇa 720). There are eight things that one with limited vision (*chaumattha*) does not know and does not see in their true nature: namely, the substance of motion (*dhammatthikāya*) up to smell and wind. However, the Arhat, Jina, and Kevalin, who possesses arisen knowledge and vision, knows and sees these very same things in their true nature: namely, the substance of motion up to wind.

Eightfold Ayurveda is taught, namely: pediatrics (kumārabhicca), internal medicine (kāyatigicchā), surgery (sālāī), extraction of splinters (sallahattā), toxicology (jaṅgōlī), demonology (bhūtavejjā), cauterization (khāratanta), and elixirs (rasāyaṇa).
Of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the devas, eight chief queens are taught, namely: Paumā, Sivā, Sacī, Añjū, Amalā, Accharā, Navamiyā, and Rohiṇī.
Of Īsāna, the lord of gods and king of the devas, eight chief queens are taught, namely: Kaṇhā, Kaṇharāī, Rāmā, Rāmarakkhittā, Vasū, Vasuguttā, Vasumittā, and Vasundharā.

It is declared that Sakka, the lord of gods, the king of the gods, has eight chief queens; it is declared that Īsāna, the lord of gods, the king of the gods, has eight chief queens. Eight great planets are declared, namely: the Moon, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, Mars, Saturn, and Ketu. Eight types of subtle vegetable organisms are declared, namely: roots, tubers, trunks, bark, branches, shoots, leaves, and flowers.

For one who does not cause harm to living beings with respect to the four senses, eightfold self-restraint is accomplished, as follows: he becomes one who does not deprive others of visual pleasure, and he becomes one who does not yoke them to visual pain; and so on, up to: he becomes one who does not deprive others of tactile pleasure, and he becomes one who does not yoke them to tactile pain.

For one who commences violence against living beings possessing four sense-faculties, eightfold non-restraint is produced, namely: by depriving them of visual pleasure, he becomes joined with visual pain; and so on, until: by depriving them of tactile pleasure, he becomes joined with tactile pain. Eight subtle things are taught, namely: subtle living beings, subtle fungi, subtle seeds, subtle green plants, subtle flowers, subtle eggs, subtle caves, and subtle moisture.

Eight generations of men in succession attained perfection, up to the complete destruction of all suffering, under King Bharata, the universal monarch of the four continents; namely: Ādityayaśas, Mahāyaśas, Atibala, Mahābala, Tejavīrya, Kattavīrya, Daṇḍavīrya, and Jalavīrya.
Pārśva, the Arhat, the supreme among men, had eight assemblies and eight *gaṇadharas*; namely: Subha, Ajjaghosa, Vasiṣṭha, Brahmachārī, Soma, Śrīdhara, Vīrabhadra, and Yaśobhadra.

Eight kinds of vision (*darśana*) are taught, namely: right vision (*samyag-darśana*), wrong vision (*mithyā-darśana*), mixed vision (*samyag-mithyā-darśana*), visual vision (*cakṣu-darśana*), non-visual vision (*acakṣu-darśana*), limited vision (*avadhi-darśana*), omniscient vision (*kevala-darśana*), and dream-vision (*svapna-darśana*). Eight kinds of time-measures (*addhōvami*) are taught, namely: the *palyōpama* (a period of time measured by the time it takes for a vast pit to be filled with or emptied of mustard seeds), the *sāgarōpama* (a period of time ten million times longer than a *palyōpama*), the *avasarpiṇī* (the descending cycle of time), the *utsarpiṇī* (the ascending cycle of time), the *pudgalaparivarta* (the time required for all matter to pass through every state of existence), past time (*atīta-addhā*), future time (*anāgata-addhā*), and all-time (*sarva-addhā*).

From the Arhat Ariṭṭhanemi down to the eighth generation of his lineage, the stage of the end of the era (*yugāntakara-bhūmi*) was brought to its conclusion when [Mahāvīra] had completed two years of religious practice (*pariyāya*).

By the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, eight kings were caused to go forth from the home life into homelessness after being shaven, namely: Vīraṅgaya, Vīrajasa, Sañjaya, Eṇijjaya, the royal sage Seya, Siva, Uddāyana, and likewise Saṅkha, the king of Kāśī.
Eightfold food is declared, namely: pleasant solid food, drink, soft food, and delicacy; and unpleasant [solid food, drink, soft food, and delicacy].

Above the Saṇaṅkumāra and Māhinda heavens, below the Brahma-loka heaven, in the Riṭṭha celestial mansion on its level floor, there are eight black streaks (kaṇharāī) described as being situated in the shape of a square courtyard. Namely: two black streaks in the east, two in the south, two in the west, and two in the north. The inner eastern black streak touches the outer southern black streak; the inner southern black streak touches the outer western black streak; the inner western black streak touches the outer northern black streak; and the inner northern black streak touches the outer eastern black streak. The two outer black streaks in the east and west are hexagonal; the two outer black streaks in the north and south are triangular; and all the inner black streaks are square.
These eight dark bands (kaṇharāī) have eight names, namely: Kaṇharāī, Mēharāī, Mahā, Mādhavatī, Vātaphalihā, Vātapalikkhōmā, Dēvaphalihā, and Dēvapalikkhōmā.

Within the eight intervals between these eight dark bands, eight celestial abodes of the world-guardians (lōgantiya-vimāṇa) are proclaimed, namely: Accī, Accimālī, Vaïrōaṇē, Pabhaṅkarē, Candābhē, Sūrābhē, Supaïṭṭhābhē, and Aggiccābhē.

In these eight celestial palaces of the world-dwellers (*lokiya*), there are eight kinds of world-dwelling gods (*lokantika devas*), namely: the Sārassatas, Māiccās, Vaṇhis, Varuṇas, Gaddatōyas, Tusitas, Avvābāhas, and Aggiccās; these are to be known. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 735)

The lifespan of these eight classes of world-protector gods (*lokiyadeva*) is declared to be eight *sāgaropamas*, neither less nor more. Eight central points of the substance of motion (*dhammatthikāya*) are declared; eight [central points] of the substance of rest (*adhammatthikāya*) are exactly the same; eight [central points] of the substance of space (*āgāsatthikāya*) are exactly the same; and eight central points of the soul (*jīva*) are declared.

The Arhat Mahāpadma will cause eight kings to go forth from the home to the homeless state after having been shaven, namely: Pauma, Paumagumma, Nalina, Nalinagumma, Paumaddhaya, Dhaṇuddhaya, Kaṇagaraha, and Bharaha.

The eight chief queens of Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, having gone into the presence of the Arhat Ariṣṭanemi, shaved their heads and went forth from the home to the homeless state; they became perfected ones (siddhas), up to the point of having abandoned all suffering.
They were as follows: Padmāvatī, Gaurī, Gandhārī, Lakṣmaṇā, Susīmā, Jambavatī, Saccabhāmā, and Rūpiṇī—the chief queens of Kṛṣṇa. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 738)
Eight main topics and eight supplementary topics are proclaimed for the *Vīriyapuvva*.

Eight destinies are proclaimed, namely: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of animals, the destiny of humans, the destiny of gods, the destiny of the perfected ones (*siddha*), the destiny of the heavy, the destiny of the rolling, and the destiny of the precipice.
The islands of the goddesses Gaṅgā, Sindhu, Rattā, and Rattavatī are each proclaimed to be eight yojanas in length and breadth.
The islands known as Ukkāmukha, Mēhamukha, Vijjumukha, and Vijjudanta are each eight hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
The Kālōda ocean is stated to be eight hundred thousand yojanas in circumference.
The inner half of the Puṣkaradvīpa is stated to be eight hundred thousand yojanas in circumference; likewise, the outer half of the Puṣkaradvīpa is also [eight hundred thousand yojanas].
Each individual universal monarch (cāurantacakravartin) possesses a golden *kākaṇī* jewel-umbrella, twelve-spoked, with eight ribs, fixed upon a stand.

It is taught that in the Magadhan *yojana*, there are eight thousand *dhanus* [in its circumference] when measured. The Jambu tree Sudarśanā is eight *yojanas* in height; at its very center, it is eight *yojanas* in width, and it is taught to be slightly more than one *yojana* in total circumference. The Kūṭaśālmalī tree is exactly the same [in dimensions].
The Timita Cave is eight yojanas in height; the Khaṇḍappavāta Cave is likewise eight yojanas in height.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara, on both banks of the great river Sītā, eight range mountains (vakkhārapavvaya) are declared, namely: Cittakūḍa, Pamhakūḍa, Nalinakūḍa, Egasela, Tikūḍa, Vesaṃmaṇakūḍa, Añjana, and Māyañjana. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara, on both banks of the great river Sītōyā, eight range mountains are declared, namely: Aṅkāvatī, Pamhāvatī, Āsīvisa, Suhāvahe, Candapavvata, Sūrapavvata, Nāgapavvata, and Dēvapavvata. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara, to the north of the great river Sītā, eight Cakravartin-conquering regions (cakkavaṭṭivijaya) are declared, namely: Kaccha, Sukaccha, Mahākaccha, Kacchagāvatī, Āvatta, Maṅgalāvatta, Pukkhalā, and Pukkhalāvatī. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara, to the south of the great river Sītā, eight Cakravartin-conquering regions are declared, namely: Vaccha, Suvaccha, Mahāvaccha, Vacchagāvatī, Ramaṇa, Ramma, Ramaṇijja, and Maṅgalāvatī. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara, to the south of the great river Sītōyā, eight Cakravartin-conquering regions are declared, namely: Pamha, Supamha, Mahapamha, Pamhagāvatī, Saṅkha, Nalina, Kumua, and Salilāvatī. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara, to the north of the great river Sītōyā, eight Cakravartin-conquering regions are declared, namely: Vappa, Suvappa, Mahāvappa, Vepagāvatī, Vaggū, Suvaggu, Gandhilla, and Gandhilāvatī.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, eight royal capitals are proclaimed; namely: Khemā, Khemapurī, Riṣṭā, Riṣṭapurī, Khaggī, Mañjūsā, Oṣadhī, and Puṇḍarīkiṇī. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītā, eight royal capitals are proclaimed; namely: Susīmā, Kuṇḍalā, Aparājitā, Prabhaṅkarā, Aṅkavatī, Padmāvatī, Subhā, and Ratnasañcayā. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītodā, eight royal capitals are proclaimed; namely: Āśāpurā, Śobhāpurā, Mahāpurā, Vijayapurā, Aparājitā, Aparā, Aśokā, and Vītaśokā. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītodā, eight royal capitals are proclaimed; namely: Vijayā, Vaijayantī, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Cakrapurā, Khagapurā, Avadhyā, and Ayodhyā.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, at the maximum limit, eight Arhats, eight Cakravartins, eight Baladevas, and eight Vāsudevas have arisen, are arising, or will arise. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītā, at the maximum limit, it is exactly the same. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītodā, at the maximum limit, it is exactly the same; likewise also to the north.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, there are eight long Veyaddha mountains; eight Timisaguhā caves; eight Khaṇḍagappavātaguhā caves; eight Kayamālaga gods; eight Naṭṭamālaga gods; eight Gaṅgākuṇḍas; eight Sindhu-kuṇḍas; eight Gaṅgā rivers; eight Sindhu rivers; eight Usabhakūḍa mountains; and eight Usabhakūḍa gods are described.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītā, there are likewise eight long Vaitāḍhya mountains, and so on, up to the eight Usabhakūṭa deities who are proclaimed to dwell there; however, here [the rivers] are Raktā and Raktavatī, and their respective reservoirs (kuṇḍas) are also [of those names]. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the south of the great river Sītōyā, there are eight long [Vaitāḍhyas], and so on, up to the eight Naṭṭamāla deities; there are eight Gaṅgā reservoirs, eight Sindhu reservoirs, eight Gaṅgā rivers, eight Sindhu rivers, eight Usabhakūṭa mountains, and eight Usabhakūṭa deities who are proclaimed to dwell there.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara and to the north of the great river Sītā, there are eight long Vaitāḍhya ranges, and so forth, up to eight Naṭṭamāla gods being described; eight Raktakuṇḍas, eight Raktāvatikuṇḍas, eight Raktās, eight Raktāvatīs, eight Ṛṣabhakūṭa mountains, and eight Ṛṣabhakūṭa gods are described.
At the very center of Mandaracūlikā, it is described as being eight yojanas in width.

In the eastern half of the continent of Dhātakīkhaṇḍa, the Ghātakī tree is taught to be eight *yojanas* in height; at its very center, it is eight *yojanas* in width, and slightly more than eight *yojanas* in total circumference. Starting from the Ghātakī tree, the entire account regarding Jambūdvīpa is to be recited, up to the Mandara-summit (*mandaracūlī*). Likewise, in the western half, starting from the Mahāghātakī tree, [the account continues] up to the Mandara-summit. Similarly, in the eastern half of the Pūrvavideha (Pukkharavaradvīpārddha) continent, starting from the Pauma (Padma) tree, [the account continues] up to the Mandara-summit. And similarly, in the western half of the Pūrvavideha continent, starting from the Mahāpauma (Mahāpadma) tree, [the account continues] up to the Mandara-summit.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, on Mount Mandara, in the Bhaddasāla forest, eight Elephant-peak summits of the quarters are declared (namely): Caümuttara, Nīlavanta, Suhasthi, Añjanāgiri, Kumuda, Palāsa, Vaḍeṃsa, and Rōyaṇāgiri. (Ṭhāṇaṅga Sutta 755)
The terrace (*jagatī*) of the continent of Jambudvīpa is eight *yojanas* in height; at its very center, it is eight *yojanas* in width.
On the southern side of Mount Mandara on the continent of Jambudvīpa, on the Mahāhimavanta range of boundary mountains, eight peaks (*kūḍa*) are declared, namely:
Siddha, Mahāhimavanta, Himavanta, Rohitā, and Harikūḍa.
Harikāntā and Harivāsa are indeed the peaks of Vairūpya.
In the *Ṭhāṇa* [Sūtra], sūtra 758, it is stated: "On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, on the Rūpya mountain range, eight peaks are proclaimed, namely:
Siddha, Rūpya, Ramyaka, Narakāntā, Buddhi, and Rūpyakūṭa."

There are peaks made of gold, jewels, and silver. (Ṭhāṇa 760) On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the east of Mount Mandara on Mount Rucakavara, eight peaks are proclaimed, namely: Riṣṭa, Tapanīya, Kāñcana, Rajata, Diśāprotsita, and Pralamba.
Añjana, Añjanapulāka, and Rūyaka are the peaks to the east [of Mount Meru].
(Ṭhāṇaṃ 762) Therein dwell eight Great Ladies of the Quarters (disākumārimahattariyā), possessing great power and so forth, with a lifespan of one *palyopama*.
They are as follows: Nandottarā, Nandā, Ānandā, and Nandivardhanā.
Vijayā, Vejayantī, Jayantī, and Aparājitā.
(Ṭhāṇaṅga 764) On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara on Mount Rucakavara, eight peaks are proclaimed, namely: Kanaka, Kāñcana, Padma, Nalina, Śaśin, and Divākara.
The Vēsamaṇa and Vēruliya peaks are to the south of Rūyaga.
(Ṭhāṇa 766) There dwell eight great queens among the Disākumāris, possessing great power and a lifespan of one *palyōpama*, as follows:
Samāhārā, Suppatiṇṇā, Suppabuddhā, and Jasōharā.
Lakṣmīvatī, Śeṣavatī, Cittaguptā, and Vasundharā.
(Ṭhāṇaṅga 768) On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the west of Mount Mandara on the excellent mountain Rucaka, eight peaks are declared; namely:
Sosthita, Amoha, Himavanta, and Mandara.
Rūpaka, Rūpakottama, Candra, and Sudarśana as the eighth.
(Ṭhāṇa 770) Therein dwell eight goddesses who are sovereigns of the quarters (disākumāri), possessing great power and a lifespan of one *palyopama*, namely: Ilādevī, Surādevī, Pṛthivī, and Padmāvatī.
Ekanāsā, Navamiyā, Sītā, and Bhaddā is the eighth.
(Ṭhāṇa 772) On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara on the Rūgavara mountain, eight peaks are proclaimed, namely: Ratna, Ratnoccaya, Sarvaratna, and Ratnasañcaya.

In Vijayā, Vejayantī, Jayantī, and Aparājitā—there dwell eight great senior goddesses of the quarters (disākumārimahattariyā), possessing great power and a lifespan of one *palyopama*. They are as follows:
Alambusā, Mitrakeśī, Pauṇḍarīkā, and Gītavāruṇī.
Āsā is in the south, while Śrī and Hrī are in the north. (Ṭhāṇa 776) Eight Great Matrons of the Quarters (Disākumārimahattariyā) residing in the lower world are enumerated:
Bhōgaṅkarā, Bhōgavatī, Subhōgā, and Bhōgamāliṇī.
Suvacchā, Vacchamittā, Vārisenā, and Balāhakā;
these eight Great Ladies of the Quarters (disākumārimahattariyā) residing in the upper world are proclaimed, namely:
Meghaṅkarā, Meghavatī, Sumedhā, and Meghamālinī.

A stream of water is variegated; a garland of flowers is beyond reproach. (Ṭhāṇa 780) Eight heavens belonging to the intermediate region are proclaimed, namely: Sōhamma up to Sahassāra. In these eight heavens, eight Indras are proclaimed, namely: Sakka up to Sahassāra. For these eight Indras, eight surrounding palaces are proclaimed, namely: Pālaē, Pupphaē, Sōmaṇasē, Sirivacchē, Nandiyāvattē, Kāmakamē, Pītimaṇē, and Vimalē.
The eighth bhikkhu-paḍimā (ascetic vow) is fulfilled according to the sūtra through sixty-four nights and two hundred and eighty-eight alms-rounds.

There are eight types of living beings involved in the cycle of existence, namely: first-moment hell-beings, non-first-moment hell-beings, first-moment animals, and so on, up to non-first-moment gods.

All living beings are declared to be of eight kinds, namely: hell-beings, male animals, female animals, males, females, gods, goddesses, and perfected beings (*siddhas*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be of eight kinds, namely: those with sensory-cognition knowledge (*ābhinibodhika-jñānī*) up to those with omniscience (*kevala-jñānī*); and those with sensory-cognition non-knowledge (*mati-ajñānī*), scriptural non-knowledge (*śruta-ajñānī*), and false-philosophical cognition (*vibhaṅga-jñānī*).
