Eightfold restraint is taught, namely: restraint with passion during the first moment of subtle-influx (sūkṣma-saṃparāya); restraint with passion during the non-first moment of subtle-influx; restraint with passion during the first moment of gross-influx (bādara-saṃparāya); restraint with passion during the non-first moment of gross-influx; restraint free from passion through subsided passions (upaśāntakaṣāya-vītarāga) during the first moment; restraint free from passion through subsided passions during the non-first moment; restraint free from passion through destroyed passions (kṣīṇakaṣāya-vītarāga) during the first moment; and restraint free from passion through destroyed passions during the non-first moment.

Eight earths are taught, namely: Ratnaprabhā up to Adhaḥsaptamī and Īṣatprāgbhārā. In the very middle region of the earth Īṣatprāgbhārā, there is a field eight *yojanas* in extent and eight *yojanas* in thickness. Eight names are taught for the earth Īṣatprāgbhārā, namely: Īṣi, or Īṣatprāgbhārā, or Tanu, or Tanutanu, or Siddhi, or Siddhalayā, or Muktī, or Muktālayā.

In eight ways one must rightly strive, exert oneself, and persevere; and in this matter, one must not be negligent. One must apply oneself to the right hearing of teachings not yet heard; one must apply oneself to the grasping and the retention of teachings already heard; one must apply oneself to the non-commission of new evil *karmas* through self-restraint (*saṃyama*); one must apply oneself to the shedding and purification of ancient *karmas* through austerity (*tapaḥ*); one must apply oneself to the gathering in of those who have not been gathered in; one must apply oneself to the instruction of novices in the sphere of conduct (*ācāra-gocara*); one must apply oneself to the performance of service for the sick without weariness; and when a dispute has arisen among fellow-monks (*sādharmika*), one must apply oneself to its pacification—being independent and unattached therein, not taking sides, remaining impartial, and thinking: "How can I bring about peace so that my fellow-monks may become quiet, free from clamor, free from strife, and free from mutual resentment?"
In the Mahāsukka and Sahassāra kalpas, the celestial palaces (vimānas) are declared to be eight hundred yojanas in height.
Of the Arhat Ariṭṭhanemi, there were eight hundred disputants who were undefeated in debate before an assembly of gods, humans, and asuras; thus, his excellence as a debater was celebrated.

Eight stages of the kevali-samudghāta (the expansion of the soul by an omniscient being) are taught, as follows: in the first moment he forms a staff; in the second moment he forms a door; in the third moment he forms a churning-stick; in the fourth moment he fills the world; in the fifth moment he withdraws from the world; in the sixth moment he withdraws the churning-stick; in the seventh moment he withdraws the door; in the eighth moment he withdraws the staff.

The ascetic, the Blessed One, Mahāvīra, had eight hundred disciples who had attained the state of *anuttaropapātika* (those reborn in the highest heavens), who were auspicious in their destination, auspicious in their station, and destined for future fortune; they possessed the supreme attainment of those reborn in the highest heavens.
Eight kinds of *vāṇamantara* (intermediate space) gods are proclaimed, namely: *pisāyas*, *bhūtas*, *jakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, *kinnaras*, *kimpurisas*, *mahōragas*, and *gandhavvas*.
For these eight kinds of *vāṇamantara* gods, eight sacred trees (*cēiyarukkha*) are proclaimed, namely: [list follows].
The *kalamba* tree belongs to the *piśācas*, the *vaṭa* to the *yakṣas*, the *tulasī* to the *bhūtas*, and the *kaṇḍaka* to the *rākṣasas*.
The *aśoka* belongs to the *kinnaras*, and the *campaka* to the *kiṃpuruṣas*. (Ṭhāṇa 792)
The *nāgarukkha* is for the *bhuyaṅgas*, and the *tendu* is for the *gandharvas*.
(Ṭhāṇa 793) Eight hundred *yojanas* above the very level and delightful ground-surface of this *Ratnaprabhā* earth, the celestial chariots (*suravimāṇa*) move in their orbits.
Eight constellations enter into conjunction with the moon in a manner that causes its eclipse: namely, Kattiyā, Rohiṇī, Punarvasū, Mahā, Cittā, Visāhā, Anurādhā, and Jeṭṭhā.
The gates of the continent of Jambūdvīpa are declared to be eight yojanas in height.
The gates of all continents and oceans are declared to be eight yojanas in height.
The minimum duration of bondage for the karma of male gender is declared to be eight years. The minimum duration of bondage for the karma of fame and renown is declared to be eight muhūrtas.

The duration of bondage for the karma of high lineage (*uccagotra*) is explained as being at least eight *muhūrtas*. Eight hundred thousand types of birth, families, and wombs are explained for three-sensed beings. Living beings have accumulated, do accumulate, or will accumulate matter formed in eight places as sinful karma; namely: from that formed in the first moment of a hell-being up to that formed in the non-first moment of a god. In this same way—regarding accumulation (*ciṇa*), gathering (*uvaciṇa*), and so on, up to exhaustion (*nijjarā*)—infinite aggregates consisting of eight space-points (*aṣṭapradeśika*) are explained.

Infinite matter-particles (*pudgala*) are taught as being immersed in eight places; likewise, infinite matter-particles are taught as being up to eight-fold dry. By nine grounds, a Śramaṇa Nirgrantha, when causing a schism in a unified community, does not overstep [his duty]. They are as follows: hostility toward the teacher (*ācārya*), hostility toward the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), hostility toward the elders (*sthavira*), hostility toward the family (*kula*), hostility toward the group (*gaṇa*), hostility toward the Saṅgha, hostility toward knowledge (*jñāna*), hostility toward vision (*darśana*), and hostility toward conduct (*cāritra*).
Nine stages of the holy life have been proclaimed, namely: the comprehension of weapons, the conquest of the world, and so forth, up to the scripture on austerities and the great comprehension.

Nine protections for celibacy (*brahmacaryagupti*) are proclaimed, as follows: 1. He frequents lodgings that are secluded, not crowded with women, not crowded with cattle, and not crowded with eunuchs. 2. He does not engage in conversation with women. 3. He does not frequent places where women reside. 4. He does not gaze upon or contemplate the beautiful and charming organs of the senses of women. 5. He does not consume highly seasoned foods. 6. He never eats food to excess. 7. He does not recall past amorous encounters or past dalliances. 8. He does not become a pursuer of sounds, nor a pursuer of forms, nor a pursuer of praise. 9. He does not become attached to pleasure and happiness. Nine protections for celibacy are proclaimed, as follows: 1. He does not frequent lodgings that are secluded, but rather those crowded with women, crowded with cattle, and crowded with eunuchs. 2. He engages in conversation with women. 3. He frequents places where women reside. 4. He gazes upon and contemplates the organs of the senses of women, and so forth. 5. He consumes highly seasoned foods. 6. He always eats food to excess. 7. He recalls past amorous encounters and past dalliances. 8. He becomes a pursuer of sounds, a pursuer of forms, and a pursuer of praise. 9. He also becomes attached to pleasure and happiness.
After nine hundred thousand billion *koṭīsāgara* aeons had elapsed, the Arhat Sumati appeared following the Arhat Abhinandana.

Nine categories of real entities (*sabbhāvapayattha*) are proclaimed, namely: living beings (*jīva*), non-living beings (*ajīva*), merit (*puṇṇa*), demerit (*pāva*), influx (*āsava*), restraint (*saṃvara*), shedding (*nijjarā*), bondage (*bandha*), and liberation (*mokkha*).

Nine types of beings involved in the cycle of existence (*saṃsārasamāvaṇṇaga*) are proclaimed, namely: earth-bodied beings up to plant-bodied beings, and those with two sense-faculties up to those with five sense-faculties.

Earth-bodied beings are declared to have nine destinations and nine origins; namely: an earth-bodied being, when being reborn among earth-bodied beings, may be reborn from among earth-bodied beings, or even from among five-sensed beings.

That same earth-bodied being, when relinquishing its state as an earth-bodied being, may go to the state of an earth-bodied being, or even to the state of a five-sensed being. The same applies to water-bodied beings, and so on up to five-sensed beings.

All living beings are declared to be of nine kinds, namely: one-sensed, two-sensed, three-sensed, four-sensed, hell-beings, five-sensed animals, humans, gods, and perfected beings (*siddhas*). Alternatively, all living beings are declared to be of nine kinds, namely: hell-beings of the first moment, hell-beings not of the first moment, and so on, up to: animals of the first moment, animals not of the first moment, humans of the first moment, humans not of the first moment, gods of the first moment, and gods not of the first moment; and perfected beings. The occupation (*ogāhaṇā*) of all living beings is declared to be of nine kinds, namely: the occupation of earth-bodied beings, the occupation of water-bodied beings, and so on, up to the occupation of plant-bodied beings, the occupation of two-sensed beings, the occupation of three-sensed beings, the occupation of four-sensed beings, and the occupation of five-sensed beings.
Living beings have wandered, are wandering, or will wander through the cycle of existence by means of nine states, namely: as earth-bodied beings, and so on, up to as five-sensed beings.

There may be the arising of disease by means of nine causes, namely: from sitting for too long, from sitting in an unhealthy posture, from excessive sleep, from excessive wakefulness, from the suppression of feces, from the suppression of urine, from traveling on a journey, from an aversion to food, and from the agitation of the objects of the senses.

The karma that obscures vision (darśanāvaraṇīya) is declared to be of nine kinds, namely: sleep (niddā), drowsiness (niddāniddā), wakeful sleep (payalā), somnambulism (payalāpayalā), intense delusion (thīṇagiddhī), obscuration of visual perception (cakkhudarśanāvaraṇa), obscuration of non-visual perception (acakkhudarśanāvaraṇa), obscuration of clairvoyant perception (ohidarśanāvaraṇa), and obscuration of omniscient perception (kevaladarśanāvaraṇa).

The asterism Abhijit joins in conjunction with the moon for more than nine muhūrtas. Nine asterisms, beginning with Abhijit, join in conjunction with the moon to its north; namely: Abhijit, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Pūrvā-bhādrapadā, Uttarā-phalgunī, Revatī, Aśvinī, and Bharaṇī.
From the level ground of this Ratnaprabhā earth, which is very even and delightful, the uppermost stars move in their course at a distance of nine hundred yojanas upward.
In Jambūdvīpa, fish nine yojanas long have entered, are entering, or will enter.
In Bhārata Varṣa on Jambūdvīpa, during this *avasarpinī*, there were nine fathers of Baladevas and Vāsudevas (as follows):
Payāvatī, Brahmā, Rudra, Soma, and Śiva.
Mahāsīha, Agnisīha, Daśārha, and the ninth, Vasudeva. [From *Ṭhāṇa* 812:
From here it begins just as in the *Samavāya*, in its entirety, until: "She will have one pregnancy and will attain perfection in the future.

In Jambūdvīpa, in Bhārata-varṣa, in the coming aeon of increase (*utsarpiṇī*), there will be nine fathers of Baladevas and Vāsudevas, and nine mothers of Baladevas and Vāsudevas; thus, just as in the *Samavāya*, in its entirety, until: "Mahābhīmasena and Suggīva, the last ones."

"These adversaries of the Vāsudevas, who are men of renown, are all indeed slain by the discus-warriors with their discs. (Ṭhāṇa 814) Each individual great treasure is declared to be nine yojanas in width; for each universal monarch (cāurantacakkavaṭṭi), nine great treasures are declared to exist (as follows): [list follows].
Nesappa, Paṇḍuka, Piṅgala, Savvarayaṇa, Mahāpauma,
Kāla, Mahākāla, Māṇavaga, Mahānihī, and Saṅkha.
(Ṭhāṇaṅga 816) In the Nesappa [treasure] are located the dwellings of villages, hamlets, towns, and cities.
[The treatise on] the harbors, market towns, fortresses, and houses;
[the treatise on] the courtesan, seeds, weights and measures, and the standard of wealth;
and the origin of seeds and wealth have been declared by Paṇḍuka. (Ṭhāṇa 817–818)
All varieties of ornaments for men and those for women,
as well as for horses and elephants, were described by Piṅgalaga in the *Nihi*.
(Ṭhāṇa 819) Regarding jewels, there are fourteen supreme gems belonging to a Cakravartin in the *Savvarayaṇa* [Nidhi].
Univocal beings arise as well as those with five senses.
(Ṭhāṇa 820) Furthermore, the origin and production of all types of garments, dyes, and cleansed cloths—all this [is described] on the Mahāpauma island. (Ṭhāṇa 821)
In the three ages, knowledge of time, the Bhavya Purāṇa, the hundred crafts, and the three types of occupations are beneficial for the world. (Ṭhāṇa.
822) Furthermore, the origin of iron and of houses occurs in the Mahākāla age.

The origin of gold, silver, jewels, pearls, crystals, and corals; the production of armor and weapons; and all the rules of warfare as well as the science of government—these were taught in Māṇava. (Ṭhāṇa 823–824)
The system of dance, the system of drama, the origin of the fourfold poetry,
and all the components of musical instruments [were established] in the Great Treasure (Mahāniddhi) at Saṅkha.
(Ṭhāṇa 825) It has a wheel-base foundation, eight in height, and nine in width.
At the mouth of the Jambū River, there are twelve long caskets shaped like chests (*mañjūsā*).
Their doors are made of beryl stones, they are fashioned of gold, and they are filled with various jewels.
Their faces have arms and jaws symmetrical with the discs of the moon and the sun. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 826–827)

Regarding those [treasures] which have a duration of many millions of years and possess names such as "Nidhi," they are indeed the abodes of gods for whom those [treasures] are inaccessible [to others],
or rather, they belong to them by way of sovereignty. (Ṭhāṇa 828) These are the nine treasures, flourishing with abundant accumulations of wealth and jewels.
Those who come under the sway of all the universal monarchs (cakravartins).
[Ṭhāṇa 829] Nine fermented liquors (vigati) are taught, namely: milk, curd, butter, ghee, oil, molasses, honey, liquor, and meat.
The body has nine channels through which it flows, namely: two ear-channels, two eye-channels, two nostrils, the mouth, the anus, and the urethra.

Nine kinds of merit are taught, namely: merit from food, merit from drink, merit from clothing, merit from shelter, merit from bedding, merit from the mind, merit from speech, merit from the body, and merit from the *namokkāra* (the fivefold salutation).
Nine sources of demerit are taught, namely: killing living beings, false speech, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, possessiveness, anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
Nine kinds of attachment to evil learning are taught, namely: [as follows].
In portents, omens, mantras, medicine, arts, obstructions, ignorance, and false doctrines—thus [are they known].
(Ṭhāṇa 835) Nine subjects of craftsmanship have been proclaimed, namely: [the list follows].

[The following are] the signs: counting, marks, astrology, ancient lore, manual arts, the ignorant, rhetoric, rites for prosperity, and medicine. (Ṭhāṇaṃ 836) The ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, had nine assemblies (gaṇas), namely: the Godāsa assembly, the Uttara-balissaha assembly, the Uddēha assembly, the Cāraṇa assembly, the Uddavāiya assembly, the Vissavāiya assembly, the Kāmaḍḍhiya assembly, the Māṇava assembly, and the Kōḍiya assembly.

By the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, alms-food purified by nine considerations has been prescribed for the ascetics, the Nirgranthas; namely: he does not kill, he does not cause to kill, nor does he approve of one who kills; he does not cook, he does not cause to cook, nor does he approve of one who cooks; he does not buy, he does not cause to buy, nor does he approve of one who buys.
Furthermore, it is declared that the divine king Īśāna, the lord of the gods, and the great king Varuṇa have nine chief queens.

The lifespan of the chief queens of Īśāna, the lord of gods and king of the devas, is declared to be nine *palyopamas*. In the celestial realm of Īśāna, the maximum lifespan of the goddesses is declared to be nine *palyopamas*.
Nine classes of gods are declared, namely:
the Sārassayas, the Ādityas, the Vaṇhis, the Varuṇas, and the Gaddatoyas.
The Tuṣitas, the Avyāvāhas, the Agniccas, and the Riṣṭas.
(Ṭhāṇa 842) Nine gods and nine divine abodes of the Avyāvāha gods are proclaimed; likewise for the Agniccas, and likewise for the Riṣṭas.

Nine tiers of Graiveyaka celestial mansions are taught, namely: the lowest-lowest tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the lower-middle tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the lower-upper tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the middle-lower tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the middle-middle tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the middle-upper tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the upper-lower tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, the upper-middle tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, and the uppermost tier of Graiveyaka celestial mansions. For these nine tiers of Graiveyaka celestial mansions, nine designations are taught, namely:

Bhaddā, Subhaddā, Sujātā, Somaṇasā, Piya-darisaṇā, Sudasaṇā, Amohā, Suppabuddhā, and Yasodharā. In the *Ṭhāṇaṃga*, 845: Ninefold transformation of matter (*āu-pariṇāma*) is taught, namely: transformation of movement (*gati-pariṇāma*), transformation of the bond of movement (*gati-bandhana-pariṇāma*), transformation of duration (*ṭhiti-pariṇāma*), transformation of the bond of duration (*ṭhiti-bandhana-pariṇāma*), upward emission of heat (*uḍḍhaṅgāra-pariṇāma*), downward emission of heat (*ahēgāra-pariṇāma*), horizontal emission of heat (*tiriyaṅgāra-pariṇāma*), long emission of heat (*dīhaṅgāra-pariṇāma*), and short emission of heat (*rahassaṅgāra-pariṇāma*).
The ninth-navemith bhikkhu-paḍimā is accomplished, as prescribed by the sūtra, in eighty-one nights and four hundred and five alms-rounds.

Nine kinds of penance (pāyacchitta) are taught, namely: that which is fit for confession (ālōyaṇā), that which is fit for repentance (paḍikkamaṇā), that which is fit for both, that which is fit for seclusion (vivega), that which is fit for extra exertion (viussagga), that which is fit for austerity (tava), that which is fit for reduction of seniority (chēya), that which is fit for root-reinstatement (mūla), and that which is fit for suspension (aṇavaṭṭhappa).
On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, in Bhāratavarṣa on the Long Vaitāḍhya mountain range, nine peaks are taught (namely:).
When Bharata is established, the names of the peaks in Bharata—Khaṇḍaga, Māṇī, Veyaḍḍha, Puṇṇa, Timisaguhā, Bharaha, and Vēsamaṇa—are the names of the peaks.
(Ṭhāṇa 850) On the island of Jambūdvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, nine peaks are declared on the Niṣadha range-encircling mountain, namely: [the list follows].

The names of the peaks on Mount Nisaha in Harivarṣa, Videha, Haridhiti, A-sītōyā, Avara-videha, and Rūyaga are as follows: [These are the names of the peaks on Mount Nisaha]. In Jambudvīpa, on Mount Mandara in the Nandana grove, nine peaks are enumerated, namely: [list follows].
Nandaṇa, Mandara, Nisaha, Haimavata, Rucaka, Sāgaracitta, Vajra, and Balakūḍa are to be known [as the peaks].
(Ṭhāṇa 854) Nine peaks are declared on Mount Mālavanta in Jambūdvīpa; namely:—

Siddha, Mālavaṃta, Uttarakuru, Kaccha, Sāgara, Rata, Sītā, Punyanāma, and Harissahakūḍa are to be known. (Ṭhāṇa 856) On the island of Jambudvīpa, on the long Veyaddha mountain in Kaccha, nine peaks are declared, namely:—

Siddha, Kaccha, Khaṇḍaga, Māṇī, Veyaddha, Puṇṇa, Timisaguhā, Kaccha, and Vesaṃmaṇa—these are the names of the peaks on the Kaccha [mountain]. (Ṭhāṇa 858) On the island of Jambūdvīpa, on the Dīrghavaitāḍhya mountain in Sukaccha, nine peaks are proclaimed; namely:—

In Siddha, Sukaccha, Khaṇḍaga, Māṇī, Veyaḍḍha, Puṇṇa, Timisaguhā, Sukaccha, and Vēsamaṇa—these are the names of the peaks in Sukaccha. (Ṭhāṇa 860). Thus, up to Pokkhalāvaī on the Long Veyaḍḍha; thus on Vaccha on the Long Veyaḍḍha; and thus up to Maṅgalāvatī on the Long Veyaḍḍha. On the island of Jambūdvīpa, on the island of Vijjuppabha, there are nine peaks on the Vakkhāra mountain, namely: [list follows].

Siddha, Vijju, Devakuru, Pamha, Kaṇaga, Sovatthī, Sīyodā, Sayajala, and Harikūḍa—these are to be known [as the peaks]. (Ṭhāṇa 862) In Jambudvīpa, on the island of Pamha Dīghaveyaḍḍha, nine peaks are enumerated, namely: Siddha, Pamha, Khaṇḍaga, Māṇī, Veyaḍḍha, Puṇṇa, Timisaguhā, Pamha, and Vesaṃmaṇa. These are the names of the peaks of Pamha; in the same manner, they exist up to Salilā in Dīghaveyaḍḍha. Likewise, there are nine peaks on Vappa Dīghaveyaḍḍha, and in the same way, up to Gandhilāvatī Dīghaveyaḍḍha, nine peaks are enumerated, namely: [the same as above].

When it is established, the names of the peaks are Gandhila, Khaṇḍaga, Māṇi, Vēyaḍḍha, Puṇṇa, Timisaguhā, Gandhilāvati, and Vēsamaṇa. (Ṭhāṇa 864) Thus, on all the long Vēyaḍḍha mountains, there are two peaks with similar names, and the remaining are those same [as previously mentioned]. On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, on the Nīlavanta range-encircling mountain, nine peaks are proclaimed, namely:—
In Siddha, Nīlavanta, Videha, Sītā, Kitti, Nārikantā, Avaravideha, Rammagakūḍa, and Uvadaṃsaṇa.
(Ṭhāṇa 866) On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, nine peaks are declared on the long Erāvata Vaitāḍhya mountain, namely: [list follows].

The names of the peaks on Mount Veyaddha are Siddhērava, Khaṇḍaga, Māṇīvēyaḍḍha, Puṇṇa, Timisaguhā, Eravata, Vēsamaṇa, and [the ninth] Eravata. (Ṭhāṇa 868) The Arhat Pārśva, the giver of men, possessed the Vajra-ṛṣabha-nārāca bone-jointing and was situated in the symmetrical square (samacaturaṃsa) formation; he was nine cubits (*rayaṇī*) in height.

In the dispensation of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, the karma of the name and lineage of a Tīrthaṅkara was produced by nine beings, namely: Seniya, Supāsa, Udāyin, Poṭṭila, the monk Daḍhāū, Saṅkha, Sata, the laywoman Sulasā, and Revatī.

This venerable Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, Rāma Baladeva, Udaya Pēḍhālaputta, Puṭṭila, Sataka the householder, Dāruka the Nirgrantha, Saccaka the son of the Nirgrantha woman, and the mendicant Ambaḍa who attained enlightenment through the Śrāvikā—all these, as well as the venerable Supārśva, the disciple of Pārśva, will, in the future *utsarpiṇī*, preach the fourfold law and attain perfection, up to the final end.

"This noble King Śreṇika of Bimbisāra, having passed away at the time of his death, will be reborn as a denizen of hell in the Sīmantaka hell within this Ratnaprabhā earth, where the lifespan is eighty-four thousand years. There he will become a hell-being—dark as the color of black collyrium, with a complexion that is intensely black—and there he will experience a sensation of pain that is blazing, intense, and difficult to endure."

When he has emerged from that hell, in the future *utsarpiṇī* age, here in this very Jambudvīpa continent, in the land of Bhāratavarṣa, at the foot of the Veyaddha mountain, in the region of Puṇḍravardhana, in the city of Śatadvāra, he will be reborn as a male child in the womb of Bhadrā, the wife of the Kulakara Saṃmuci. Then, after nine months have passed and seven and a half nights and days, that wife Bhadrā will give birth to a boy with delicate hands and feet, whose body possesses complete and unimpaired five senses, and who is endowed with auspicious marks, characteristics, and a beautiful form. On the night that the boy is born, on that very night, in the city of Śatadvāra, both inside and outside, there will fall showers of gold dust (*bhāragga*), showers of silver dust (*kumbhagga*), showers of lotuses (*pauma*), and showers of jewels (*rayaṇa*).

Then, when eleven days had passed for that boy—once the impurity-removing rites were completed and the twelfth day had arrived—his parents will give him this appropriate name derived from his qualities: "Since, upon the birth of this boy, a rain of gold, a rain of jewels, a rain of lotuses, and a rain of gems fell throughout our city, both inside and outside, let the name of this boy be Mahāpauma."

Then his parents will give that boy the name Mahāpauma. When his parents know that the boy Mahāpauma has reached a little more than eight years of age, they will consecrate him with a very grand royal consecration. He will then become the king there, ruling the kingdom like a great Himalaya, Mahāmalaya, Mandara, or Mahendra mountain, [with all the description of a king] until he dwells presiding over his realm.

Then, at another time, two gods of great power and great happiness—namely Puṇṇabhadda and Maṇibhadda—performed the task of marshaling the army for King Mahāpauma. Thereupon, many lords, chiefs, ministers, feudal lords, householders, merchants, guild-leaders, caravan leaders, and others in the city of Sataduvāra called one another and said: "O dear sirs, since two gods of great power and great happiness—namely Puṇṇabhadda and Maṇibhadda—are performing the task of marshaling the army for our King Mahāpauma, therefore, O dear sirs, let 'Devasena' become a second name for our King Mahāpauma. Consequently, a second name, Devasena, came to belong to that King Mahāpauma.

Then, on a certain occasion, there will arise for King Devasena a pre-eminent elephant-treasure, white as the surface of a conch shell and possessing four tusks. When King Devasena has mounted that pre-eminent elephant-treasure, white as the surface of a conch shell and possessing four tusks, he will frequently pass through and out of the city of Śatadvāra right through its middle. Then, many lords of the realm, chief ministers, and others in the city of Śatadvāra will call out to one another and say: "O beloved ones, since a pre-eminent elephant-treasure, white as the surface of a conch shell and possessing four tusks, has arisen for our King Devasena, let 'Vimalavāhana' (the Pure-Rider) be his third name, O beloved ones! And so, King Devasena will have a third name, Vimalavāhana.

Then King Vimalavāhana, having lived for thirty years in the midst of the household life, when his parents had gone to the world of the gods and he had been granted permission by his elders and preceptors, and having awakened to the unsurpassed path of liberation in the autumn season, shall—being greeted and praised with those delightful, lovely, dear, pleasing, agreeable, sublime, auspicious, blissful, blessed, auspicious, and glorious words by the world-protectors and the gods who are like his own life—go forth from the home to the homeless state, having become shaven-headed and having taken a single divine garment, in the Subhūmibhāga park outside the city.

For more than twelve years, that Blessed One will remain with his body constantly surrendered and his possessions renounced; whatever obstacles may arise—whether from gods, humans, or animals—he will endure, tolerate, patiently bear, and withstand them all. Then that Blessed One will become a wandering mendicant, restrained in movement, restrained in speech, and so forth, until he is a protector of celibacy, free from "mine-ness," possessing nothing, with ties severed, undefiled, like a bronze vessel released from its impurities, as described in the *Bhāvanā* chapter, up to: like a well-kindled fire, blazing with intense splendor.
In a bronze vessel, a conch shell, a living being, the sky, the wind, the essence, water,
a lotus leaf, a tortoise, a bird, a rhinoceros, and a bhāraṇḍa;
an elephant, a bull, a lion, a king of mountains, and the unshakeable ocean— *Thāṇa* 873.
Like the moon, the sun, gold, and the earth, they are as if well-sacrificed. (Ṭhāṇa 874)

There shall be no obstruction whatsoever for that Blessed One. That obstruction is declared to be fourfold, namely: an egg, a boat, a hold, or a grip. In whichever direction he desires, in that very direction he shall wander—unobstructed, purified, lightened, and free from bonds—cultivating his self through self-restraint. For that Blessed One, as he cultivates his self by means of supreme knowledge, supreme vision, supreme conduct, and likewise by his discourse, his mode of life, uprightness, gentleness, lightness, patience, liberation, restraint, truth, self-restraint, austerity, virtue, good conduct, purity, and the path of the fruit of final liberation; and while abiding in the interval between meditations, there shall arise in him infinite, supreme, unimpeded, unobstructed, complete, and perfect supreme, excellent knowledge and vision.

Then that Blessed One will become an Arhat, a Jina, a Kevalin, omniscient and all-seeing; he will know and behold the conduct of the world with its gods, humans, and asuras. He will know and behold the coming and going, the staying, the passing away, and the rebirth of all living beings in the entire world; their thoughts, mental states, what has been eaten, done, and experienced; their public deeds and secret deeds. Being an Arhat, a partaker of the state of an Arhat, at whatever time he abides in the activity of mind, speech, or body, he will dwell knowing and beholding all the states of all living beings in the entire world.

Then, by means of that supreme, excellent, absolute knowledge and vision (*kevalavarajñānadarśana*), the Blessed One, having perceived the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, will endure, tolerate, patiently bear, and overcome all the hardships (*upasargas*) that may arise for the Śramaṇas and Nirgranthas—whether they be divine, human, or animal. Then that Blessed One will become a monk (*anagāra*): restrained in movement (*iryāsamita*), restrained in speech (*bhāṣāsamita*), and so forth, just as Lord Vardhamāna [did], in full detail, until he is "engaged in the yoga of non-action" (*avyāpāravīryayogayukta*). As that Blessed One wanders about in this manner of life, when twelve years and thirteen fortnights have passed, while the thirteenth year is still in progress, there will arise in him supreme knowledge and vision, just as described in the *Bhāvanā* chapter; he will become a Conqueror (*jina*), an omniscient one, an all-seer. He will wander about teaching the Dharma, which includes the five great vows with their respective reflections (*sabhāvanā*) and the six classes of living beings (*ṣaḍjīvanikāya*), including the hell-beings and so forth.

"Just as, venerable sir, one basis of violence has been taught by me for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, even so the Arhat Mahāpadma will also proclaim one basis of violence for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas. Just as, venerable sir, two kinds of bondage have been taught by me for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, namely: the bondage of attachment (*pejja*) and the bondage of aversion (*dōsa*), even so the Arhat Mahāpadma will also proclaim two kinds of bondage for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, namely: the bondage of attachment and the bondage of aversion. Just as, venerable sir, three rods have been taught by me for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, namely: the rod of mind (*maṇa-daṇḍa*), the rod of speech (*vaya-daṇḍa*), and the rod of body (*kāya-daṇḍa*), even so the Arhat Mahāpadma will also proclaim three rods for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, namely: the rod of mind, the rod of speech, and the rod of body."

Just as, O Venerable One, I have declared four passions (*kaṣāya*) for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas—namely, the passion of anger up to the passion of greed—and five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*), [and] six classes of living beings (*ṣaḍjīvanikāya*) have been declared—namely, the earth-bodied beings up to those with sound, up to those with touch, and the mobile-bodied beings—in the very same way, the Arhat Mahāpadma will also teach the six classes of living beings for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, namely: the earth-bodied beings up to the mobile-bodied beings.

Just as, O Venerable One, seven bases of fear, eight bases of pride, nine rules for the protection of celibacy, and tenfold conduct of a śramaṇa have been taught by me, so too [have been taught] everything up to the thirty-three types of afflictions.

Just as, O Venerable One, I have declared for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, the state of nakedness, the state of being shaven-headed, not bathing, not cleaning the teeth, not using an umbrella, not using footwear, sleeping on the ground, sleeping on a plank, sleeping on a wooden board, the plucking out of hair, living in celibacy, entering the houses of others, and so forth, up to subsisting on whatever food is obtained—exactly in that same way, the Arhat Mahāpadma will also proclaim for the Śramaṇas, the Nirgranthas, the state of nakedness, and so forth, up to subsisting on whatever food is obtained.

"Just as, O Venerable One, I have prohibited for the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas food that is *ādhākarmika*, or *uddēśika*, or mixed with raw grain (*mīsajāya*), or *adhyavapūraka*, or putrid, or purchased, or received on credit, or stolen, or unpermitted, or brought [to them], or food from a wilderness, or food from a time of famine, or food for the sick, or food for a storm, or food for guests, or food consisting of roots, or food consisting of tubers, or food consisting of fruits, or food consisting of seeds, or food consisting of greens—just so will the Arhat Mahāpadma also prohibit for the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas food that is *ādhākarmika* up to food consisting of greens. Just as, O Venerable One, I have proclaimed for the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas the Dharma consisting of the five great vows, along with confession, and being unclothed (*acelaka*), just so the Arhat Mahāpadma will proclaim for the Śramaṇas Nirgranthas the Dharma consisting of the five great vows, along with confession, and being unclothed."

"Just as, O Venerable Sir, I have prescribed for the lay followers (*śramaṇopāsaka*) the twelvefold duty of a lay follower consisting of the five minor vows (*aṇuvrata*) and the seven disciplinary vows (*śikṣāvrata*), even so will the Arhat Mahāpadma also prescribe for the lay followers the twelvefold duty of a lay follower, starting from the five minor vows.

Just as, O Venerable Sir, I have prohibited for the naked mendicant monks (*nirgrantha śramaṇa*) the alms-food of a bed-maker or the alms-food of a king, even so will the Arhat Mahāpadma also prohibit for the naked mendicant monks the alms-food of a bed-maker or the alms-food of a king."
Just as, O Venerable One, I have nine gaṇas and eleven gaṇadharas, even so there will be nine gaṇas and eleven gaṇadharas for the Arhat Pārśva.

"Just as, O Venerable One, I, having lived for thirty years in the midst of household life, having become shaven-headed, having gone forth from the home to the homeless state, having completed twelve years and thirteen fortnights of the stage of an imperfect sage (*chadmastha*), having completed the stage of a perfected sage (*kevalin*) for thirty years less thirteen fortnights, and having completed forty-two years of the stage of asceticism (*śrāmaṇya*), shall—having lived out my full lifespan of seventy-two years—attain perfection and make an end to all suffering; even so, Mahāpadma the Arhat, having lived for thirty years in the midst of household life... [and] having gone forth... for twelve years... [and] having lived out his full lifespan of seventy-two years, shall attain perfection and make an end to all suffering."
The same conduct and practice that belongs to the Arhat Tīrthaṅkara Mahāvīra also belongs to the Arhat Mahāpadma.
(Ṭhāṇa 876) Nine constellations are declared to be behind the moon (as follows): [list].
The constellations Abhijit, Śravaṇā,
Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Hasta, and Citrā— these nine are the western [asterisms].
(Ṭhāṇa 878) In the celestial realms Ānata, Prāṇata, Āraṇa, and Acyuta, the palaces are declared to be nine hundred yojanas in height.

The lineage-founder Vimalavāhana was nine *ghanaśata*s in height. When nine *koṭākoṭis* of *sāgaropamas* had elapsed in this current *avasarpinī*, the Arhat Ṛṣabha, the descendant of Kośala, established the *tīrtha*.
The islands Ghanadanta, Laṭṭhadanta, Gūḍhadanta, and Śuddhadanta are each described as being nine hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth.

Nine courses of the great planet Sukra are taught, namely: the horse-course, the elephant-course, the serpent-course, the bull-course, the cow-course, the snake-course, the iron-course, the deer-course, and the Vaisānara-course.
Nine types of karma produced by the non-kaṣāya passions are taught, namely: female gender, male gender, neuter gender, laughter, attachment, aversion, fear, sorrow, and disgust.

Nine hundred thousand principal classes of species and wombs are taught for four-sensed beings; nine hundred thousand principal classes of species and wombs are taught for five-sensed terrestrial animals, both those that crawl on their bellies and those that move on land. Living beings have accumulated, are accumulating, or will accumulate matter formed into nine categories as sinful karma; namely: matter formed into the category of earth-bodied beings, up to matter formed into the category of five-sensed beings. In the same way, there is accumulation (*ciṇa*), further accumulation (*uvaciṇa*), and so forth, up to the shedding (*nijjarā*) of that very matter.
Infinite aggregates consisting of nine space-points are taught; likewise, up to infinite particles of matter possessing ninefold dryness are taught.

Ten principles for the stability of the world (*logatthitī*) are taught, as follows: 1. That living beings (*jīvā*), having died here and there, are reborn again and again in those very same places—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 2. That for living beings, sinful karma (*pāve kammē*) is constantly and continuously being performed—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 3. That for living beings, deluding karma (*mōhaṇijjē pāvē kammē*) is constantly and continuously being performed—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 4. That it has never been so, nor will it ever be, that living beings become non-living beings (*ajīvā*), or that non-living beings become living beings—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 5. That it has never been so, nor will it ever be, that mobile beings (*tasā pāṇā*) will cease to exist and stationary beings (*thāvarā pāṇā*) will come to be, or that stationary beings will cease to exist and mobile beings will come to be—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 6. That it has never been so, nor will it ever be, that the world (*lōgē*) will become the non-world (*alōgē*), or that the non-world will become the world—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 7. That it has never been so, nor will it ever be, that the world will enter the non-world, or that the non-world will enter the world—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 8. As far as the world extends, so far extend living beings; as far as living beings extend, so far extends the world—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 9. As long as there is the movement and transition (*gatipariyāē*) of living beings and matter (*poggalā*), so long does the world exist; as long as the world exists, so long does the movement and transition of living beings and matter continue—this is one principle for the stability of the world. 10. At all the boundaries of the world (*lōgantēsu*), matter (*poggalā*) is made to be touched without being bound by a tether (*abaddhapāsapuṭṭhā*) due to its dryness (*lukkhattāē*), whereby living beings and matter are not able to go outside the boundaries of the world—this is one principle for the stability of the world.
Ten kinds of sounds are taught (as follows):
the sound of a draft, a solid mass, dryness, breaking, and decay; long, short, distinct, the sound of a kākī, and the sound of a bell. (Ṭhāṇa 890)

Ten objects of the senses are taught as having passed away, namely: some heard sounds partially; some heard sounds completely; some saw forms partially; some saw forms completely; some smelled odors partially; some tasted flavors partially; some tasted flavors completely; some [experienced] odors, tastes, and touches partially; and some experienced touches completely. Ten objects of the senses are taught as being present, namely: some hear sounds partially, up to experiencing touches completely. Ten objects of the senses are taught as being future, namely: some will hear sounds partially, up to experiencing touches completely.

In ten situations, matter (*pudgala*) may move: namely, it may move while being ingested; it may move while being transformed; it may move while breathing out; it may move while breathing in; it may move while being experienced [as karma]; it may move while being worn away [through karmic exhaustion]; it may move while being manifested [through psychic power]; it may move while being transmuted; it may move when possessed by a spirit (*yakṣa*); or it may move when affected by wind.

There are ten grounds for the arising of anger, namely: (1) pleasant sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells have been taken away from me; (2) unpleasant sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells have been brought to me; (3) pleasant sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells are being taken away from me; (4) unpleasant sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells are being brought to me; (5) pleasant sounds, touches, tastes, forms, and smells will be taken away from me; (6) unpleasant sounds, etc., will be brought to me; (7) pleasant sounds, etc., will be taken away from me; (8) unpleasant sounds, etc., have been, are being, or will be brought to me; (9) pleasant and unpleasant sounds, etc., have been, are being, or will be taken away from me; (10) I am behaving correctly toward my teachers and preceptors, yet my teachers and preceptors have behaved wrongly toward me.

Restraint is declared to be of ten kinds, namely: restraint regarding the earth-body, up to restraint regarding the plant-body; restraint regarding two-sensed beings, three-sensed beings, four-sensed beings, and five-sensed beings; and restraint regarding non-living matter. Non-restraint is declared to be of ten kinds, namely: non-restraint regarding the earth-body, water-body, fire-body, air-body, and plant-body, up to non-restraint regarding non-living matter.

Ten kinds of restraint are taught, namely: restraint of the ear-faculty, up to restraint of the touch-faculty, restraint of the mind, restraint of speech, restraint of the body, restraint of requisites, and restraint regarding the needle-point; ten kinds of non-restraint are taught, namely: non-restraint of the ear-faculty, up to non-restraint regarding the needle-point.

One might become arrogant on account of ten grounds, namely: on account of birth, or on account of family, up to on account of sovereignty; or thinking, "Nagas and Suparnas come quickly to me"; or thinking, "A superhuman state, a distinction, knowledge, and vision have arisen in me."

Ten kinds of concentration (*samādhi*) are taught, namely: abstention from taking life, abstention from false speech, abstention from taking what is not given, abstention from sexual activity, abstention from possessiveness, carefulness in movement (*iryā-samiti*), carefulness in speech (*bhāṣā-samiti*), carefulness in seeking alms (*eṣaṇā-samiti*), carefulness in receiving, handling, and putting away utensils and requisites (*ādāna-bhaṇḍa-matta-nikṣepaṇā-samiti*), and carefulness in the disposal of excrement, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, and perspiration (*uccāra-pāsavaṇa-khēla-sindhāṇaga-jalla-pāriṭṭhāvaṇiyā-samiti*). Ten kinds of non-concentration (*asamādhi*) are taught, namely: taking life up to possessiveness; lack of carefulness in movement up to lack of carefulness in the disposal of excrement, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, and perspiration.

Ten kinds of renunciation are taught (as follows): that by consent, by anger, by exhaustion, by a dream, by a promise, by remembrance, by illness, by being unattended, by divine command, and by following after a calf. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 898)

The tenfold duty of a monk (*śramaṇadharma*) is taught as follows: forbearance, freedom from attachment, uprightness, gentleness, lightness, truthfulness, self-restraint, austerity, renunciation, and living in celibacy. The tenfold service (*vaiyāvṛtya*) is taught as follows: service to the preceptor (*ācārya*), service to the teacher (*upādhyāya*), service to the elder (*sthavira*), service to the ascetic (*tapasvin*), service to the sick (*glāna*), service to the novice (*śaikṣa*), service to the family (*kula*), service to the community (*gaṇa*), service to the order (*saṅgha*), and service to one's fellow practitioners (*sādharmika*).

Tenfold transformation of the soul is taught, namely: transformation of state of existence (*gati-pariṇāma*), transformation of sense organs (*indriya-pariṇāma*), transformation of passions (*kaṣāya-pariṇāma*), transformation of coloration (*leśyā-pariṇāma*), transformation of activity (*yoga-pariṇāma*), transformation of possession (*upayoga-pariṇāma*), transformation of knowledge (*jñāna-pariṇāma*), transformation of vision (*darśana-pariṇāma*), transformation of conduct (*cāritra-pariṇāma*), and transformation of sex (*veda-pariṇāma*). Tenfold transformation of non-soul is taught, namely: transformation of bondage (*bandhana-pariṇāma*), transformation of state of existence (*gati-pariṇāma*), transformation of shape (*saṃsthāna-pariṇāma*), transformation of division (*bheda-pariṇāma*), transformation of color (*varṇa-pariṇāma*), transformation of taste (*rasa-pariṇāma*), transformation of smell (*gandha-pariṇāma*), transformation of touch (*sparśa-pariṇāma*), transformation of lightness-heaviness (*agurulaghu-pariṇāma*), and transformation of sound (*śabda-pariṇāma*).

Ten kinds of atmospheric conditions are declared to be unsuitable for recitation (*asajjhāya*), namely: whirlwind, dust-storm, thunder, lightning, crash of thunder, storm, firebrand of a *yakṣa*, smoke, mist, and a cloud of dust. Ten kinds of terrestrial conditions are declared to be unsuitable for recitation, namely: a bone, flesh, blood, a place near an impure thing, a place near a cemetery, an eclipse of the moon, an eclipse of the sun, a fall [of a meteor], a royal disturbance, and a bodily excretion within the vicinity of the dwelling.

For one who does not cause injury to living beings possessing the five senses, tenfold self-restraint (*saṃyama*) is accomplished; namely: he becomes one who does not deprive others of the pleasure of sound, and he becomes one who is not joined with the pain of sound, and so on, until he becomes one who is not joined with the pain of touch.

For one who commences violence against living beings by means of the five sense organs, tenfold non-restraint is produced, namely: having deprived them of the pleasure consisting of sound, he becomes joined with suffering consisting of sound; and so on, up to: having deprived them of the pleasure consisting of touch, he becomes joined with suffering consisting of touch. Ten subtle things are taught, namely: the subtle living being, the subtle fungus, and so on, up to the subtle moisture, the subtle calculation, and the subtle division.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the south of Mount Mandara, ten great rivers join the Ganges and the Sindhu; namely: the Jaunā, Sarayū, Āvī, Kośī, Mahī, Satadru, Vitastā, Vibhāsā, Airāvatī, and Candrabhāgā.

On the island of Jambudvīpa, to the north of Mount Mandara, ten great rivers join the Raktā and the Raktavatī; namely: the Kṛṣṇā, Mahākṛṣṇā, Nīlā, Mahānīlā, Mahātīrā, Indrā, Indrasenā, Susenā, Vārisenā, and Mahābhogā.

In the land of Bharata on the continent of Jambūdvīpa, ten royal capitals are enumerated, namely: Campā, Mathurā, Vārāṇasī, Śrāvastī, likewise Sāketa, Hastināpura, Kampilla, Mithilā, Kauśāmbī, and Rājagṛha. (Ṭhāṇa 906)
In these ten royal capitals, ten kings became shaven-headed and went forth as ascetics, namely: Bharata, Sagara, Maghavan, Sanatkumāra, Śānti, Kuṃthu, Ara, Mahāpadma, Hariṣeṇa, and Jayanāman.

On Mount Mandara in the continent of Jambūdvīpa, the height above the surface of the earth is ten hundred yojanas; its width at the base is ten thousand yojanas, and its width at the summit is ten hundred yojanas; thus it is declared to have a total extent of ten times ten thousand yojanas.

On the island of Jambūdvīpa, in the very middle region of Mount Mandara, upon the upper and lower minor terraces of this Jewel-Lustre Earth (*Rayaṇappabhā Puḍhavī*), there exists the eight-parted Axis (*Ruyaga*). From it, these ten directions issue forth, namely: the East, the Southeast, the South, the Southwest, the West, the Northwest, the North, the Northeast, the Upward direction, and the Downward direction. For these ten directions, ten designations are proclaimed (as follows):—
Indrā, Aggī, Jammā, Nēratī, Vāruṇī, Vāyavvā, Sōmā, Īsāṇī, Vimalā, and Tamā are to be known [as the ten directions]. (Ṭhāṇa 910)

In the salt ocean, ten thousand yojanas of land are declared to be suitable for grazing cattle; in the salt ocean, ten thousand yojanas are declared to be the expanse of the water. All the great subterranean abysses (mahāpātālas) are declared to be fifty thousand yojanas in depth; at their base, they are declared to be ten thousand yojanas in width; in the middle portion, by way of a single-unit line (egapaēsiyā sēḍhī), they are declared to be fifty thousand yojanas in width; and at the top, at the mouth, they are declared to be ten thousand yojanas in width.

The walls of those great netherworlds (mahāpātāla) are made entirely of adamant (vajra), uniform throughout, and ten hundred yojanas in thickness. All the small netherworlds (khuddāpātāla) are also declared to be ten hundred yojanas in depth; at their base, they are ten hundred yojanas in width; at their broad middle section, they are ten hundred yojanas in width along a single-layered line (seḍhī); and at the top, at the mouth, they are ten hundred yojanas in width. The walls of those small netherworlds are also made entirely of adamant, uniform throughout, and ten yojanas in thickness.

The Mandara mountains of Ghāyaisaṇḍa are ten hundred yojanas in height above the earth's surface, slightly less than ten thousand yojanas in width at the base, and ten hundred yojanas in width at the top; the Mandara mountains of Pukkhara-vara-dīvaḍḍha are likewise ten hundred yojanas in height, and so forth.

All the Vattaveyaḍḍha mountains are ten hundred yojanas in height upward, ten hundred *gavyūtis* in height above the ground, equal everywhere and shaped like a palanquin, and are declared to be ten hundred yojanas in width.
On the island of Jambudvīpa, ten regions are taught, namely: Bharata, Airāvata, Haimavata, Hairaṇyavata, Harivarṣa, Ramyakavarṣa, Pūrvavideha, Aparavideha, Devakuru, and Uttarakuru.
At the base of the Mānuṣottara mountain, the width is taught to be one thousand two hundred and twenty yojanas.

All the Añjana mountains are ten hundred yojanas in height; at their base they are ten thousand yojanas in width, and at the top they are ten hundred yojanas in width. All the Dadhimukha mountains are ten hundred yojanas in height, equal in width everywhere, shaped like a palaga (plank), and ten thousand yojanas in width.

All the Ratikara mountains are ten hundred yojanas in height, ten hundred *gavyūtis* in depth, equal everywhere and shaped like cymbals (*jhallari*), and are declared to be ten thousand yojanas in width.

The Rucakavara mountain is declared to be ten hundred *gavyūtis* in depth, ten thousand yojanas in width at its base, and ten hundred yojanas in width at the top; the same applies to the Kuṇḍalavara mountain as well.

Ten types of substance-consideration (*dravyānuyoga*) are taught, namely: substance-consideration, mother-consideration, synonymous-consideration, instrument-consideration, assigned and unassigned, cultivated and uncultivated, external and internal, eternal and non-eternal, knowledge of suchness, and knowledge of non-suchness.

At the base of Mount Tigiñchikūṭa, the mountain of emergence belonging to Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asurakumāras, the extent is taught to be one thousand two hundred and twenty *yojanas* in width.

Of Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asurakumāras, the great king Soma’s mountain of omen, Somappabha, is ten hundred yojanas in height, ten hundred *gavyūtis* in depth, and at its base it is ten hundred yojanas in width.
Of Camara, the lord of the Asuras and king of the Asurakumāras, the great king Yama’s mountain of omen, Yamappabha, is exactly the same; likewise for Varuṇa, and likewise for Vaiśramaṇa.
At the foot of Mount Utpāta, the mountain of the lord of the Vairocanas, King Vairoyaṇa, [the palaces] are declared to be one thousand two hundred and twenty yojanas in extent.
For Bala, the lord of the Vairocanas, King Vairoyaṇa, it is exactly the same as for the world-protectors of Camara; that which applies to them applies to Bala as well.

Of Dharaṇa, the lord of the Nāgakumāras and king of the Nāgakumāras, on the mountain Dharaṇaprabha, there is a height of one thousand yojanas, a depth of one hundred *gavyūtas*, and at its base, a width of one thousand yojanas.

Of Dharaṇa, the lord of the Nāgakumāras and king of the Nāgakumāras, on the mountain Mahākālaprabha in the great forest Kālavāna, which is one hundred yojanas in height—[the description] is exactly the same [as that of Śaṅkhaśekhara], and so on up to Saṅkhavāla; likewise for Bhūtānanda, and likewise for the World-Protectors (Lokapālas). Just as it is for Dharaṇa, so it should be recited for all the Stanitakumāras together with their World-Protectors; for all of them, the mountains of emergence (uppāyapavvaya) should be recited with names corresponding to their own.

The mountain of Sakkappahe on the eastern side of Sakka, the lord of gods and king of the gods, is ten thousand yojanas in height, ten thousand *gavyūtas* in depth, and ten thousand yojanas in width at its base.
Just as it is for Sakka, so it is for all the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) and for all the Indras down to Accue; the dimensions of them all are one and the same.

The maximum body size of gross vegetable-bodied beings is taught to be ten hundred yojanas; the maximum body size of five-sensed aquatic animals is taught to be ten hundred yojanas; the maximum body size of five-sensed terrestrial animals that move by crawling on the belly is taught to be ten hundred yojanas.
From the time of the Arhat Sambhava, ten thousand koṭis of sāgaropamas had elapsed when the Arhat Abhinandana appeared.

Ten kinds of infinity are taught, namely: nominal infinity, conventional infinity, substantial infinity, numerical infinity, spatial infinity, oneness-infinity, twoness-infinity, partial-extension infinity, total-extension infinity, and eternal infinity.

Ten subjects (*vastu*) are taught for the *Utpāda-pūrva*, and ten minor subjects (*cūlavastu*) are taught for the *Astināstipravāda-pūrva*. Ten types of transgression (*pratiṣevaṇā*) are taught, namely:

Arrogance, negligence, lack of attention, illness, emergencies, suspicion, haste, fear, malice, and deliberation. (Āvaśyaka Niryukti 925) Ten faults of confession (ālocanā-doṣa) are taught, namely: [the above ten].
Having shaken [the mind] and having inferred, whatever is seen—whether gross or subtle, concealed, full of sound, crowded with many people, or overturned—he follows after that very thing. (Ṭhāṇa 927)

An ascetic endowed with ten qualities is worthy of confessing his own faults, namely: being well-born, being of noble lineage, and so forth as described in the *Aṣṭasthāna* up to: patient, self-controlled, free from deceit, and without subsequent regret. An ascetic endowed with ten qualities is worthy of receiving confession, namely: possessing right conduct (*ācāra*), possessing right study (*āhāra*), and so forth up to: one who perceives danger, one who loves the Dharma, and one who is firm in the Dharma. Ten kinds of penance are prescribed, namely: that which requires confession (*ālocanā-arha*), and so forth up to: that which requires suspension (*anavasthāpya-arha*) and that which requires re-initiation (*pārāñcika-arha*).

Ten kinds of wrong belief (mithyātva) are taught, namely: the perception of non-dharma as dharma; the perception of dharma as non-dharma; the perception of what is not the path as the path; the perception of the path as not the path; the perception of non-living beings as living beings; the perception of living beings as non-living beings; the perception of the unworthy as worthy; the perception of the worthy as unworthy; the perception of the unliberated as liberated; and the perception of the liberated as unliberated.

The Arhat Candraprabha, having lived out his full lifespan of one million years, became perfected (siddha), up to the point of having abandoned all suffering. The Arhat Dharma, having lived out his full lifespan of one million years, became perfected, up to the point of having abandoned all suffering. The Arhat Namī, having lived out his full lifespan of ten thousand years, became perfected, up to the point of having abandoned all suffering.

The lion among men, Vāsudeva, having lived out his full lifespan of one million years, was reborn as a hell-being in the sixth hell, Tamā. The Arhat Nemi, ten *dhanus* in height, having lived out his full lifespan of one thousand years, attained perfection and passed beyond all suffering.
Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva, ten *dhanus* in height, having lived out his full lifespan of one thousand years, was reborn as a hell-being in the third hell, Vālukaprabhā.

Ten types of gods dwelling in the *bhavana* (celestial abodes) are taught, namely: the Asura-kumāras up to the Sthaniya-kumāras. For these ten types of gods dwelling in the *bhavana*, ten sacred trees (*caitya-vṛkṣa*) are taught, namely: The *Aśvattha*, the *Saptaparṇa*, the *Sāmalī*, the *Udumbara*, the *Śirīṣa*, the *Dadhiparṇa*, the *Vañjula*, the *Palāśa*, the *Vāghātaka*, and the *Kaṇikāra* tree. (Āyāraṅga Sutta, Ṭhāṇaṃga Sutta 932)

Ten kinds of happiness are proclaimed (as follows): health, long life, wealth, sensual pleasures, contentment, the enjoyment of existing comforts, renunciation, and thereafter, freedom from affliction. (Ṭhāṇa 934)

Ten kinds of obstacles (*uvaghāta*) are taught, namely: obstacle regarding procurement (*uggama*), obstacle regarding acquisition (*uppāyaṇa*), obstacle regarding seeking (*esaṇa*), obstacle regarding preparation (*parikamma*), obstacle regarding avoidance (*pariharaṇa*), obstacle regarding knowledge (*nāṇa*), obstacle regarding vision (*daṃsana*), obstacle regarding conduct (*caritta*), obstacle regarding lack of respect (*aciyatta*), and obstacle regarding protection (*sārakkhaṇa*). Ten kinds of purifications (*visōhī*) are taught, namely: purification regarding procurement (*uggama*), purification regarding acquisition (*uppāyaṇa*), and so on, up to purification regarding protection (*sārakkhaṇa*).

Ten types of defilements (*saṅkleśa*) are taught, namely: defilement of requisites (*upadhi*), defilement of lodgings (*upāśraya*), defilement of passions (*kaṣāya*), defilement of food and drink (*bhaktapāna*), defilement of mind (*manas*), defilement of speech (*vāk*), defilement of body (*kāya*), defilement of knowledge (*jñāna*), defilement of vision (*darśana*), and defilement of conduct (*cāritra*).
Ten types of non-defilements (*asaṅkleśa*) are taught, namely: non-defilement of requisites, and so on, up to non-defilement of conduct.

Ten types of powers (*bala*) are taught, namely: the power of the sense of hearing, and so on, up to the power of the sense of touch; the power of knowledge (*jñāna-bala*), the power of vision (*darśana-bala*), the power of conduct (*cāritra-bala*), the power of austerity (*tapas-bala*), and the power of vigor (*vīrya-bala*).

Ten kinds of truth are taught (as follows):— the truth of common usage, the truth of convention, the truth of designation, the truth of form, the truth of reference, the truth of worldly practice, the truth of state, the truth of application as the tenth, and the truth of analogy. (Ṭhāṇa 939)

Ten kinds of falsehood are declared (as follows): anger, pride, deceit, greed, attachment, as well as aversion, laughter, delusion, intimidation, and the tenth is based on [false] teaching. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 941)

Ten kinds of truth-and-falsehood (*saccāmōsa*) are taught, namely: mixed with what has arisen (*uppannamīsaē*), mixed with what has passed away (*vigatamīsaē*), mixed with what has both arisen and passed away (*uppannavigatamīsaē*), mixed with the living (*jīvamīsaē*), mixed with the non-living (*ajīvamīsaē*), mixed with both living and non-living (*jīvājīvamīsaē*), mixed with the infinite (*anantamīsaē*), mixed with the limited (*parittamīsaē*), mixed with time (*addhāmīsaē*), and mixed with half-time (*addhaddhāmīsaē*). Ten designations for the *Diṭṭhivāya* (the Doctrine of Views) are taught, namely: it is called *Diṭṭhivāya*, or *Hēuvāya* (the Doctrine of Causes), or *Bhūyavāya* (the Doctrine of Beings), or *Taccāvāya* (the Doctrine of Reality), or *Sammāvāya* (the Doctrine of Rightness), or *Dhammāvāya* (the Doctrine of Dharma), or *Bhāsāvijaya* (Victory over Speech), or *Puvvagata* (that which has gone before), or *Anujōgagata* (that which follows the sequence), or "that which brings happiness to all breathers, beings, souls, and existents" (*savvapāṇabhūtajīvasattasuhāvaha*).
The weapons are declared to be of ten kinds (as follows):
the weapon of fire, poison, salt, oiliness, alkaline, sourness, the ill-directed mind, speech, body, and disposition, as well as non-restraint. (Ṭhāṇa 945)
Ten faults are declared (as follows):

the fault of its origin (*tajjātadosa*), the fault of the destruction of intelligence (*matibhaṅgadosa*), the fault of the patron (*pasatthāradosa*), the fault of avoidance (*pariharaṇadosa*), the fault of the characteristics, causes, and reasons (*salakkhaṇakāraṇahēudosā*), and the fault of the object of transfer and suppression (*saṅkamaṇaniggahavatthudosā*). (Ṭhāṇa 947)

Ten kinds of specific faults (*visesa*) are declared (as follows): the fault of the object (*vatthu*), the fault of its kind (*tajjāta-dosa*), the fault of the same purpose (*egaṭṭhiya*), the fault of the cause (*kāraṇa*), the fault of the present (*paḍuppanna*), the eighth being the fault of the permanent (*nicca*), the fault brought about by oneself (*attaṇā uvaṇīta*), and the specific fault (*visesa*); these are the ten. (Ṭhāṇa 949)
Ten kinds of pure vocal activity are taught, namely: the sound *caṃ*, the sound *maṃ*, the sound *piṃ*, the sound *sēyaṃ*, unity, diversity, combination, transformation, and separation.
Ten kinds of giving are taught, namely:
out of compassion, for the sake of gathering [disciples], out of fear, out of pity, out of shame, and out of respect.
Furthermore, it is said that in the seventh and eighth principles, one both intends to do and does [the deed].

(Ṭhāṇa 952) Tenfold destinies are taught, namely: the destiny of hell-beings, the destiny of the intermediate state for hell-beings; the destiny of animals, the destiny of the intermediate state for animals; [the destiny of human beings, the destiny of the intermediate state for human beings; the destiny of gods, the destiny of the intermediate state for gods]; the destiny of the perfected ones, and the destiny of the intermediate state for the perfected ones.

Ten types of "shaven ones" (muṇḍa) are taught, namely: the shaven one regarding the sense of hearing, the shaven one regarding the sense of sight, the shaven one regarding the sense of smell, the shaven one regarding the sense of taste, the shaven one regarding the sense of touch, the shaven one regarding anger, the shaven one regarding pride, the shaven one regarding deceit, the shaven one regarding greed, and the shaven one regarding the head.
Ten kinds of calculation are taught, namely:
preliminary operation (parikamma), practical application (vavahāra), the cord (rajjū), the heap (rāsī), and the art of fractions (kalā-savaṇṇa).
As many as there are [categories], so too are the *vaggō*, the *dhaṇṇō*, the *vaggavaggō*, and the *kappō*. (Ṭhāṇa 956) Tenfold renunciation (*paccakkhāṇa*) is taught (as follows):

that which is future, that which is past, that which is accompanied by a limit (*kōḍīsahiya*), that which is restricted (*niyaṇṭita*), that which is with conditions (*sāgāra*), and that which is without conditions (*aṇāgāra*).

The renunciation (*paccakkhāṇa*) regarding quantity is of ten kinds: that which is limited, that which is without remainder, and that which is numerical, as well as that which pertains to time. [Thāṇa 958] Tenfold proper conduct (*sāmāyārī*) is taught (as follows):
*icchā*, *micchā*, *tahakkārō*, *āvassiyā*, *nisīhiyā*, *āpucchaṇā*, and *paḍipucchā*.
Giving, invitation, and formal admission—at the proper time, the code of conduct (sāmācārī) is tenfold. (Ṭhāṇa 960)

During the period when he was still a householder, on the final night, the ascetic Blessed One Mahāvīra, having seen these ten great dreams, awoke. They were as follows: 1. He saw in a dream that he had conquered a great *tāla*-demon of terrifying form and blazing appearance; having seen this, he awoke. 2. He saw in a dream a great white cock; having seen this, he awoke. 3. He saw in a dream a great male cuckoo with variegated and beautiful wings; having seen this, he awoke. 4. He saw in a dream a great pair of garlands made entirely of jewels; having seen this, he awoke. 5. He saw in a dream a great herd of white bulls; having seen this, he awoke. 6. He saw in a dream a great lotus pond in full bloom on all sides; having seen this, he awoke. 7. He saw in a dream the great sun blazing with radiance; having seen this, he awoke. 8. He saw in a dream the Mount Mānuṣottara encircled and surrounded on all sides by his own tail, which had the color of beryl; having seen this, he awoke. 9. He saw in a dream himself seated upon an excellent lion-throne atop the peak of Mount Mandara; having seen this, he awoke.

Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great, terrifyingly shaped and blazing palm-demon (*tālapisāya*) being defeated, and upon waking, the deluding karma (*mōhaṇijja-kamma*) was uprooted by the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra from its very foundation. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great, white-winged male cuckoo, and upon waking, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, dwells having attained pure meditation (*sukkajjhāṇa*). Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great, male cuckoo with variegated and beautiful wings, and upon waking, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, proclaims, explains, demonstrates, shows, illustrates, and teaches the twelve-fold collection of scriptures (*duvālasaṅga gaṇipiḍaga*), which contains both his own doctrine and that of others, and is variegated and beautiful—namely, the *Āyāra* up to the *Diṭṭhivāya*. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great pair of garlands made entirely of jewels, and upon waking, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, proclaims the two-fold Dharma, namely: the householder’s Dharma (*agāradhamma*) and [the renunciant’s Dharma]. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great herd of white cows, and upon waking, the fourfold community (*saṅgha*) of the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra arose, namely: monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great lotus lake blooming on all sides, and upon waking, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, proclaims the four kinds of gods, namely: the residents of the underworld (*bhavaṇavāsī*), the denizens of the intermediate space (*vāṇamantara*), the celestial luminaries (*jōisiya*), and the gods of the heavens (*vēmāṇiya*). Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great ocean with waves and surges... and upon waking, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, has crossed over the beginningless, endless, long-lasting, and four-cornered wilderness of *saṃsāra*. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great sun... and upon waking, infinite and unsurpassed [knowledge] up to [omniscience] has arisen for the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great [throne] of beryl... and upon waking, magnificent fame, praise, renown, and glory circulate throughout the world of gods, humans, and asuras for the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra. Thus indeed is the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra. Because the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, saw in a dream a single, great Mount Mandara above the peak of Mandara... and upon waking, the ascetic, the Blessed One Mahāvīra, standing in the midst of an assembly of gods, humans, and asuras, proclaims, explains, and teaches the Dharma as proclaimed by the Kevalins.
Ten types of right view accompanied by attachment are taught (as follows):

natural inclination, teaching-based inclination, scriptural authority-based inclination, inclination toward the scriptures and the seeds [of the doctrine], as well as inclination through comprehension, inclination through expansion, inclination toward action, inclination toward summary, and inclination toward the Dharma. (Ṭhāṇaṃga 963)

Ten perceptions are taught, namely: the perception of food, up to the perception of possession; the perception of anger, up to the perception of greed; the perception of the world, and the perception of delusion.
For hell-beings, there are likewise ten perceptions; thus continuously, up to the Vaimānika gods.
Hell-beings dwell experiencing ten kinds of sensations, namely: cold, heat, hunger, thirst, itching, exhaustion, fear, sorrow, old age, and disease.

There are ten things that an ordinary person (chaumattha) does not know and does not see in their true nature: namely, the substance of motion (dhammatthikāya), and so on, up to air; whether this person will become a Jina or will not become a Jina; and whether this person will bring an end to all suffering or will not bring an end to all suffering. These same things, however, [he knows and sees] when he is an Arhat possessing arisen knowledge and vision, up to: whether this person will become a Jina or will not become a Jina; and whether this person will bring an end to all suffering or will not bring an end to all suffering.

Ten *daśās* (sections) are taught, namely: the *Karmavipākadaśās*, the *Upāsakadaśās*, the *Antagaḍadaśās*, the *Anuttaropapātikadaśās*, the *Ācāradaśās*, the *Praśnavyākaraṇadaśās*, the *Bandhadaśās*, the *Dogiddhidaśās*, the *Dīrghadaśās*, and the *Saṃkṣepitadaśās*. There are ten chapters (*adhyayana*) in the *Karmavipākadaśās*:
Miyāputta, Gottāsa, Aṇḍa, Sagaḍa, Yāvara, the Brāhmaṇa Nandiṣeṇa, Soriya, Udumbara, Sahasuddāha, Āmalaka, Kumāra, and the Licchavi. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 968)
In the *Upāsakadaśāḥ*, ten chapters are taught (namely):
Ānanda, Kāmadeva, Cūlaṇī’s father the householder Suradeva, Cullaśataka, the householder Kuṇḍakoliya, Saddālaputra, Mahāśataka, Nandinī’s husband, and Lēyā’s husband. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 970)
In the Antagaḍadasās, ten chapters are proclaimed (as follows):
Nami, Mātaṅga, Sōmila, Rāmagutta, Sundasaṇa, Jamālī, Magālī, Kiṅkasa, Cillaṭa, and Phāla, as well as Ambaḍaputta—these are the ten who have been declared [to have reached the end]. (Ṭhāṇa 972)
In the *Aṇuttarovavātiyadasā* ten chapters are proclaimed (namely):
Isidāsa, Ghaṇṇa, Suṇakkhatta, Kātiya, Saṇṭhāṇa, Sālibhadra, Ānanda, Tetali, Daśārṇabhadra, and Atimukta—these are declared to be the ten. (Ṭhāṇaṅga 974)

In the *Āyāra-dasā*, ten chapters are proclaimed, namely: the twenty places of non-concentration (*asamāhi-ṭṭhāṇā*), the twenty-one strengths (*sabala*), the thirty-three disrespectfulnesses (*āsāyaṇāo*), the eightfold excellence of a leader (*gaṇi-sampayā*), the ten bases for mental concentration (*citta-samāhi-ṭṭhiṇā*), the eleven lay practitioner vows (*uvāsaga-paḍimāo*), the twelve mendicant vows (*bhikkhu-paḍimāo*), the ritual of the rainy season retreat (*pajjōsavaṇā-kappa*), the thirty points of delusion (*mōhaṇijja-ṭṭhāṇā*), and the place of self-restraint (*ājāi-ṭṭhāṇaṁ*). In the *Paṇhāvāgaraṇa-dasā*, ten chapters are proclaimed, namely: Similes (*uvamā*), Calculations (*saṅkhā*), Discourses spoken by Sages (*isibhāsiyāiṁ*), Discourses spoken by Teachers (*āyariya-bhāsiyāiṁ*), Discourses spoken by Mahāvīra (*mahāvīra-bhāsiyāiṁ*), Questions on the Khōmaga cloth (*khōmagapasiṇāiṁ*), Questions on the Komala cloth (*kōmalapasiṇāiṁ*), Questions on the mirror (*addāgapasiṇāiṁ*), Questions on the thumb (*aṅguṭṭhapasiṇāiṁ*), and Questions on the arm (*bāhupasiṇāiṁ*).

Ten chapters of the *Bandhadaśā* are proclaimed, namely: *Bandha*, *Mokkha*, *Devaddhi*, *Daśāramaṇḍala*, *Ācāryavipratipatti*, *Upādhyāyavipratipatti*, *Bhāvanā*, *Vimukti*, *Sāta*, and *Karman*. Ten chapters of the *Dōgeddhi-daśā* are proclaimed, namely: *Vāda*, *Vivāda*, *Upavāta*, *Sukhetta*, *Kasiṇa*, *Bāyālīsa-sumiṇa*, *Tīsa-mahāsumiṇa*, *Bāvattari-savvasumiṇa*, *Hāra*, and *Rāma-gutta*. These ten have been thus declared. Ten chapters of the *Dīhadasā* are proclaimed, namely: *Canda*, *Sūra*, *Sukka*, *Siridevī*, *Pabhāvatī*, *Dīvasamuddovavattī*, *Bahuputtī*, *Mandarētī*, the elder *Sambhūtivijaya*, and the elder *Pamha*. [And] *Ūsāsanīsāsa*. Ten chapters of the *Saṅkhēviya-daśā* are proclaimed, namely: *Khuḍḍiyā-vimāṇapavibhattī*, *Mahalliyā-vimāṇapavibhattī*, *Aṅgacūliyā*, *Vaggacūliyā*, *Vivāhacūliyā*, *Aruṇōvavāta*, *Varuṇōvavāta*, *Garulōvavāta*, *Vēlandharōvavāta*, and *Vēsamaṇōvavāta*.

The duration of an *osappiṇī* (descending cycle) is ten *koṭākoṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*; the duration of an *ussappiṇī* (ascending cycle) is ten *koṭākoṭīs* of *sāgaropamas*. Ten kinds of hell-beings are taught, namely: those born immediately after [the end of the world], those born successively; those who have just descended [into the realm], those who have descended successively; those who have just begun to consume food, those who consume food successively; those who have just attained full development (*paryāpti*), those who have attained full development successively; the final ones, and the non-final ones. In this same manner, it continues without interruption up to the *vaimānika* gods.

In the fourth earth, Paṅkaprabhā, one million hell-abodes are taught; in the first earth, Ratnaprabhā, the minimum lifespan of the hell-beings is taught to be ten thousand years; in the fourth earth, Paṅkaprabhā, the maximum lifespan of the hell-beings is taught to be ten sāgaropamas; in the fifth earth, Dhūmaprabhā, the minimum lifespan of the hell-beings is taught to be ten sāgaropamas; for the Asurakumāras, the minimum lifespan is taught to be ten thousand years; and likewise up to the Stanitakumāras, and for the gross vegetable-bodied beings, the maximum lifespan is taught to be ten thousand years.
The minimum lifespan of the Vāṇamaṃtara gods is taught to be ten thousand years.
In the Brahma-loka kalpa, the maximum lifespan of the gods is taught to be ten sāgaropamas; in the Lāntaka kalpa, the minimum lifespan of the gods is taught to be ten sāgaropamas.

By ten conditions, living beings produce karma leading to future auspiciousness, namely: by being free from worldly motives, by being endowed with right view, by being engaged in proper conduct, by being patient and enduring, by having conquered the senses, by being free from deceit, by not being partial to others' doctrines, by being a good ascetic, by being devoted to the teaching, and by promoting the teaching.

Ten types of application based on expectation (*āsaṃsappaōga*) are taught, namely: application based on expectation for this world, application based on expectation for the next world, application based on expectation for both worlds, application based on expectation for life, application based on expectation for death, application based on expectation for sensual pleasures (*kāma*), application based on expectation for enjoyments (*bhōga*), application based on expectation for gain (*lābha*), application based on expectation for honor (*pūyā*), and application based on expectation for respect (*sakkāra*).

Ten types of phenomena (*dhamma*) are taught, namely: the phenomenon of the village (*gāmadhamma*), the phenomenon of the city (*nagaradhamma*), the phenomenon of the kingdom (*raṭṭhadhamma*), the phenomenon of the religious sect (*pāsaṇḍadhamma*), the phenomenon of the family (*kuladhamma*), the phenomenon of the group (*gaṇadhamma*), the phenomenon of the community (*saṅghadhamma*), the phenomenon of the scriptures (*suyadhamma*), the phenomenon of conduct (*carittadhamma*), and the phenomenon of the astikāyas (*atthikāyadhamma*).

Ten kinds of elders are declared, namely: village elders, town elders, country elders, praised elders, family elders, group elders, community elders, elders by birth, elders by learning, and elders by seniority. Ten kinds of sons are declared, namely: the son of one's own body, the son of the field, the son given, the son received, the son born of the breast, the son of a secret marriage, the son of a woman of loose character, the son of a pregnant bride, the son purchased, and the religious disciple.

For the Kevalin, ten unsurpassed qualities are proclaimed, namely: unsurpassed knowledge, unsurpassed vision, unsurpassed conduct, unsurpassed austerity, unsurpassed vigor, unsurpassed forbearance, unsurpassed liberation, unsurpassed uprightness, unsurpassed gentleness, and unsurpassed lightness.

In the Samayakṣetra, ten Kuru regions are proclaimed, namely: five Devakurus and five Uttarakurus. Therein, ten very great and magnificent great trees are proclaimed, namely: the Jambū Sudaṃsaṇā, the Dhāyaï-rukkha, the Mahādhāyaï-rukkha, the Paüma-rukkha, the Mahāpaüma-rukkha, and five Kūṭa-sāmalīs. Therein, ten gods of great power and influence dwell, namely: Aṇāḍhita, the lord of Jambudvīpa; Sudaṃsaṇa; Piyandaṇa; Poṇḍarīka; Mahāpoṇḍarīka; and five Garuḍas, the Vēṇudevas.

One should recognize a deeply degenerate age (*dussama*) by ten conditions, namely: it rains out of season; it does not rain at the proper time; non-ascetics are honored; ascetics are not honored; people have adopted wrong views toward their teachers; sounds are unpleasant, and so on, up to tactile sensations being unpleasant. One should recognize a deeply flourishing age (*susama*) by ten conditions, namely: it does not rain out of season, and so on, up to tastes being pleasant and tactile sensations being pleasant.
During the age of extreme prosperity (*susamasusamā*), ten kinds of trees come forth for the purpose of enjoyment, namely: [the list follows].

Mataṅga, Bhiṅga, Tuḍitaṅga, Dīva, Joti, Cittaṅga, Cittarasa, Maṇiyaṅga, Gēhāgāra, and Aṇiyaṇa. In Jambudvīpa, in the region of Bhāratavarṣa, during the past *utsarpiṇī*, there were ten Kulakaras. (Namely as follows—).

Sayāñjala, Sayāyu, Anantasena, Ajitasena, Kakkasena, Bhīmasena, Mahābhīmasena as the seventh, Daḍharaha, Dasaraha, and Sayaraha.
